11questions

Bone cement (PMMA): Properties, technique & complications

PMMA material behaviour, modern cementing technique, and the mechanism of cemented stem failure/loosening.

6 of 7 sittings2021, 2022 (x2), 2023 (x2), 2024S (x3), 2024F, 2025 (x2)

  • PMMA is an interdigitating grout, not an adhesive. It is strongest in compression, weakest in tension and shear; Young's modulus sits between cortical bone and metal, so it acts as a load-transfer buffer.
  • Polymerisation is exothermic (peak ~70–120 °C at the interface in vivo, buffered by blood and bone); the reaction proceeds through doughing, working and setting phases.
  • Modern (3rd/4th generation) technique = canal preparation with pulsatile lavage, distal plug, retrograde filling with a gun, pressurisation, vacuum mixing/centrifugation to reduce porosity, and a stem centraliser. Pressurisation and a clean, dry, lavaged interface are the biggest determinants of cement mantle quality.
  • Failure typically begins as debonding at the stem–cement interface → cement mantle fracture → subsidence into varus with a distal pedestal. Mantle should be ≥2 mm and uniform; thin mantles (<2 mm), voids and blood laminations are failure risks.
  • Antibiotic-loaded cement: elution is a surface phenomenon and falls exponentially; high-dose (>2 g per 40 g) is for treatment/spacers, low-dose for prophylaxis. High doses reduce mechanical strength; heat-stable antibiotics (vancomycin, tobramycin, gentamicin) are used.
  • Bone cement implantation syndrome: hypotension/hypoxia/arrhythmia during pressurisation, particularly in hemiarthroplasty for hip fracture — communicate with anaesthesia, lavage well, and avoid over-pressurising a fragile canal.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics: Orthopaedic Implants; Arthroplasty: Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • Vaishya R et al. Bone cement. J Clin Orthop Trauma 2013.
  • Jafari SM et al. Do tantalum and titanium cups show similar results? / cemented fixation reviews, CORR.
  • AAOS/OrthoInfo & AOA National Joint Replacement Registry — cemented vs cementless stem survivorship in the elderly.
10questions

Biomechanics: Plate fixation principles (locking, LC-DCP, buttress, pre-tension)

Understanding what each plate function does mechanically — compression, neutralisation, buttress, bridging — and the specific advantages/limitations of locked constructs.

6 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2022, 2023 (x2), 2024S, 2024F (x2), 2025 (x2)

  • Locked plates are internal fixators: screws lock to the plate, so the construct does not rely on plate–bone friction. Advantages: preserves periosteal blood supply, resists loss of reduction in osteoporotic/metaphyseal bone, no need to precisely contour the plate. Disadvantage: locking a plate does not reduce the fracture, and a stiff construct over a short working length can suppress callus.
  • LC-DCP vs DCP: the undercut (limited-contact) undersurface reduces plate–periosteum contact and improves cortical perfusion, gives a more even distribution of stiffness along the plate (reducing stress risers at screw holes), and allows screw angulation in both directions.
  • Far cortical locking / dynamic locking screws deliberately reduce near-cortex stiffness so motion at the fracture is more symmetric (near and far cortex), promoting callus. The classic error with a laterally applied locked plate is asymmetric motion — near cortex moves, far cortex does not gap — creating a nonunion.
  • Plate pre-tensioning/pre-bending: for a transverse fracture, slightly over-bending the plate at the fracture ensures the far cortex compresses when the screws are tightened; a perfectly straight plate compresses the near cortex and gaps the far cortex.
  • Buttress (antiglide) plating converts shear into compression at an oblique fracture; the plate must be applied on the side of the apex/vertex of the shear and be fixed proximal to it. Under-contoured plates work as antiglide.
  • Titanium has a lower modulus (~110 GPa) than stainless steel (~200 GPa) — a titanium plate is less stiff for the same geometry, is more notch-sensitive, and produces fewer MRI artefacts; stainless is stronger/ductile and easier to contour.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Implants: Plates.
  • Perren SM. Evolution of the internal fixation of long bone fractures. JBJS Br 2002.
  • Bottlang M et al. Far cortical locking can improve healing of fractures stabilised with locking plates. JBJS Am 2010.
  • Gardner MJ et al. The mechanical behaviour of locking compression plates. J Orthop Trauma.
  • AO Foundation Principles of Fracture Management, 3rd ed.
10questions

Perioperative medicine: Analgesia, opioids & ERAS

Multimodal analgesia, opioid stewardship, ERAS pathways, and specific perioperative medication issues (DMARDs, GLP-1 agonists, penicillin allergy).

4 of 7 sittings2022 (x2), 2023, 2024S (x4), 2024F (x3)

  • Multimodal analgesia (acetaminophen + NSAID + regional block ± short-course opioid) reduces opioid consumption, nausea and length of stay. Peri-articular local infiltration analgesia in TKA/THA is at least equivalent to femoral nerve block without motor blockade/fall risk.
  • The single strongest predictor of persistent post-operative opioid use is pre-operative opioid use; other risks are mental-health comorbidity, substance use, and higher initial prescription size/duration. Opioid prescribing quantity — not pain severity — drives leftover pills and diversion.
  • ERAS in arthroplasty: pre-op education, carbohydrate loading/avoidance of prolonged fasting, TXA, spinal anaesthesia, multimodal analgesia, LIA, avoidance of drains/urinary catheters, same-day mobilisation. Reduces LOS and complications without increasing readmission.
  • GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide/'Ozempic'): delayed gastric emptying → retained gastric contents and aspiration risk despite standard fasting; current anaesthesia guidance is to hold the weekly agent before elective surgery and consider gastric ultrasound/RSI.
  • DMARDs: continue conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine) through surgery; hold biologics and time surgery at the end of the dosing cycle, restarting ~14 days post-op once the wound looks satisfactory. Taper glucocorticoids to the lowest possible dose.
  • Reported penicillin 'allergy' is usually not true IgE allergy (>90% of labelled patients tolerate penicillin). Substituting vancomycin/clindamycin is associated with higher SSI rates — allergy delabelling or cefazolin challenge is preferred; true anaphylaxis is the exception.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Medical Conditions; Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • Goesling J, Brummett CM et al. Persistent opioid use after major surgery. JAMA Surg 2017.
  • Goodman SM et al. ACR/AAHKS guideline for perioperative management of antirheumatic medication. J Arthroplasty 2022.
  • American Society of Anesthesiologists consensus guidance on GLP-1 receptor agonists, 2023.
  • Blumenthal KG et al. Impact of a reported penicillin allergy on surgical site infection risk. Clin Infect Dis 2018.
  • Soffin EM, YaDeau JT. Enhanced recovery after surgery for primary hip and knee arthroplasty. Br J Anaesth 2016.
8questions

Surgical site infection prevention & antibiotic prophylaxis

Evidence-based SSI prevention bundles, timing/dosing of prophylaxis, and what does and does not work.

5 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2024S, 2024F (x3), 2025

  • Prophylaxis: first-generation cephalosporin (cefazolin) within 60 min of incision (120 min for vancomycin), weight-adjusted (≥2 g, 3 g if >120 kg), re-dosed at ~2 half-lives (cefazolin q4h) or after >1500 mL blood loss. Discontinue within 24 h post-op.
  • Proven measures: chlorhexidine–alcohol skin preparation, hair removal with clippers (not razors) or not at all, normothermia, glycaemic control, avoidance of preoperative shaving, and appropriate antibiotic timing. Nasal S. aureus screening/decolonisation with mupirocin reduces staphylococcal SSI.
  • Not supported / harmful: routine prolonged post-op antibiotics, iodine-impregnated drapes as a stand-alone, and using vancomycin routinely in place of cefazolin for a non-verified penicillin allergy.
  • Intrawound vancomycin powder is widely used in spine and some trauma; the OVIVA/VANCO-type data show reduced gram-positive infection but a shift toward gram-negative organisms and a risk of seroma/nonunion signals in some series — the exam answer is usually 'reduces gram-positive infection but selects for gram-negative organisms'.
  • Dental prophylaxis after arthroplasty: current AAOS/ADA position is that routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not required for most patients; it is considered for the immunocompromised, poorly controlled diabetics, and within the first 1–2 years for a small subset — shared decision-making.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics; Arthroplasty.
  • Berríos-Torres SI et al. CDC Guideline for the Prevention of Surgical Site Infection. JAMA Surg 2017.
  • AAOS/ADA Appropriate Use Criteria — Management of Patients with Orthopaedic Implants Undergoing Dental Procedures.
  • PREP-IT Investigators (Canadian-led). Aqueous-PREP and PREPARE trials — skin antisepsis in open and closed fractures. Lancet 2022 / NEJM 2024.
6questions

Compartment syndrome: Diagnosis & management

Diagnosis in the awake and the obtunded patient, pressure thresholds, at-risk injuries, and the consequences of a missed compartment syndrome.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022 (x2), 2023, 2024S

  • Diagnosis in the awake patient is clinical: pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, and a tense compartment. Pulselessness, paralysis and pallor are late. Serial examination beats a single pressure reading.
  • In the obtunded/ICU patient, compartment pressure monitoring is required. Use a ΔP (diastolic BP − compartment pressure) < 30 mmHg as the threshold; measure within 5 cm of the fracture. An absolute pressure alone over-diagnoses.
  • Highest-risk injuries: high-energy tibial shaft fractures (most common overall), forearm fractures, and — proportionally — young men, tibial plateau/Schatzker VI with knee dislocation, and vascular injury with reperfusion. Open fractures do not protect against compartment syndrome.
  • Prevention/reduction: avoid circumferential casts, split/bivalve and release padding (releasing the cast reduces pressure more than splitting alone), keep the limb at heart level (not elevated), and treat hypotension.
  • A missed compartment syndrome results in Volkmann ischaemic contracture, and late imaging may show calcification within myonecrotic muscle. Late fasciotomy of established necrosis (>24–48 h with no functional muscle) risks infection and is generally avoided.
  • Paediatric differences: the classic '3 A's' — increasing Analgesia requirement, Anxiety, Agitation — often precede pain, and children may not reliably report pain out of proportion.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas: Acute Compartment Syndrome.
  • McQueen MM, Court-Brown CM. Compartment monitoring in tibial fractures: the pressure threshold for decompression. JBJS Br 1996.
  • Bae DS et al. Acute compartment syndrome in children. J Pediatr Orthop 2001.
  • Schmidt AH. Acute compartment syndrome. Injury 2017; and JAAOS review.
6questions

Professionalism: Closing/terminating practice & duty of care

The physician's obligations when winding down a practice or ending a therapeutic relationship, and when non-compliance discharges duty.

4 of 7 sittings2021, 2023 (x2), 2024S, 2025 (x2)

  • Closing a practice requires: reasonable advance notice to patients (generally ≥3 months, per most Canadian colleges), arranging transfer of ongoing care, ensuring records are retained/transferred securely for the mandated period (commonly 10 years from last visit, or 10 years past the age of majority for minors), and notifying the College and CMPA.
  • You cannot abandon a patient. Terminating a relationship requires written notice, provision of urgent/interim care for a reasonable period, assistance in finding another provider, and transfer of records on request.
  • Legitimate reasons to terminate include a breakdown of trust, abusive behaviour, persistent non-adherence that makes safe care impossible, or a conflict of interest — not the patient's cost, complexity, or a filed complaint.
  • Non-compliance alone does not automatically discharge duty: you must document counselling about risks, offer alternatives, confirm capacity, and give notice before withdrawing. Emergency care must still be provided.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • CMPA. Ending the doctor–patient relationship and Closing or leaving a practice (good practice guidance).
  • CPSO Policy: Ending the Physician–Patient Relationship; Closing a Practice.
  • CanMEDS 2015 Physician Competency Framework — Professional role.
5questions

Biomechanics: Stress-strain curve, modulus & material properties

Reading the stress-strain curve and knowing which material property each region represents.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2025

  • Stress = force/area; strain = change in length/original length. The slope of the elastic region = Young's modulus (stiffness) — a material property independent of geometry.
  • Yield point separates elastic (recoverable) from plastic (permanent) deformation. Past the yield point, deformation is permanent — the classic exam stem.
  • Ultimate tensile strength = the highest stress reached. Area under the whole curve = toughness (energy absorbed to failure); area under the elastic portion = resilience.
  • Brittle materials (PMMA, ceramic) fail at/near the yield point with little plastic deformation; ductile materials (stainless steel) deform substantially first. Tendon has a low modulus with a long toe region; bone is stiffer and fails earlier — the classic 'two curves' figure.
  • Bone is viscoelastic and anisotropic: it is stiffer and stronger at higher strain rates, and strongest in compression, weaker in tension, weakest in shear. Modulus order: ceramic > cobalt-chrome > stainless steel > titanium > cortical bone > PMMA > cancellous bone > UHMWPE.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System, 4th ed.
  • Einhorn TA, Buckwalter JA. Orthopaedic Basic Science (AAOS).
5questions

Biostatistics: Bias, randomization & confounding

Which design feature controls which threat to validity.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024S

  • Randomisation controls confounding, including unmeasured confounders — this is its unique property and the usual exam answer. It does not eliminate measurement or observer bias.
  • Blinding controls performance, detection and observer bias. Allocation concealment prevents selection bias at enrolment (distinct from blinding).
  • Intention-to-treat analysis preserves randomisation and protects against attrition/crossover bias; per-protocol analysis re-introduces it.
  • Other tools: restriction, matching, stratification and multivariable adjustment control measured confounders only. Propensity scores likewise.
  • A baseline imbalance in a single variable after proper randomisation is expected by chance; the response is to adjust for it in the analysis, not to declare the randomisation failed.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Research Summaries.
  • Bhandari M, Joensson A. Clinical Research for Surgeons. Thieme.
  • Schulz KF, Grimes DA. Series on epidemiology and clinical research design. Lancet.
  • CONSORT 2010 Statement.
5questions

Biostatistics: Outcome measures & PROMs

Reliability, validity and responsiveness of patient-reported outcome measures, and which instrument is best validated in each region.

5 of 7 sittings2021, 2022, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • Reliability = reproducibility (test–retest, inter-/intra-observer, internal consistency). Validity = measures what it claims (content, criterion, construct). Responsiveness = ability to detect true change over time. An instrument can be highly reliable and still invalid.
  • Region-specific instruments outperform generic ones (SF-36, EQ-5D) for detecting change, but generic instruments allow cross-disease comparison and utility/QALY estimation.
  • Foot & ankle: the FAAM and FAOS have the strongest psychometric support; the AOFAS score is widely used but poorly validated (it mixes clinician-measured and patient-reported items). PROMIS instruments are increasingly the preferred general measure.
  • MCID (minimal clinically important difference) is the smallest change patients perceive as beneficial; a statistically significant difference smaller than the MCID is not clinically meaningful — a recurring stem with distal radius/DASH data.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Research Summaries.
  • Hunt KJ, Hurwit D. Use of patient-reported outcome measures in foot and ankle research. JBJS Am 2013.
  • SooHoo NF et al. Evaluation of the validity of the AOFAS clinical rating systems. Foot Ankle Int 2003.
  • Hung M et al. PROMIS in orthopaedics. JBJS Rev.
5questions

Metal hypersensitivity & implant allergy

Delayed-type hypersensitivity to implant metals — how it presents, how (poorly) it is diagnosed, and how it differs from ALTR.

4 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2023, 2024S

  • Type IV (delayed, T-cell mediated) hypersensitivity. Nickel is the commonest sensitiser, then cobalt and chromium; cross-reactivity between nickel and cobalt is common. Titanium and tantalum are the least immunogenic.
  • Population sensitisation (~10–15%, higher in women) vastly exceeds the rate of symptomatic implant failure — a positive patch test in an asymptomatic patient predicts nothing.
  • There is no validated diagnostic test. Patch testing and lymphocyte transformation testing (LTT) have poor specificity; diagnosis is one of exclusion after ruling out infection, loosening, instability and referred pain.
  • Distinguish from adverse local tissue reaction/ALVAL from metal wear debris (a metal-ion, not allergic, phenomenon) — the latter has raised serum Co/Cr and a pseudotumour on MARS MRI.
  • Routine pre-operative screening is not recommended. In a patient with a convincing history of cutaneous metal allergy, using a hypoallergenic (oxidised zirconium, titanium-nitride coated, or all-polyethylene) implant is reasonable but not evidence-mandated.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: General.
  • Granchi D et al. Metal hypersensitivity testing in patients undergoing joint replacement. JBJS Br 2012.
  • Schmidt AH, Frisch NB. Metal hypersensitivity in total joint arthroplasty. JAAOS 2019.
5questions

Osteoporosis: Diagnosis, pharmacology & fragility fracture care

Post-fragility-fracture care, drug classes and mechanisms, and calcium/vitamin D.

3 of 7 sittings2021, 2022 (x3), 2024S

  • A fragility fracture is a sentinel event: ~50% of patients with a hip fracture had a prior fragility fracture. A distal radius fracture in a patient >50 mandates BMD testing and fracture-risk assessment (FRAX/CAROC). Fracture liaison services close the well-documented treatment gap.
  • Antiresorptives: bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, zoledronate — inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in osteoclasts), denosumab (RANKL monoclonal antibody), raloxifene, calcitonin, oestrogen. Anabolic: teriparatide/abaloparatide (intermittent PTH). Romosozumab (sclerostin antibody) is dual-action.
  • Teriparatide is the classic 'not an antiresorptive' distractor. Denosumab must not be stopped abruptly — rebound vertebral fractures occur; transition to a bisphosphonate.
  • Osteoporosis Canada: 1000–1200 mg elemental calcium daily (diet preferred over supplements) and 800–2000 IU vitamin D3 for adults at risk. High-dose intermittent vitamin D bolus dosing increases falls and is not recommended.
  • Osteoporosis is defined by BMD T-score ≤ −2.5, or by a hip/vertebral fragility fracture regardless of BMD.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Systemic Disease; Medical Conditions.
  • Osteoporosis Canada. 2023 Clinical Practice Guideline for the management of osteoporosis. CMAJ 2023.
  • AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Hip Fractures in Older Adults, 2021.
  • Bogoch ER et al. (Canadian) Effective initiation of osteoporosis diagnosis and treatment after fragility fracture. JBJS Am 2006.
5questions

Tribology: Bearing surfaces, wear & lubrication

Lubrication regimes, wear mechanisms and modern polyethylene.

5 of 7 sittings2021, 2022, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • Lubrication regimes: boundary (surfaces contact, lubricant plays little role), mixed, and fluid-film/hydrodynamic (surfaces fully separated by a fluid layer — the ideal, favoured by a larger head, smoother surface and lower roughness ratio λ >3). Ceramic-on-ceramic and metal-on-metal can approach fluid-film; metal-on-poly runs in boundary/mixed.
  • Wear mechanisms: adhesive, abrasive, third-body, fatigue (delamination/pitting) and corrosion. Modes 1–4 describe articulation between intended/unintended surfaces.
  • Volumetric wear rises with the square of the head radius; linear wear does not. Metal-on-metal has low volumetric wear but generates vastly more particles (nanometre-sized) than metal-on-poly, hence high particle number with low volume — the classic MoM vs MoP stem.
  • Highly cross-linked polyethylene: gamma or electron-beam irradiation creates cross-links (↓ wear) but leaves free radicals → oxidation and embrittlement. Remelting (above melt temperature) eliminates free radicals but reduces mechanical strength/fatigue resistance; annealing (below melt) preserves strength but leaves residual free radicals. Vitamin-E doping quenches free radicals without a thermal penalty.
  • Particle size ~0.2–0.8 µm is most biologically active for macrophage-mediated osteolysis (RANKL-driven). Osteolysis is a biological, not a mechanical, failure.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: General; Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • Kurtz SM. UHMWPE Biomaterials Handbook, 3rd ed.
  • Kurtz SM et al. Advances in highly crosslinked UHMWPE. CORR 2011.
  • Australian AOANJRR / CJRR annual reports — bearing surface survivorship.
5questions

VTE prophylaxis in orthopaedics

Risk stratification, agent choice and the specific evidence base in arthroplasty, hip fracture and below-knee injury.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2022 (x2), 2023, 2024S

  • Arthroplasty: aspirin is non-inferior to rivaroxaban for symptomatic VTE prophylaxis after an initial 5-day rivaroxaban lead-in (EPCAT II, Anderson, NEJM 2018 — Canadian). Aspirin is cheaper, needs no monitoring and has less bleeding. Mechanical prophylaxis and early mobilisation are adjuncts.
  • The weakest evidence base is for mechanical prophylaxis alone (IPC/stockings) after hip arthroplasty and for warfarin — a recurring 'least evidence' stem.
  • Isolated below-knee injury/immobilisation: routine pharmacologic prophylaxis is not indicated for all patients; use risk stratification (previous VTE, malignancy, obesity, OCP, immobilisation duration). Achilles rupture and ankle fracture with prolonged non-weightbearing casting carry the highest risk in this group.
  • Spine and arthroscopy: chemoprophylaxis is generally not routine; balance against epidural haematoma risk. In AIS surgery in an adolescent, mechanical prophylaxis and early mobilisation, not anticoagulation, are the answer.
  • HIT: an immune, IgG-mediated reaction to heparin–PF4 complexes causing thrombocytopenia with thrombosis (not bleeding), typically at day 5–10; treatment is to stop all heparin (including flushes/LMWH) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, fondaparinux, DOAC). Warfarin alone is contraindicated acutely (limb gangrene).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Medical Conditions.
  • Anderson DR et al. Aspirin or rivaroxaban for VTE prophylaxis after hip or knee arthroplasty (EPCAT II). NEJM 2018.
  • AAOS CPG: Preventing Venous Thromboembolic Disease in Patients Undergoing Elective Hip and Knee Arthroplasty.
  • Falck-Ytter Y et al. ACCP Antithrombotic Therapy and Prevention of Thrombosis, 9th ed. Chest 2012.
4questions

Biomechanics: Working length, fracture gap strain & callus

Strain theory, working length and how construct choices change healing.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • Interfragmentary strain theory (Perren): tissue differentiates according to the strain it experiences. <2% strain → primary/direct bone healing (requires absolute stability, contact/lag compression). 2–10% → secondary healing with callus. >10% → fibrous tissue/nonunion.
  • Working length = the distance between the two points of fixation closest to the fracture (the unsupported segment). A longer working length → lower construct stiffness, lower strain at the fracture, more motion and more callus. It is the single most powerful modifier of a locked-plate construct.
  • For the same implant, a comminuted (multi-fragmentary) fracture distributes displacement over many gaps → lower strain per gap → callus forms readily. A simple transverse fracture concentrates displacement in one gap → high strain → this is why transverse fractures treated with a bridge plate fail to heal and require absolute stability or a longer working length.
  • Increasing callus stiffness: reducing the gap, adding a lag screw, shortening working length. Factors that do not increase early callus stiffness: increasing plate length alone (increases working length), removing screws near the fracture.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics.
  • Perren SM. Physical and biological aspects of fracture healing. CORR 1979.
  • Stoffel K et al. Biomechanical testing of the LCP — how can stability in locked internal fixators be controlled? Injury 2003.
  • Claes LE, Heigele CA. Magnitudes of local stress and strain along bony surfaces predict course and type of fracture healing. J Biomech 1999.
4questions

Bone biology: Remodelling, resorption & calcium homeostasis

Cell biology of resorption and the clinical face of calcium disorders.

3 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2022

  • Osteoclasts are haematopoietic (monocyte/macrophage lineage), multinucleated, and resorb via a ruffled border sealing zone using carbonic anhydrase (H+ ) and cathepsin K/TRAP. Osteoblasts are mesenchymal in origin.
  • RANKL (osteoblast/stromal) binds RANK on osteoclast precursors → differentiation and activation. OPG is the decoy receptor that blocks this. The RANKL:OPG ratio governs bone turnover; denosumab is a RANKL antibody.
  • PTH: intermittent = anabolic (teriparatide); continuous = catabolic (hyperparathyroidism). Calcitonin inhibits osteoclasts. 1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D increases intestinal calcium absorption.
  • Hypercalcaemia — 'stones, bones, abdominal groans, psychic moans': polyuria, polydipsia, constipation, confusion/psychosis, short QT. Carpopedal spasm is hypo-calcaemia, the classic distractor.
  • Bone remodelling unit sequence: activation → resorption → reversal → formation → quiescence.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Systemic Disease.
  • Einhorn TA, Buckwalter JA. Orthopaedic Basic Science (AAOS), 4th ed.
  • Boyle WJ, Simonet WS, Lacey DL. Osteoclast differentiation and activation. Nature 2003.
4questions

Bone graft, substitutes & BMP

Osteogenic/osteoinductive/osteoconductive properties, and how each substitute behaves.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2024F, 2025

  • Autograft is the only graft that is osteogenic and osteoinductive and osteoconductive. Cancellous autograft (iliac crest, RIA) is the gold standard; RIA yields large volumes (>40 mL) with growth-factor content comparable to iliac crest and less donor-site pain, at the cost of femoral fracture risk.
  • BMPs (BMP-2, BMP-7) are osteoinductive members of the TGF-β superfamily; they act by recruiting and inducing differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into osteoblasts — the classic mechanism answer. They signal through SMAD pathways. Concerns: heterotopic bone, seroma, cervical spine airway swelling (off-label), cost, and possible oncogenic signal.
  • Calcium phosphate (e.g. injectable CaPO₄ cement) has higher compressive strength and slower resorption than calcium sulfate, and is osteoconductive only. In tibial plateau fractures it reduces articular subsidence compared with autograft/iliac crest — a repeated stem.
  • Calcium sulfate resorbs quickly (weeks–months) and provides no meaningful structural support. DBM is osteoconductive with variable osteoinductivity (lot-dependent). Allograft is osteoconductive (± weak induction) and structurally useful.
  • Hindfoot/ankle fusion: rhPDGF-BB with β-tricalcium phosphate has been shown to be non-inferior/equivalent to autograft — the recurring 'bone substitute equivalent to autograft for hindfoot fusion' answer.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics; Foot and Ankle.
  • DiGiovanni CW et al. rhPDGF-BB/β-TCP vs autograft in ankle and hindfoot fusion. JBJS Am 2013.
  • Russell TA, Leighton RK (Canadian). Comparison of autogenous bone graft and calcium phosphate cement in tibial plateau fractures. JBJS Am 2008.
  • Bishop JA, Einhorn TA. Bone graft substitutes. JAAOS.
4questions

Cartilage biology: Composition, chondrocytes & injury response

Zonal architecture, matrix composition and the limits of intrinsic repair.

3 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2025

  • Composition by wet weight: ~70–80% water, 10–20% type II collagen, 5–10% proteoglycan (aggrecan). Chondrocytes occupy only ~1–5% of the volume, are avascular/aneural/alymphatic and rely on diffusion — hence poor intrinsic healing.
  • Zones: superficial/tangential (collagen parallel to surface, highest water & collagen, lowest proteoglycan — resists shear), middle (oblique), deep/radial (perpendicular collagen, highest proteoglycan, largest chondrocytes), tidemark, calcified cartilage.
  • Type II collagen provides tensile strength; proteoglycans provide compressive stiffness by binding water. Chondrocytes are metabolically active but do not divide meaningfully in adults.
  • Superficial (chondral-only) injuries do not heal. Injuries that penetrate subchondral bone gain access to marrow elements and heal with fibrocartilage (type I collagen), which is mechanically inferior and degrades over time.
  • Ageing decreases water content and proteoglycan size; osteoarthritis increases water content early, with proteoglycan loss and collagen network disruption.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics; Sports.
  • Buckwalter JA, Mankin HJ. Articular cartilage: structure, composition and function. Instr Course Lect.
  • Sophia Fox AJ et al. The basic science of articular cartilage. Sports Health 2009.
4questions

Necrotizing soft tissue infection

Recognition, microbiology and treatment of necrotising fasciitis.

3 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2022, 2024F

  • Type I is polymicrobial (aerobes + anaerobes) and is the most common overall, typically in diabetics/immunocompromised, perineum and abdominal wall. Type II is monomicrobial, classically group A Streptococcus (± S. aureus), and occurs in healthy young patients. Type III includes Vibrio (marine exposure) and clostridial myonecrosis.
  • Pain out of proportion, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, bullae, skin anaesthesia and crepitus. Imaging must not delay surgery; gas on plain film is specific but insensitive.
  • LRINEC score (CRP, WBC, Hb, Na, creatinine, glucose) supports but never excludes the diagnosis — a low score does not rule it out.
  • Treatment: emergent, aggressive serial débridement is the single determinant of survival, plus broad-spectrum antibiotics (carbapenem or pip-tazo + vancomycin) with clindamycin to suppress exotoxin/M-protein production. IVIG is adjunctive in streptococcal toxic shock. Delay to débridement is the strongest predictor of mortality.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas: Necrotizing Fasciitis.
  • Stevens DL et al. IDSA Practice Guidelines for Skin and Soft Tissue Infections. Clin Infect Dis 2014.
  • Wong CH et al. The LRINEC score. Crit Care Med 2004.
  • Anaya DA, Dellinger EP. Necrotizing soft-tissue infection: diagnosis and management. Clin Infect Dis 2007.
4questions

Professionalism: Informed consent & capacity

Elements of valid consent, emergency exceptions and capacity assessment.

4 of 7 sittings2021, 2022, 2024S, 2025

  • Valid consent requires: capacity, voluntariness, disclosure of the nature of the procedure, material risks, alternatives (including no treatment) and expected outcomes, and the patient's understanding. Canadian standard (Reibl v Hughes) is the modified objective 'reasonable patient' test — what a reasonable person in the patient's position would want to know, not what a reasonable physician would disclose.
  • In a true emergency where the patient lacks capacity and no substitute decision-maker is reachable, you may treat under the emergency doctrine — provide the treatment necessary to preserve life or limb, document the emergency, and obtain consent as soon as an SDM is available. You do not delay to search for family.
  • Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate; it is not determined by diagnosis or by agreeing/disagreeing with you. A capable patient may refuse even life-saving surgery.
  • Disclosure of who will perform the operation, including trainee involvement, is part of consent — patients must be told that residents/fellows will participate and in what role. Concealing this is not acceptable.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • Reibl v Hughes [1980] 2 SCR 880 (Supreme Court of Canada).
  • CMPA. Consent: A guide for Canadian physicians, 4th ed.
  • CanMEDS 2015 — Professional and Communicator roles.
4questions

Professionalism: Social media, photography & AI

Digital professionalism: patient images, online conduct and generative AI in scholarly work.

2 of 7 sittings2024S, 2024F (x3)

  • Clinical photography requires separate, explicit consent for each intended use (record, teaching, publication, social media). Images must be de-identified, stored on institutionally approved (not personal) devices, and consent must be documented and revocable.
  • Social media: no patient-identifiable information even in a 'closed' group; maintain professional boundaries (do not accept friend requests from current patients); do not give individualised medical advice online; identify conflicts of interest and disclose industry relationships.
  • Generative AI (e.g. ChatGPT) in manuscripts: AI cannot be listed as an author because it cannot take responsibility or attest to integrity. Its use must be disclosed in the methods/acknowledgements, and the human authors remain fully accountable for accuracy, originality and any fabricated references. ICMJE and most journals now require this.
  • A patient covertly recording a consultation: respond calmly and non-defensively, do not terminate the encounter, explore why they felt the need to record, and offer a formal summary/copy of the note. In most Canadian provinces one-party consent recording is legal.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • ICMJE Recommendations — Defining the Role of Authors and Contributors (AI section), 2023.
  • CMPA. Social media: the opportunities, the realities; Using patient images.
  • CMA Policy: Social Media and Canadian Physicians.
4questions

Radiation safety & imaging in pregnancy

ALARA, dose figures and imaging the pregnant trauma patient.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2025

  • ALARA: time, distance, shielding. Scatter is the main occupational exposure. Dose falls with the inverse square of distance — stepping back one metre is more effective than most shielding. Stand on the image-intensifier side (away from the source/under-table tube), and the surgeon's hands should never be in the primary beam.
  • Mini C-arm delivers far less dose than a standard C-arm; the highest doses to the surgeon come from large-C-arm lateral imaging (spine, pelvis, acetabulum) and from holding limbs.
  • Fetal risk: the accepted cumulative threshold for deterministic effects is 50 mGy (5 rad); teratogenesis is greatest at 2–15 weeks. A single extremity radiograph gives a negligible fetal dose (<0.01 mGy) — less than background. No single diagnostic study exceeds the threshold, and a CT of the pelvis is not contraindicated when clinically necessary in trauma.
  • In the pregnant trauma patient: resuscitate the mother first (best fetal therapy), left lateral tilt after ~20 weeks to offload the IVC, obtain necessary imaging with abdominal shielding when it does not obscure the field, involve obstetrics early, and give Rh immunoglobulin to Rh-negative mothers. Avoid tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: General; Medical Conditions.
  • ACOG Committee Opinion 723: Guidelines for Diagnostic Imaging During Pregnancy and Lactation, 2017.
  • Mastrangelo G et al. Increased cancer risk among surgeons in an orthopaedic hospital. Occup Med.
  • Singer G. Occupational radiation exposure to the surgeon. JAAOS 2005.
3questions

Atypical femoral fracture & bisphosphonate-related bone disease

ASBMR diagnostic criteria and management of AFF.

3 of 7 sittings2021, 2022, 2024F

  • Location: subtrochanteric or diaphyseal femur, from just distal to the lesser trochanter to just proximal to the supracondylar flare. Major features: minimal/no trauma, transverse or short-oblique orientation, non-comminuted, medial spike if complete, localised periosteal/endosteal thickening of the lateral cortex ('beaking'), and generalised cortical thickening.
  • Prodromal thigh or groin pain is present in a majority; ~30–50% are bilateral, so image the contralateral femur (full-length radiographs; MRI/bone scan if radiographs are negative).
  • Risk factors: long-duration bisphosphonate use (risk rises after ~3–5 years), denosumab, glucocorticoids, Asian ethnicity, and femoral bowing/varus. Absolute risk remains low and is far outweighed by fracture prevention benefit for most treated patients.
  • Management: stop the antiresorptive, optimise calcium/vitamin D, consider teriparatide. Complete fractures need cephalomedullary nailing. Incomplete fractures with a dreaded black line and pain, or that fail conservative treatment, should be prophylactically nailed. Healing is slow and nonunion/delayed union is common; reaming and correcting varus/bow are important.
  • The classic technical trap: a bowed, varus femur with thick diaphyseal cortices — the nail cannot be forced into a straight path, so nailing in varus with a lateral start point causes malreduction and failure.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Lower Extremity Trauma; Systemic Disease.
  • Shane E et al. Atypical subtrochanteric and diaphyseal femoral fractures: second report of a task force of the ASBMR. J Bone Miner Res 2014.
  • Egol KA et al. Healing delayed but generally reliable after bisphosphonate-associated complete femur fractures. CORR 2014.
3questions

Biostatistics: Study design — RCT, observational, meta-analysis

Hierarchy of evidence, what each design can and cannot answer, and threats to meta-analysis validity.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2023, 2024F

  • RCT is the strongest design for a therapeutic question because randomisation balances known and unknown confounders. It is poorly suited to rare outcomes, harms, and prognosis. Cohort studies are best for prognosis and incidence; case-control for rare outcomes/etiology (yields an odds ratio, not a relative risk or incidence).
  • Observational studies cannot establish causation and are vulnerable to selection, information and confounding bias; they can, however, have better external validity than a narrowly enrolled RCT.
  • Threats to meta-analysis validity: publication bias (assessed with funnel plot/Egger test), clinical and statistical heterogeneity, poor quality of included studies, inappropriate pooling, and duplicate/overlapping data. High heterogeneity (I² >50–75%) means the pooled estimate may be meaningless — it is a reason to explore subgroups or use a random-effects model, and it does not simply mean 'more studies are needed'.
  • Fixed-effects assumes one true effect; random-effects assumes a distribution of true effects and gives wider confidence intervals — appropriate when heterogeneity is present.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Research Summaries.
  • Bhandari M et al. (Canadian) Users' guide to the orthopaedic literature series. JBJS Am.
  • Higgins JPT et al. Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions.
  • PRISMA 2020 Statement.
3questions

Biostatistics: Type I/II error, power & sample size

Error types, power, and what drives sample size.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2024S (x2)

  • Type I (α) error = rejecting a true null = a false-positive result ('finding a difference that isn't there'). Type II (β) error = failing to reject a false null = a false-negative ('missing a real difference'). Power = 1 − β, conventionally 0.80.
  • A small trial showing a benefit that a larger, multicentre trial subsequently fails to confirm is the classic scenario for a type I error in the first study.
  • Sample size increases when: the expected effect size is smaller, event rates are low, variance is larger, α is set lower (0.01 vs 0.05), power is set higher (90% vs 80%), the test is two-sided, or dropout is anticipated. The smaller the difference you want to detect, the larger the trial.
  • Underpowered trials do not 'prove no difference' — absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Reporting a confidence interval is more informative than a p-value alone.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Research Summaries.
  • Bhandari M, Joensson A. Clinical Research for Surgeons.
  • Lochner HV, Bhandari M, Tornetta P. Type-II error rates (beta errors) of randomised trials in orthopaedic trauma. JBJS Am 2001.
3questions

Bone healing: Stages, primary vs secondary & modifiers

Phases of fracture healing and factors that modify it.

2 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021

  • Secondary (indirect) healing: haematoma/inflammation (0–7 d) → soft callus/fibrocartilage (chondrogenesis, ~2–3 wk) → hard callus (endochondral ossification — new bone laid down on a cartilage scaffold) → remodelling (Wolff's law, months–years). The 'new bone forming on a scaffold' stem = hard callus/endochondral ossification.
  • Primary (direct) healing occurs only with absolute stability and <2% strain: cutting cones cross the fracture (Haversian remodelling) with no callus. Radiographic callus after compression plating of a simple fracture means the construct is failing.
  • Inflammation is essential — a controlled inflammatory phase drives healing; NSAIDs (especially non-selective and COX-2 inhibitors) impair early healing in animal models and are associated with nonunion in clinical series, so short courses are preferred in high-risk fractures.
  • Negative modifiers: smoking (the strongest modifiable factor), diabetes, malnutrition, infection, NSAIDs, bisphosphonates (delay remodelling), radiation, vascular disease. Vitamin D deficiency is very common in fracture patients and should be corrected, though supplementation alone has not been shown to accelerate union.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics; Orthopaedic Dilemmas: Nonunion.
  • Einhorn TA, Gerstenfeld LC. Fracture healing: mechanisms and interventions. Nat Rev Rheumatol 2015.
  • Marquez-Lara A et al. NSAIDs and bone healing. JBJS Rev 2016.
3questions

Genetics & molecular pathology in orthopaedics

Recurring gene/mutation associations tested on the exam.

3 of 7 sittings2021, 2023, 2024S

  • Achondroplasia — FGFR3 gain-of-function, autosomal dominant, >80% sporadic (advanced paternal age). Thanatophoric dysplasia and hypochondroplasia also FGFR3.
  • Osteogenesis imperfecta — COL1A1/COL1A2 (type I collagen); most types autosomal dominant, but type II (perinatal lethal) is the classically autosomal-recessive/new-mutation severe form. Types VII–VIII (CRTAP, LEPRE1) are recessive.
  • Multiple hereditary exostoses — EXT1/EXT2, AD. Diaphyseal aclasis with malignant transformation risk ~1–5% (higher with EXT1 and pelvic/proximal lesions).
  • Ollier/Maffucci — IDH1/IDH2 somatic mosaicism (not inherited). Fibrous dysplasia — GNAS1 post-zygotic mutation (McCune-Albright when polyostotic + café-au-lait + endocrinopathy).
  • Ewing sarcoma — t(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1. Synovial sarcoma — t(X;18) SS18-SSX. Myxoid liposarcoma — t(12;16) FUS-DDIT3. ALT/WDL and dedifferentiated liposarcoma — MDM2/CDK4 amplification. Neurofibromatosis 1 — NF1 (neurofibromin), AD, 50% sporadic. Diastrophic dysplasia — DTDST, AR. Pseudoachondroplasia — COMP.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology; Pediatrics.
  • Weiss SW, Goldblum JR. Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors, 7th ed.
  • WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone, 5th ed, 2020.
3questions

Heterotopic ossification

Risk factors, natural history, prophylaxis and timing of excision.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2025 (x2)

  • Highest-risk orthopaedic scenarios: acetabular fracture surgery via an extended iliofemoral or Kocher-Langenbeck approach (extensive gluteal muscle stripping), THA, elbow trauma/burns, and traumatic brain or spinal cord injury. Male sex, ankylosing spondylitis, DISH, prior HO and hypertrophic OA increase risk.
  • Pathophysiology: mesenchymal cells differentiate into osteoblasts under BMP signalling; mature lamellar bone forms in soft tissue. Bone scan turns positive earliest; alkaline phosphatase rises; radiographic maturity takes 6–12 months.
  • Prophylaxis: single-dose radiation (700–800 cGy within 24 h pre-op or 72 h post-op) or indomethacin for 2–6 weeks. Both work; radiation avoids GI effects but may impair fracture/trochanteric osteotomy healing and is contraindicated in the young because of malignancy risk.
  • Excision only once mature and symptoms (loss of motion/impingement) justify it — historically 6–12 months, though earlier excision is increasingly accepted in the elbow. Excision should be followed by prophylaxis.
  • Brooker classification is used at the hip; most HO is asymptomatic and radiographic only, and it does not all resolve by 6 months.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas: Heterotopic Ossification; Pelvis and Acetabulum.
  • Baird EO, Kang QK. Prophylaxis of heterotopic ossification — an updated review. J Orthop Surg Res 2009.
  • Firoozabadi R et al. Heterotopic ossification in acetabular fracture surgery. JAAOS 2017.
3questions

Nerve injury: Classification, degeneration & recovery

Seddon/Sunderland, Wallerian degeneration and the order of recovery.

3 of 7 sittings2023, 2024S, 2025

  • Seddon: neurapraxia (conduction block, no Wallerian degeneration, full recovery days–weeks), axonotmesis (axon disrupted, endoneurium intact — recovers by regeneration), neurotmesis (complete transection, requires repair). Sunderland I–V maps onto these (I = neurapraxia; II–IV = degrees of axonotmesis; V = neurotmesis).
  • Regeneration proceeds at ~1 mm/day (1 inch/month) after a ~3–4 week lag. Recovery is proximal to distal — the muscle closest to the injury recovers first.
  • Radial nerve palsy with a humeral shaft fracture: brachioradialis is the first muscle to recover; the last is typically extensor indicis proprius/extensor pollicis longus. For a mid-forearm ulnar nerve laceration, intrinsic hand function (interossei/adductor pollicis) is the last to return, and often does not.
  • Advancing Tinel sign indicates regenerating axons. EMG/NCS is most informative at ~3–4 weeks (fibrillations appear); a normal study before then does not exclude injury.
  • Timing of repair: clean sharp laceration → primary repair; blunt/avulsion → tag and repair at 3 weeks; no recovery by 3–6 months → explore, with nerve grafting or transfer. Muscle motor end-plates degenerate irreversibly by ~18–24 months.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas: Nerve Injury; Upper Extremity Nerve Pathology.
  • Seddon HJ. Three types of nerve injury. Brain 1943; Sunderland S. Nerves and Nerve Injuries.
  • Shao YC et al. Radial nerve palsy associated with fractures of the shaft of the humerus: a systematic review. JBJS Br 2005.
3questions

Professionalism: Equity, diversity & care of trans/gender-diverse patients

Respectful, evidence-informed care of transgender and gender-diverse patients, and equity in the profession.

3 of 7 sittings2023, 2024S, 2024F

  • Use the patient's chosen name and pronouns; ask, do not assume. Record the legal name where required for administrative purposes but use the chosen name in communication. Do not ask about gender-affirming surgery or anatomy unless clinically relevant to the presenting problem.
  • Gender-affirming hormone therapy: oestrogen therapy carries a VTE risk that is relevant to perioperative planning, but current guidance is generally not to routinely stop hormones before orthopaedic surgery — decisions should be individualised with the prescriber, weighing thrombotic risk against the psychological harm of interruption.
  • Organ-based screening and physiologic reference ranges should follow the organs present, not the recorded gender marker (e.g. bone density interpretation, haemoglobin norms).
  • Women remain markedly under-represented in orthopaedic surgery — the lowest proportion of any surgical specialty in both Canada and the US — with documented disparities in mentorship, referral patterns, industry payments and academic promotion. Reported burnout rates in orthopaedic surgeons are comparable to, not lower than, other surgical specialties, and are higher in residency.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • Coleman E et al. WPATH Standards of Care, version 8. Int J Transgend Health 2022.
  • Rohde RS et al. Where are the women in orthopaedic surgery? CORR 2016.
  • CMA National Physician Health Survey; Canadian Orthopaedic Association diversity reports.
3questions

Tranexamic acid & blood management

Mechanism, routes, efficacy and safety of TXA.

3 of 7 sittings2023, 2024S, 2024F

  • TXA is a lysine analogue that competitively blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, preventing its binding to fibrin and thereby inhibiting fibrinolysis. It stabilises existing clot; it does not promote new clot formation.
  • In arthroplasty, TXA reduces blood loss and transfusion by roughly 30–50%. IV, topical/intra-articular and oral routes are equivalent for TKA/THA; combined routes give little additional benefit. Oral TXA is the cheapest.
  • Safety: multiple large studies and meta-analyses show no increase in VTE, including in patients with a history of VTE, coronary stents or CVA — current AAOS/ICM consensus considers these not to be absolute contraindications. True contraindications are limited (acquired defective colour vision, active intravascular clotting, subarachnoid haemorrhage in some guidance).
  • In trauma, CRASH-2 showed a mortality benefit when given within 3 hours of injury, with harm if given after 3 hours. Earlier is better.
  • Restrictive transfusion (threshold ~70–80 g/L, or symptoms) is as safe as liberal transfusion after hip fracture surgery (FOCUS trial) — transfuse for symptoms, not a number.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: General; Trauma: General.
  • Fillingham YA et al. AAHKS/AAOS/Hip & Knee Society Combined Clinical Practice Guideline on TXA. J Arthroplasty 2018.
  • CRASH-2 Collaborators. Effects of tranexamic acid on death and vascular occlusive events in trauma patients. Lancet 2010.
  • Carson JL et al. Liberal or restrictive transfusion in high-risk patients after hip surgery (FOCUS). NEJM 2011.
3questions

Trunnionosis, modularity & adverse local tissue reaction

Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion at modular junctions.

2 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2024F

  • Trunnionosis is fretting and crevice corrosion at the head–neck (or neck–stem) taper, releasing metal debris and ions and producing an ALTR/pseudotumour that can look identical to MoM disease — even with a ceramic or polyethylene bearing.
  • Factors that increase risk: larger head diameter (higher frictional torque), longer head/neck offset (skirted heads), dissimilar metals (mixed alloy) at the junction, smaller/shorter trunnion designs, high patient BMI and activity, and contamination of the taper at assembly.
  • Minimising risk: assemble a clean and dry taper, impact firmly once along the axis, avoid skirted/extra-long heads and large metal heads, avoid unnecessary modularity (modular neck stems have a poor track record), and consider ceramic heads.
  • Work-up of a painful metal-bearing or modular THA: rule out infection first (ESR/CRP, aspiration), then serum cobalt and chromium, and MARS MRI. Elevated cobalt disproportionate to chromium suggests taper corrosion rather than bearing wear.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • Cooper HJ et al. Corrosion at the head–neck taper as a cause for adverse local tissue reactions after THA. JBJS Am 2012.
  • Kwon YM et al. Evaluation of the painful metal-on-metal hip. JAAOS 2014.
2questions

Biostatistics: Diagnostic test performance (sens/spec/PPV/NPV)

2×2 table calculations and the effect of prevalence.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2023

  • Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) — 'of those with disease, how many test positive'. Specificity = TN/(TN+FP). SnNout: a highly Sensitive test, when Negative, rules out. SpPin: a highly Specific test, when Positive, rules in.
  • PPV = TP/(TP+FP); NPV = TN/(TN+FN). Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test; PPV and NPV depend on prevalence. As prevalence falls, PPV falls and NPV rises — a key exam concept for screening.
  • Likelihood ratios are prevalence-independent: LR+ = sens/(1−spec); LR− = (1−sens)/spec. LR+ >10 or LR− <0.1 substantially changes post-test probability.
  • Practical tip: build the 2×2 with disease across the top and test result down the side, fill in the totals first, then compute along rows (predictive values) or columns (sensitivity/specificity).
References2
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Research Summaries.
  • Bhandari M, Guyatt GH. How to appraise a diagnostic test. World J Surg 2005.
2questions

Biostatistics: Incidence, prevalence & epidemiology

Definitions and their relationship.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2025

  • Incidence = the number of new cases in a defined population over a defined time period (a rate). Prevalence = the total number of existing cases at a point (or over a period) in time (a proportion).
  • Prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration of disease. Chronic conditions of long duration (osteoarthritis) have high prevalence with modest incidence; rapidly fatal or rapidly cured conditions have low prevalence despite high incidence.
  • Prevalence is what you need for interpreting a diagnostic test (pre-test probability) and for health-services planning; incidence is what you need for causation and risk-factor studies.
  • Anything that improves survival without curing a disease increases prevalence without changing incidence — a classic distractor.
References2
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Research Summaries.
  • Rothman KJ. Epidemiology: An Introduction, 2nd ed.
2questions

Casting & splinting materials

Material properties and the cast index.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2023

  • Fibreglass: stronger for the same weight, lighter, water-resistant, radiolucent, sets faster, and is more durable. Plaster of Paris: cheaper, better moulding/conformability, and lower exothermic risk if applied correctly — superior moulding is the advantage of plaster, not fibreglass, and is the standard distractor.
  • Plaster burns are related to high dip-water temperature, >8-ply thickness, and setting on a pillow (insulation). Use cool water and support on the palms, not fingertips.
  • Cast index = internal cast width on the lateral view ÷ internal width on the AP view, measured at the fracture. A value >0.8 predicts loss of reduction in paediatric distal radius/forearm fractures. Related measures: three-point index, gap index, and the padding index.
  • Good moulding beats a thick cast — a well-moulded, three-point cast with an appropriate cast index is the single best predictor of maintained reduction.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatric Trauma: Upper Extremity.
  • Chess DG et al. Cast index in predicting outcome of distal radius fractures in children. J Pediatr Orthop 1994.
  • Webb GR et al. The cast index as a predictor of redisplacement. JBJS Am 2006.
2questions

Chronic exertional compartment syndrome

Diagnosis and risk factors for CECS.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2021

  • Exercise-induced, reproducible pain/tightness relieved by rest, usually the anterior compartment of the leg; may have transient paraesthesia or foot drop. The examination is normal at rest — examine immediately after exercise.
  • Diagnosis is by dynamic intracompartmental pressure measurement (Pedowitz criteria): resting >15 mmHg, 1 min post-exercise >30 mmHg, or 5 min post-exercise >20 mmHg.
  • Risk factors: young athletes/military recruits, running and repetitive impact sport, anabolic steroid or creatine use, eccentric training, and rapid increases in training volume. Being older and sedentary is protective — the usual 'except' answer.
  • Treatment: activity modification, gait retraining (forefoot strike running reduces anterior compartment pressures); definitive treatment is fasciotomy of the involved compartments, with good results anteriorly and less predictable results for the deep posterior compartment.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports.
  • Pedowitz RA et al. Modified criteria for the objective diagnosis of chronic compartment syndrome of the leg. Am J Sports Med 1990.
  • Diebal AR et al. Forefoot running improves pain and disability associated with chronic exertional compartment syndrome. AJSM 2012.
2questions

Muscle physiology: Fibre types & contraction mechanics

Fibre typing and modes of contraction.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2024S

  • Type I (slow twitch): oxidative, high mitochondria/myoglobin/capillary density, fatigue-resistant, low force, red — postural muscles (soleus). Type II (fast twitch): glycolytic (IIb/IIx) or fast-oxidative-glycolytic (IIa), high force, rapid fatigue, white — used for sprinting/power. Immobilisation preferentially atrophies type I.
  • Eccentric contraction = the muscle lengthens while generating force (the load exceeds the force produced). It generates the highest force of the three modes, uses the least metabolic energy per unit force, and produces the most delayed-onset muscle soreness/damage. Concentric = shortening; isometric = no length change.
  • Force–velocity relationship: force falls as concentric shortening velocity increases, and rises with eccentric lengthening velocity. Length–tension: peak active force occurs at optimal sarcomere overlap.
  • Denervated muscle fibrillates on EMG; reinnervation produces polyphasic potentials and fibre-type grouping.
References2
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics.
  • Lieber RL. Skeletal Muscle Structure, Function, and Plasticity, 3rd ed.
2questions

Osteogenesis imperfecta

Sillence classification, inheritance and orthopaedic management.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2023

  • Defect in type I collagen quantity or quality (COL1A1/COL1A2). Sillence: I mildest, AD, blue sclerae, normal stature; II perinatal lethal (autosomal recessive/new dominant mutation — the classic 'which is recessive' answer); III progressively deforming, severe, most severe survivable form; IV moderate, normal/white sclerae.
  • Features: fragility fractures, blue sclerae (I, II), dentinogenesis imperfecta, hearing loss, ligamentous laxity, wormian skull bones, basilar invagination, scoliosis, olecranon apophyseal avulsion fractures.
  • Medical treatment: bisphosphonates increase BMD and reduce fracture rate and pain, especially in types III/IV; they do not correct deformity. Vitamin D/calcium optimisation and physiotherapy.
  • Surgery: realignment osteotomy with telescoping/expandable intramedullary rods (Fassier-Duval) rather than plates — plates create stress risers in brittle bone. Scoliosis progresses and braces are ineffective (rib deformation); early fusion is often required.
  • Key differential from non-accidental injury: OI is suggested by family history, blue sclerae, dentinogenesis, wormian bones and low BMD; NAI by metaphyseal corner fractures, posterior rib fractures, and injuries inconsistent with the developmental stage.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics; Systemic Disease.
  • Sillence DO et al. Genetic heterogeneity in osteogenesis imperfecta. J Med Genet 1979.
  • Glorieux FH et al. Cyclic administration of pamidronate in children with severe osteogenesis imperfecta. NEJM 1998.
2questions

Professionalism: Medicolegal (CMPA) & referral responsibility

CMPA assistance and the division of responsibility between referring and consulting physicians.

1 of 7 sittings2024F (x2)

  • CMPA assistance is discretionary, not insurance. It generally covers medico-legal matters arising from professional work in Canada. Assistance for legal actions commenced outside Canada is limited — the usual exception is care provided to a Canadian patient by a member practising in Canada; work performed abroad, telemedicine to patients located outside Canada, or actions filed in a foreign jurisdiction (especially the US) are typically not covered without prior arrangement.
  • Referral responsibility: the referring physician remains responsible for the patient until care is accepted and assumed; they must ensure the referral is actually received and follow up on a critical result. The consultant is responsible for communicating findings and recommendations back in a timely manner.
  • For a critical finding (e.g. radiograph suggesting osteosarcoma) where the family does not attend, both physicians share a duty to make reasonable attempts to contact the patient and document those attempts — the referring physician cannot assume the consultant has taken over, and vice versa.
  • Adverse events: disclose promptly, factually and empathetically; an apology for the outcome is protected under apology legislation in most provinces and does not constitute an admission of liability.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • CMPA. Assistance eligibility; Consultations and referrals: closing the loop; Disclosing harm from healthcare delivery.
  • Canadian Medical Protective Association Annual Report.
2questions

Professionalism: Physician impairment & burnout

Definitions, obligations and the specific epidemiology of burnout in orthopaedics.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2024S

  • The AMA defines impairment as the inability to practise medicine safely and reliably because of a physical, mental or substance-use condition. Impairment is a functional determination — a diagnosis alone (e.g. depression, being in recovery) is not impairment.
  • Obligations: physicians have a duty to protect patients, which includes self-reporting and reporting a colleague whose impairment endangers patients. The first step is usually a supportive, confidential approach to the colleague and referral to the provincial physician health program; mandatory College reporting applies when patients are at risk.
  • Burnout (Maslach): emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation, reduced personal accomplishment. Orthopaedic surgeons report rates comparable to or higher than most other specialties; residents and early-career surgeons and women report higher rates. It is a systems problem more than an individual resilience problem.
  • Drivers: administrative/EMR burden, loss of autonomy, work–home conflict, and a culture that discourages help-seeking. Effective interventions are largely organisational (workload, schedule control, team support).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • AMA Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 9.3.2 — Physician responsibilities to impaired colleagues.
  • Shanafelt TD et al. Burnout and satisfaction with work–life balance among US physicians. Arch Intern Med / Mayo Clin Proc series.
  • Ames SE et al. Burnout in orthopaedic surgeons. JBJS Am 2017.
2questions

Professionalism: Prescribing for family/self

Boundaries of treating oneself, family and close friends.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2023

  • Canadian College policies and the CMA Code of Ethics direct that physicians should not treat themselves or members of their immediate family except for a minor condition or in an emergency when no other physician is available. This includes prescribing.
  • Reasons: loss of objectivity, incomplete history and examination, no proper record, failure to address sensitive issues, and inadequate follow-up.
  • Narcotics, controlled substances and psychotropics must never be prescribed for oneself or family. Prescribing for a recurrent chronic condition (e.g. recurrent lumbar disc disease) for a spouse is not a minor, self-limited condition and is therefore not appropriate — arrange proper care even if inconvenient.
  • If care is provided in a genuine emergency, document it fully and transfer care as soon as practical.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • CMA Code of Ethics and Professionalism, 2018.
  • CPSO Policy: Physician Treatment of Self, Family Members, or Others Close to Them.
  • CMPA. Treating family members: proceed with caution.
2questions

Professionalism: Resident involvement & overlapping surgery

Disclosure of trainee participation and supervision standards.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2025

  • Patients must be told before the operation that residents/fellows will be involved and in what capacity — this is a required element of informed consent, and it applies regardless of how much of the case the trainee performs.
  • The attending surgeon retains full responsibility, must be immediately available, and must personally perform or directly supervise the critical portions of the procedure. Graded responsibility is appropriate and should be described honestly, not concealed.
  • 'Overlapping' surgery (non-critical portions of two cases overlap with the attending present for all critical portions) is permissible with disclosure and a qualified backup surgeon identified. Concurrent surgery (critical portions overlapping) is not acceptable.
  • Studies of resident involvement in arthroplasty and trauma show comparable outcomes with modestly longer operative times — a point that can be shared honestly with patients.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • American College of Surgeons Statements on Principles — Intraoperative responsibility of the primary surgeon.
  • CMPA. The role of residents in patient care; Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada — supervision standards.
2questions

Professionalism: Truth-telling & breaking bad news

The ethical basis for disclosure and how to deliver it.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2025

  • Truth-telling flows primarily from respect for autonomy — a patient cannot make an informed decision without accurate information — supported by beneficence, non-maleficence and fidelity. Withholding a serious diagnosis (therapeutic privilege) is now regarded as almost never justified.
  • Exceptions are narrow: a competent patient may explicitly waive their right to information and delegate it, and disclosure may be timed/staged for a patient in acute crisis. Family requests to withhold a diagnosis from a competent adult do not override the patient's right to know.
  • Use a structured approach (SPIKES): Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Empathy, Strategy/Summary. Deliver in person, without jargon, with a warning shot, in small pieces, checking understanding, and allow silence.
  • Document the discussion, offer written information and a second meeting, and arrange support.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • Baile WF et al. SPIKES — a six-step protocol for delivering bad news. Oncologist 2000.
  • Beauchamp TL, Childress JF. Principles of Biomedical Ethics, 8th ed.
2questions

Tendon repair biology & suture materials

Repair strength determinants and suture characteristics.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2023

  • Repair strength is proportional to the number of core suture strands crossing the repair site (a 4-strand repair is roughly twice as strong as a 2-strand). Adding a peripheral epitendinous suture adds ~20–50% strength and improves gliding by tidying the repair.
  • Other determinants: suture calibre and material, locking versus grasping configuration, purchase length (~1 cm from the cut end), and knot placement. Repairs are weakest at 5–21 days as they soften before remodelling.
  • For tendon-to-tendon anastomosis, a Pulvertaft weave is the strongest construct and is the standard for tendon transfers; end-to-end/Kessler-type repairs are weaker.
  • Suture reactivity: monofilament non-absorbable (nylon, polypropylene) causes the least tissue reaction; braided multifilament (silk, braided polyester) causes the most and harbours bacteria. Absorbable braided (Vicryl) is intermediate. Silk is the most reactive of the common sutures.
  • Post-repair rehabilitation with early controlled motion improves excursion and strength versus immobilisation — motion is the strongest modifier of adhesion formation.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand.
  • Strickland JW. Development of flexor tendon surgery. J Hand Surg Am 2000.
  • Tang JB. Indications, methods, postoperative motion and outcome evaluation of primary flexor tendon repairs. J Hand Surg Eur 2007.
1question

Biomechanics: Joint reaction force & offloading (cane use)

Free-body analysis of the hip and the mechanics of offloading.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • The hip joint reaction force in single-leg stance is roughly 2.5–3× body weight, because the abductor moment arm is short (~5 cm) relative to the body-weight moment arm (~15 cm) — a roughly 3:1 mechanical disadvantage.
  • A cane held in the contralateral hand markedly reduces the joint reaction force (by up to ~50%) because it lengthens the effective moment arm across the body and reduces the abductor force required. A cane in the ipsilateral hand shortens the lever arm and increases joint reactive force — the recurring exam answer.
  • Other measures that reduce hip JRF: increasing femoral offset (lengthens the abductor lever arm), medialising the acetabular cup, weight loss, and carrying loads on the ipsilateral side. Trendelenburg lurch is the body's own compensation (shifting the centre of gravity over the affected hip).
  • Increasing offset reduces JRF and improves abductor efficiency but increases torque on the stem/trunnion and polyethylene wear rate.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • Neumann DA. Biomechanical analysis of selected principles of hip joint protection. Arthritis Care Res 1989.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System.
1question

Biostatistics: Health economics & cost analysis

Choosing the right economic analysis.

1 of 7 sittings2020

  • When two interventions have equivalent clinical outcomes, the correct analysis is a cost-minimisation analysis — you simply compare costs. This is the standard exam answer.
  • Cost-effectiveness analysis compares cost per natural unit of outcome (cost per fracture prevented). Cost-utility analysis uses a preference-weighted unit — cost per QALY — and permits comparison across diseases. Cost-benefit analysis converts everything to dollars.
  • Willingness-to-pay thresholds in Canada are commonly cited around $50,000/QALY. An intervention that is both cheaper and better is 'dominant'.
  • Include direct medical, direct non-medical and indirect (productivity) costs, and state the perspective (societal, payer, hospital) and time horizon; discount future costs and benefits.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Research Summaries.
  • Drummond MF et al. Methods for the Economic Evaluation of Health Care Programmes, 4th ed.
  • Bozic KJ et al. Health economics in orthopaedics. JBJS Am.
1question

Biostatistics: MCID & clinical vs statistical significance

Interpreting a small but statistically significant difference.

1 of 7 sittings2023

  • The MCID is the smallest change in an outcome score that patients perceive as beneficial. A difference that is statistically significant (p<0.05) but smaller than the MCID is not clinically important — the classic distal radius stem (DASH difference of 5 with an MCID of 10).
  • A large trial can make a trivial difference statistically significant; a small trial can miss an important one. Always report and interpret the effect size and confidence interval alongside the p-value.
  • Related concepts: MDC (minimal detectable change — the smallest change beyond measurement error), PASS (patient acceptable symptom state), and SCB (substantial clinical benefit). MCID is anchor- or distribution-based and varies with the population and baseline severity.
  • Common orthopaedic MCIDs to recognise: DASH ~10, Constant ~10, WOMAC/HOOS/KOOS ~8–10, VAS pain ~2/10 (or ~20 mm).
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Research Summaries.
  • Copay AG et al. Understanding the minimum clinically important difference. Spine J 2007.
  • Bhandari M et al. Users' guide to the orthopaedic literature. JBJS Am.
1question

Biostatistics: Number needed to treat & effect measures

Converting risk differences into NNT.

1 of 7 sittings2021

  • Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = control event rate − treatment event rate. NNT = 1/ARR. Reamed nails 5% nonunion vs unreamed 10% → ARR = 0.05 → NNT = 20.
  • Relative risk reduction (RRR) = ARR/control event rate — here 50%, which sounds far more impressive than an NNT of 20. Relative measures exaggerate benefit when baseline risk is low; always ask for the absolute numbers.
  • NNH (number needed to harm) is calculated the same way from the absolute risk increase. NNT is time-dependent and population-dependent — an NNT quoted without a time frame is incomplete.
  • A smaller NNT means a more effective treatment; NNT approaching infinity means no effect.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Research Summaries.
  • Laupacis A, Sackett DL, Roberts RS. An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment. NEJM 1988.
  • SPRINT Investigators. Reamed vs unreamed nailing of tibial shaft fractures. JBJS Am 2008.
1question

Biostatistics: Survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier)

Interpreting survivorship curves in arthroplasty and oncology.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • Kaplan-Meier estimates the probability of an event-free interval over time and correctly handles censored data (patients lost to follow-up or who die of unrelated causes) — this is its main advantage over a simple percentage.
  • The curve steps down only when an event occurs; censored patients appear as tick marks and reduce the number at risk without counting as failures. The right-hand tail is the least reliable part because few patients remain at risk — always inspect the number-at-risk table and the widening confidence interval.
  • The end point must be explicitly defined (revision for any cause, revision for aseptic loosening, radiographic loosening); changing the end point changes the curve dramatically. Competing risks (death in an elderly cohort) inflate KM failure estimates — a competing-risks (cumulative incidence) analysis is more accurate in registry data.
  • The log-rank test compares two curves; Cox proportional hazards permits adjustment for covariates and yields a hazard ratio.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Research Summaries; Arthroplasty.
  • Murray DW, Carr AJ, Bulstrode C. Survival analysis of joint replacements. JBJS Br 1993.
  • Canadian Joint Replacement Registry (CIHI) annual reports.
1question

Complex regional pain syndrome

Diagnosis and management of CRPS.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • Diagnosis is clinical, using the Budapest criteria: continuing pain disproportionate to the inciting event, plus symptoms in ≥3 of 4 categories and signs in ≥2 of 4 categories (sensory — hyperalgesia/allodynia; vasomotor — temperature/colour asymmetry; sudomotor/oedema; motor/trophic — weakness, tremor, dystonia, hair/nail/skin changes), with no better explanation.
  • Type I (formerly RSD) has no identifiable nerve lesion; type II (causalgia) follows a defined nerve injury. Distal radius fracture is the classic orthopaedic trigger.
  • Investigations are supportive only: three-phase bone scan (periarticular uptake) has moderate sensitivity; radiographs may show patchy osteopenia late. No test confirms or excludes the diagnosis.
  • Management: early mobilisation and intensive physiotherapy/occupational therapy including desensitisation, mirror therapy and graded motor imagery — movement is the mainstay. Adjuncts: neuropathic agents (gabapentinoids, amitriptyline), bisphosphonates, and sympathetic blocks in refractory cases. Vitamin C 500 mg daily for 50 days after distal radius fracture reduces incidence in several trials, although the evidence has been challenged.
  • Prolonged immobilisation and repeated surgery worsen it.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas; Wrist and Hand.
  • Harden RN et al. Validation of proposed diagnostic criteria (the 'Budapest Criteria') for CRPS. Pain 2010.
  • Zollinger PE et al. Effect of vitamin C on frequency of reflex sympathetic dystrophy in wrist fractures. Lancet 1999 / JBJS Am 2007.
1question

MRI physics & contrast (gadolinium)

When gadolinium adds information and its risks.

1 of 7 sittings2020

  • Gadolinium is paramagnetic and shortens T1, so enhancing tissue appears bright on T1 post-contrast images. It requires an intact/leaky vasculature to accumulate — enhancement indicates vascularity and perfusion.
  • Useful for: distinguishing solid tumour from cystic/necrotic components, abscess (rim enhancement) from phlegmon, recurrent disc herniation (non-enhancing) from post-operative scar (enhances), infection, and assessing tumour response to chemotherapy.
  • Not needed for routine meniscal, ligamentous or most degenerative imaging. Intra-articular gadolinium (MR arthrography) is used for labral tears and cartilage.
  • Risks: nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30) with older linear agents — screen renal function; gadolinium deposition in the dentate nucleus/basal ganglia with repeated linear agent exposure (clinical significance uncertain); allergic reactions are rare. Avoid in pregnancy unless essential (gadolinium crosses the placenta).
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology; Principles of Orthopaedics.
  • ACR Manual on Contrast Media, 2023.
  • Kanal E et al. ACR guidance document on MR safe practices.
1question

Negative pressure wound therapy

What VAC therapy does and does not do.

1 of 7 sittings2021
