  • Mechanism: macrodeformation (wound contraction), microdeformation (cellular stretch stimulating granulation), removal of exudate/oedema, and a moist, closed environment. It increases granulation tissue and reduces wound surface area and dressing changes.
  • In open fractures it reduces the need for free flaps in some series and is a useful temporising dressing, but it does not replace timely débridement and definitive soft-tissue coverage — delay to coverage remains the driver of infection.
  • Contraindications/cautions: untreated osteomyelitis, necrotic tissue/eschar in the wound (débride first), malignancy in the wound, exposed vessels/nerve/anastomoses or bowel, and active bleeding/anticoagulation. Do not place directly over exposed vessels.
  • Incisional NPWT over closed high-risk incisions (pilon, calcaneus, acetabulum, revision arthroplasty) reduces wound complications and drainage in several trials.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas; Trauma.
  • Stannard JP et al. Incisional negative pressure wound therapy after high-risk lower extremity fractures. J Orthop Trauma 2012.
  • Blum ML et al. Negative pressure wound therapy reduces deep infection rate in open tibial fractures. J Orthop Trauma 2012.
1question

Operating-room safety & aerosol-generating procedures

Aerosol generation in orthopaedic procedures.

1 of 7 sittings2021

  • Highest aerosol/particle generation comes from high-speed powered instruments and irrigation: pulse lavage, oscillating saws, high-speed burrs, reaming, and electrocautery smoke. Suctioning and dressing changes generate far less.
  • Ranking used in exam stems: pulse lavage > power saw/burr/reamer > suction > simple dressing change or manual traction/reduction. Manual, non-powered manoeuvres are the least aerosol-generating.
  • Mitigation: use bulb-syringe or low-pressure irrigation instead of pulse lavage where feasible, local exhaust/smoke evacuation, N95/eye protection, minimise personnel and door openings, and allow appropriate air-exchange time.
  • Laminar flow and body exhaust suits reduce airborne particles, although registry data have questioned whether laminar flow reduces deep infection in arthroplasty.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics.
  • Canadian Orthopaedic Association / AAOS COVID-19 guidance on aerosol-generating orthopaedic procedures, 2020.
  • Hirschmann MT et al. COVID-19 and orthopaedic surgery — aerosol generation. KSSTA 2020.
1question

Professionalism: Environmental sustainability of surgery

Reducing the carbon and waste footprint of the OR.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • The operating room generates ~20–30% of hospital waste and a disproportionate share of energy use. The largest single lever in most analyses is anaesthetic gas selection — avoiding desflurane and nitrous oxide (desflurane has a global-warming potential many times that of sevoflurane) and using low fresh-gas flows or total intravenous anaesthesia.
  • Other high-yield measures: reducing single-use items and rightsizing custom packs (unused opened items are a major waste stream), reprocessing/reusable instruments and gowns, correct waste segregation (biohazard waste costs and pollutes far more than general waste, and most OR waste is mis-sorted into it), and powering down ventilation/lighting in unused ORs.
  • Recycling alone has a comparatively small effect; procurement and gas choices dominate. Reducing procedure volume of low-value care is also a legitimate lever.
  • This maps to the CanMEDS Leader role and stewardship of finite health-care resources.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • MacNeill AJ et al. The impact of surgery on global climate: a carbon footprinting study of operating theatres. Lancet Planet Health 2017.
  • Canadian Coalition for Green Health Care; CASCADES Canada OR sustainability toolkits.
1question

Professionalism: Ethical principles (beneficence/justice)

The four principles and how they are worded on exams.

1 of 7 sittings2022

  • Beneficence — the positive duty to act for the patient's good: 'prevent evil or harm, remove evil or harm, and do and promote good' is the classic textbook phrasing of beneficence.
  • Non-maleficence — 'first, do no harm'; the negative duty to refrain from causing harm. Autonomy — respect for self-determination (consent, confidentiality, truth-telling). Justice — fair distribution of benefits, risks and resources.
  • Utilitarianism is a consequentialist framework maximising overall good, distinct from the four-principles approach; deontology judges acts by duties/rules regardless of outcome.
  • Fidelity (keeping promises), veracity (truthfulness) and confidentiality are derivative duties. Most exam vignettes hinge on autonomy versus beneficence.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • Beauchamp TL, Childress JF. Principles of Biomedical Ethics, 8th ed, 2019.
  • CMA Code of Ethics and Professionalism, 2018.
1question

Septic arthritis of the native joint (adult)

Diagnosis and management of the acutely infected native joint.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • Synovial fluid analysis is the key test: WBC generally >50,000/mm³ with >90% neutrophils supports septic arthritis, though lower counts occur in immunocompromised, gonococcal and partially treated cases. Crystals and infection can coexist — finding crystals does not exclude sepsis.
  • Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism overall; Neisseria gonorrhoeae in sexually active young adults (migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustular rash; culture is often negative — use nucleic acid testing).
  • Blood cultures before antibiotics; obtain aspirate before antibiotics whenever possible. Radiographs are usually normal early.
  • Treatment: urgent joint drainage (arthroscopic or open lavage; serial aspiration is acceptable for some joints such as the knee in selected cases) plus IV antibiotics. Cartilage damage from chondrolytic enzymes begins within hours — delay is the key predictor of poor outcome.
  • Prosthetic joints follow different thresholds (much lower synovial WBC cut-offs) and different management pathways.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas; Medical Conditions.
  • Margaretten ME et al. Does this adult patient have septic arthritis? JAMA 2007.
  • Mathews CJ et al. Bacterial septic arthritis in adults. Lancet 2010.

9questions

Surgical approaches: Hip & pelvis

Internervous intervals, structures at risk and indications for the standard hip/pelvis approaches.

7 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022 (x2), 2023, 2024S (x2), 2024F, 2025

  • Smith-Petersen (anterior): internervous interval between sartorius/rectus femoris (femoral nerve) and tensor fascia lata (superior gluteal nerve). At risk: lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (superficial, most common complication), ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery (deep). It gives excellent access to the anterior column/hip capsule but poor access to the posterior column and the femur.
  • Kocher-Langenbeck (posterior): for posterior wall/column acetabular fractures. At risk: sciatic nerve (keep the knee flexed and hip extended), superior gluteal neurovascular bundle in the greater sciatic notch (limits proximal retraction), and the medial femoral circumflex artery — protect the quadratus femoris and the obturator externus to preserve the femoral head blood supply.
  • Stoppa / anterior intrapelvic: through the rectus abdominis midline into the space of Retzius. You routinely see the quadrilateral surface, pelvic brim, obturator neurovascular bundle and the corona mortis (anastomosis between the obturator and external iliac/inferior epigastric vessels, ~5 cm from the symphysis) — the corona must be identified and ligated.
  • Hemipelvectomy/obturator anatomy: the obturator artery and nerve exit through the obturator canal in the superolateral (upper outer) quadrant of the obturator foramen.
  • Surgical hip dislocation (Ganz): trochanteric flip osteotomy with an anterior capsulotomy; the structure that must be protected is the deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery, which runs posterior to obturator externus and anterior to the superior gemellus, inferior gemellus and obturator internus tendons — hence obturator externus must be preserved and the tendons released only as needed.
  • Ilioinguinal approach gives access to the anterior column and quadrilateral plate through three windows (lateral to iliopsoas/LFCN; between iliopsoas and femoral vessels; medial to the femoral vessels/spermatic cord).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Pelvis and Acetabulum; Arthroplasty.
  • Hoppenfeld S, deBoer P, Buckley R. Surgical Exposures in Orthopaedics: The Anatomic Approach, 5th ed.
  • Gänz R et al. Surgical dislocation of the adult hip. JBJS Br 2001.
  • Cole JD, Bolhofner BR. Acetabular fracture fixation via a modified Stoppa limited intrapelvic approach. CORR 1994.
6questions

Brachial plexus & peripheral nerve anatomy of the upper limb

Plexus organisation, named branch levels and clinically important trifurcations.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2021 (x2), 2024S, 2024F (x2)

  • Plexus: Roots (C5–T1) → Trunks (upper C5-6, middle C7, lower C8-T1) → Divisions (behind the clavicle) → Cords (named for their relationship to the axillary artery) → Branches. 'Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer.'
  • Preganglionic (root avulsion) signs: Horner syndrome, winged scapula (long thoracic, off the roots), rhomboid weakness (dorsal scapular), elevated hemidiaphragm (phrenic), intact sensory nerve action potentials with absent sensation, and pseudomeningocele on MRI. These indicate a poor prognosis and are not amenable to graft — nerve transfer is needed.
  • Upper trunk (C5-6, Erb) injury: weak shoulder abduction/external rotation, elbow flexion and supination; the arm sits adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated ('waiter's tip'). Lower trunk (C8-T1, Klumpke) affects intrinsics with Horner syndrome.
  • The radial nerve trifurcates into the radial nerve proper, the branch to medial triceps/anconeus and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm on the medial side of the humerus, proximal to the spiral groove (medial to and above the triangular interval) — a repeated stem.
  • Axillary artery branches by part relative to pectoralis minor: 1st part — supreme thoracic; 2nd part — thoracoacromial, lateral thoracic; 3rd part (distal to pectoralis minor) — subscapular (largest), anterior humeral circumflex, posterior humeral circumflex.
  • Brachial plexus reconstruction priority: elbow flexion first, then shoulder stability/abduction and external rotation, then hand sensation, then wrist/finger function.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Nerve Pathology; Shoulder and Elbow.
  • Hoppenfeld S, deBoer P, Buckley R. Surgical Exposures in Orthopaedics, 5th ed.
  • Shin AY, Spinner RJ, Bishop AT. Adult traumatic brachial plexus injuries. JAAOS 2005.
5questions

Surgical approaches: Elbow & forearm

Choosing the correct interval for radius, coronoid and distal humerus exposure.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2024S (x2), 2024F, 2025

  • Henry (anterior/volar) approach to the radius: internervous interval between brachioradialis (radial nerve) and pronator teres (median nerve) proximally, and brachioradialis and FCR distally. Best for proximal-third radius shaft fractures (e.g. gunshot) and for the anterior radial head with an intact LCL. Protect the radial artery medially; supinate to move the PIN laterally and release supinator from its radial insertion.
  • Thompson (dorsal) approach: between ECRB (radial nerve) and EDC (PIN); the PIN is directly at risk within supinator — identify it. Used for middle/distal-third radius.
  • Kocher: between anconeus (radial) and ECU (PIN) — for radial head/capitellum. Stay anterior to the midline of the radial head and keep the forearm pronated to protect the PIN; the LCL originates from the lateral epicondyle and must be preserved (stay anterior to the equator).
  • Coronoid exposure: an over-the-top or medial (Hotchkiss 'over-the-top', or FCU-splitting Taylor-Scham) approach gives the best access to a large anteromedial coronoid facet fracture; the ulnar nerve must be identified and protected. A lateral approach is adequate only for a small tip fragment approached through the radial head defect.
  • Posterior humerus/radial nerve: a posterior triceps-splitting or paratricipital approach gives the most extensive exposure of the posterior humerus and the radial nerve in the spiral groove; the modified posterior (Gerwin) extensile approach mobilises the radial nerve for the widest exposure.
  • Olecranon osteotomy for a complex intra-articular distal humerus fracture: a chevron (apex distal) osteotomy at the bare area of the trochlear notch, pre-drilled before osteotomising, gives ~57% of the articular surface and is repaired with a tension band or plate.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma; Elbow.
  • Hoppenfeld S, deBoer P, Buckley R. Surgical Exposures in Orthopaedics, 5th ed.
  • Ring D, Jupiter JB. Surgical exposure of coronoid fractures. Tech Hand Up Extrem Surg.
3questions

Surgical approaches: Cervical spine

The Smith-Robinson anterior approach and its structures at risk.

3 of 7 sittings2021, 2022, 2024F

  • The anterior (Smith-Robinson) approach uses the interval medial to the sternocleidomastoid and the carotid sheath, and lateral to the strap muscles, trachea and oesophagus. The carotid sheath (carotid artery, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve) is retracted laterally — the vagus nerve lies within the carotid sheath.
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve: courses in the tracheo-oesophageal groove. On the left it loops under the aortic arch and has a longer, more predictable course; on the right it loops around the subclavian artery and is more variable — hence many surgeons favour a left-sided approach for low cervical levels. Injury causes hoarseness and vocal cord paresis.
  • Superior laryngeal nerve (external branch, to cricothyroid) is at risk with high (C3-4) exposure — injury causes loss of high-pitch phonation, the classic 'professional singer cannot hit high notes' stem.
  • Hypoglossal nerve at C2-3 (tongue deviation); sympathetic chain on the longus colli laterally (Horner syndrome); oesophagus (perforation — devastating); thoracic duct on the left at the cervicothoracic junction.
  • Dysphagia is the commonest post-operative complaint, related to retraction time, multi-level surgery, plate profile and prevertebral swelling.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Surgical Techniques.
  • Smith GW, Robinson RA. The treatment of certain cervical spine disorders by anterior removal of the intervertebral disc. JBJS Am 1958.
  • Hoppenfeld S, deBoer P, Buckley R. Surgical Exposures in Orthopaedics, 5th ed.
3questions

Surgical approaches: Distal tibia & ankle

Anterolateral vs anteromedial exposure of the pilon and the limits of each.

1 of 7 sittings2024F (x3)

  • Anterolateral approach: interval lateral to the tibialis anterior/extensor group; the superficial peroneal nerve emerges from the fascia ~10–12 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral malleolus and crosses the field — it is the structure most at risk and the practical proximal limit of the exposure. The anterior neurovascular bundle (deep peroneal nerve, anterior tibial artery) is retracted medially.
  • It provides excellent access to the anterolateral (Chaput) fragment, the syndesmosis and the fibula from a single incision, with a more robust soft-tissue envelope than the anteromedial approach.
  • Anteromedial approach gives better access to the medial and central articular surface but has a thinner soft-tissue envelope; the classic error is combining an anteromedial tibial incision with a direct lateral fibular incision, leaving a narrow skin bridge — the historical rule is ≥7 cm between incisions to reduce skin necrosis.
  • Reduce soft-tissue complications in pilon fractures with: staged management (spanning external fixation first, definitive fixation at 7–14 days once the skin wrinkles), fibular fixation only if it aids reduction, careful incision planning, and consideration of a posterolateral approach for posterior fragments.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Lower Extremity Trauma: Pilon.
  • Herscovici D et al. Anterolateral approach to the tibial plafond. J Orthop Trauma 2005.
  • Sirkin M, Sanders R et al. A staged protocol for soft tissue management in the treatment of complex pilon fractures. J Orthop Trauma 1999.
3questions

Surgical approaches: Knee & tibia

Posterior and posterolateral exposure of the knee and tibial plateau.

3 of 7 sittings2023, 2024S, 2025

  • Lobenhoffer (posteromedial) approach: patient prone or in a floppy-lateral position; the interval is between the medial head of gastrocnemius (retracted laterally, protecting the popliteal neurovascular bundle) and semimembranosus/pes. It gives direct access to the posteromedial fragment of a bicondylar plateau fracture for buttress plating — the fragment that a lateral plate cannot control.
  • Direct posterior (S-shaped/Trickey) approaches allow PCL avulsion fixation but require dissection of the popliteal fossa; the medial sural cutaneous nerve and the popliteal vessels are at risk.
  • Posterolateral corner exposure (layered anatomy of the lateral knee, Seebacher): Layer I — iliotibial tract and superficial biceps femoris; Layer II — patellar retinaculum and patellofemoral ligaments; Layer III — lateral (superficial and deep) capsular layer containing the LCL, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament, arcuate ligament and fabellofibular ligament. The peroneal nerve must be identified posterior to the biceps femoris.
  • For posterior column plateau fractures, prone positioning with a posterior or posteromedial approach is superior to attempting reduction from anterior; the posteromedial fragment is a marker of instability and needs buttress support.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Lower Extremity Trauma: Tibial Plateau; Sports.
  • Lobenhoffer P et al. The posteromedial approach to the tibial plateau. Unfallchirurg / Oper Orthop Traumatol.
  • Seebacher JR et al. The structure of the posterolateral aspect of the knee. JBJS Am 1982.
  • LaPrade RF et al. The anatomy of the posterolateral aspect of the knee. AJSM.
3questions

Surgical approaches: Thoracolumbar spine

Anterior/retroperitoneal exposure and the thoracolumbar junction.

3 of 7 sittings2021, 2022, 2023

  • Anterior retroperitoneal lumbar approach: the order of structures encountered from medial to lateral at the L4-5 level is great vessels (aorta/IVC and iliac vessels) → sympathetic chain → psoas → ureter (which crosses over the iliac vessels and is swept anteriorly with the peritoneum) → genitofemoral nerve on the psoas surface. The genitofemoral nerve lies on the anteromedial surface of psoas and is the structure typically identified there.
  • Risks: retrograde ejaculation from superior hypogastric plexus injury (approach L5-S1 in men from the left, use blunt dissection, avoid monopolar cautery), vascular injury (left iliac vein at L4-5), ureteric injury, and lumbar plexus injury with lateral transpsoas approaches (L4-5 highest risk).
  • Thoracic approach at T11-12: a thoracoabdominal or transthoracic-retroperitoneal exposure requires taking down the diaphragm at its peripheral attachment (leaving a cuff for repair). The 11th and 12th ribs are usually resected; the thoracic duct lies on the right, and the segmental vessels can be ligated — but ligating multiple segmentals on the left, especially T8–L1, risks spinal cord ischaemia (artery of Adamkiewicz).
  • The left side is preferred for thoracic and thoracolumbar approaches: the aorta is more forgiving to mobilise than the thin-walled vena cava, and the liver is avoided.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Surgical Techniques.
  • Hoppenfeld S, deBoer P, Buckley R. Surgical Exposures in Orthopaedics, 5th ed.
  • Sasso RC et al. Retrograde ejaculation after anterior lumbar interbody fusion. Spine 2003.
2questions

Biceps musculotendinous anatomy & rotation

The 90° rotation of the distal biceps and its clinical consequences.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2023

  • The biceps musculotendinous unit undergoes an approximately 90° external (lateral) rotation as it travels from the proximal to the distal attachment. Consequently, the fibres of the short head come to lie distal on the radial tuberosity and the long head proximal; the tendon inserts on the ulnar (medial) side of the tuberosity.
  • Functional implication: the long head contributes more to supination (a more proximal, eccentric insertion gives a longer moment arm) and the short head more to flexion power.
  • Anatomic repair must restore the footprint on the posterior-ulnar aspect of the tuberosity to recover supination strength; a repair placed too anteriorly loses supination moment arm.
  • The lacertus fibrosus (bicipital aponeurosis) may keep the tendon from retracting — an intact lacertus with a ruptured tendon gives a less obvious deformity, and the Hook test is the most accurate physical examination test for a complete distal biceps rupture.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Elbow.
  • Athwal GS, Steinmann SP, Rispoli DM (Canadian). The distal biceps tendon: footprint and relevant clinical anatomy. J Hand Surg Am 2007.
  • O'Driscoll SW, Goncalves LB, Dietz P. The hook test for distal biceps tendon avulsion. AJSM 2007.
2questions

Foot & ankle neuroanatomy (plantar nerves, dorsomedial cutaneous)

Named cutaneous and motor branches tested repeatedly.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2025

  • The first branch of the lateral plantar nerve (Baxter's nerve) innervates abductor digiti minimi (and supplies quadratus plantae, flexor digitorum brevis and the long plantar ligament). Its entrapment between the abductor hallucis fascia and the quadratus plantae causes chronic heel pain without night pain, sometimes with atrophy of ADM.
  • The dorsomedial cutaneous nerve to the hallux is a branch of the superficial peroneal nerve (medial dorsal cutaneous branch). It is at risk during a dorsomedial approach for hallux valgus/bunion surgery and its injury causes a painful neuroma over the medial hallux — a repeated stem.
  • The deep peroneal nerve supplies the first dorsal web space and extensor digitorum brevis. The tibial nerve divides into medial and lateral plantar nerves in the tarsal tunnel; the medial calcaneal branch supplies the heel pad and can arise proximal to the tunnel.
  • Ankle arthroscopy anteromedial portal: made just medial to tibialis anterior, at risk to the saphenous nerve and vein. The anterolateral portal is lateral to peroneus tertius and endangers the superficial peroneal nerve (intermediate dorsal cutaneous branch) — the classic 'first portal' answer depends on which portal is named, so read carefully.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Baxter DE, Pfeffer GB. Treatment of chronic heel pain by surgical release of the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve. CORR 1992.
  • Ferkel RD, Small HN, Gittins JE. Complications in foot and ankle arthroscopy. CORR 2001.
2questions

Gait cycle

Phases, percentages and muscle activity.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2024S

  • Stance = ~60% of the cycle, swing = ~40%. Double-limb support occupies ~20% (two periods of ~10%) and disappears with running — the defining difference between walking and running.
  • Stance phases: initial contact/heel strike (0%), loading response, midstance, terminal stance/heel off, pre-swing/toe off (~60%). Swing: initial, mid, terminal.
  • Muscle activity: tibialis anterior is eccentrically active at heel strike to control foot slap and again in swing for clearance; the gastrocsoleus is active in terminal stance for push-off; quadriceps act eccentrically in loading response; hip abductors (gluteus medius) act in single-limb stance to prevent contralateral pelvic drop.
  • Normal cadence ~100–115 steps/min; walking velocity ~80 m/min. Centre of gravity is lowest at double support and highest at midstance; vertical displacement ~5 cm.
  • The subtalar joint pronates through loading response (unlocking the transverse tarsal joints for shock absorption) and supinates in terminal stance (locking the midfoot into a rigid lever for push-off).
References2
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics; Foot and Ankle.
  • Perry J, Burnfield JM. Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function, 2nd ed.
2questions

Shoulder girdle & pectoralis major anatomy

Insertional anatomy relevant to repair and to TSA.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2024S

  • Pectoralis major has a clavicular head (medial half of the clavicle) and a sternocostal head (sternum, upper six costal cartilages, external oblique aponeurosis). The tendon inserts on the lateral lip of the bicipital groove as a bilaminar (two-layered) tendon: the clavicular head inserts anteriorly and more distally, while the sternal head fibres twist to insert posteriorly and more proximally — the characteristic 180° twist.
  • Innervation: lateral pectoral nerve (C5-7) to the clavicular head, medial pectoral nerve (C8-T1) to the sternocostal head. Blood supply is chiefly the pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery (from the axillary artery), not the intercostals.
  • Rupture typically occurs at the humeral insertion or musculotendinous junction, most often during bench press eccentric loading; the sternal head tears first. Repair restores adduction and internal rotation strength.
  • The superior border of pectoralis major is a reliable landmark for humeral head height in shoulder arthroplasty (~5.6 cm from the top of the humeral head to the superior border of the pectoralis major insertion).
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder.
  • Fung L, Wong B, Ravichandiran K, Agur A, Rindlisbacher T, Elmaraghy A (Canadian). Three-dimensional study of pectoralis major muscle and tendon architecture. Clin Anat 2009.
  • Murachovsky J et al. Pectoralis major tendon reference for humeral head height. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2006.
2questions

Spinal cord & nerve root anatomy

Tract anatomy and how it maps to incomplete cord syndromes.

1 of 7 sittings2020 (x2)

  • Ascending: dorsal columns (ipsilateral proprioception, vibration, light touch — decussate in the medulla); lateral spinothalamic (contralateral pain and temperature — decussate within 1–2 levels of entry). Descending: lateral corticospinal tract (ipsilateral motor, decussates in the medulla).
  • Somatotopy in the lateral corticospinal tract places cervical/upper-extremity fibres most medial and sacral fibres most lateral — the anatomic basis for central cord syndrome affecting the arms more than the legs.
  • Blood supply: a single anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds (motor, spinothalamic); paired posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns. The artery of Adamkiewicz (usually left, T9–L2) is the dominant thoracolumbar radicular feeder — hence anterior cord syndrome after aortic or thoracolumbar surgery.
  • The cord ends at the conus medullaris (L1-2 in adults); below that is the cauda equina (lower motor neuron). The zone of partial preservation applies only to a complete (ASIA A) injury and refers to the dermatomes/myotomes with some preserved function below the neurological level.
  • Bulbocavernosus reflex return marks the end of spinal shock (typically 24–48 h); accurate ASIA classification requires that spinal shock has resolved.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spine Trauma.
  • ASIA/ISCoS International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury, 2019 revision.
  • Kirshblum SC et al. Reference for the 2011/2019 ISNCSCI. J Spinal Cord Med.
2questions

Vascular anatomy: Medial femoral circumflex & femoral head blood supply

The blood supply of the femoral head and how to protect it.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2025

  • The deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA) is the dominant supply to the adult femoral head, via the superior retinacular (lateral epiphyseal) vessels. It arises from the profunda femoris, runs between pectineus and iliopsoas, then along the inferior border of obturator externus.
  • Critical relationship: the deep branch passes posterior/deep to the obturator externus tendon and anterior (superficial) to the tendons of the superior gemellus, obturator internus and inferior gemellus before piercing the capsule at the superior-posterior femoral neck. This is why obturator externus must be preserved during surgical hip dislocation, while the short external rotators above it may be released.
  • Minor contributions: lateral femoral circumflex artery (anterior/inferior retinacular), and the artery of the ligamentum teres (from the obturator artery) which is significant in children but contributes little in adults.
  • Clinical consequences: displaced femoral neck fractures, posterior hip dislocations, and slipped capital femoral epiphysis (especially unstable slips) all threaten this supply and cause AVN. In children the retinacular vessels are the sole supply after the age of ~4 years because the physis is a barrier.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity; Pediatrics.
  • Gautier E, Ganz K, Krügel N, Gill T, Ganz R. Anatomy of the medial femoral circumflex artery and its surgical implications. JBJS Br 2000.
  • Trueta J, Harrison MHM. The normal vascular anatomy of the femoral head in adult man. JBJS Br 1953.
1question

Adductor canal & thigh anatomy

Contents of the adductor (Hunter's) canal.

1 of 7 sittings2020

  • The adductor canal runs from the apex of the femoral triangle to the adductor hiatus, bounded by vastus medialis (anterolateral), adductor longus and magnus (posteromedial), and the sartorius/subsartorial fascia (roof).
  • Contents: superficial femoral artery, femoral vein, saphenous nerve, and the nerve to vastus medialis. The sciatic nerve is not in the adductor canal — it lies in the posterior compartment and is therefore the structure least at risk with an anteromedial mid-thigh stab wound (the recurring answer).
  • Adductor canal block spares quadriceps strength (mostly sensory, saphenous) compared with a femoral nerve block, reducing fall risk after TKA — the basis of modern ERAS analgesia.
  • The profunda femoris and its perforators lie posterior to adductor longus; the femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics.
  • Hoppenfeld S, deBoer P, Buckley R. Surgical Exposures in Orthopaedics, 5th ed.
  • Kim DH et al. Adductor canal block versus femoral nerve block for TKA. Anesthesiology 2014.
1question

Hip musculature & secondary abductors

Primary and secondary abductors of the hip.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • Primary abductors: gluteus medius (principal), gluteus minimus, and tensor fascia lata — all innervated by the superior gluteal nerve.
  • Secondary abductors (contribute when the hip is in certain positions): piriformis, superior portion of gluteus maximus, sartorius, and rectus femoris. Obturator externus, adductor magnus, pectineus and the adductor group are adductors, not abductors — the usual 'which is not a secondary abductor' answer comes from this list.
  • Superior gluteal nerve injury (from an over-aggressive direct lateral or anterolateral split, or from proximal retraction in the greater sciatic notch) produces a Trendelenburg gait — keep the split within ~5 cm of the tip of the greater trochanter.
  • Restoring femoral offset lengthens the abductor moment arm, improving abductor efficiency and reducing joint reactive force and polyethylene wear.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • Neumann DA. Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System, 3rd ed.
  • Hoppenfeld S, deBoer P, Buckley R. Surgical Exposures in Orthopaedics.
1question

Sesamoid anatomy & biomechanics

The hallux sesamoid complex.

1 of 7 sittings2020

  • The two sesamoids sit within the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis (medial/tibial and lateral/fibular heads) inside the plantar plate. The medial (tibial) sesamoid is larger, more distally placed and bears more weight — it is more often injured, fractured or affected by osteonecrosis. The FHL tendon runs in the groove between them.
  • Function: they increase the moment arm of the FHB (a pulley effect), absorb and distribute weightbearing load beneath the first metatarsal head, and protect the FHL. They bear up to ~50% of body weight in stance and up to 3× in push-off.
  • During gait the sesamoids translate distally with the metatarsal head as the MTP dorsiflexes; loss of this excursion (hallux rigidus, post-surgical scarring) limits dorsiflexion.
  • Bipartite medial sesamoid occurs in ~10–30% (often bilateral) and is the main mimic of fracture — an axial/sesamoid view and comparison with the contralateral foot help. Turf toe involves the plantar plate and sesamoid complex; proximal sesamoid migration on radiographs indicates complete plantar plate disruption.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Dedmond BT et al. The hallucal sesamoid complex. JAAOS 2006.
  • Anderson RB, McCormick JJ. Turf toe. JAAOS 2010.
1question

Spring ligament complex

Components and role in the medial longitudinal arch.

1 of 7 sittings2020

  • The spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament complex has three components: the superomedial calcaneonavicular ligament (the largest and most important, blending with the deltoid and forming a sling under the talar head), the medioplantar oblique, and the inferoplantar longitudinal calcaneonavicular ligaments.
  • It supports the head of the talus, maintains the medial longitudinal arch, and is the static restraint to talar head plantar-medial subluxation. The posterior tibial tendon is the principal dynamic restraint.
  • Chronic posterior tibial tendon dysfunction leads to attenuation of the spring ligament, and the flatfoot deformity does not fully correct with tendon reconstruction alone — spring ligament repair/reconstruction is often required. It is also the structure allowing talar head 'peek-a-boo' medially in progressive collapsing foot deformity.
  • The superomedial component is contiguous with the tibiocalcaneal portion of the superficial deltoid, which is why deltoid insufficiency and spring ligament failure often coexist in valgus ankle/hindfoot deformity.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Davis WH et al. Gross, histological, and microvascular anatomy of the spring ligament complex. Foot Ankle Int 1996.
  • Deland JT. The adult acquired flatfoot and spring ligament complex. Foot Ankle Clin.
1question

Upper extremity anatomic relationships

Frequently tested positional relationships in the arm and forearm.

1 of 7 sittings2022

  • At the elbow, from lateral to medial in the antecubital fossa: 'TAN' — Tendon (biceps), Artery (brachial), Nerve (median). The radial nerve lies lateral, between brachialis and brachioradialis.
  • In the distal forearm, from radial to ulnar: radial artery, FCR, palmaris longus, median nerve (deep and just radial/deep to palmaris), FDS, ulnar artery and ulnar nerve (with the ulnar nerve ulnar to the artery in Guyon's canal).
  • In the arm the radial nerve is posterior in the spiral groove, then crosses the lateral intermuscular septum ~10 cm proximal to the lateral epicondyle to lie anterior between brachialis and brachioradialis; the ulnar nerve is posterior to the medial epicondyle; the median nerve and brachial artery run medially, the nerve crossing from lateral to medial to the artery in the mid-arm.
  • In the carpal tunnel the median nerve is the most superficial and radial structure; the recurrent motor branch classically arises extraligamentously and radially (but has multiple variants). The palmar cutaneous branch arises ~5 cm proximal to the wrist crease and is at risk with an over-radial carpal tunnel incision.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Nerve Pathology; Wrist and Hand.
  • Hoppenfeld S, deBoer P, Buckley R. Surgical Exposures in Orthopaedics, 5th ed.
  • Netter FH. Atlas of Human Anatomy, 7th ed.
