13questions

Metastatic bone disease: Workup, prophylactic fixation & prognosis

The single most tested oncology topic: work-up of a destructive bone lesion in an adult, deciding who needs prophylactic fixation, and construct selection.

7 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2022 (x4), 2023 (x2), 2024S (x2), 2024F, 2025

  • Never biopsy a destructive lesion in an adult over 40 without a full work-up — the commonest cause is metastasis, and the primary can usually be found non-invasively. Standard work-up: history and physical (including breast, prostate, thyroid, skin), CBC, ESR/CRP, electrolytes, calcium, ALP, LDH, SPEP/UPEP with serum free light chains (myeloma), PSA, TSH; plain films of the whole involved bone; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; and a bone scan (or PET) for whole-body staging. This finds the primary in ~85% of cases.
  • MRI of the lesion is for local staging, not for finding the primary. If a primary is still not identified, then biopsy — through a tract that can be excised with the definitive resection, planned by the treating oncologic surgeon.
  • Commonest primaries metastasising to bone: breast, prostate, lung, renal, thyroid ('BLT with Kosher Pickle'). Renal and thyroid are classically hypervascular — embolise within 24–48 h before surgery or expect catastrophic bleeding. Lung has the worst prognosis; breast/prostate/thyroid/myeloma the best.
  • Mirels' score (site, pain, lesion type, size) ≥9/12 predicts impending fracture and warrants prophylactic fixation. Other classic indications: >50% cortical destruction, a lesion >2.5 cm, a lesion in the peritrochanteric/subtrochanteric femur, or functional/mechanical pain with weightbearing (the most reliable single clinical indicator).
  • Prophylactic fixation before fracture gives less pain, shorter hospital stay, faster rehabilitation and better function than fixation after fracture. Construct principle: protect the entire bone (long cephalomedullary nail for the femur), assume the lesion will not heal, and use cement augmentation; consider endoprosthetic replacement for a solitary, destructive, or radioresistant (renal) lesion in a patient with a reasonable life expectancy.
  • A solitary bone metastasis with a controlled primary and long expected survival (classically renal cell) is the exception where wide en-bloc resection with reconstruction can improve survival — otherwise the goal is palliative and durable fixation.
  • Post-operative radiotherapy to the whole surgical field reduces progression and reoperation; start after wound healing (~2–3 weeks). Bisphosphonates/denosumab reduce skeletal-related events.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Systemic Disease/Metastatic Bone Disease.
  • Mirels H. Metastatic disease in long bones: a proposed scoring system for diagnosing impending pathologic fractures. CORR 1989 (reprinted 2003).
  • Rougraff BT, Kneisl JS, Simon MA. Skeletal metastases of unknown origin: a prospective study of a diagnostic strategy. JBJS Am 1993.
  • Bickels J, Dadia S, Lidar Z. Surgical management of metastatic bone disease. JBJS Am 2009.
  • Wedin R, Bauer HCF. Surgical treatment of skeletal metastatic lesions of the proximal femur. JBJS Br 2005.
7questions

Osteosarcoma & variants

Conventional osteosarcoma and the surface/low-grade variants, with their differing prognosis.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2021 (x2), 2022 (x2), 2023, 2025

  • Conventional high-grade intramedullary osteosarcoma: bimodal age (peak in the second decade), metaphysis of the distal femur > proximal tibia > proximal humerus. Radiographs show a mixed lytic/blastic lesion with aggressive periosteal reaction (Codman triangle, sunburst) and soft-tissue extension. Elevated ALP and LDH are prognostic.
  • Histology: malignant spindle cells producing osteoid — this is the defining feature. Treatment is neoadjuvant chemotherapy → wide resection → adjuvant chemotherapy. The strongest prognostic factor is percentage tumour necrosis after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (>90% = good responder); presence of metastases at diagnosis is the worst.
  • Parosteal osteosarcoma: surface of the posterior distal femur, low grade, 3rd–4th decade, best prognosis of all osteosarcomas (>90% survival). It grows as a heavily ossified stalked mass with a cleavage plane; medullary canal involvement occurs in a minority and predicts a worse outcome/higher grade. Treated by wide resection alone — no chemotherapy if low grade.
  • Periosteal osteosarcoma: surface of the diaphysis of the tibia/femur, intermediate grade, chondroblastic, with perpendicular periosteal reaction. Prognosis intermediate — better than conventional, worse than parosteal. Usually resection ± chemotherapy.
  • Telangiectatic osteosarcoma: purely lytic with fluid-fluid levels — the classic mimic of an aneurysmal bone cyst. It has a high rate of pathologic fracture (~25%), but with modern chemotherapy the prognosis is at least as good as conventional osteosarcoma.
  • Secondary osteosarcoma arises in Paget disease or previously irradiated bone; it occurs in older patients and has a poor prognosis. Low-grade central osteosarcoma is easily confused histologically with fibrous dysplasia — the key discriminator is permeative growth and MDM2/CDK4 positivity.
  • Metastases are to lung first, then bone. Skip metastases within the same bone mandate whole-bone MRI before resection.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Malignant Bone Tumors.
  • Ritter J, Bielack SS. Osteosarcoma. Ann Oncol 2010.
  • Okada K et al. Parosteal osteosarcoma: a clinicopathological study. JBJS Am 1994.
  • Bacci G et al. Telangiectatic osteosarcoma of the extremity: neoadjuvant chemotherapy in 24 cases. Acta Orthop Scand.
  • WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone, 5th ed, 2020.
7questions

Soft-tissue sarcoma: Staging, biopsy & prognosis

Principles of staging, the cardinal rules of biopsy, and what actually drives survival.

4 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2023, 2024S (x3), 2025

  • Grade is the single most important prognostic factor for soft-tissue sarcoma, followed by size (>5 cm), depth (deep to fascia) and the presence of metastases. Margin status predicts local recurrence, not survival — a distinction frequently tested.
  • Any soft-tissue mass that is >5 cm, deep to fascia, painful, or enlarging must be assumed malignant until proven otherwise. Image with MRI with contrast before biopsy, and stage the chest with CT (lung is the dominant metastatic site; myxoid liposarcoma is the exception with extrapulmonary/retroperitoneal and spinal metastases).
  • Biopsy principles: longitudinal incision in line with the definitive resection, through (not between) compartments, meticulous haemostasis, drain in line with the incision, and — ideally — performed at the centre that will do the definitive surgery. Poorly planned biopsies alter management, worsen outcomes and increase amputation rates (Mankin's classic studies).
  • Core-needle biopsy is accurate in experienced hands and is preferred over FNA (which cannot grade or assess architecture). Open incisional biopsy remains the gold standard when core is non-diagnostic.
  • Treatment: limb-salvage wide resection plus radiotherapy gives local control equivalent to amputation with better function. Radiotherapy timing — pre-operative radiation uses a lower dose and smaller field with better long-term function/fibrosis but roughly double the acute wound complication rate; post-operative radiation has fewer wound problems but more late fibrosis (the Canadian NCIC SR2 trial, O'Sullivan, Lancet 2002).
  • Chemotherapy has a limited role in adult soft-tissue sarcoma generally (unlike osteosarcoma/Ewing), but is used in chemosensitive histologies (rhabdomyosarcoma, synovial sarcoma in young patients).
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Malignant lesions.
  • Mankin HJ, Lange TA, Spanier SS. The hazards of biopsy in patients with malignant primary bone and soft-tissue tumors. JBJS Am 1982 / 1996 update.
  • O'Sullivan B et al. (Canadian, NCIC-CTG SR2) Preoperative versus postoperative radiotherapy in soft-tissue sarcoma of the limbs. Lancet 2002.
  • Rosenberg SA et al. The treatment of soft-tissue sarcomas of the extremities. Ann Surg 1982.
  • Enneking WF, Spanier SS, Goodman MA. A system for the surgical staging of musculoskeletal sarcoma. CORR 1980.
6questions

Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (MFH)

UPS of bone and soft tissue — the diagnosis of exclusion, and its treatment.

6 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • UPS (formerly malignant fibrous histiocytoma) is a diagnosis of exclusion: a high-grade pleomorphic sarcoma with no identifiable line of differentiation. Modern immunohistochemistry re-classifies many historic 'MFH' cases as dedifferentiated liposarcoma, leiomyosarcoma or myxofibrosarcoma.
  • Soft-tissue UPS is one of the commonest adult sarcomas, typically a deep, painless, enlarging mass in the thigh of a patient in the 5th–7th decade. UPS of bone is rare (<5% of primary bone malignancies), lytic and permeative with a wide zone of transition, and often presents with pathologic fracture.
  • UPS of bone is treated like osteosarcoma: neoadjuvant chemotherapy → wide resection → adjuvant chemotherapy — a repeatedly tested point that distinguishes it from soft-tissue UPS, where chemotherapy has a much more limited role and treatment is wide resection plus radiotherapy.
  • It may arise secondarily in a bone infarct, Paget disease or irradiated bone. Prognosis is grade- and stage-dependent, with 5-year survival roughly 50–60%; metastases go to lung.
  • Radiographically there is no matrix production — an aggressive purely lytic destructive lesion in an adult, which is why metastasis, myeloma and lymphoma must be excluded first.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Malignant Bone Tumors; Miscellaneous Lesions.
  • Nishida Y et al. Malignant fibrous histiocytoma of bone. Cancer.
  • WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone, 5th ed, 2020.
  • Fletcher CDM. The evolving classification of soft tissue tumours. Histopathology 2014.
5questions

Atypical lipomatous tumour, liposarcoma & lipoma

The ALT/WDL spectrum, MDM2, and the risk of dedifferentiation.

3 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2023 (x2)

  • Atypical lipomatous tumour (ALT) = well-differentiated liposarcoma (WDL) — the same lesion with different names by site. 'ALT' is used in the extremity/trunk (surgically resectable, excellent prognosis); 'WDL' in the retroperitoneum/mediastinum (unresectable, high mortality from local effects).
  • ALT/WDL does not metastasise in its well-differentiated state — this is a classic true/false stem. It can dedifferentiate (roughly 2% in the extremity, up to 20% retroperitoneally) into a high-grade sarcoma with metastatic potential. Saying 'they do not dedifferentiate' or 'they metastasise' are both wrong.
  • MDM2 and CDK4 amplification (12q13-15 ring/giant marker chromosomes) is the defining molecular feature and is used by FISH to distinguish ALT/WDL from a benign lipoma when the histology is equivocal — MDM2 is characteristically positive, not rarely positive.
  • MRI: a predominantly fatty mass with thick (>2 mm) septations, nodular non-adipose areas, <75% fat content, or size >10 cm suggests ALT/WDL rather than a simple lipoma. Deep, large, and non-homogeneous lesions warrant referral.
  • Treatment is marginal or wide excision; local recurrence in the extremity is roughly 10–20% (higher retroperitoneally) and recurrence is the main risk, not metastasis. Radiotherapy is not routine for ALT of the extremity.
  • Other liposarcoma subtypes: myxoid/round cell — t(12;16) FUS-DDIT3, occurs in younger patients, is radiosensitive, and characteristically metastasises to extrapulmonary sites (other soft tissue, retroperitoneum, spine) — hence whole-body/spinal imaging. Pleomorphic liposarcoma is the highest grade and most aggressive.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Miscellaneous/Soft Tissue Lesions.
  • Weiss SW, Rao VK. Well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipoma) of deep soft tissue. Am J Surg Pathol 1992.
  • Kransdorf MJ et al. Imaging of fatty tumors: distinction of lipoma and well-differentiated liposarcoma. Radiology 2002.
  • Sirvent N et al. Detection of MDM2-CDK4 amplification by FISH in 200 paraffin-embedded tumor samples. Am J Surg Pathol 2007.
5questions

Chondrosarcoma

Grading, location, primary vs secondary, and why chondrosarcoma is treated surgically.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • Chondrosarcoma is the commonest primary bone sarcoma of adults over 50 (osteosarcoma dominates in children). Common sites: pelvis, proximal femur, proximal humerus, scapula and ribs — axial/proximal lesions.
  • Chondrosarcoma is radioresistant and chemoresistant — the treatment is wide surgical resection. This is the single most important management point. Low-grade (grade I / atypical cartilaginous tumour) lesions of the extremity may be treated with extended intralesional curettage, but pelvic and axial lesions must be resected en bloc because local recurrence there is high and often fatal.
  • Grade determines behaviour: grade I (ACT) rarely metastasises; grade II/III metastasise to lung. Location in the pelvis is the strongest predictor of local recurrence; larger size and higher grade predict metastasis. Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma (a low-grade cartilage tumour with a high-grade non-cartilaginous component) has a dismal prognosis (<10% 5-year survival).
  • Secondary chondrosarcoma arises in a pre-existing osteochondroma (~1–5% risk, higher in MHE and in pelvic/proximal lesions) or enchondroma (Ollier/Maffucci). Secondary lesions are usually low grade with a better prognosis than primary chondrosarcoma — a repeated exam distinction. Growth of an osteochondroma after skeletal maturity, pain, or a cartilage cap >2 cm in an adult are the red flags.
  • Distinguishing enchondroma from low-grade chondrosarcoma is one of the hardest problems in orthopaedic oncology: favour chondrosarcoma with pain (not attributable to another cause), endosteal scalloping >2/3 cortical thickness, cortical destruction/expansion, soft-tissue mass, size >5 cm, and axial location. Histology alone is unreliable.
  • Clear cell chondrosarcoma is the low-grade epiphyseal variant (mimics chondroblastoma but in an adult); mesenchymal chondrosarcoma is high grade, occurs in the young, and is chemosensitive.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Benign Cartilage Tumors; Malignant Bone Tumors.
  • Gelderblom H et al. The clinical approach towards chondrosarcoma. Oncologist 2008.
  • Fiorenza F et al. Risk factors for survival and local control in chondrosarcoma of bone. JBJS Br 2002.
  • Ahmed AR et al. Secondary chondrosarcoma in osteochondroma: report of 107 patients. CORR 2003.
5questions

Giant cell tumour of bone

Behaviour, treatment options, denosumab, and the rare 'benign metastasising' phenomenon.

5 of 7 sittings2021, 2023, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • GCT is a benign but locally aggressive tumour of skeletally mature patients (20–40 years, slight female predominance) arising in the epiphysis/metaphysis extending to subchondral bone — classically distal femur, proximal tibia, distal radius and sacrum. Radiographically an eccentric, lytic, well-defined lesion without a sclerotic rim, often extending to within 1 cm of the joint surface.
  • Histology: multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells on a background of mononuclear stromal cells — the neoplastic cell is the mononuclear stromal cell, which expresses RANKL and recruits the giant cells. H3F3A (histone H3.3) mutation is characteristic.
  • Standard treatment is extended intralesional curettage — high-speed burr, plus an adjuvant (phenol, liquid nitrogen, argon beam, hydrogen peroxide) — with cementation or bone grafting. PMMA cementation is preferred: it allows early detection of recurrence at the cement–bone interface, provides immediate structural support, and the exothermic reaction may kill residual cells. Local recurrence is ~10–25%, usually within 2 years.
  • Wide resection is reserved for extensive articular destruction, expendable bones (proximal fibula, distal ulna), or repeated recurrence — it lowers recurrence but at a functional cost.
  • Denosumab (RANKL antibody) dramatically reduces tumour activity and induces a peripheral bone rim; it is used for unresectable/axial/sacral disease and to downstage before surgery. Caution: it makes the tumour hard and sclerotic and may obscure margins; recurrence is common after stopping, and it does not replace surgery for resectable disease.
  • Benign pulmonary 'metastases' occur in ~2–5% of histologically benign GCT — they are typically indolent, may regress spontaneously, and do not indicate malignancy. Chest imaging is nevertheless part of staging. Frank malignant transformation is rare and is strongly associated with previous radiotherapy, which should be avoided.
  • GCT of the sacrum/spine is difficult, has a high recurrence rate, and is where denosumab and serial embolisation have the greatest role.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Miscellaneous Benign/Giant Cell Tumor.
  • Turcotte RE (Canadian) et al. Giant cell tumor of long bone: a Canadian Sarcoma Group study. CORR 2002.
  • Thomas D et al. Denosumab in patients with giant-cell tumour of bone. Lancet Oncol 2010.
  • Errani C et al. Giant cell tumor of the extremity: a review of 349 cases. Cancer Treat Rev 2010.
4questions

Osteochondroma & multiple hereditary exostoses

The commonest benign bone tumour, its complications and the syndromic form.

3 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2024S, 2024F

  • An osteochondroma is a cartilage-capped bony projection with cortical and medullary continuity with the underlying bone — this continuity is the diagnostic feature and distinguishes it from a parosteal osteosarcoma or periosteal chondroma. Sessile or pedunculated, metaphyseal, pointing away from the joint.
  • It arises from displaced physeal cartilage and grows only until skeletal maturity. Growth after skeletal maturity, new pain, or a cartilage cap >2 cm in an adult is the red flag for secondary chondrosarcoma (~1% solitary; up to 5% in MHE).
  • Causes of pain: mechanical irritation/bursa formation over the lesion, fracture of the stalk, impingement on adjacent tendons/muscles, neurovascular compression (peroneal nerve at the proximal fibula, pseudoaneurysm of the popliteal artery at the distal femur), and malignant transformation. Pain from the marrow/medullary canal is not a mechanism — the classic 'not a cause of pain' distractor.
  • Multiple hereditary exostoses (MHE/hereditary multiple osteochondromas): autosomal dominant, EXT1/EXT2. Features: short stature, multiple lesions, and characteristic deformities — forearm deformity with ulnar shortening, radial bowing and radial head subluxation/dislocation, ankle valgus from fibular shortening, coxa valga and genu valgum. Deformity progresses with growth and is more severe with EXT1.
  • Surgery: excise symptomatic lesions at the base including the perichondrium and full cartilage cap (incomplete excision recurs, particularly in skeletally immature children). Address forearm/ankle deformity with guided growth, ulnar lengthening or corrective osteotomy as indicated. Routine prophylactic excision of asymptomatic lesions is not indicated.
  • Subungual exostosis (Dupuytren exostosis) of the distal phalanx is a related but distinct entity.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Benign Cartilage Tumors.
  • Murphey MD et al. Imaging of osteochondroma: variants and complications. RadioGraphics 2000.
  • Stieber JR, Dormans JP. Manifestations of hereditary multiple exostoses. JAAOS 2005.
  • Porter DE et al. Severity of disease and risk of malignant change in hereditary multiple exostoses. JBJS Br 2004.
4questions

Spine tumours & SINS score

Assessing instability and the approach to metastatic and primary spine tumours.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2024F, 2025

  • Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS) components: location (junctional/mobile/semi-rigid/rigid), mechanical pain (pain with movement/loading — this carries the highest weighted single clinical variable and is the strongest predictor), bone lesion quality (lytic/mixed/blastic), spinal alignment, vertebral body collapse, and posterolateral involvement of spinal elements. Score 0–6 stable, 7–12 indeterminate (surgical consult), 13–18 unstable.
  • SINS assesses stability only — it says nothing about neurological compromise or oncologic prognosis. Use it alongside the ESCC (Bilsky) grade for cord compression and a survival estimate (Tokuhashi/Tomita) to decide on surgery.
  • Metastatic epidural cord compression: Patchell's RCT showed that decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy is superior to radiotherapy alone for ambulation and continence in patients with a single-level lesion and reasonable life expectancy. Separation surgery plus stereotactic body radiotherapy is the modern paradigm.
  • Radiosensitivity guides the plan: lymphoma, myeloma, Ewing and small-cell are highly radiosensitive; breast/prostate intermediate; renal cell, melanoma, thyroid, sarcoma and GI are relatively radioresistant — the classic 'least responsive to radiation' answer is renal cell/melanoma/sarcoma. Renal metastases must be embolised before surgery.
  • Primary spine tumours by location: posterior elements — osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma, ABC, osteochondroma; vertebral body — haemangioma, giant cell tumour, chordoma, eosinophilic granuloma (vertebra plana), metastasis, myeloma. In paediatric spine the commonest primary bone tumours are osteoid osteoma/osteoblastoma and ABC; the commonest benign vertebral body lesion overall is haemangioma.
  • A destructive vertebral body lesion in an adult over 40 with weight loss = metastasis or myeloma until proven otherwise. Preservation of the disc space with vertebral body destruction favours tumour; disc destruction favours infection (with tuberculosis the classic exception that spares the disc and produces large paraspinal abscesses).
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spine Oncology.
  • Fisher CG (Canadian, Spine Oncology Study Group) et al. A novel classification system for spinal instability in neoplastic disease (SINS). Spine 2010.
  • Patchell RA et al. Direct decompressive surgical resection in the treatment of spinal cord compression caused by metastatic cancer. Lancet 2005.
  • Laufer I et al. The NOMS framework. Oncologist 2013.
  • Bilsky MH et al. Reliability analysis of the epidural spinal cord compression scale. J Neurosurg Spine 2010.
4questions

Unicameral & aneurysmal bone cysts

Two cystic lesions of childhood — differentiating features and treatment.

4 of 7 sittings2021, 2023, 2024F, 2025

  • Unicameral (simple) bone cyst (UBC): central, metaphyseal, well-defined lytic lesion in the proximal humerus (most common) and proximal femur in the first two decades. Classically asymptomatic until pathologic fracture — the 'fallen leaf/fallen fragment' sign (a fragment of cortex lying dependently in the fluid-filled cyst) is pathognomonic.
  • UBC management: most non-displaced pathologic fractures of the proximal humerus are treated non-operatively (sling/immobilisation) first — the fracture heals and a proportion of cysts heal or shrink. Persistent/recurrent cysts are treated with aspiration and injection (steroid, bone marrow, DBM) or curettage with grafting ± decompression cannulated screws. Proximal femoral lesions are more likely to need internal fixation because of the mechanical demand.
  • Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC): eccentric, expansile, 'blown out' lytic lesion with a thin rim, containing blood-filled spaces with fluid-fluid levels on MRI/CT. Occurs in the metaphysis of long bones and in the posterior elements of the spine, in the first two decades, and is often painful, including night pain.
  • ABC is now known to be a true neoplasm with a USP6 gene rearrangement in primary lesions. It can be secondary to another lesion — always exclude telangiectatic osteosarcoma, GCT, chondroblastoma and osteoblastoma, so tissue diagnosis is essential.
  • ABC treatment to minimise recurrence: intralesional curettage with a high-speed burr and adjuvant, plus pre-operative selective arterial embolisation — this is the standard answer for a spinal/pedicle ABC in a child. Serial embolisation alone, sclerotherapy (doxycycline, polidocanol) and denosumab are alternatives for surgically inaccessible lesions. Recurrence is ~10–20% and is highest in young children with open physes.
  • En-bloc resection of a spinal ABC gives the lowest recurrence but at a high morbidity cost in a child — intralesional treatment with embolisation is preferred where feasible.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Benign Cystic Lesions.
  • Wilkins RM. Unicameral bone cysts. JAAOS 2000.
  • Cottalorda J, Bourelle S. Modern concepts of primary aneurysmal bone cyst. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg 2007.
  • Boriani S et al. Aneurysmal bone cysts of the mobile spine: report on 41 cases. Spine 2001.
  • Oliveira AM et al. USP6 and CDH11 oncogenes identify the neoplastic cell in primary aneurysmal bone cysts. Am J Pathol 2004.
3questions

Desmoid tumour (fibromatosis)

A benign but locally destructive fibroblastic tumour with a paradoxical management pathway.

3 of 7 sittings2023, 2024F, 2025

  • Desmoid tumours (aggressive fibromatosis) are locally aggressive but do not metastasise. They are typically painful and firm — the notion that they are painless like most benign soft-tissue tumours is a common distractor.
  • Molecular basis: sporadic lesions have CTNNB1 (β-catenin) mutations; multifocal/mesenteric desmoids are associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (Gardner syndrome) via APC mutations — a patient with multifocal desmoids needs colonoscopy and genetic assessment.
  • Risk factors: previous trauma or surgical scar, pregnancy/oestrogen exposure, and young adulthood (peak 20–40 years, female predominance).
  • Management has shifted decisively toward initial active surveillance, because a substantial proportion stabilise or regress spontaneously. Surgery is no longer first-line: local recurrence after resection is high (20–60%) and margin status correlates poorly with recurrence, so radical resection is not justified.
  • Second-line options: systemic therapy (tamoxifen/NSAIDs historically; methotrexate–vinblastine, tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sorafenib/pazopanib, and now gamma-secretase inhibitors (nirogacestat)), radiotherapy for symptomatic unresectable disease, and cryoablation. Surgery is reserved for progressive, symptomatic, functionally threatening disease.
  • MRI shows a T2-hypointense, infiltrative lesion with a 'fascial tail' — a low T2 signal soft-tissue mass is a useful clue.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Benign Fibrous Lesions/Miscellaneous.
  • Kasper B et al. Desmoid Tumor Working Group. An update on the management of sporadic desmoid-type fibromatosis: a European consensus. Ann Oncol 2017.
  • Bonvalot S et al. Spontaneous regression of primary abdominal wall desmoid tumors. Ann Surg Oncol 2013.
  • Gounder MM et al. Nirogacestat in desmoid tumors (DeFi trial). NEJM 2023.
2questions

Bone-forming tumours (general)

The osteoid-producing family and how to separate them.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2024S

  • The bone-forming family: osteoma (dense, cortical, skull/facial — associated with Gardner syndrome), osteoid osteoma (<2 cm nidus, NSAID-responsive night pain), osteoblastoma (>2 cm, aggressive, spine posterior elements), and osteosarcoma and its variants (malignant osteoid production).
  • The unifying histologic feature is production of osteoid by tumour cells. Benign lesions show osteoblastic rimming and organised trabeculae; osteosarcoma shows malignant pleomorphic cells producing lace-like osteoid with permeation of pre-existing bone.
  • Low-grade central osteosarcoma and parosteal osteosarcoma are the two malignant lesions most often mistaken for benign disease (fibrous dysplasia and osteochondroma/myositis ossificans respectively) — MDM2/CDK4 immunohistochemistry distinguishes them.
  • Bone island (enostosis) is a benign 'don't touch' focus of compact bone with spiculated blending margins and typically no uptake on bone scan — a helpful discriminator from a blastic metastasis, which is hot.
  • Blastic lesions in an adult: prostate and breast metastasis, lymphoma, Paget disease, bone island, osteosarcoma.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Benign Bone Tumors; Malignant Bone Tumors.
  • WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone, 5th ed, 2020.
  • Greenspan A. Bone island (enostosis): current concept. Skeletal Radiol 1995.
2questions

Enchondroma, Ollier & Maffucci

Benign intramedullary cartilage lesions and their syndromic, malignant-prone forms.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2025

  • Enchondroma is a benign intramedullary hyaline cartilage lesion; the hand (proximal phalanx most common) is the commonest site, where it is the most frequent bone tumour and often presents with pathologic fracture. Radiographs show a lucent lesion with punctate/'ring and arc' chondroid calcification and endosteal scalloping.
  • Solitary enchondroma of the hand: treat a pathologic fracture first (let it heal), then curette and graft if symptomatic. Malignant transformation of a solitary hand enchondroma is very rare — chondrosarcoma of the hand is rare and, when it occurs, is usually in the setting of Ollier disease.
  • Ollier disease (enchondromatosis): multiple, often unilateral/asymmetric enchondromas causing limb-length discrepancy and angular deformity. Maffucci syndrome = enchondromatosis plus soft-tissue haemangiomas (spindle cell haemangiomas), and carries the highest risk of malignancy.
  • Both are due to somatic mosaic IDH1/IDH2 mutations and are therefore not inherited — the classic genetic counselling answer is that the risk to offspring is not increased.
  • Malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma: roughly 25–40% in Ollier and higher (approaching 100% for some malignancy overall) in Maffucci, which also carries a risk of non-skeletal malignancies (gliomas, visceral, ovarian). Lifelong surveillance is required; new pain or growth after maturity warrants imaging.
  • Radiographic surveillance points for transformation: cortical destruction, deep endosteal scalloping, soft-tissue mass, and interval growth.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Benign Cartilage Tumors.
  • Pansuriya TC et al. Somatic mosaic IDH1 and IDH2 mutations are associated with enchondroma and spindle cell hemangioma in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome. Nat Genet 2011.
  • Verdegaal SHM et al. Incidence, predictive factors and prognosis of chondrosarcoma in patients with Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome. Oncologist 2011.
2questions

Ewing sarcoma

The small round blue cell tumour of childhood.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2023

  • Ewing sarcoma is the second commonest primary bone malignancy of children/adolescents (peak 5–25 years), with a strong predilection for Caucasian patients and for the diaphysis of long bones and the flat bones (pelvis, scapula, ribs) — a diaphyseal lesion in a child is Ewing until proven otherwise.
  • Radiographs: permeative, moth-eaten destruction with 'onion-skin' lamellated periosteal reaction and a large soft-tissue mass often out of proportion to the bony change.
  • Clinically it mimics osteomyelitis: pain, fever, raised ESR/CRP and leukocytosis. Every suspicious 'osteomyelitis' should have tissue sent for histology and every tumour biopsy sent for culture.
  • Molecular hallmark: t(11;22)(q24;q12) EWSR1-FLI1 fusion (~85%), with variant translocations (EWSR1-ERG). Immunohistochemistry is CD99 (MIC2) positive, distinguishing it from lymphoma (CD45+).
  • Treatment: neoadjuvant multi-agent chemotherapy, then local control (wide surgical resection preferred where feasible, radiotherapy where resection is not), then adjuvant chemotherapy. Ewing is one of the few radiosensitive bone sarcomas, but surgery gives better local control when the lesion is resectable.
  • Prognostic factors: presence of metastases at diagnosis (worst), pelvic/axial location, large tumour volume, poor chemotherapy response (necrosis), older age and elevated LDH. Localised disease has ~70% survival; metastatic disease ~20–30%.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Malignant Bone Tumors.
  • Grier HE et al. Addition of ifosfamide and etoposide to standard chemotherapy for Ewing's sarcoma. NEJM 2003.
  • Delattre O et al. The Ewing family of tumors — a subgroup of small-round-cell tumors defined by specific chimeric transcripts. NEJM 1994.
  • Bernstein M et al. Ewing's sarcoma family of tumors: current management. Oncologist 2006.
2questions

Fibrous dysplasia & fibrous lesions

Fibrous dysplasia, non-ossifying fibroma and osteofibrous dysplasia.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2025

  • Fibrous dysplasia: a developmental GNAS1 post-zygotic mutation producing a 'ground-glass' lytic lesion with a well-defined sclerotic rim ('rind sign'). Histology shows irregular woven bone trabeculae in a fibrous stroma — 'alphabet soup'/'Chinese characters' — without osteoblastic rimming (the key discriminator from osteofibrous dysplasia and low-grade osteosarcoma).
  • Shepherd's crook deformity of the proximal femur is characteristic of polyostotic disease. McCune-Albright syndrome = polyostotic FD + café-au-lait macules with irregular 'coast of Maine' borders + endocrinopathy (precocious puberty). Mazabraud syndrome = FD + intramuscular myxomas.
  • Management: observe asymptomatic lesions; bisphosphonates reduce pain. When fixation is needed, use load-sharing intramedullary devices, not plates and screws — the abnormal bone will not incorporate graft, cortical/cancellous autograft is resorbed and replaced by dysplastic bone, and plates fail. Cortical allograft is more durable than cancellous graft. Correct deformity with osteotomy plus IM fixation.
  • Non-ossifying fibroma (fibrous cortical defect): an eccentric, cortically based, lucent lesion with a sclerotic scalloped margin in the metaphysis of a child — a 'don't touch' lesion that resolves with maturity. Treat only for pathologic fracture or if >50% of the bone width/>33 mm (Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome when multiple with café-au-lait spots).
  • Osteofibrous dysplasia: anterior tibial cortex ('bowing of the tibia') in the first decade, histologically has osteoblastic rimming and is closely related to adamantinoma — the two are on a spectrum and biopsy/observation is important because adamantinoma is a low-grade malignancy requiring wide resection.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Benign Fibrous Lesions.
  • DiCaprio MR, Enneking WF. Fibrous dysplasia: pathophysiology, evaluation, and treatment. JBJS Am 2005.
  • Stanton RP et al. The surgical management of fibrous dysplasia of bone. Orphanet J Rare Dis 2012.
  • Most MJ et al. Osteofibrous dysplasia and adamantinoma. JAAOS 2010.
2questions

Langerhans cell histiocytosis

The 'great mimicker' of childhood bone lesions.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2022

  • LCH (eosinophilic granuloma when limited to bone) is a clonal proliferation of Langerhans dendritic cells, most often in the first decade. It is the great mimicker — it can look like anything, from a benign lytic lesion to a permeative aggressive lesion with periosteal reaction.
  • Commonest sites: skull (punched-out lesion with 'bevelled edge' from unequal inner/outer table involvement), femur, pelvis, ribs and spine. In the spine it produces vertebra plana (symmetric vertebral body collapse with preserved disc spaces) — the classic paediatric cause.
  • Histology: Langerhans cells with grooved 'coffee-bean' nuclei, CD1a and S100 positive, with Birbeck granules (tennis-racket shaped) on electron microscopy and eosinophil infiltration. BRAF V600E mutations are present in a substantial proportion.
  • Spectrum: solitary eosinophilic granuloma (best prognosis) → multifocal unisystem (Hand-Schüller-Christian: skull lesions, diabetes insipidus, exophthalmos) → multisystem (Letterer-Siwe: infants, visceral involvement, poor prognosis). Skeletal survey (or whole-body MRI) is required to stage.
  • Treatment of solitary bone lesions is usually observation — many heal spontaneously — or intralesional steroid injection/curettage for painful or structurally threatening lesions. Vertebra plana usually reconstitutes vertebral height with growth and rarely requires surgery; bracing for comfort. Low-dose radiotherapy is reserved for lesions threatening the cord/optic nerve. Multisystem disease requires chemotherapy.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Miscellaneous Lesions; Pediatrics.
  • Kilpatrick SE et al. Langerhans' cell histiocytosis (histiocytosis X) of bone: a clinicopathologic analysis of 263 pediatric and adult cases. Cancer 1995.
  • Hoover KB et al. Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Skeletal Radiol 2007.
2questions

Lymphoma of bone

Primary and secondary lymphoma of bone — a great mimic.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2024F

  • Primary lymphoma of bone is usually diffuse large B-cell, presenting in the 4th–7th decade with a permeative, moth-eaten diaphyseal/metaphyseal lesion of the femur, pelvis or spine. The classic clinical clue is a patient who feels well and has surprisingly few systemic symptoms despite extensive bone destruction.
  • Radiographs often underestimate the disease; MRI shows extensive marrow replacement and a soft-tissue mass with relatively preserved cortex (permeating through Haversian canals). This mismatch between a large soft-tissue component and an intact-looking cortex is characteristic.
  • Histology: sheets of small round blue cells that are CD45/LCA positive — the key immunohistochemical distinction from Ewing sarcoma (CD99 positive) and metastatic small-cell carcinoma.
  • Treatment is primarily chemotherapy (R-CHOP) plus radiotherapy; surgery is reserved for impending or actual pathologic fracture and for biopsy. Prognosis for primary bone lymphoma is relatively good (5-year survival often >70–80%).
  • In a patient with known lymphoma and a new painful lytic lesion, restage before assuming it is lymphoma — a second primary or a different metastasis is possible, and the treating oncologist's plan (radiation vs surgery) depends on the tissue diagnosis.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Systemic Disease.
  • Mulligan ME et al. Radiologic features of primary lymphoma of bone. AJR 1999.
  • Beal K et al. Primary bone lymphoma: treatment results and prognostic factors. Cancer 2006.
2questions

Osteoid osteoma & osteoblastoma

Two osteoblastic lesions separated largely by size and behaviour.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2024S

  • Osteoid osteoma: a nidus <1.5–2 cm with surrounding reactive sclerosis, most often in the proximal femur/femoral neck and the tibial diaphysis, and in the posterior elements of the spine (a classic cause of painful scoliosis in an adolescent, with the lesion on the concavity of the curve).
  • Classic pain: night pain relieved by NSAIDs/aspirin — mediated by prostaglandin E2 produced by the nidus. Intra-articular lesions may present atypically with an effusion and synovitis rather than the classic pattern. CT is the best study for the nidus; bone scan shows a 'double density' sign.
  • Natural history is spontaneous resolution over years, so NSAIDs alone are a legitimate treatment. Definitive treatment for those who fail or cannot tolerate NSAIDs is CT-guided radiofrequency ablation (>90% success). Open excision is reserved for lesions adjacent to the spinal cord or skin where RFA thermal injury is a concern.
  • Osteoblastoma: histologically similar but >2 cm, more aggressive and expansile, less reactive sclerosis, pain that is not typically relieved by NSAIDs, and a predilection for the posterior elements of the spine and the sacrum. It does not regress spontaneously.
  • Osteoblastoma treatment is intralesional curettage (extended, with adjuvant) or marginal excision; recurrence is ~10–20% and the aggressive variant can be confused with osteosarcoma. Pre-operative embolisation may be used for large vascular spinal lesions.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Benign Bone Tumors.
  • Rosenthal DI et al. Percutaneous radiofrequency treatment of osteoid osteomas. JBJS Am 1998.
  • Frassica FJ et al. Osteoid osteoma: diagnostic problems. JBJS Am.
  • Lucas DR et al. Osteoblastoma: clinicopathologic study of 306 cases. Hum Pathol 1994.
2questions

Paediatric bone lesions: Differential diagnosis of the aggressive lesion

Building a differential for a destructive lesion with periosteal reaction in a child.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2025

  • An aggressive-looking lytic/permeative lesion with periosteal reaction and a soft-tissue mass in a child under 5: think Langerhans cell histiocytosis, osteomyelitis, Ewing sarcoma, leukaemia/lymphoma, neuroblastoma metastasis and (less likely under 5) osteosarcoma.
  • Age is the single most useful discriminator: under 5 — LCH, leukaemia, neuroblastoma metastasis, infection; 5–20 — Ewing, osteosarcoma, LCH, osteomyelitis; over 40 — metastasis, myeloma, lymphoma, chondrosarcoma. Osteosarcoma is rare under 5 and is usually the 'least likely' answer in a toddler.
  • Systemic features matter: fever, night sweats and raised inflammatory markers occur in both Ewing sarcoma and osteomyelitis — this overlap is why every 'infection' that does not behave typically must be biopsied and every biopsy sent for culture, and every culture specimen sent for histology.
  • Leukaemia is the commonest childhood malignancy and can present with bone pain, refusal to weightbear, metaphyseal lucent bands and a normal-to-low WBC — always check the blood film and consider marrow assessment.
  • Neuroblastoma metastases in a child under 5 produce permeative lytic lesions, periosteal reaction, and often periorbital ecchymosis; check urine catecholamines (VMA/HVA) and abdominal imaging.
  • The MRI/biopsy sequence in a child: plain radiographs first (most diagnostic single study), then MRI of the whole bone, then staging (CT chest, bone scan/PET, marrow), then biopsy at the treating centre.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology; Pediatrics.
  • Kaste SC. Imaging pediatric bone sarcomas. Radiol Clin North Am.
  • Arndt CAS, Crist WM. Common musculoskeletal tumors of childhood and adolescence. NEJM 1999.
2questions

Radiation therapy & radiation-associated fracture

Radiosensitivity of tumours and the behaviour of irradiated bone.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2024S

  • Radiosensitivity ranking: highly sensitive — lymphoma, myeloma, Ewing sarcoma, seminoma, small-cell lung; intermediate — breast, prostate; relatively resistant — renal cell, melanoma, thyroid, sarcoma (osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma), GI adenocarcinoma. The 'least responsive to radiation' answer is almost always renal cell, melanoma, or chondrosarcoma.
  • Radiation-associated (insufficiency) fractures occur in irradiated bone, most classically the femoral neck after pelvic radiotherapy and the pelvis/sacrum. They are typically transverse, occur at 1–5 years or later after treatment, heal slowly with a high nonunion rate, and have poor surrounding soft tissue.
  • Irradiated bone has impaired osteoblast function, reduced vascularity and reduced healing capacity — plan for load-sharing intramedullary fixation, vascularised graft, or endoprosthetic replacement rather than conventional plating and grafting, and expect a prolonged union time.
  • Radiation-induced sarcoma (Cahan criteria): arises in the radiation field, after a latency of at least 3–4 years, with different histology from the original tumour. Most are osteosarcoma or UPS, and prognosis is poor. This is the reason radiotherapy is avoided in benign disease (e.g. GCT) and in children where possible.
  • Prophylactic pinning of the femoral neck before pelvic radiotherapy is not routine, but a low threshold for imaging new hip/groin pain in a previously irradiated patient is essential.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology.
  • Cahan WG et al. Sarcoma arising in irradiated bone. Cancer 1948 (reprinted 1998).
  • Baxter NN et al. Risk of pelvic fractures in older women following pelvic irradiation. JAMA 2005.
  • Helmstedter CS et al. Pathologic fractures after surgery and radiation for soft tissue tumors. CORR 2001.
1question

Benign soft-tissue tumours

Recognising the common benign soft-tissue masses and their red flags.

1 of 7 sittings2024F

  • Lipoma is by far the commonest soft-tissue tumour: soft, mobile, subcutaneous, and follows fat signal on all MRI sequences with complete suppression on fat-saturated images. Deep, large (>10 cm), septated or heterogeneous fatty lesions must be treated as ALT/WDL until proven otherwise.
  • Ganglion cyst — the commonest hand/wrist mass; fluid-filled, transilluminates, T2 bright and non-enhancing (except a thin rim). Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath (localised TGCT) — the second commonest hand mass; a firm, painless nodule, characteristically low signal on T1 and T2 from haemosiderin.
  • Schwannoma vs neurofibroma: a schwannoma is eccentric to the nerve and can be shelled out preserving the nerve; a neurofibroma is intimately involved with the nerve fascicles and cannot be excised without sacrificing it. Both may show a 'target sign' and 'split fat sign'. NF1 raises concern for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour.
  • Haemangioma — serpiginous vessels, phleboliths on radiograph, pain that varies with activity/position. Elastofibroma dorsi — periscapular, bilateral in a third, characteristic striated fat.
  • Red flags mandating referral and MRI before excision: size >5 cm, deep to fascia, rapid growth, pain, and firmness/fixation. Any of these means 'plan it as a sarcoma until proven otherwise', because an unplanned excision compromises the definitive operation.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Miscellaneous Lesions; Wrist and Hand.
  • Kransdorf MJ, Murphey MD. Imaging of Soft Tissue Tumors, 3rd ed.
  • Weiss SW, Goldblum JR. Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors, 7th ed.
1question

Benign surface lesions of bone (Nora lesion/BPOP, periosteal chondroma)

Surface lesions of the small bones — a common source of diagnostic confusion.

1 of 7 sittings2022

  • Nora lesion (bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation, BPOP): a surface lesion of the small bones of the hands and feet (proximal phalanx most typical) in young adults. Radiographically a well-defined ossified mass on the cortical surface without medullary continuity — this distinguishes it from an osteochondroma.
  • MRI shows a cartilage-capped surface lesion; T2 bright cartilage cap arising from the periosteum. Histology shows the characteristic 'blue bone' with disorganised cartilage, bone and spindle cells — alarming but benign.
  • It has a high local recurrence rate (up to 50%) after excision, so complete excision including the underlying periosteum/cortical base is recommended. It does not metastasise.
  • Differential for a surface lesion of a phalanx: osteochondroma (medullary continuity), periosteal chondroma (cortical scalloping with a sclerotic base, chondroid matrix), BPOP, subungual exostosis, florid reactive periostitis, and (rarely) periosteal/parosteal osteosarcoma.
  • Because the histology is worrisome, correlation with the radiographic appearance and consultation with a bone pathologist is essential to avoid over-treatment.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Benign Bone Tumors; Wrist and Hand.
  • Nora FE, Dahlin DC, Beabout JW. Bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferations of the hands and feet. Am J Surg Pathol 1983.
  • Meneses MF et al. Bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation of bone (Nora's lesion). Am J Surg Pathol 1993.
1question

Multiple myeloma & plasma cell disease

The commonest primary malignancy of bone.

1 of 7 sittings2022

  • Multiple myeloma is the commonest primary malignant tumour of bone in adults (metastasis is more common overall but is not primary). Peak incidence in the 6th–7th decade.
  • Presentation — CRAB: hyperCalcaemia, Renal insufficiency, Anaemia, Bone lesions. Radiographs show multiple punched-out lytic lesions without sclerotic margins; the skull, spine, ribs and pelvis are typical. Diffuse osteopenia with vertebral compression fractures is a common presentation.
  • Myeloma lesions are frequently cold on technetium bone scan because they are purely osteolytic with suppressed osteoblastic activity — skeletal survey, whole-body low-dose CT, or whole-body MRI/PET is required rather than bone scan. This is a repeated exam point.
  • Diagnosis: SPEP/UPEP with immunofixation, serum free light chains, β2-microglobulin, and bone marrow biopsy showing >10% clonal plasma cells. Bence-Jones proteinuria. Solitary plasmacytoma may precede myeloma by years.
  • Treatment is medical (proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulators, anti-CD38 antibodies, stem cell transplant) plus bisphosphonates/denosumab for skeletal-related events and radiotherapy for painful lesions (myeloma is highly radiosensitive). Surgery is for impending/actual pathologic fracture and spinal instability; vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty for painful compression fractures.
  • Prognosis has improved markedly with modern therapy — a patient with myeloma and a femoral lesion may have years of life and deserves durable fixation.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Systemic Disease.
  • Rajkumar SV. Multiple myeloma: 2022 update on diagnosis, risk stratification and management. Am J Hematol 2022.
  • International Myeloma Working Group updated criteria for the diagnosis of multiple myeloma. Lancet Oncol 2014.
  • Dhodapkar MV. Skeletal complications of myeloma. Blood.
1question

Myositis ossificans

Heterotopic bone in muscle — and the critical distinction from parosteal osteosarcoma.

1 of 7 sittings2023

  • Myositis ossificans typically follows blunt trauma (classically thigh/brachialis) and presents as a firm, painful, enlarging mass 2–4 weeks after injury, sometimes with fever and a raised ALP — closely mimicking a sarcoma.
  • Zonal phenomenon is the diagnostic key: myositis ossificans matures from the periphery inward, so the mineralisation is most dense at the periphery with a lucent immature centre, and there is a lucent cleft separating it from the underlying bone. Parosteal osteosarcoma is the opposite — densest centrally, and it is continuous with/attached to the cortex.
  • The lesion mineralises on radiographs at ~3–6 weeks and matures over 6–12 months. Serial radiographs at 2–3 week intervals are far more useful than an early biopsy — early biopsy is dangerous because the immature proliferative centre looks histologically like a sarcoma and has led to unnecessary amputations.
  • Treatment is expectant: rest, gentle range of motion, and analgesia. Excise only if mature (stable radiographic appearance, normal ALP, quiescent bone scan, usually ≥6–12 months) and symptomatic from impingement or restricted motion. Early excision leads to recurrence.
  • Myositis ossificans progressiva (fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva) is a distinct, devastating genetic disorder (ACVR1 mutation) with congenital hallux valgus — biopsy and surgery are contraindicated because they provoke flares.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Miscellaneous Lesions; Orthopaedic Dilemmas.
  • Parikh J et al. The imaging features of post-traumatic myositis ossificans, with emphasis on MRI. Clin Radiol 2002.
  • Walczak BE et al. Myositis ossificans. JAAOS 2015.
1question

Pigmented villonodular synovitis / TGCT

Diffuse and localised tenosynovial giant cell tumour.

1 of 7 sittings2023

  • PVNS is now termed tenosynovial giant cell tumour (TGCT): localised (the commonest tumour of the hand/tendon sheath, nodular, low recurrence) and diffuse (intra-articular, classically the knee, then hip/ankle, with a high recurrence rate).
  • It is a neoplastic process driven by a CSF1 gene translocation producing a landscape effect (a minority of neoplastic cells recruiting a large population of macrophages).
  • Clinical: a young adult with recurrent atraumatic haemorrhagic (brown/serosanguinous) effusions, swelling and stiffness. Radiographs may show periarticular erosions on both sides of the joint with preserved joint space and no osteopenia — distinguishing it from inflammatory arthritis.
  • MRI is diagnostic: nodular synovial masses with low signal on T1 and T2 and 'blooming' artefact on gradient-echo sequences from haemosiderin. This blooming is the classic finding.
  • Treatment: complete synovectomy (arthroscopic ± open, often combined anterior and posterior in the knee) for diffuse disease; local excision for nodular disease. Recurrence is high in diffuse disease (up to 50%). Adjuvant radiosynoviorthesis and CSF1R inhibitors (pexidartinib) are options for refractory/unresectable disease. Malignant transformation is rare.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology: Miscellaneous Lesions; Sports.
  • Ravi V et al. Diffuse-type tenosynovial giant cell tumor. Curr Opin Oncol 2011.
  • Tap WD et al. Pexidartinib for advanced tenosynovial giant cell tumour (ENLIVEN). Lancet 2019.
  • Murphey MD et al. PVNS: radiologic-pathologic correlation. RadioGraphics 2008.
1question

Polyostotic lesions & differential diagnosis

Which lesions occur in multiple bones.

1 of 7 sittings2022

  • Classic polyostotic entities: fibrous dysplasia (McCune-Albright), enchondromatosis (Ollier/Maffucci), multiple hereditary exostoses, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, metastases, myeloma, hyperparathyroidism (brown tumours), Paget disease, and multifocal osteomyelitis/CRMO.
  • Lesions that are essentially always solitary: osteoid osteoma, chondroblastoma, chondromyxoid fibroma, unicameral bone cyst and adamantinoma — these are the usual 'which of these does not have a polyostotic form' answers. Giant cell tumour is very rarely multifocal (associated with Paget disease).
  • Non-ossifying fibromas can be multiple in Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome (multiple NOFs, café-au-lait spots, mental retardation, hypogonadism) and in neurofibromatosis.
  • Practical approach to a patient with multiple bone lesions: age >40 → metastasis/myeloma until proven otherwise (SPEP, CT CAP, bone scan). Age <30 → fibrous dysplasia, enchondromatosis, LCH, MHE, and infection.
  • Bone scan or whole-body MRI is the appropriate screening study when polyostotic disease is suspected.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology.
  • Greenspan A, Jundt G, Remagen W. Differential Diagnosis in Orthopaedic Oncology, 2nd ed.
  • WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone, 5th ed, 2020.
1question

Tumour imaging & general principles

Choosing and interpreting imaging in musculoskeletal oncology.

1 of 7 sittings2024F

  • Plain radiographs remain the single most useful study for characterising a bone lesion: they define the zone of transition (narrow = indolent, wide/permeative = aggressive), periosteal reaction, matrix (chondroid = rings/arcs; osteoid = cloud-like), and location within the bone (epiphysis/metaphysis/diaphysis; central/eccentric/cortical/surface).
  • MRI defines local extent, soft-tissue involvement, marrow replacement, neurovascular relationships and skip lesions — image the entire involved bone including both adjacent joints. Contrast distinguishes solid from cystic/necrotic tissue and identifies the best biopsy target.
  • CT best shows matrix mineralisation, cortical integrity and the nidus of an osteoid osteoma, and is required for staging the chest. Bone scan screens the whole skeleton for polyostotic disease and metastases; PET-CT assesses metabolic activity, response to chemotherapy and occult metastases.
  • Fluid-fluid levels on MRI are not specific for ABC — they occur in telangiectatic osteosarcoma, GCT, chondroblastoma and secondary ABC in other lesions.
  • Lodwick classification of the zone of transition (IA geographic with sclerotic rim → III permeative) correlates with aggressiveness. 'Don't touch' lesions include NOF, bone island, myositis ossificans, avulsive cortical irregularity and osteochondroma with continuity.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Oncology.
  • Miller TT. Bone tumors and tumorlike conditions: analysis with conventional radiography. Radiology 2008.
  • Costelloe CM, Madewell JE. Radiography in the initial diagnosis of primary bone tumors. AJR 2013.

19questions

Distal radius fracture: Indications, fixation & outcomes

The single most tested hand topic: acceptable parameters, who benefits from surgery, technique pitfalls and complications.

7 of 7 sittings2020, 2021 (x3), 2022, 2023 (x2), 2024S (x3), 2024F (x3), 2025 (x6)

  • Acceptable non-operative parameters (adults): radial inclination ≥15° (normal ~22°), radial height/length within 2–3 mm (normal ~11 mm), volar tilt from 0° to 20° dorsal-neutral (normal 11° volar), articular step-off <2 mm, and no DRUJ instability. Loss of radial inclination/height causes ulnar-sided load transfer and loss of grip.
  • Predictors of secondary displacement after reduction: age >60–65, dorsal comminution, initial dorsal tilt >20°, initial radial shortening, intra-articular extension, and an associated ulnar fracture. Age >40 alone is not a strong predictor — the exam distractor.
  • In patients over 65, multiple RCTs and the AAOS CPG show that radiographic malalignment correlates poorly with function: at one year, DASH/PRWE outcomes after cast treatment are equivalent to volar locking plate fixation, though grip strength and early function favour surgery. Function, not radiographs, drives the decision in the low-demand elderly.
  • Volar locking plate is the workhorse. Key technical points: place the plate proximal to the watershed line — a plate distal to it abrades FPL and FDP and is the leading cause of flexor tendon rupture (FPL first); check the skyline/tangential view for dorsal screw penetration causing extensor tendon rupture; and restore volar tilt before locking.
  • The volar lunate facet fragment is the critical fragment: it is small, ulnar and volar, sits distal to the watershed line, and if not captured the carpus subluxes volarly with the fragment — the classic post-operative failure. It requires a dedicated volar rim plate, hook plate, or wire/suture fixation.
  • EPL rupture occurs classically after a minimally displaced/non-displaced distal radius fracture treated non-operatively (watershed of the third dorsal compartment at Lister's tubercle, from attrition/ischaemia in an intact tight compartment) — the counter-intuitive but repeatedly tested association. Treatment is EIP-to-EPL tendon transfer (direct repair is not possible due to attrition).
  • Bridge plating (radius-to-second/third metacarpal) is useful for highly comminuted intra-articular or osteoporotic fractures and polytrauma, allowing immediate weightbearing through the limb; it is removed at 3–4 months. External fixation relies on ligamentotaxis, which cannot reduce a depressed die-punch fragment or restore volar tilt, and over-distraction causes stiffness and CRPS.
  • Acute carpal tunnel syndrome after distal radius fracture requires urgent release. Persistent/worsening median symptoms after an initially successful CTR — think incomplete release distally, or injury to the palmar cutaneous branch (tender Tinel over the radial aspect of the distal wrist crease with normal two-point discrimination in the digits).
References7
