  • AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Distal Radius Fractures, 2020.
  • Arora R et al. A comparative study of clinical and radiologic outcomes of unstable distal radius fractures in patients older than 70. J Orthop Trauma 2009.
  • Lafontaine M, Hardy D, Delince P. Stability assessment of distal radius fractures. Injury 1989.
  • Harness NG et al. Loss of fixation of the volar lunate facet fragment in fractures of the distal part of the radius. JBJS Am 2004.
  • Soong M et al. Volar locking plate implant prominence and flexor tendon rupture. JBJS Am 2011.
  • Chung KC et al. WRIST Group. Volar locking plate vs percutaneous pinning vs external fixation in older adults. JBJS Am 2019.
11questions

Extensor tendon injuries: EPL rupture, sagittal band & deformities

The extensor mechanism: sagittal band, oblique retinacular ligament, and the classic deformities.

6 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021 (x2), 2022 (x2), 2023, 2024S (x2), 2024F (x2)

  • Sagittal band rupture ('boxer's knuckle'): traumatic dislocation of the extensor tendon at the MCP joint, usually ulnar subluxation from a radial sagittal band tear, most often the middle finger. Acute injuries (<2–3 weeks) can be treated in a relative motion extension splint/MCP extension splint for 4–6 weeks; chronic injuries need sagittal band reconstruction.
  • Swan-neck deformity = PIP hyperextension + DIP flexion. Causes: chronic mallet (extensor lag at DIP with proximal migration of the lateral bands), volar plate laxity at the PIP, intrinsic tightness, and FDS insufficiency. In rheumatoid disease it is driven by MCP volar subluxation and intrinsic tightness.
  • Boutonnière deformity = PIP flexion + DIP hyperextension, from central slip rupture with volar migration of the lateral bands. Test with Elson's test (PIP flexed 90° over a table edge, resisted PIP extension → a rigid DIP indicates central slip rupture). Treat acutely with PIP extension splinting leaving the DIP free for 6 weeks.
  • Oblique retinacular ligament (Landsmeer): passes volar to the PIP axis and dorsal to the DIP axis, linking PIP and DIP motion — its role is to coordinate/couple DIP extension with PIP extension. Tightness causes a fixed DIP in extension (positive Haines-Zancolli test).
  • Intrinsic tightness (Bunnell test): PIP flexion is limited when the MCP is held in extension and improves with the MCP flexed. Extrinsic extensor tightness is the opposite — PIP flexion is limited with the MCP flexed and improves with the MCP extended. The stem 'cannot extend the PIP with the MCP flexed but can with the MCP extended' points to the extrinsic/intrinsic balance and to a central slip or intrinsic problem.
  • Vaughan-Jackson syndrome: attritional rupture of the extensor tendons over a prominent, dorsally subluxed distal ulna (caput ulnae) in rheumatoid arthritis, progressing from ulnar to radial — the EDM/EDC to the small finger ruptures first (compartment 5, then 4). Treatment is Darrach/Sauvé-Kapandji plus tendon transfer or side-to-side suturing; direct repair is not possible.
  • Mannerfelt lesion is the flexor equivalent: FPL rupture from attrition against a scaphoid osteophyte on the volar radiocarpal joint in rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Intersection syndrome involves the first and second dorsal compartments — pain and crepitus ~4 cm proximal to the wrist where the first compartment (APL/EPB) crosses over the second (ECRL/ECRB). Distinguish from de Quervain (first compartment, at the radial styloid).
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand.
  • Rockwell WB, Butler PN, Byrne BA. Extensor tendon: anatomy, injury, and reconstruction. Plast Reconstr Surg 2000.
  • Catalano LW et al. Sagittal band reconstruction. J Hand Surg Am.
  • Williams K, Terrono AL. Treatment of boutonniere finger deformity in rheumatoid arthritis. J Hand Surg Am 2011.
  • Chim H, Elhassan B et al. Vaughan-Jackson syndrome. J Hand Surg Am.
7questions

Carpal tunnel syndrome & median nerve compression

Diagnosis, distinguishing distal from proximal compression, and complications of release.

7 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • Carpal tunnel syndrome: night symptoms in the median distribution, positive Tinel/Phalen/Durkan compression, thenar atrophy in advanced disease. Two-point discrimination is a late finding; Semmes-Weinstein monofilament (threshold) testing is more sensitive early.
  • Distinguishing CTS from proximal median compression (pronator syndrome): the palmar cutaneous branch arises ~5 cm proximal to the wrist and travels superficial to the transverse carpal ligament, so it is spared in CTS. Therefore numbness over the thenar eminence/palm indicates a lesion proximal to the carpal tunnel. Pronator syndrome also lacks prominent night symptoms and has a positive Tinel in the proximal forearm.
  • Compression sites in pronator syndrome: ligament of Struthers (supracondylar process), lacertus fibrosus, between the two heads of pronator teres, and the proximal arch of FDS. Carpal tunnel is not a site of pronator syndrome — the classic 'all are compression sites except' answer.
  • Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome is purely motor (FPL, FDP index/middle, pronator quadratus) — inability to make an 'OK' sign, with no sensory loss.
  • Endoscopic vs open release: endoscopic gives a faster return to work and less scar/pillar pain in the first weeks but has equivalent outcomes at 3–6 months. The commonest complication of endoscopic release is transient neurapraxia (usually of the median or ulnar nerve or their branches); the feared complication is incomplete release and irreversible nerve laceration.
  • Persistent or recurrent symptoms after release: the commonest cause is incomplete release of the distal transverse carpal ligament/distal antebrachial fascia. Recurrence after an initial symptom-free period suggests scarring or a new pathology; a positive Tinel over the radial aspect of the distal wrist crease with intact digital two-point discrimination points to a palmar cutaneous branch neuroma from an incision placed too radially.
  • Bilateral CTS in an older patient with cardiac disease/CHF should prompt consideration of transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis — send the tenosynovium for Congo red staining at the time of release. Bilateral CTS often precedes the cardiac diagnosis by several years.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Nerve Pathology; Wrist and Hand.
  • AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, 2016.
  • Sotelo-Garza A, Buck-Gramcko D. Compression syndromes of the median nerve. Hand Clin.
  • Vosbikian MM et al. Carpal tunnel release: open vs endoscopic. JAAOS.
  • Sperry BW et al. Tenosynovial and cardiac amyloidosis in patients undergoing carpal tunnel release. J Am Coll Cardiol 2018.
6questions

Metacarpal & phalangeal fractures

Acceptable deformity by ray, indications for surgery, and outcomes of malunion.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2021 (x2), 2024S (x2), 2024F

  • Acceptable apex-dorsal angulation for metacarpal neck fractures increases from radial to ulnar because of the increasing CMC mobility: index ~10°, middle ~20°, ring ~30–40°, small finger ~50–60°. No rotational deformity is acceptable in any digit — 5° of malrotation produces ~1.5 cm of digital overlap.
  • Indications for open reduction of a metacarpal fracture: malrotation, multiple fractures, open fracture, unacceptable angulation, shortening >5 mm (pseudoclawing/extensor lag), intra-articular displacement, and associated soft-tissue injury. Angulation within the acceptable range in an isolated small-finger neck fracture is not an indication.
  • Metacarpal shortening: each 2 mm of shortening produces roughly 7° of extensor lag, and about 8% loss of grip strength — the repeated 'lady with a metacarpal fracture, 2 mm shortening, 10° angulation' stem. In practice, up to 5 mm of shortening in the ring/small finger is well tolerated functionally.
  • Phalangeal fractures: the commonest complication of non-operative treatment is stiffness/loss of motion from adhesions, not malunion or nonunion — the extensor mechanism and flexor sheath are intimately adherent to the phalanx. Early protected motion is the priority.
  • Tuft fractures: treat the nail bed and soft tissue, not the bone. Options include splinting for comfort, nail bed repair, trephination for a subungual haematoma. Formal ORIF with a plate is not a treatment for a tuft fracture — the usual 'all are potential methods except' answer.
  • The 'fight bite' (tooth-strike over the MCP): assume joint penetration and extensor tendon injury; requires irrigation and débridement of the joint, antibiotics covering Eikenella corrodens (amoxicillin-clavulanate), and radiographs for retained tooth fragments. Never close primarily.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand.
  • Strauch RJ, Rosenwasser MP, Lunt JG. Metacarpal shaft fractures: the effect of shortening on the extensor tendon mechanism. J Hand Surg Am 1998.
  • Kollitz KM et al. Metacarpal fractures: treatment and complications. Hand 2014.
  • Henry MH. Fractures of the proximal phalanx and metacarpals in the hand. JAAOS 2008.
6questions

PIP and MCP joint injuries & fracture-dislocations

Dorsal and volar PIP fracture-dislocations, and the irreducible MCP dislocation.

4 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2022 (x2), 2024F, 2025

  • Dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation management is driven by the percentage of the volar base of the middle phalanx involved, because that is where the volar plate and collateral ligaments attach: <30–40% — stable, treat with extension-block splinting and early motion; 30–50% — tenuous, extension-block pinning or ORIF; >50% — unstable, requires hemi-hamate autograft arthroplasty, volar plate arthroplasty, dynamic external fixation, or ORIF.
  • The '50% volar lip fracture' stem = hemi-hamate arthroplasty (the dorsal-distal hamate reproduces the concave articular surface of the middle phalanx base). Dorsal block splinting is inadequate for this degree of instability.
  • Volar PIP dislocation implies central slip injury — treat with PIP extension splinting for 6 weeks, leaving the DIP free, or you get a boutonnière. An irreducible volar dislocation is blocked by the lateral band buttonholed around the condyle (or interposed central slip); rotatory volar dislocations are classically irreducible by closed means.
  • Irreducible dorsal MCP dislocation (complex dislocation) — usually the index finger. The block to reduction is the interposed volar plate, with the metacarpal head buttonholed between the lumbrical (radial) and flexor tendons (ulnar), and the natatory/superficial transverse ligaments tightening around the neck. Radiographic clue is a sesamoid within the joint space.
  • Reduction technique: do NOT apply longitudinal traction and hyperextension — this converts a simple dislocation into a complex one by drawing the volar plate into the joint. Instead flex the wrist (relaxing the flexors), apply volar-directed pressure on the base of the proximal phalanx to slide it over the metacarpal head, with the MCP flexed.
  • Post-reduction, all PIP/MCP injuries need early protected motion — stiffness is the dominant complication of these joints.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand.
  • Williams RM, Kiefhaber TR, Sommerkamp TG, Stern PJ. Treatment of unstable dorsal proximal interphalangeal fracture/dislocations using a hemi-hamate autograft. J Hand Surg Am 2003.
  • Kiefhaber TR, Stern PJ. Fracture dislocations of the proximal interphalangeal joint. J Hand Surg Am 1998.
  • Kaplan EB. Dorsal dislocation of the metacarpophalangeal joint of the index finger. JBJS Am 1957.
5questions

Scapholunate instability, SLAC wrist & carpal collapse

SL dissociation, DISI/VISI, and the surgical menu for degenerative carpal collapse.

3 of 7 sittings2020 (x3), 2023, 2025

  • The dorsal component of the scapholunate interosseous ligament is the strongest and most important stabiliser; secondary stabilisers are the scaphotrapezial-trapezoid ligament, the radioscaphocapitate and the dorsal intercarpal ligament. Radiographic signs: SL gap >3 mm ('Terry Thomas'), a cortical ring sign from the flexed scaphoid, and an SL angle >70° (normal 30–60°).
  • DISI = dorsal intercalated segment instability: the lunate extends (dorsiflexes), SL angle >70° — associated with scapholunate dissociation and with scaphoid nonunion. VISI = the lunate flexes, SL angle <30° — the commonest cause is lunotriquetral ligament injury/ulnar-sided carpal instability. This is a repeated distinction.
  • Progression: dynamic instability (only on stress views/clenched fist) → static instability → SLAC (scapholunate advanced collapse): Stage I radial styloid–scaphoid arthritis; Stage II entire radioscaphoid joint; Stage III capitolunate/midcarpal arthritis; Stage IV pancarpal. The radiolunate joint is characteristically spared until very late because of the congruent lunate facet.
  • Treatment by stage: acute repair ± dorsal capsulodesis for a repairable ligament; ligament reconstruction (e.g. SLIC/three-ligament tenodesis) for chronic reducible deformity; radial styloidectomy for stage I; proximal row carpectomy (PRC) or scaphoid excision with four-corner fusion (4CF) for stage II–III; total wrist fusion (or arthroplasty) for stage IV.
  • PRC requires an intact capitate head and lunate fossa — it converts the wrist to a capitate-on-lunate-fossa articulation, so it is contraindicated when the capitolunate joint is arthritic (SLAC III). PRC preserves more motion; 4CF preserves more grip strength and carpal height. In patients under 35, 4CF is often favoured (higher demands), though this is debated.
  • The 'piece of pie' sign (a triangular lunate on the AP view) and a disrupted Gilula arc with an overlapping lunate-capitate on the lateral indicate a perilunate or lunate dislocation — a missed emergency.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Wrist.
  • Watson HK, Ballet FL. The SLAC wrist: scapholunate advanced collapse pattern of degenerative arthritis. J Hand Surg Am 1984.
  • Kitay A, Wolfe SW. Scapholunate instability: current concepts in diagnosis and management. J Hand Surg Am 2012.
  • Cohen MS, Kozin SH. Degenerative arthritis of the wrist: proximal row carpectomy versus scaphoid excision and four-corner arthrodesis. J Hand Surg Am 2001.
4questions

Dupuytren disease

Diathesis, treatment options and complications.

4 of 7 sittings2022, 2023, 2024S, 2024F

  • A fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia driven by myofibroblasts and type III collagen, with Northern European ancestry, autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance. Diseased cords are named for the normal bands they replace (pretendinous, central, lateral, spiral, natatory, Grayson's ligament).
  • The spiral cord displaces the neurovascular bundle centrally (midline), superficially and proximally — this is why digital nerve injury occurs during PIP-level dissection, especially with a PIP contracture.
  • Dupuytren diathesis predicts aggressive disease and recurrence: bilateral disease, ectopic disease (Ledderhose plantar fibromatosis, Peyronie disease, Garrod knuckle pads), a positive family history, early age of onset (<50), and male sex. Ectopic/extra-palmar disease and bilaterality are the strongest indicators — the usual 'most suggestive of aggressive disease' answer.
  • Indications for treatment: MCP contracture ≥30°, any PIP contracture, or a positive tabletop test with functional impairment. MCP contractures correct better and more durably than PIP contractures (the PIP has volar plate and check-rein contracture).
  • Options: collagenase clostridium histolyticum injection and percutaneous needle aponeurotomy (faster recovery, higher recurrence) versus open limited/segmental fasciectomy (lower recurrence, longer recovery) versus dermofasciectomy with full-thickness skin graft (lowest recurrence, for recurrent/diathesis-positive disease).
  • The commonest complication of open palmar fasciectomy is a wound-healing problem/haematoma and skin necrosis, with digital nerve injury (~2–5%) the most feared. Complex regional pain syndrome, flare reaction and stiffness also occur. Recurrence is the rule rather than the exception with long follow-up.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand.
  • Hindocha S, Bayat A et al. Dupuytren's diathesis revisited: evaluation of prognostic indicators. J Hand Surg Am 2006.
  • Hurst LC et al. Injectable collagenase clostridium histolyticum for Dupuytren's contracture (CORD I). NEJM 2009.
  • Denkler K. Surgical complications associated with fasciectomy for Dupuytren's disease. Hand 2010.
4questions

Flexor tendon injury, pulleys & repair

Pulley biomechanics, venting, and repair strength.

3 of 7 sittings2022, 2023 (x2), 2025

  • Pulley system: annular pulleys A1–A5 and cruciate pulleys C1–C3. A2 (over the proximal phalanx) and A4 (over the middle phalanx) are the most biomechanically important — their loss causes bowstringing, loss of digital flexion arc and decreased mechanical efficiency (an increase in the moment arm with loss of excursion efficiency).
  • Modern evidence supports venting — releasing part of A4 and up to the distal half of A2 — to allow tendon glide and repair without significant biomechanical penalty. Complete A2 release, however, causes measurable bowstringing, increased work of flexion, loss of the flexion arc and reduced DIP/PIP motion. Preserve the A2 pulley or vent it partially.
  • Repair strength is proportional to the number of core strands crossing the repair; a 4- or 6-strand core repair with an epitendinous suture permits early active motion protocols. Aim for 1 cm purchase and avoid gapping (>3 mm gap predicts rupture and adhesion).
  • Excessive shortening of the FDP (e.g. >1 cm at repair) produces the quadriga effect — because the FDP tendons share a common muscle belly, over-shortening one tendon limits excursion of the others, causing weak grip and incomplete flexion of the adjacent digits. Over-lengthening produces a lumbrical-plus finger (paradoxical PIP extension on attempted flexion).
  • Jersey finger (FDP avulsion, ring finger most common, Leddy-Packer classification): type I retracts to the palm (both vincula ruptured) and must be repaired within 7–10 days; types II and III retract less and can be repaired later. When placing a suture anchor in the distal phalanx, pull-out strength is greatest when the anchor is inserted at ~45° to the cortex, angled away from the direction of pull (deadman angle), in the distal phalanx base.
  • Zone II ('no-man's land') repairs have the greatest risk of adhesion; early controlled motion protocols (Duran, Kleinert, or early active motion) are essential.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand.
  • Tang JB. Venting the A4 and A2 pulleys in flexor tendon repair. J Hand Surg Eur 2007/2014.
  • Moriya K, Tang JB et al. Effects of venting the A4 pulley on gliding resistance. J Hand Surg Eur.
  • Leddy JP, Packer JW. Avulsion of the profundus tendon insertion in athletes. J Hand Surg Am 1977.
  • Strickland JW. Flexor tendon injuries: repair and rehabilitation. JAAOS 1995.
4questions

Perilunate dislocation & lesser arc injury

The greater and lesser arc patterns and the ligaments involved.

4 of 7 sittings2021, 2023, 2024F, 2025

  • Mayfield stages of progressive perilunar instability: I scapholunate dissociation → II capitolunate dislocation (perilunate) → III lunotriquetral disruption → IV lunate dislocation (the lunate is extruded volarly into the carpal tunnel, 'spilled teacup' sign).
  • Lesser arc injuries are purely ligamentous and travel around the lunate: scapholunate, radioscaphocapitate/capitolunate, lunotriquetral, and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments. The radioscaphoid ligament / radiolunate ligaments and the volar ulnolunate are not part of the lesser arc pattern in the classic teaching — the exam typically asks which ligament is not injured.
  • Greater arc injuries pass through bone: trans-scaphoid, trans-capitate, trans-triquetral, trans-styloid perilunate fracture-dislocations. A trans-scaphoid perilunate dislocation is the commonest greater arc pattern.
  • This injury is missed in up to 25% of cases on initial presentation — the AP view shows a triangular 'piece of pie' lunate with disrupted Gilula's arcs; the lateral shows loss of collinearity of the radius–lunate–capitate axis.
  • Treatment: urgent closed reduction to decompress the median nerve, followed by open reduction and ligament repair with K-wire or screw fixation — usually through a combined dorsal and volar approach. Carpal tunnel release is performed if there is acute median neuropathy. Closed treatment alone gives poor results.
  • Even with prompt anatomic treatment, post-traumatic arthritis and stiffness are common; delayed presentation (>6–8 weeks) is often better served by salvage (PRC or fusion).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Wrist.
  • Mayfield JK, Johnson RP, Kilcoyne RK. Carpal dislocations: pathomechanics and progressive perilunar instability. J Hand Surg Am 1980.
  • Herzberg G et al. Perilunate dislocations and fracture-dislocations: a multicenter study. J Hand Surg Am 1993.
  • Stanbury SJ, Elfar JC. Perilunate dislocation and perilunate fracture-dislocation. JAAOS 2011.
4questions

Scaphoid fracture & nonunion

Diagnosis, immobilisation, and the management of nonunion with deformity.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2024S, 2025

  • Blood supply is retrograde from the dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery entering the dorsal ridge, supplying ~80% of the scaphoid including the entire proximal pole. Hence the more proximal the fracture, the higher the rate of nonunion and AVN.
  • Non-displaced waist fracture: union rates ~90% with cast immobilisation. Multiple RCTs (including the Canadian-led SWIFFT and earlier trials) show no difference between a short-arm thumb spica and a short-arm cast including or excluding the thumb, and no clear benefit from a long-arm cast. Percutaneous screw fixation gives a faster return to work/sport with equivalent union rates and a small complication risk.
  • Displaced fractures (>1 mm step, lateral intrascaphoid angle >35°, or a humpback deformity) require ORIF. CT along the scaphoid axis defines displacement; MRI is the most sensitive early test for an occult fracture (radiographs may be normal for 2 weeks).
  • Scaphoid nonunion with DISI/humpback deformity: the flexed distal pole causes carpal collapse. Treatment is open reduction with a structural (corticocancellous, volar wedge) bone graft and screw fixation to restore scaphoid length and correct the DISI — a non-structural cancellous graft will not correct the deformity.
  • Proximal pole nonunion with AVN requires a vascularised bone graft (1,2-intercompartmental supraretinacular artery pedicle from the distal radius, or a free medial femoral condyle graft). Untreated nonunion progresses to SNAC wrist (scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse) in a pattern analogous to SLAC.
  • Established SNAC/SLAC with radioscaphoid arthritis is treated with salvage (PRC or four-corner fusion) rather than attempted union.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Wrist.
  • Gelberman RH, Menon J. The vascularity of the scaphoid bone. J Hand Surg Am 1980.
  • Dias JJ et al. SWIFFT trial: cast treatment versus surgical fixation for scaphoid waist fractures. Lancet 2020.
  • Clay NR et al. Need the thumb be immobilised in scaphoid fractures? JBJS Br 1991.
  • Jones DB, Bürger H, Bishop AT, Shin AY. Free vascularized medial femoral condyle bone graft for scaphoid nonunions. JBJS Am 2008.
3questions

Kienböck disease

Lunate osteonecrosis: staging, vascular anatomy and treatment by ulnar variance.

2 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2022

  • Osteonecrosis of the lunate, typically in men 20–40 years. Lichtman staging: I — normal radiographs, MRI shows oedema; II — sclerosis without collapse; IIIA — lunate collapse with normal carpal alignment; IIIB — collapse with fixed scaphoid flexion (ring sign) and carpal collapse (radioscaphoid angle >60°); IV — pancarpal arthritis.
  • Vascular anatomy is central: the lunate is supplied by volar and dorsal branches from the radial artery, anterior interosseous and ulnar recurrent arteries, entering through the volar and dorsal poles. Approximately 20% of lunates have a single (volar) vessel and no intraosseous anastomosis, making them vulnerable. Intraosseous patterns are described as Y, I and X by Gelberman. The articular cartilage surface has no vascular contribution — the classic 'all affect lunate vascularity except' answer relates to the cartilage covering ~80% of the lunate leaving little area for vessel entry.
  • Negative ulnar variance is associated with Kienböck (increased radiolunate shear/load), although the relationship is not causal in all cases.
  • Treatment is guided by stage and ulnar variance: stage I–II/IIIA with negative ulnar variance → joint-levelling radial shortening osteotomy (the most reliable procedure). With neutral or positive variance → capitate shortening, vascularised bone graft (4+5 ECA pedicle from the distal radius), or a radial wedge/core decompression.
  • Stage IIIB → proximal row carpectomy or scaphocapitate/STT limited fusion. Stage IV → salvage: PRC (if the capitate head and lunate fossa are intact), total wrist fusion, or arthroplasty. Lunate excision alone causes carpal collapse and is not recommended without a stabilising procedure.
  • Immobilisation/observation remains appropriate for stage I disease and in children, where the natural history is much more favourable.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Wrist.
  • Gelberman RH et al. The vascularity of the lunate bone and Kienböck's disease. J Hand Surg Am 1980.
  • Lichtman DM et al. Kienböck's disease: a new algorithm for the 21st century. J Wrist Surg 2017.
  • Bain GI, Begg M. Arthroscopic assessment and classification of Kienböck's disease. Tech Hand Up Extrem Surg.
3questions

Rheumatoid hand & wrist

The characteristic deformities and their mechanics.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2024S, 2025

  • The primary lesion is proliferative synovitis (pannus) destroying capsule, ligament and tendon. Wrist deformity precedes and drives the hand deformity — this is the essential concept: radial deviation and supination of the carpus at the wrist causes compensatory ulnar deviation (ulnar drift) of the fingers at the MCP joints ('zig-zag' collapse).
  • Ulnar drift results from: radial deviation of the metacarpals at the wrist, attenuation of the radial sagittal bands with ulnar and volar subluxation of the extensor tendons, the normal ulnar-directed pull of the flexors and intrinsics, and volar plate/collateral attenuation. The cause is not simply intrinsic tightness alone.
  • Caput ulnae syndrome: dorsal subluxation of the distal ulna with supination of the carpus, causing painful DRUJ, dorsal prominence, and attritional extensor tendon rupture (Vaughan-Jackson) beginning at the small finger.
  • The commonest carpal deformity in the rheumatoid wrist is radial deviation with volar and ulnar translocation of the carpus (carpal supination and ulnar translation), with loss of carpal height and scapholunate dissociation.
  • Mannerfelt lesion — FPL rupture from attrition over a volar scaphoid osteophyte. Treated with tendon graft, transfer (FDS ring) or IP fusion, plus excision of the offending spur.
  • Wrist surgery: synovectomy with DRUJ reconstruction (Darrach or Sauvé-Kapandji) early; radiolunate (Chamay) partial fusion for ulnar translocation with a preserved midcarpal joint; total wrist arthrodesis for pancarpal destruction — durable, pain-relieving, and the workhorse in a heavily deformed rheumatoid wrist, positioned in slight extension. Bilateral fusion should be considered carefully (perineal care).
  • Perioperative DMARD management: continue methotrexate/hydroxychloroquine/sulfasalazine; hold biologics and schedule surgery at the end of the dosing interval, restarting ~14 days post-operatively once the wound is satisfactory.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand; Systemic Disease.
  • Chung KC, Pushman AG. Current concepts in the management of the rheumatoid hand. J Hand Surg Am 2011.
  • Feldon P, Terrono AL, Nalebuff EA. Rheumatoid arthritis and other connective tissue diseases. In Green's Operative Hand Surgery.
  • Goodman SM et al. 2022 ACR/AAHKS perioperative antirheumatic medication guideline. J Arthroplasty 2022.
3questions

Ulnar nerve compression at the wrist (Guyon canal)

Localising an ulnar nerve lesion by examination.

3 of 7 sittings2022, 2024S, 2024F

  • Guyon's canal boundaries: floor — transverse carpal ligament and hypothenar muscles; roof — volar carpal ligament and palmaris brevis; ulnar — pisiform and FCU; radial — hook of hamate. The ulnar nerve lies ulnar to the ulnar artery.
  • Zone I (proximal to bifurcation) — mixed motor and sensory. Zone II (deep motor branch, around the hook of hamate) — pure motor with no sensory loss. Zone III (superficial sensory branch) — pure sensory to the volar small and ulnar ring finger.
  • Key localising principle: the dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve arises ~5–8 cm proximal to the wrist and does not pass through Guyon's canal. Therefore:
  • • Numbness on the dorso-ulnar hand = lesion proximal to the wrist (forearm/elbow).
    • Sparing of the dorso-ulnar hand with volar small-finger numbness = lesion at/distal to Guyon's canal.
    • The stem 'ulnar-side forearm laceration with dorsal hand and small-finger numbness, no motor deficit and no volar cutaneous loss' localises to the dorsal cutaneous branch in the distal forearm — proximal to Guyon's canal.
  • Causes at the wrist: ganglion (most common), hook of hamate fracture/nonunion, ulnar artery thrombosis (hypothenar hammer syndrome), repetitive pressure (cyclists' palsy), anomalous muscle. Imaging (MRI/ultrasound) is warranted because a compressive mass is common.
  • Froment sign — thumb IP flexion when pinching (recruiting FPL, median-innervated) to compensate for a weak adductor pollicis (ulnar). Jeanne sign is compensatory MCP hyperextension. Wartenberg sign is small-finger abduction from unopposed EDM.
  • Cubital tunnel (elbow-level) compression additionally weakens FCU and FDP to the small/ring fingers, and has dorsal cutaneous sensory loss — the two features distinguishing it from a wrist-level lesion.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Nerve Pathology.
  • Shea JD, McClain EJ. Ulnar-nerve compression syndromes at and below the wrist. JBJS Am 1969.
  • Gross MS, Gelberman RH. The anatomy of the distal ulnar tunnel. CORR 1985.
  • Earp BE et al. Ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist. JAAOS 2014.
2questions

Bennett fracture & thumb CMC injuries

Deforming forces and reduction manoeuvre.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2024S

  • A Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the base of the first metacarpal with a volar-ulnar fragment held reduced by the anterior oblique (volar beak) ligament, which anchors it to the trapezium.
  • Deforming forces on the metacarpal shaft: abductor pollicis longus pulls the shaft proximally, dorsally and radially (shortening and subluxation); adductor pollicis pulls the distal metacarpal into adduction and supination; the extensor pollicis longus/brevis add extension. The volar-ulnar fragment stays put.
  • Reduction manoeuvre: longitudinal traction, palmar abduction, pronation, and direct pressure over the base of the metacarpal. Note that pronation, not supination, is the correct rotational component — a repeated 'which is false' item.
  • Treatment: closed reduction and percutaneous pinning (metacarpal to trapezium and/or to the index metacarpal) is adequate for most fractures with small fragments; ORIF with a screw for fragments >15–20% of the articular surface or with >1–2 mm displacement. Anatomic reduction reduces (but does not eliminate) later CMC arthritis.
  • A Rolando fracture is the comminuted T- or Y-shaped intra-articular base fracture — more difficult, worse prognosis, often treated with ORIF, external fixation or pinning depending on comminution.
  • Thumb ulnar collateral ligament (skier's thumb) injury: a Stener lesion (the adductor aponeurosis interposed between the retracted UCL and its insertion) prevents healing and mandates surgical repair. Suspect it with >30° of laxity in 30° flexion, >15–20° side-to-side difference, or a palpable mass. Chronic UCL insufficiency causes weak key/pinch grip and eventual MCP instability and arthritis.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand.
  • Bennett EH. Fractures of the metacarpal bones. Dublin J Med Sci 1882.
  • Soyer AD. Fractures of the base of the first metacarpal. JAAOS 1999.
  • Stener B. Displacement of the ruptured ulnar collateral ligament of the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb. JBJS Br 1962.
2questions

Distal radioulnar joint instability & TFCC

Stabilisers of the DRUJ, ulnar styloid fractures, and ulnocarpal impaction.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2024F

  • The deep fibres of the distal radioulnar (dorsal and volar radioulnar) ligaments of the TFCC — the ligamentum subcruentum inserting at the fovea — are the primary stabilisers of the DRUJ. The pronator quadratus, ECU subsheath, interosseous membrane (distal oblique bundle) and the ulnar capsule are secondary stabilisers.
  • An ulnar styloid tip fracture is usually irrelevant to DRUJ stability; a basilar (base) ulnar styloid fracture disrupts the foveal insertion of the TFCC and is associated with instability. But the decision to fix is based on the examination of DRUJ stability after fixing the radius, not on the radiograph.
  • Algorithm after distal radius ORIF: reduce and fix the radius anatomically → examine the DRUJ. If stable, no further treatment. If reducible but unstable, immobilise in supination in a long-arm/Muenster cast (or pin the ulna to the radius) for ~6 weeks. If irreducible, open the joint — an entrapped ECU tendon or TFCC is the usual block, and the TFCC is repaired to the fovea. Fixing a small styloid tip fragment does not restore stability.
  • Ulnocarpal impaction (abutment): ulnar-sided wrist pain worse with grip and ulnar deviation, from positive ulnar variance — congenital, or acquired after distal radius malunion with radial shortening, or after radial head excision (Essex-Lopresti). Radiographs show cystic/sclerotic changes in the ulnar head, lunate and triquetrum; MRI shows a central TFCC perforation (degenerative, Palmer 2) and lunate oedema.
  • Treatment of ulnocarpal impaction: activity modification and injection, then ulnar shortening osteotomy (which also tightens the ulnocarpal ligaments) or an arthroscopic wafer procedure (contraindicated with a large DRUJ arthritic change or with instability).
  • Palmer classification: class 1 = traumatic (1A central perforation, 1B ulnar/foveal avulsion ± styloid fracture, 1C ulnocarpal ligament, 1D radial avulsion); class 2 = degenerative (ulnocarpal impaction spectrum). Peripheral (1B) tears are vascular and repairable; central (1A) tears are avascular and are débrided.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Wrist.
  • Palmer AK, Werner FW. The triangular fibrocartilage complex of the wrist. J Hand Surg Am 1981.
  • May MM, Lawton JN, Blazar PE. Ulnar styloid fractures associated with distal radius fractures: incidence and implications for distal radioulnar joint instability. J Hand Surg Am 2002.
  • Nakamura T et al. The functional anatomy of the DRUJ ligaments. J Hand Surg Br.
2questions

Hand tumours & ganglion cysts

The commonest masses of the hand and their behaviour.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2024S

  • Ganglion cyst is the commonest soft-tissue mass of the hand/wrist (60–70%): dorsal (scapholunate ligament origin, ~70%), volar radial (radioscaphoid/STT joint, adjacent to the radial artery), flexor sheath (retinacular, A1 pulley) and mucous cyst (DIP joint, associated with an osteophyte). Transilluminates; MRI/ultrasound is only needed when atypical.
  • Management: observation is appropriate — many resolve spontaneously. Aspiration has a high recurrence rate (~50%+). Excision requires removal of the stalk and a cuff of the joint capsule to minimise recurrence (~5–15%). For a mucous cyst, the associated DIP osteophyte must be excised or it recurs; nail deformity is a common presenting feature.
  • Giant cell tumour of tendon sheath (localised TGCT) is the second commonest hand mass: a firm, painless, slow-growing nodule on the volar/radial digit; low signal on both T1 and T2 from haemosiderin. Treat with marginal excision; recurrence 10–20%.
  • Epidermal inclusion cyst (post-traumatic, fingertip), lipoma, glomus tumour (subungual, exquisitely painful, cold-sensitive, pinpoint tenderness — Love's test/Hildreth's test), and schwannoma are the other common benign lesions.
  • Enchondroma is the commonest primary bone tumour of the hand and frequently presents as a pathologic fracture of a proximal phalanx. Let the fracture heal, then curette and graft if symptomatic.
  • Malignancy in the hand is rare; the commonest is squamous cell carcinoma of the skin/nail bed (a chronic non-healing 'paronychia' or nail bed lesion should be biopsied), then epithelioid sarcoma — the classic mimic of a benign nodule or 'ganglion' in a young adult that recurs and ulcerates. Any hand mass that recurs, ulcerates or grows must be biopsied.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand; Oncology.
  • Thornburg LE. Ganglions of the hand and wrist. JAAOS 1999.
  • Athanasian EA. Bone and soft tissue tumors. In Green's Operative Hand Surgery.
  • Murphey MD et al. Imaging of musculoskeletal neurogenic tumors. RadioGraphics.
2questions

Hook of hamate fracture

The classic athlete's injury and its complications.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2024F

  • Occurs in athletes gripping a club, bat or racquet — golfers, baseball/softball players, hockey players and tennis players — from a direct blow of the handle against the hypothenar eminence, usually in the non-dominant/lead hand (the hand at the butt of the club).
  • Presents with ulnar-sided palmar wrist pain, tenderness directly over the hook, pain with resisted small-finger flexion, and sometimes ulnar nerve symptoms (deep motor branch, zone II) or ulnar artery thrombosis.
  • Radiographs are frequently normal — the carpal tunnel view and the supinated oblique view help, but CT is the diagnostic study of choice.
  • Complications: nonunion (very common because of the tenuous blood supply and shear from the transverse carpal ligament/pisohamate ligament), attritional rupture of the flexor tendons to the small and ring fingers, ulnar neuropathy and ulnar artery thrombosis.
  • For a symptomatic nonunion in an athlete, excision of the hook fragment is the treatment of choice — it gives reliable pain relief and rapid return to sport with negligible functional loss. ORIF is reserved for selected acute fractures. Immobilisation of an established nonunion is unlikely to succeed.
  • Protect the ulnar nerve and artery during excision; the deep motor branch curves around the hook.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Wrist.
  • Stark HH et al. Fracture of the hook of the hamate. JBJS Am 1989.
  • Scheufler O et al. Hook of hamate fractures: critical evaluation of different therapeutic procedures. Plast Reconstr Surg 2005.
  • Bansal A et al. Hook of hamate fractures in athletes. Hand.
1question

Distal radius malunion & corrective osteotomy

Indications and planning for corrective osteotomy.

1 of 7 sittings2021

  • Malunion is the commonest complication of distal radius fracture. Symptomatic malunion causes pain, loss of grip strength, limited rotation, DRUJ incongruity and midcarpal instability (adaptive carpal malalignment).
  • The best indication for corrective osteotomy is a symptomatic malunion in a young, active patient with preserved joint surfaces and good motion, particularly with dorsal tilt >20°, radial shortening >5 mm, radial inclination <10°, or an incongruent DRUJ. Malalignment alone in an asymptomatic or low-demand elderly patient is not an indication.
  • Correct early where possible — early osteotomy (within 3–6 months) is technically easier, the soft tissues are more compliant, and adaptive carpal changes are reversible. Established radiocarpal arthritis is a contraindication (salvage instead).
  • Planning requires bilateral wrist radiographs and CT to quantify deformity in all three planes; 3D planning and patient-specific guides improve accuracy. Extra-articular osteotomy uses an opening (volar approach with structural graft or a locking plate) or closing wedge; intra-articular osteotomy is more demanding.
  • Address the ulnar side: an isolated ulnar shortening osteotomy may suffice when the primary problem is ulnocarpal impaction from radial shortening without significant tilt deformity; consider a Darrach or Sauvé-Kapandji in the older patient with DRUJ arthritis.
  • Outcomes are good for pain, grip strength and rotation, though full restoration of motion is uncommon; concurrent carpal tunnel release is often required.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma; Wrist and Hand.
  • Fernandez DL. Correction of post-traumatic wrist deformity in adults by osteotomy, bone-grafting and internal fixation. JBJS Am 1982.
  • Prommersberger KJ, Lanz UB. Corrective osteotomy of the distal radius. Tech Hand Up Extrem Surg.
  • Haghverdian JC et al. Complications of corrective osteotomies for extra-articular distal radius malunion. J Hand Surg Am 2019.
1question

Hand infections & felon/flexor sheath sepsis

Recognising and treating the surgical hand infection.

1 of 7 sittings2023

  • Kanavel's four cardinal signs of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis: (1) fusiform swelling of the digit, (2) the digit held in slight flexion, (3) tenderness along the flexor sheath, and (4) pain on passive extension (the most sensitive and earliest sign). Treatment is urgent irrigation of the sheath plus IV antibiotics; delay causes tendon necrosis and adhesion.
  • Felon — a closed-space infection of the distal pulp septa causing throbbing pain and pressure necrosis. Requires incision and drainage (a mid-lateral or volar longitudinal incision avoiding the flexor sheath and the digital nerves); do not use a fish-mouth incision.
  • Paronychia (perionychium) is the commonest hand infection — drain by elevating the eponychial fold ± partial nail plate removal. Herpetic whitlow is a viral vesicular infection that must not be incised.
  • Bite wounds: human bites (fight bite over the MCP) — Eikenella corrodens, treat with amoxicillin-clavulanate, explore the joint and extensor tendon, never close primarily. Cat bites — Pasteurella multocida, deep puncture, high infection rate. Dog bites — Pasteurella, Staph, Strep.
  • Atypical infections: a chronic granulomatous 'inflammatory' hand mass with an indolent course, especially with aquarium or fish/water exposure, suggests Mycobacterium marinum or another atypical mycobacterium — requires special culture media at 30–32 °C, held for several weeks, and prolonged multi-drug therapy. Sporotrichosis follows rose thorn/soil exposure.
  • Acute calcific periarthritis/tendinitis is the great mimic of infection: acute pain, redness and warmth around a joint (often near the metacarpal head or the flexor carpi ulnaris insertion), afebrile with normal WBC, and amorphous calcification adjacent to the joint on radiographs. Treatment is NSAIDs, not surgery.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand.
  • Kanavel AB. Infections of the Hand, 1912.
  • Osterman M, Draeger R, Stern P. Acute hand infections. J Hand Surg Am 2014.
  • Patel DB et al. Hand infections: anatomy, types and spread of infection, imaging findings. RadioGraphics 2014.
1question

Tendon transfers in the hand

Principles of transfer and the standard transfers for each palsy.

1 of 7 sittings2021

  • Principles: correct the deformity/supple joints first, adequate soft-tissue bed, expendable donor, one tendon one function, synergistic donor, straight line of pull, and adequate excursion (wrist ~33 mm, finger extensors ~50 mm, finger flexors ~70 mm) and strength (a transferred tendon loses roughly one grade of power).
  • Low ulnar nerve palsy (claw hand): MCP hyperextension of the ring and small fingers with PIP/DIP flexion from intrinsic loss. Correct with an anti-claw procedure: Zancolli capsulodesis, Bouvier-positive → static MCP block; or Modified Stiles-Bunnell (FDS ring transfer to the lateral bands), Brand (ECRB/ECRL + graft) transfers. Restore key pinch with an adductorplasty (ECRB or FDS to adductor pollicis) for a positive Froment sign.
  • The stem 'elderly patient with thumb weakness, difficulty grasping, MCP hyperextension of the thumb and clawing of the ring and small fingers' describes a low ulnar nerve palsy — the transfer must restore thumb adduction/key pinch and correct clawing.
  • Radial nerve palsy (the classic triad): pronator teres → ECRB (wrist extension), FCU (or FCR) → EDC (finger extension), palmaris longus → EPL (thumb extension). FCR-based transfers preserve wrist ulnar deviation balance.
  • Low median nerve palsy (loss of opposition): opponensplasty — EIP (Burkhalter), FDS ring (Bunnell), abductor digiti minimi (Huber, favoured in children/congenital), or palmaris longus with graft (Camitz — the transfer of choice in advanced carpal tunnel syndrome, done at the time of release).
  • Pulvertaft weave is the strongest tendon-to-tendon junction and is the standard for transfers; tension is set with the wrist and digits in the resting posture and checked with the tenodesis effect.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand; Upper Extremity Nerve Pathology.
  • Sammer DM, Chung KC. Tendon transfers: part I & II. Plast Reconstr Surg 2009.
  • Davis TRC. Principles of tendon transfers of median, radial, and ulnar nerves. In Green's Operative Hand Surgery.
  • Camitz H. Surgical treatment of paralysis of opponens muscle of thumb. Acta Chir Scand 1929.
1question

Thumb CMC arthritis & denervation

Treatment options for basal thumb arthritis, including denervation.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • Thumb CMC (trapeziometacarpal) arthritis is common in women over 50. Eaton-Littler staging: I — joint space widening/synovitis; II — slight narrowing with debris <2 mm; III — significant narrowing with osteophytes >2 mm; IV — pantrapezial (STT involvement).
  • Examination: positive grind test, tenderness at the CMC joint, adduction contracture with compensatory MCP hyperextension in advanced disease. First-line treatment is a thumb spica orthosis, NSAIDs and corticosteroid injection.
  • Surgical options: trapeziectomy alone, trapeziectomy with ligament reconstruction and tendon interposition (LRTI), suspensionplasty/suture button, CMC arthrodesis (for young, high-demand labourers — durable and strong but loses motion and risks nonunion), volar ligament reconstruction (Eaton-Littler) for stage I instability in the young, and prosthetic arthroplasty.
  • Systematic reviews and RCTs (including Cochrane) show no clear superiority of LRTI over simple trapeziectomy, and LRTI has more complications and longer operative time. This is an important evidence point.
  • CMC denervation (excision of the articular branches — from the superficial radial nerve, the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve and the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve supplying the joint) is a motion-preserving, joint-preserving option that relieves pain without altering biomechanics. It is attractive in high-demand patients and does not preclude later definitive surgery, but pain relief is less predictable and less durable.
  • MCP hyperextension >30° must be addressed at the time of surgery (volar plate capsulodesis, sesamoidesis or MCP fusion) or the reconstruction will fail.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand.
  • Wajon A et al. Surgery for thumb (trapeziometacarpal joint) osteoarthritis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015.
  • Eaton RG, Glickel SZ. Trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis: staging as a rationale for treatment. Hand Clin 1987.
  • Loréa P et al. Denervation of the trapeziometacarpal joint. Chir Main.
1question

Thumb ulnar collateral ligament injury

Skier's/gamekeeper's thumb and the Stener lesion.

1 of 7 sittings2023

  • Mechanism is forced radial deviation/abduction of the thumb MCP (ski pole, fall on an abducted thumb). Acute = skier's thumb; chronic attritional = gamekeeper's thumb.
  • Examination: laxity >30–35° in 30° of MCP flexion (isolating the proper UCL), or >15–20° more than the contralateral side, indicates a complete tear. Test in both full extension (accessory collateral/volar plate) and 30° flexion (proper collateral). Local anaesthetic improves the reliability of the examination. Obtain radiographs before stressing to exclude a displaced avulsion fracture.
  • Stener lesion (~60–80% of complete tears): the torn UCL retracts proximally and becomes trapped superficial to the adductor aponeurosis, which interposes between the ligament and its insertion on the proximal phalanx. Healing is then impossible and surgical repair is required. A palpable tender mass proximal to the MCP joint suggests it; ultrasound or MRI confirms it.
  • Partial (stable) tears heal well in a thumb spica cast/orthosis for 4–6 weeks. Complete tears, a Stener lesion, or a displaced/rotated avulsion fragment (>2–3 mm displacement or involving >20% of the articular surface) require repair with a suture anchor.
  • Consequence of untreated UCL insufficiency: chronic pain and weakness of key/pinch grip, MCP instability, and eventual post-traumatic MCP arthritis. Chronic cases are treated with reconstruction (free tendon graft) or MCP arthrodesis.
  • Radial collateral ligament injuries are less common, tend to occur more distally, and rarely form a Stener-equivalent lesion.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand.
  • Stener B. Displacement of the ruptured ulnar collateral ligament of the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb. JBJS Br 1962.
  • Heyman P et al. Injuries of the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint. JBJS Am 1993.
  • Rhee PC, Jones DB, Kakar S. Management of thumb metacarpophalangeal ulnar collateral ligament injuries. JBJS Am 2012.
1question

Trigger finger & stenosing tenosynovitis

Pathophysiology and evidence-based treatment.

1 of 7 sittings2021

  • Stenosing tenosynovitis at the A1 pulley — a size mismatch between the thickened flexor tendon/sheath and the pulley, causing catching, locking and pain, most often in the ring finger and thumb. It is a tendon-sheath rather than a tendon problem.
  • Strongly associated with diabetes mellitus (and thyroid disease, rheumatoid arthritis, amyloidosis, gout, and carpal tunnel syndrome). Diabetic patients have more severe, multi-digit disease and respond less well to injection.
  • Corticosteroid injection is first-line, with success of roughly 60–90% in non-diabetics after one or two injections; success is materially lower in diabetics (~50%) and in long-standing disease, multi-digit involvement, and young patients. Expect a transient rise in blood glucose for several days after injection in diabetics and counsel accordingly.
  • Surgical release (open or percutaneous) of the A1 pulley has >95% success. Do not release the A1 pulley of the thumb without care for the radial digital nerve, which crosses obliquely and superficially at the level of the A1 pulley. In rheumatoid arthritis, do not release the A1 pulley — it accelerates ulnar drift; perform a flexor tenosynovectomy and/or FDS slip resection instead.
  • Paediatric trigger thumb is a distinct entity: a fixed IP flexion deformity with a palpable Notta's node, usually presenting at 1–3 years; a proportion resolve spontaneously, and release is highly successful if needed.
  • Persistent triggering after release suggests an incomplete release, a retained FDS slip, or triggering at another level.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Hand.
  • Ryzewicz M, Wolf JM. Trigger digits: principles, management, and complications. J Hand Surg Am 2006.
  • Baumgarten KM et al. Corticosteroid injection in diabetic patients with trigger finger. JBJS Am 2007.
  • Fiorini HJ et al. Surgery for trigger finger. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018.
1question

Wrist arthroscopy & ulnar-sided wrist pain

A structured approach to the ulnar-sided wrist.

1 of 7 sittings2021

  • Ulnar-sided wrist pain is the 'low back pain of the wrist'. Differential: TFCC tear, ulnocarpal impaction, DRUJ instability/arthritis, LT ligament injury, ECU tendinitis or subluxation, pisotriquetral arthritis, hook of hamate fracture, ulnar artery thrombosis, ulnar nerve compression.
  • Localise by anatomy: dorsal-ulnar → ECU, DRUJ, TFCC dorsal; volar-ulnar → pisotriquetral, FCU, ulnar artery/nerve, hook of hamate, LT; central → TFCC/ulnocarpal impaction.
  • Provocative tests: fovea sign (tenderness in the soft spot between the ulnar styloid and FCU — highly sensitive for foveal TFCC/LT pathology), ulnocarpal stress test (axial load with ulnar deviation and rotation), piano key/ballottement for DRUJ instability, and the ECU synergy test for ECU tendinitis.
  • For a baseball player with volar-ulnar wrist pain and a negative ECU examination, the next step is dedicated imaging — MRI (ideally arthrogram) — and consideration of hook of hamate fracture (CT) and pisotriquetral pathology; wrist arthroscopy is the diagnostic gold standard for intra-articular pathology when imaging is equivocal.
  • Wrist arthroscopy allows direct assessment of the TFCC (the 'trampoline test' and 'hook test' for foveal detachment), the SL and LT interosseous ligaments (Geissler grading I–IV), and cartilage. Radiocarpal portals are named for their relationship to the extensor compartments (3-4, 4-5, 6R, 6U); the 6U portal risks the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve.
  • Treatment follows the diagnosis: peripheral TFCC tears are repaired; central tears are débrided; ulnocarpal impaction is treated by ulnar shortening; DRUJ instability by foveal repair.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Wrist and Hand: Wrist.
  • Tay SC et al. The 'ulnar fovea sign' for defining ulnar wrist pain. J Hand Surg Am 2007.
  • Geissler WB et al. Intracarpal soft-tissue lesions associated with an intra-articular fracture of the distal end of the radius. JBJS Am 1996.
  • Sachar K. Ulnar-sided wrist pain: evaluation and treatment. J Hand Surg Am 2012.
