8questions

Distal humerus fracture: ORIF vs total elbow arthroplasty

Fixation principles, the elderly distal humerus, and when to choose arthroplasty.

6 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 (x2), 2024F (x2), 2025

  • Fixation principles (O'Driscoll): place as many screws as possible in the distal fragments, each screw should engage a fragment on the opposite side, all screws should lock the columns together, use long screws that pass through a plate and engage the other column, and achieve plate fixation on both columns with plates that are strong enough not to fail before union. Parallel versus perpendicular (orthogonal) plating are both acceptable; parallel plating allows longer distal screws.
  • Olecranon osteotomy is required for adequate visualisation of a complex intra-articular (AO type C) fracture — a chevron (apex distal) osteotomy at the bare area of the trochlear notch, pre-drilled and pre-tapped before osteotomising, exposing ~57% of the articular surface. Complications: nonunion, symptomatic hardware (very common — up to 30–50% require removal), and the osteotomy precludes conversion to total elbow arthroplasty in the same setting.
  • Identify and protect the ulnar nerve routinely in every distal humerus ORIF. Whether to transpose is debated — some evidence suggests in-situ decompression has a lower rate of post-operative ulnar neuritis than routine transposition — but identification is mandatory.
  • Elderly, comminuted, intra-articular distal humerus fracture: total elbow arthroplasty (TEA) gives better and more predictable early function and Mayo Elbow Performance Scores than ORIF, with a lower reoperation rate in the RCT literature (McKee, Canadian). It is best for low-demand patients over ~65 with osteoporotic comminution or pre-existing inflammatory arthritis. The permanent trade-off is a lifetime lifting restriction (roughly 2–5 kg single-event, 1–2 kg repetitive).
  • TEA is contraindicated in the young, high-demand patient, in the presence of active infection, and with an absent/incompetent triceps. Distal humeral hemiarthroplasty is an alternative for a coronal shear/articular fracture with intact columns.
  • Non-operative treatment ('bag of bones') in a frail, unfit elderly patient can give a surprisingly functional, painless pseudarthrosis with acceptable ROM, though strength and stability are poor — it remains a legitimate option when surgery is unsafe.
  • Fishtail deformity is a late paediatric complication of a distal humerus fracture (usually a lateral condyle, supracondylar or T-condylar fracture, or AVN of the medial trochlear ossification centre) producing a central defect in the trochlea. It is generally asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic, is not associated with progressive cubitus varus, and is usually a radiographic finding requiring no treatment.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma: Distal Humerus; Shoulder and Elbow: Elbow.
  • McKee MD, Veillette CJH, Hall JA et al. (Canadian) A multicenter, prospective, randomized, controlled trial of open reduction–internal fixation versus total elbow arthroplasty for displaced intra-articular distal humeral fractures in elderly patients. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2009.
  • O'Driscoll SW. Optimizing stability in distal humeral fracture fixation. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2005.
  • Sanchez-Sotelo J, Torchia ME, O'Driscoll SW. Complex distal humeral fractures: internal fixation with a principle-based parallel-plate technique. JBJS Am 2007.
  • Nauth A, McKee MD et al. Distal humeral fractures in adults. JBJS Am 2011.
6questions

Radial head fracture & arthroplasty (overstuffing)

Mason classification, ORIF vs replacement, and detecting an overstuffed implant.

5 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2022, 2024S, 2024F

  • Mason classification: I — non-displaced/minimally displaced (<2 mm); II — displaced partial articular; III — comminuted whole-head; IV — with elbow dislocation. Treatment: Mason I — early motion; Mason II — ORIF if displaced and blocking motion; Mason III — replacement (or ORIF if 3 or fewer simple fragments).
  • Radial head excision alone is acceptable only in the isolated, stable elbow with an intact MCL, interosseous membrane and no coronoid injury. In the setting of instability (terrible triad, Essex-Lopresti, MCL injury) excision causes proximal radial migration, valgus instability and wrist pain.
  • Detecting overstuffing is a repeated stem: the most reliable radiographic sign is incongruity/asymmetric widening of the ulnohumeral (medial) joint space on a true AP view — the lateral aspect of the ulnohumeral joint 'gaps' or the joint becomes asymmetric. Comparison with the contralateral elbow is helpful. Intra-operatively, use the lateral edge of the coronoid (the proximal margin of the lesser sigmoid notch) as the reference for the height of the native radial head, and check that the ulnohumeral joint is congruent.
  • Consequences of overstuffing (as little as 2.5 mm, certainly 4 mm): capitellar cartilage wear/erosion, loss of terminal extension, painful stiffness, and eventual radiocapitellar arthritis. Under-stuffing causes instability.
  • Persistent posterolateral instability after radial head arthroplasty, with the elbow dislocating in supination, suggests: unrepaired LCL/LUCL, an under-sized (short) implant, an unaddressed coronoid fracture, or a malaligned/loose implant. Overstuffing is not a cause of persistent dislocation — it causes stiffness — the classic 'all are potential causes except' answer.
  • Essex-Lopresti injury: radial head fracture + interosseous membrane rupture + DRUJ disruption. Always examine the wrist in a patient with a radial head fracture; excision here is disastrous.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma: Radial Head.
  • Athwal GS, King GJW et al. (Canadian) Radial head arthroplasty: overstuffing. J Hand Surg Am 2009 / J Shoulder Elbow Surg.
  • Frank SG, Grewal R, Johnson J, Faber KJ, King GJW, Athwal GS. Determination of correct implant size in radial head arthroplasty to avoid overlengthening. JBJS Am 2009.
  • Ring D, Quintero J, Jupiter JB. Open reduction and internal fixation of fractures of the radial head. JBJS Am 2002.
6questions

Terrible triad & complex elbow instability

The three-component injury and its stepwise surgical algorithm.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2022 (x2), 2023 (x2), 2025

  • The terrible triad = elbow dislocation + radial head fracture + coronoid fracture. It results from a valgus–posterolateral rotatory mechanism, so the soft-tissue injury proceeds lateral to medial, beginning with the LUCL.
  • Surgical algorithm from deep to superficial: (1) fix or replace the radial head (it is the critical secondary valgus stabiliser and a key restraint to posterolateral instability); (2) address the coronoid — a type I (tip) fracture often does not require fixation once the radial head and LCL are restored, whereas type II/III (>50%, or an anteromedial facet fracture) must be fixed; (3) repair the LCL/LUCL to the isometric point on the lateral epicondyle — this is the single most important step; (4) assess stability, and only then consider MCL repair or a hinged external fixator.
  • In an elderly patient with a terrible triad, the structure least likely to require fixation is the small coronoid tip fragment — a repeatedly tested point. The radial head and LCL take priority.
  • Repair or replace the radial head; excision alone is contraindicated in this setting because it removes the key stabiliser. If the head is unreconstructible (>3 fragments), replace it.
  • Protect the LUCL during any lateral approach: it originates from the isometric point at the centre of the capitellum on the lateral epicondyle and inserts on the crista supinatoris of the ulna. Dissection must remain anterior to the midaxis (equator) of the radial head and the forearm should be pronated to move the PIN away.
  • Post-operative protocol: early motion in a stable arc, with the forearm in pronation if the LCL was repaired (and supination if the MCL was the primary repair), overhead active motion to use gravity as a stabiliser, and avoidance of varus stress. Persistent instability after all three steps warrants a hinged external fixator or internal joint stabiliser.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma: Elbow.
  • Pugh DMW, Wild LM, Schemitsch EH, King GJW, McKee MD (Canadian). Standard surgical protocol to treat elbow dislocations with radial head and coronoid fractures. JBJS Am 2004.
  • Ring D, Jupiter JB, Zilberfarb J. Posterior dislocation of the elbow with fractures of the radial head and coronoid. JBJS Am 2002.
  • Mathew PK, Athwal GS, King GJW. Terrible triad injury of the elbow: current concepts. JAAOS 2009.
5questions

Distal biceps tendon rupture & repair

Diagnosis, one- vs two-incision technique, and the consequences of non-operative treatment.

5 of 7 sittings2021, 2023, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • Mechanism: eccentric load on a flexed, supinated elbow, typically in a man in the 4th–5th decade; smoking and anabolic steroid use are risk factors. The tendon usually ruptures from the radial tuberosity.
  • Diagnosis: the hook test (the examiner cannot hook a finger under the lateral edge of the tendon in the antecubital fossa with the elbow flexed 90° and supinated) is the most accurate physical test (near 100% sensitivity/specificity in the original series). An intact lacertus fibrosus limits retraction and may mask the deformity ('reverse Popeye' with proximal migration is more obvious when the lacertus tears).
  • Non-operative treatment leaves a predictable deficit: roughly 40–50% loss of supination strength and endurance, and ~30% loss of flexion strength, with cramping and fatigue on repetitive rotation. Supination is affected more than flexion — this is what a patient must be told before choosing non-operative management.
  • One-incision (anterior) technique uses suture anchors/cortical button/interference screw through a single anterior approach — the principal risk is lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve neurapraxia (the most common complication overall) and PIN injury if dissection strays around the radial neck (keep the forearm supinated and avoid retractors around the neck; place retractors subperiosteally).
  • Two-incision (Boyd-Anderson, modified muscle-splitting) technique reduces anterior neurovascular risk but historically carried a risk of proximal radioulnar synostosis and heterotopic ossification; the modified muscle-splitting approach (avoiding subperiosteal exposure of the ulna) has largely mitigated this. Comparative studies show similar strength; the one-incision technique has more transient nerve symptoms, the two-incision technique more HO.
  • Anatomic footprint restoration on the posterior-ulnar aspect of the radial tuberosity maximises the supination moment arm. Chronic ruptures (>4–6 weeks) with retraction may require a graft (Achilles or semitendinosus).
  • Heterotopic ossification/synostosis is the classic complication associated with distal biceps repair — the exam 'all are true except' often hinges on which technique carries which risk.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Elbow.
  • O'Driscoll SW, Goncalves LB, Dietz P. The hook test for distal biceps tendon avulsion. AJSM 2007.
  • Grewal R, Athwal GS, MacDermid JC, Faber KJ, Drosdowech DS, King GJW (Canadian). Single versus double-incision technique for the repair of acute distal biceps tendon ruptures: a randomized clinical trial. JBJS Am 2012.
  • Baker BE, Bierwagen D. Rupture of the distal tendon of the biceps brachii: operative versus non-operative treatment. JBJS Am 1985.
  • Athwal GS, Steinmann SP, Rispoli DM. The distal biceps tendon: footprint and relevant clinical anatomy. J Hand Surg Am 2007.
5questions

Medial ulnar collateral ligament injury & Tommy John

The valgus stabiliser of the elbow, diagnosis, and reconstruction.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2023, 2024S, 2024F

  • The anterior band of the MCL is the primary restraint to valgus stress from 20° to 120° of flexion — the functional arc of throwing. In full extension, the primary valgus stabilisers are the bony articulation (olecranon in the fossa) and the anterior capsule, with the MCL contributing roughly one third — the repeatedly tested 'valgus stabiliser in extension' answer is the olecranon/bony congruity (with the posterior band of the MCL contributing in flexion).
  • The radial head is the secondary valgus stabiliser, which is why radial head excision in an MCL-deficient elbow is catastrophic.
  • Diagnosis: medial elbow pain in an overhead thrower during late cocking/early acceleration, loss of velocity and control. Examination — the moving valgus stress test (O'Driscoll) is the most sensitive and specific physical test; the milking manoeuvre and valgus stress at 30° are also used. Stress radiographs and dynamic ultrasound show medial gapping; MR arthrography is the most accurate imaging test for a partial undersurface (T-sign) tear.
  • Valgus extension overload: repetitive valgus with forced extension causes posteromedial olecranon osteophytes and chondral wear in the posteromedial olecranon fossa — an athlete with posterior/posteromedial pain at ball release. Isolated osteophyte resection in an MCL-deficient elbow accelerates MCL failure (remove only the osteophyte, not native olecranon).
  • Ulnar neuritis is common in the throwing athlete because of traction, and must be assessed. Little Leaguer's elbow is the paediatric equivalent (medial epicondyle apophysitis).
  • Reconstruction (Tommy John) uses palmaris longus (or gracilis) in a figure-of-eight (Jobe), docking or DANE-TJ configuration. Return to the same level of play is roughly 80–90%, but return takes 12–18 months. In a non-throwing athlete or a low-demand patient, MCL injury rarely requires surgery. UCL repair with internal brace is emerging for proximal avulsions in young athletes with a faster return.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Elbow; Sports.
  • O'Driscoll SW, Lawton RL, Smith AM. The 'moving valgus stress test' for medial collateral ligament tears of the elbow. AJSM 2005.
  • Jobe FW et al. Reconstruction of the ulnar collateral ligament in athletes. JBJS Am 1986.
  • Cain EL et al. Outcome of ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction of the elbow in 1281 athletes. AJSM 2010.
  • Morrey BF, An KN. Articular and ligamentous contributions to the stability of the elbow joint. AJSM 1983.
5questions

Simple elbow dislocation & posterolateral rotatory instability

The Horii circle, examination for PLRI and treatment of the simple dislocation.

3 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021 (x2), 2025

  • The elbow dislocates in a predictable lateral-to-medial sequence (O'Driscoll's Horii circle): (1) LUCL/lateral collateral complex → (2) anterior and posterior capsule → (3) MCL (posterior band, then anterior band). Therefore the MCL does not have to tear for the elbow to dislocate — the classic true/false item.
  • The LUCL avulses from the humeral (lateral epicondyle) origin far more often than from its ulnar insertion — this is why repair to the isometric point on the lateral epicondyle is the standard.
  • Posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI) is the commonest pattern of chronic elbow instability, resulting from LUCL insufficiency. Tests: lateral pivot-shift test (supination + valgus + axial load with the arm overhead, best under anaesthesia), posterolateral rotatory drawer, chair push-up sign, tabletop relocation test, and the stand-up test. The varus stress test is not a test for PLRI — the classic 'which cannot be used to assess PLRI' answer.
  • Simple (ligamentous) elbow dislocation treatment: closed reduction, then assess stability through a full arc. If the elbow is stable in extension but opens with valgus stress, and remains concentrically reduced, early active motion in a functional arc (with a sling/hinged brace) is the treatment of choice — early motion gives better outcomes than prolonged immobilisation. The Canadian-led multicentre RCT showed early mobilisation is safe and superior to immobilisation.
  • Immobilise for no more than 1–2 weeks; the dominant complication of a simple dislocation is stiffness/flexion contracture, not recurrent instability (recurrence is <2%).
  • Instability that persists after reduction, or a fracture-dislocation, changes the algorithm entirely — those require operative stabilisation.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma: Elbow; Shoulder and Elbow.
  • O'Driscoll SW, Bell DF, Morrey BF. Posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow. JBJS Am 1991.
  • O'Driscoll SW, Morrey BF, Korinek S, An KN. Elbow subluxation and dislocation: a spectrum of instability. CORR 1992.
  • Schreiber JJ et al. An online video investigation into the mechanism of elbow dislocation. J Hand Surg Am 2013.
  • Iordens GIT et al. Early mobilisation versus plaster immobilisation of simple elbow dislocations (FuncSiE RCT). Br J Sports Med 2017.
4questions

Total elbow arthroplasty

Indications, design, and why TEA loosens sooner than TKA.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2024F, 2025

  • Indications: inflammatory arthritis (the historical gold-standard indication), comminuted distal humerus fracture in the low-demand elderly, post-traumatic arthritis and distal humeral nonunion in older patients. Contraindications: young/high-demand patient, active infection, absent triceps/poor soft tissues, and inability to comply with lifting restrictions.
  • Designs: linked (semi-constrained, 'sloppy hinge') — allows a few degrees of varus/valgus and rotation, tolerates ligamentous insufficiency and bone loss; unlinked (unconstrained) — requires competent collateral ligaments and adequate bone stock, transmits less stress to the interface but risks instability. Convertible systems exist.
  • Why TEA loosens earlier than TKA: the elbow is a non-weightbearing joint with a small surface area and a long lever arm — a load applied at the hand generates a large moment at the elbow. Forces across the elbow can reach 3× body weight with lifting. The small bone stock and thin cortices of the distal humerus and proximal ulna provide limited fixation surface, and the constrained/linked articulation transmits torque directly to the cement–bone interface. Combined with the fact that patients use the arm freely, this produces earlier aseptic loosening.
  • Lifetime restrictions are the price of TEA: single-event lifting limited to roughly 2–5 kg and repetitive lifting to 1–2 kg. Patients must be counselled explicitly — non-compliance is a major cause of failure.
  • Complications: aseptic loosening (usually humeral), infection (higher than hip/knee, ~3–5%, and much higher in rheumatoid patients), ulnar neuropathy, triceps insufficiency, periprosthetic fracture, and bushing wear in linked designs.
  • Periprosthetic humeral fracture around a TEA is classified by location relative to the stem (Mayo). Well-fixed stem with a fracture distal/around the stem tip → ORIF with plate and cerclage ± strut allograft; loose stem → revision with a longer stem ± allograft-prosthetic composite.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Elbow.
  • Morrey BF, Adams RA. Semiconstrained arthroplasty for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis of the elbow. JBJS Am 1992.
  • Voloshin I, Schippert DW, Kakar S et al. Complications of total elbow replacement: a systematic review. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2011.
  • Sanchez-Sotelo J. Total elbow arthroplasty. Open Orthop J / JAAOS reviews.
3questions

Cubital tunnel syndrome & ulnar nerve transposition

Sites of compression and the commonest site of persistent symptoms after transposition.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2025

  • Sites of ulnar nerve compression around the elbow (proximal to distal): the arcade of Struthers (~8 cm proximal to the medial epicondyle), the medial intermuscular septum, the medial epicondyle/cubital tunnel retinaculum (Osborne's ligament), the anconeus epitrochlearis (anomalous muscle) and the deep flexor–pronator aponeurosis / FCU fascia (Osborne's fascia between the two heads of FCU). The ligament of Struthers with a supracondylar process compresses the median nerve, not the ulnar — the classic distractor.
  • Presentation: paraesthesia in the small and ring fingers, worse with elbow flexion and at night, weakness of the first dorsal interosseous and adductor pollicis (Froment sign), and — distinguishing it from Guyon's canal compression — loss of sensation on the dorso-ulnar hand (dorsal cutaneous branch) and weakness of FDP to the small finger.
  • The commonest site of persistent or recurrent compression after anterior transposition is the medial intermuscular septum (and the fascial edges/deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis) — if the septum is not adequately excised, the transposed nerve kinks over it. This is the answer to 'most common site of persistent compression after transposition'.
  • Evidence: for idiopathic cubital tunnel syndrome, in-situ decompression gives equivalent outcomes to anterior transposition with less surgical morbidity and fewer complications, and is the preferred first-line operation. Transposition is reserved for subluxating nerves, revision surgery, valgus deformity, and after distal humerus trauma.
  • Endoscopic in-situ release is an alternative. Medial epicondylectomy is an older option with a risk of MCL injury and persistent medial elbow pain.
  • Non-operative measures: night extension splinting (avoid prolonged elbow flexion), activity modification, and nerve gliding — effective for mild/intermittent symptoms without motor deficit. Established intrinsic wasting predicts incomplete recovery.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Nerve Pathology.
  • Bartels RHMA et al. Prospective randomized controlled study comparing simple decompression versus anterior subcutaneous transposition for idiopathic neuropathy of the ulnar nerve at the elbow. Neurosurgery 2005.
  • Palmer BA, Hughes TB. Cubital tunnel syndrome. J Hand Surg Am 2010.
  • Macadam SA, Gandhi R, Bezuhly M, Lefaivre KA (Canadian). Simple decompression versus anterior subcutaneous and submuscular transposition of the ulnar nerve for cubital tunnel syndrome: a meta-analysis. J Hand Surg Am 2008.
3questions

Olecranon fracture & tension band fixation

Tension band mechanics, plate fixation, and the elderly comminuted olecranon.

3 of 7 sittings2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • The tension band principle converts the distracting/tensile force of the triceps into compression at the articular (far) surface during elbow flexion. It requires an intact opposite (anterior) cortex — a comminuted or oblique fracture with anterior cortical comminution will collapse and is not suitable for tension banding.
  • Tension band is appropriate for simple, transverse, non-comminuted (Mayo type IIA) fractures. Technique: two parallel K-wires engaging the anterior ulnar cortex (or intramedullary), a figure-of-eight 18-gauge wire through a transverse drill hole in the dorsal ulna distal to the fracture, knotted on both sides, with the wire deep to the triceps.
  • Tension band with heavy non-absorbable suture (FiberWire) instead of metal wire is increasingly used because symptomatic hardware and hardware removal — the dominant complication of olecranon tension banding, occurring in up to 50–80% of patients — is markedly reduced, with comparable biomechanical strength and union rates. This is the modern answer to 'wire versus suture'.
  • Comminuted olecranon fractures (Mayo IIB/III) require plate fixation — a contoured dorsal plate wrapping over the tip of the olecranon, with a long screw down the medullary canal. Restore the depth of the trochlear notch; do not compress a comminuted fracture (it narrows the notch and causes stiffness).
  • Elderly, low-demand patients with a comminuted olecranon fracture: two strong alternatives to ORIF exist — non-operative treatment (which gives surprisingly good functional results with a painless extension lag in low-demand patients — the Duckworth RCT) and fragment excision with triceps advancement (for fragments involving <50% of the articular surface with an intact coronoid, giving good function and avoiding hardware problems). ORIF in osteoporotic bone has a high complication and reoperation rate.
  • Beware the olecranon fracture that is really a transolecranon fracture-dislocation — the ulnohumeral joint translates with the ulna and the radial head remains aligned with the ulna. The key is anatomic restoration of the trochlear notch.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma: Olecranon.
  • Duckworth AD, Clement ND, White TO, Court-Brown CM, McQueen MM. Plate versus tension-band wire fixation for olecranon fractures: a prospective randomized trial. JBJS Am 2017.
  • Duckworth AD et al. Operative versus non-operative management of olecranon fractures in the elderly: a randomised controlled trial. Bone Joint J 2017.
  • Carofino BC, Santangelo SA, Kabadi M, Mazzocca AD, Browner BD. Olecranon fractures repaired with FiberWire or metal wire tension banding: a biomechanical comparison. Arthroscopy 2007.
3questions

Posterior interosseous nerve & radial tunnel syndrome

PIN compression sites and how to avoid iatrogenic injury.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2023, 2025

  • Five sites of compression in the radial tunnel (proximal to distal): (1) fibrous bands at the radiocapitellar joint, (2) the leash of Henry (radial recurrent vessels), (3) the medial edge of ECRB, (4) the proximal (fibrous) edge of the supinator — the arcade of Frohse, the most common site, and (5) the distal edge of the supinator. The arcade of Frohse is the commonest site of PIN compression.
  • PIN syndrome is a motor palsy — finger and thumb extension weakness with radial deviation on wrist extension (ECRL is innervated proximally, ECU is not) and no sensory loss (the PIN is purely motor after the superficial radial branch departs). Radial tunnel syndrome is pain without motor deficit — tenderness ~4 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle over the mobile wad, pain with resisted supination and resisted middle-finger extension.
  • Radial tunnel syndrome coexists with, and is frequently misdiagnosed as, lateral epicondylitis; injection of local anaesthetic into the radial tunnel that relieves the pain supports the diagnosis. Surgical results for radial tunnel syndrome are less predictable than for a true PIN palsy.
  • Avoiding iatrogenic PIN injury when plating the proximal radius: pronate the forearm to move the PIN away from the operative field (it moves laterally/away with pronation), and release the supinator from its insertion on the radius subperiosteally (staying on bone) rather than dissecting within the muscle. Avoid retractors placed around the radial neck — this is a well-documented cause of PIN palsy.
  • In a paediatric Monteggia with a PIN palsy, the palsy is almost always a neurapraxia that resolves spontaneously once the radial head is reduced — the next step is anatomic reduction of the ulna/radial head and observation, not nerve exploration. Explore only if there is no recovery by ~3 months (EMG at 6 weeks).
  • Complete PIN palsy that fails to recover is managed with tendon transfers (as for radial nerve palsy, but wrist extension is preserved so PT-to-ECRB is unnecessary).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Nerve Pathology.
  • Spinner M. The arcade of Frohse and its relationship to posterior interosseous nerve paralysis. JBJS Br 1968.
  • Lubahn JD, Cermak MB. Uncommon nerve compression syndromes of the upper extremity. JAAOS 1998.
  • Diliberti T et al. Anatomical considerations regarding the posterior interosseous nerve during posterolateral approaches to the proximal part of the radius. JBJS Am 2000.
2questions

Elbow arthroscopy: Portals & nerve risk

Portal anatomy and which nerve is at greatest risk.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2024S

  • Elbow arthroscopy has the highest rate of neurological complication of any joint arthroscopy (transient nerve injury reported in up to 5–10%). Distend the joint before portal placement (this displaces the neurovascular structures anteriorly), flex the elbow to 90°, and use nick-and-spread technique.
  • Portals closest to neurovascular structures: the anteromedial portal (distal, made from inside-out or 2 cm distal and anterior to the medial epicondyle) lies closest to the median nerve and brachial artery — it is the classic answer to 'which portal is closest to a neurovascular structure'. The anterolateral portal endangers the radial nerve/PIN (as close as 3–7 mm).
  • Proximal portals are safer: the proximal anteromedial portal (2 cm proximal to the medial epicondyle, anterior to the intermuscular septum) is the safest anterior working portal — the median nerve and brachial artery are further away (~12–20 mm) and the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve is the structure at greatest risk. The proximal anterolateral portal is safer than the standard anterolateral portal for the radial nerve.
  • Overall, the most commonly injured nerve in elbow arthroscopy is the ulnar nerve in some series (particularly with medial portals, in patients with a subluxating nerve or previous transposition — a previously transposed ulnar nerve is a relative contraindication to medial portal placement without first identifying the nerve), while the PIN/radial nerve is the most commonly injured with anterolateral portal placement and anterior capsular work.
  • Contraindications/high-risk situations: previous ulnar nerve transposition (must identify the nerve first), significant distorted anatomy from prior surgery or HO, and severe ankylosis with a contracted capsule (the nerves lie closer to the capsule).
  • Posterior portals (posterolateral, direct posterior/transtriceps) risk the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve and the ulnar nerve medially.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Elbow.
  • Lynch GJ, Meyers JF, Whipple TL, Caspari RB. Neurovascular anatomy and elbow arthroscopy: inherent risks. Arthroscopy 1986.
  • Kelly EW, Morrey BF, O'Driscoll SW. Complications of elbow arthroscopy. JBJS Am 2001.
  • Stothers K, Day B, Regan WR (Canadian). Arthroscopy of the elbow: anatomy, portal sites, and a description of the proximal lateral portal. Arthroscopy 1995.
2questions

Elbow stiffness, contracture & hinged external fixation

Post-traumatic contracture and the axis of rotation.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2024F

  • The elbow is the joint most prone to post-traumatic stiffness because of its highly congruent articulation, intracapsular ligaments, and the propensity of the brachialis to form heterotopic bone. A functional arc of 30–130° of flexion and 50–50° of rotation (Morrey) covers most activities of daily living, though modern task analysis suggests a wider arc is needed for contemporary activities (e.g. mobile phone use).
  • Contracture is classified as intrinsic (articular — incongruity, adhesion, HO within the joint) or extrinsic (capsular, ligamentous, HO outside the joint). Treatment: static progressive/dynamic splinting first; then open or arthroscopic contracture release (capsulectomy) once the fracture has united and the patient has plateaued (usually >6 months).
  • The axis of rotation of the elbow (flexion–extension) passes through the centre of the trochlea and the centre of the capitellum, seen on a true lateral as the centre of the concentric circles formed by the capitellum and trochlear sulcus. This is the reference point for a hinged external fixator — the fixator's hinge must be aligned precisely with this axis or the fixator will drive the joint and cause pain, subluxation and loss of motion.
  • Hinged fixation is used for persistent instability after ligament repair, complex fracture-dislocations, chronic instability requiring protection during ligament healing, and to protect an interposition arthroplasty. It allows motion while maintaining concentric reduction.
  • Elbow arthrofibrosis with HO is treated by excision once mature; radiation or indomethacin prophylaxis is given afterwards. Neurologic injury (head injury, burns) is the strongest risk factor for elbow HO.
  • During any release, the ulnar nerve must be decompressed/transposed if pre-operative flexion is <100–110°, because restoring flexion tensions a previously scarred nerve and causes post-operative ulnar neuropathy.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Elbow.
  • Morrey BF, Askew LJ, Chao EY. A biomechanical study of normal functional elbow motion. JBJS Am 1981.
  • Cheung EV, Adams R, Morrey BF. Post-traumatic elbow stiffness. JAAOS 2010.
  • Ring D, Jupiter JB. Operative release of complete ankylosis of the elbow due to heterotopic bone. JBJS Am 2003.
2questions

Lateral epicondylitis

Natural history, prognostic factors and the evidence for treatment.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2025

  • Lateral epicondylitis ('tennis elbow') is an angiofibroblastic tendinosis of the ECRB origin — a degenerative, not inflammatory, process (hence 'epicondylosis'). Peak incidence 35–55 years; most patients are not tennis players.
  • Natural history is favourable: 80–90% resolve within 12 months regardless of treatment. This is the single most important counselling point and the basis for a 'wait and see' policy.
  • Factors associated with poor outcome at 1 year: high baseline pain intensity, long symptom duration, manual/repetitive occupational demands, involvement of the dominant arm, coexisting neck/shoulder pain, poor coping/psychological distress (kinesiophobia, catastrophising), and a workers' compensation claim. Psychosocial factors predict outcome more strongly than physical findings.
  • Corticosteroid injection gives short-term (2–6 week) relief but worse outcomes at 6–12 months than physiotherapy or wait-and-see, with higher recurrence — a landmark and frequently tested finding (Bisset, BMJ 2006; Coombes, JAMA 2013). Eccentric strengthening and physiotherapy are the mainstay.
  • Other options: counterforce bracing, topical/oral NSAIDs (short-term), extracorporeal shockwave therapy (mixed evidence), PRP (inconsistent evidence, no clear superiority to placebo in the best trials), and — after at least 6–12 months of failed non-operative treatment — surgical débridement of the ECRB origin (open, percutaneous or arthroscopic) with ~80–90% success.
  • Always consider the alternative diagnoses: radial tunnel syndrome, PLRI, radiocapitellar plica, cervical radiculopathy (C6) and osteochondral pathology, particularly when the pain is more distal or does not respond as expected.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Elbow; Sports.
  • Bisset L et al. Mobilisation with movement and exercise, corticosteroid injection, or wait and see for tennis elbow: randomised trial. BMJ 2006.
  • Coombes BK, Bisset L, Vicenzino B. Efficacy and safety of corticosteroid injections and other injections for management of tendinopathy. Lancet 2010 / JAMA 2013.
  • Nirschl RP, Pettrone FA. Tennis elbow: the surgical treatment of lateral epicondylitis. JBJS Am 1979.
2questions

Triceps tendon rupture

The rarest tendon rupture and its associations.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2025

  • Triceps rupture is the least common of all tendon ruptures. It typically occurs at the olecranon insertion (an avulsion, often with a bony flake) rather than at the musculotendinous junction, from an eccentric load on a contracting triceps or a fall on an outstretched hand.
  • Associations: anabolic steroid use, local corticosteroid injection, chronic renal failure/secondary hyperparathyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, olecranon bursitis and previous olecranon surgery, and (rarely) after total elbow arthroplasty.
  • Diagnosis: a palpable defect, weakness of active extension against gravity, and a 'flake sign' (a small avulsed fleck of olecranon bone) on the lateral radiograph — pathognomonic. A partial tear may still allow active extension against gravity because of the intact lateral triceps expansion and anconeus, so the modified Thompson-type test (extension against resistance with the arm supported) and MRI are needed to avoid missing a tear.
  • Complete ruptures require surgical repair — transosseous suture through cruciate bone tunnels or suture anchors, with an anatomic footprint repair. Delayed repair is more difficult and may require a graft (Achilles allograft or anconeus rotation).
  • Partial tears with intact extension against gravity (<50% of the tendon) may be treated non-operatively in extension splinting for 4–6 weeks, with good results in low-demand patients.
  • Post-operative protocol: protected extension with gradual flexion, avoiding resisted extension for 3 months. Re-rupture and loss of terminal extension are the principal complications.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Elbow.
  • Yeh PC, Dodds SD, Smart LR, Mazzocca AD, Sethi PM. Distal triceps rupture. JAAOS 2010.
  • van Riet RP, Morrey BF, Ho E, O'Driscoll SW. Surgical treatment of distal triceps ruptures. JBJS Am 2003.
2questions

Varus posteromedial rotatory instability

The anteromedial coronoid facet fracture pattern.

1 of 7 sittings2021 (x2)

  • Varus posteromedial rotatory instability (VPMRI) results from a varus + posteromedial rotatory + axial load mechanism, producing a characteristic triad: an anteromedial coronoid facet fracture (O'Driscoll type 2), an LCL/LUCL avulsion, and (in higher grades) an olecranon/posterior bundle MCL injury — but characteristically no radial head fracture, which distinguishes it from the terrible triad.
  • The anteromedial facet of the coronoid is unsupported by the ulnar metaphysis and, when fractured, allows the trochlea to subside into varus — producing rapid, severe post-traumatic arthritis if left untreated.
  • The injury is easily missed on plain radiographs because the joint may look congruent on the AP; look for subtle varus tilt/asymmetry of the ulnohumeral joint on the AP and a 'double density' at the coronoid. CT with 3D reconstruction is essential and is the study that makes the diagnosis.
  • Treatment: ORIF of the anteromedial coronoid facet through a medial (over-the-top or FCU-splitting) approach with a buttress plate, plus repair of the LCL laterally. Non-operative treatment of a displaced anteromedial facet fracture leads to varus collapse and early arthritis.
  • Examination for residual instability includes the varus stress test and gravity varus stress test; post-operative rehabilitation avoids varus stress (no unsupported arm abduction/shoulder abduction with the elbow flexed) and uses overhead motion protocols.
  • The O'Driscoll coronoid classification: type 1 tip (terrible triad); type 2 anteromedial facet (VPMRI); type 3 basal (transolecranon fracture-dislocations, requiring fixation).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma: Elbow.
  • O'Driscoll SW, Jupiter JB, Cohen MS, Ring D, McKee MD. Difficult elbow fractures: pearls and pitfalls. Instr Course Lect 2003.
  • Doornberg JN, Ring D. Fracture of the anteromedial facet of the coronoid process. JBJS Am 2006.
  • Chan K, Athwal GS et al. Can we treat select terrible triad injuries nonoperatively? CORR 2014.
1question

Elbow anatomy & general principles

Carrying angle, articulation and basic kinematics.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • The elbow comprises three articulations in one capsule: ulnohumeral (hinge/ginglymus), radiocapitellar (pivot/rotation and axial load transfer) and proximal radioulnar (trochoid). It is one of the most congruent and inherently stable joints in the body.
  • Normal carrying angle is ~11–14° of valgus in men and ~13–16° in women, measured in full extension with the forearm supinated. Cubitus varus ('gunstock deformity') is the classic malunion of a paediatric supracondylar fracture.
  • Load transmission: approximately 60% of the axial load across the elbow passes through the radiocapitellar joint in extension — which is why radial head excision transfers load to the ulnohumeral joint and to the wrist.
  • The flexion–extension axis passes through the centres of the capitellum and trochlea (see the concentric circles on a true lateral). Forearm rotation occurs about an axis from the centre of the radial head to the fovea of the distal ulna.
  • Primary stabilisers: the ulnohumeral articulation (especially the coronoid and the olecranon), the anterior bundle of the MCL, and the LCL/LUCL complex. Secondary stabilisers: the radial head, the common flexor and extensor origins, and the capsule. Stability requires at least the bony articulation plus one collateral ligament.
  • Range of motion: normal 0–140° flexion, 75° pronation, 85° supination; the functional arc is 30–130° flexion and 50–50° rotation.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Elbow.
  • Morrey BF, An KN. Stability of the elbow: osseous constraints. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2005.
  • Morrey BF, Askew LJ, Chao EY. A biomechanical study of normal functional elbow motion. JBJS Am 1981.
