12questions

Rotator cuff tears: Natural history, repair indications & healing

The single most tested shoulder topic: who to repair, what predicts healing, and the irreparable tear.

7 of 7 sittings2020 (x4), 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024S, 2024F (x2), 2025 (x2)

  • Factors predicting poor healing/worse outcome after repair — the most consistently tested list: increasing age (the strongest single factor), larger tear size and retraction, higher Goutallier fatty infiltration grade (grade 3–4 is the strongest structural predictor of failure), muscle atrophy (Warner/tangent sign), chronicity, smoking, diabetes, osteoporosis and workers' compensation status. Fatty infiltration is irreversible and does not improve after repair.
  • Early/acute surgical repair should be considered for: an acute traumatic tear in a young or active patient (especially with a sudden loss of function), an acute tear with pseudoparalysis, a subscapularis tear, and a tear associated with a shoulder dislocation in a patient over 40. Chronic, degenerative, small tears in older patients can be managed non-operatively first.
  • A medium-sized degenerative cuff tear in a middle-aged patient: multiple RCTs show that structured physiotherapy achieves good outcomes in a majority, but repair reduces tear progression and gives modestly better pain/function scores at 1–2 years; retear rates rise with age and tear size. Non-operatively managed tears progress in size in ~half of patients over 2–5 years, and progression correlates with symptom development.
  • Massive/irreparable tear signs: acromiohumeral interval <7 mm, superior escape/static superior migration of the humeral head, Goutallier 3–4 fatty infiltration, positive tangent sign, tear retracted to the glenoid (Patte 3), and pseudoparalysis. Preserved active elevation is not a sign of irreparability — the classic 'all are signs except'.
  • Massive irreparable tear with pseudoparalysis in a 75-year-old → reverse total shoulder arthroplasty is the most predictable treatment. Options for the younger patient without arthritis: superior capsular reconstruction (SCR) — best for an irreparable supraspinatus tear with an intact or repairable subscapularis and a functioning teres minor, no arthritis, and no static superior escape; latissimus dorsi/lower trapezius tendon transfer for posterosuperior tears; partial repair; débridement/biceps tenotomy; subacromial balloon spacer.
  • Teres minor matters: it is the main remaining external rotator in a massive posterosuperior tear and is critical to a good outcome after reverse arthroplasty. Fatty infiltration of teres minor predicts a poor result from rTSA (persistent external rotation lag, positive Hornblower sign) and may warrant a concurrent latissimus/teres major transfer.
  • The commonest complication of arthroscopic rotator cuff repair is retear/failure of healing (structural failure, 20–90% depending on tear size and age), followed by stiffness. Nerve injury and infection (Cutibacterium acnes) are uncommon.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder.
  • Goutallier D et al. Fatty muscle degeneration in cuff ruptures: pre- and postoperative evaluation by CT scan. CORR 1994.
  • Moosmayer S et al. Tendon repair compared with physiotherapy in the treatment of rotator cuff tears: a randomized controlled study with 5-year follow-up. JBJS Am 2014/2019.
  • MOON Shoulder Group (Kuhn JE et al). Effectiveness of physical therapy in treating atraumatic full-thickness rotator cuff tears. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2013.
  • Mihata T et al. Superior capsule reconstruction to restore superior stability in irreparable rotator cuff tears. Arthroscopy 2013.
  • AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Rotator Cuff Injuries, 2019.
11questions

Reverse total shoulder arthroplasty: Indications, biomechanics & complications

The biomechanics of the reverse, component positioning, and the classic complications.

6 of 7 sittings2020 (x4), 2022 (x2), 2023, 2024S (x2), 2024F, 2025

  • Biomechanical principle (Grammont): medialise and distalise the centre of rotation. Medialisation increases the deltoid moment arm and recruits more anterior/posterior deltoid fibres; distalisation tensions the deltoid. The semi-constrained articulation converts the deltoid into the prime mover, compensating for an absent cuff.
  • Scapular notching (erosion of the inferior scapular neck by the humeral component in adduction) is reduced by: inferior placement of the glenosphere with inferior overhang, inferior tilt of the baseplate, a larger glenosphere, a lateralised glenosphere/bony increased-offset (BIO-RSA), and a more valgus (135°) humeral neck-shaft angle. Superior placement with superior tilt increases notching and baseplate failure.
  • Lateralisation improves rotation, reduces notching and improves the wrapping/tension of the remaining cuff, but increases stress at the baseplate–bone interface and on the acromion (raising the risk of acromial/scapular spine fracture) and increases deltoid tension.
  • Instability is the commonest early complication. Contributing factors: subscapularis deficiency, insufficient deltoid tension (under-lengthening), component malposition (excessive humeral retroversion or a superiorly placed glenosphere), a lateral offset humeral tray, soft-tissue impingement and a poor deltoid. Measures that improve stability: increasing the glenosphere diameter, inferior positioning, adequate deltoid tension/lengthening, a more constrained/deeper humeral liner, and repairing the subscapularis where possible.
  • Scapular spine and acromial stress fractures (Levy classification) occur in ~1–10%; risk factors are osteoporosis, rheumatoid arthritis, female sex, greater lengthening/distalisation, excessive lateralisation, and superior baseplate screw placement penetrating the scapular spine. Presentation is new pain and loss of elevation months after a successful arthroplasty — the classic 5-year post-rTSA scenario.
  • Anterior instability in an rTSA is associated with subscapularis insufficiency, insufficient tension, and component malposition; glenosphere lateralisation is protective, not causative — a common 'which is not associated' item.
  • Stress on the acromion in abduction is decreased by reducing lateralisation and by avoiding excessive distalisation; healing of the tuberosities in a reverse for fracture improves external rotation specifically (and functional outcome scores), which is why tuberosity repair is emphasised in fracture arthroplasty.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder.
  • Boileau P, Watkinson DJ, Hatzidakis AM, Balg F (Canadian co-author). Grammont reverse prosthesis: design, rationale, and biomechanics. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2005.
  • Gutiérrez S et al. Biomechanical comparison of component position and hardware failure in the reverse shoulder prosthesis. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2007/2008.
  • Levy JC et al. Classification of postoperative acromial fractures following reverse shoulder arthroplasty. JBJS Am 2013.
  • Werner CML et al. Treatment of painful pseudoparesis due to irreparable rotator cuff dysfunction with the Delta III reverse-ball-and-socket total shoulder prosthesis. JBJS Am 2005.
8questions

Anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty: Glenoid, subscapularis & outcomes

Glenoid component choice, the Walch classification, subscapularis management and technical errors.

6 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024S, 2024F (x2)

  • The all-polyethylene cemented pegged glenoid component has the best long-term survivorship and lowest revision rate in registry and clinical data, and is the standard answer to 'best glenoid component for anatomic TSA'. Pegged designs outperform keeled; metal-backed glenoids have a substantially higher failure rate (polyethylene dissociation, backside wear, osteolysis) and have largely been abandoned.
  • Glenoid loosening is the commonest cause of failure of an anatomic TSA. Radiolucent lines are common; the key risk factors are eccentric (posterior) wear, retroversion, an unbalanced/eccentric load ('rocking horse' phenomenon from superior migration in cuff deficiency), and inadequate bone preparation.
  • Anatomic TSA is contraindicated in rotator cuff arthropathy — the unopposed superior pull of the deltoid produces superior migration and eccentric superior loading of the glenoid, generating a rocking-horse mechanism that causes early glenoid loosening. This is the reason a reverse is used instead.
  • Walch classification of glenoid morphology: A1/A2 concentric (A2 with medial erosion); B1 posterior joint-space narrowing with sclerosis/osteophytes; B2 biconcave with a posteriorly worn neoglenoid; B3 monoconcave with posterior wear and >15° retroversion or >70% posterior humeral head subluxation; C dysplastic (retroversion >25°); D anteverted/anterior subluxation. B2/B3 are the technical challenge — options include eccentric reaming (limited, loses bone), augmented glenoid components, bone grafting, and reverse arthroplasty.
  • Improving glenoid exposure: complete inferior capsular release, release of the subscapularis with the anterior capsule, humeral head resection first, removal of inferior humeral and glenoid osteophytes, adequate retractor placement, and releasing/mobilising the long head of biceps and the superior capsule. Excessive external rotation of the arm actually worsens exposure — internal rotation and adduction with posterior levering deliver the glenoid.
  • Subscapularis management: lesser tuberosity osteotomy, subscapularis peel and subscapularis tenotomy all give comparable clinical outcomes in randomised and comparative studies; the lesser tuberosity osteotomy heals bone-to-bone and may improve the belly-press/lift-off, but no technique is clearly superior. Whichever is used, protect the repair for 6 weeks and avoid active internal rotation and passive external rotation beyond the intra-operative safe zone.
  • Oversizing/anteriorly offsetting the humeral head overstuffs the joint: it over-tensions the anterior soft tissues, decreases external rotation, increases joint reaction force, risks subscapularis failure, and accelerates glenoid wear — the answer to 'what is the risk of implanting an oversized humeral component anteriorly'.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder.
  • Walch G et al. Morphologic study of the glenoid in primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis. J Arthroplasty 1999; Bercik MJ et al. modified Walch classification. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2016.
  • Bohsali KI, Wirth MA, Rockwood CA. Complications of total shoulder arthroplasty. JBJS Am 2006/2017.
  • Lapner PLC, Sabri E, Rakhra K, Bell K, Athwal GS (Canadian). Comparison of lesser tuberosity osteotomy to subscapularis peel in shoulder arthroplasty: a randomized controlled trial. JBJS Am 2012.
  • Papadonikolakis A, Matsen FA. Metal-backed glenoid components have a higher rate of failure and fail by different modes in comparison with all-polyethylene components. JBJS Am 2014.
7questions

Anterior shoulder instability & glenoid bone loss

Risk factors for recurrence, the glenoid track, and choosing a procedure.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2024S, 2024F (x2), 2025 (x2)

  • Risk factors for recurrent instability after a first-time anterior dislocation: young age (the strongest — under 20 years carries up to 80–90% recurrence), male sex, participation in contact/collision or overhead sport, ligamentous laxity/hyperlaxity, and glenoid or humeral bone loss. A first dislocation over the age of 40 is more likely to be associated with a rotator cuff tear than with recurrence.
  • The best predictor of glenoid bone loss is the number of dislocation episodes/recurrent instability events — bone loss is progressive with each event. Imaging assessment: 3D CT with the humeral head digitally subtracted is the gold standard for quantifying glenoid bone loss (best-fit circle method on the en-face view); MRI is reasonable but less precise.
  • Glenoid track concept (Yamamoto/Di Giacomo): the glenoid track ≈ 83% of the glenoid diameter minus the glenoid bone loss. If the Hill-Sachs interval exceeds the track it is 'off-track' (engaging) and needs to be addressed; if it lies within the track it is 'on-track'.
  • Treatment algorithm: <13–15% glenoid bone loss with an on-track Hill-Sachs → arthroscopic Bankart repair (a 7% loss with a small on-track lesion is comfortably in this group — the answer to that stem). 13–20% (subcritical) with an off-track lesion → Bankart plus remplissage, or a bone procedure; >20–25% ('critical') → bone block procedure (Latarjet/coracoid transfer or free bone graft — distal tibial allograft, iliac crest).
  • The Latarjet works by three mechanisms: the bone block increasing the glenoid arc, the sling effect of the conjoint tendon across the subscapularis, and repair of the capsule to the CA ligament stump. Risks: neurovascular injury (musculocutaneous and axillary nerves), graft nonunion/resorption, hardware problems and later arthritis. Recurrence after Latarjet is low (~5%).
  • Distal tibial osteoarticular allograft is an alternative for revision/large defects — it restores an articular cartilage surface and a matching radius of curvature. Fresh-frozen (non-irradiated) allograft is preferred over irradiated allograft: irradiation (particularly >25 kGy) degrades collagen crosslinks, reduces mechanical strength and impairs incorporation, with higher graft failure. Fresh-frozen grafts retain better biomechanical properties, at a theoretically higher (still very low) disease-transmission risk.
  • Posterior instability is far less common, usually atraumatic/repetitive (blocking lineman, bench press) or from a seizure/electrocution. It presents with pain rather than frank instability, is associated with glenoid retroversion and dysplasia, and a posterior labral (reverse Bankart) tear. The mechanism of a traumatic posterior dislocation is a fall on an outstretched, flexed, adducted and internally rotated arm.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder.
  • Di Giacomo G, Itoi E, Burkhart SS. Evolving concept of bipolar bone loss and the Hill-Sachs lesion: from 'engaging/non-engaging' to 'on-track/off-track'. Arthroscopy 2014.
  • Burkhart SS, De Beer JF. Traumatic glenohumeral bone defects and their relationship to failure of arthroscopic Bankart repairs. Arthroscopy 2000.
  • Balg F, Boileau P. The instability severity index score. JBJS Br 2007.
  • Provencher MT et al. Distal tibia allograft for anterior shoulder instability. Arthroscopy / AJSM.
  • Hurley ET, Mullett H et al. Arthroscopic Bankart repair versus conservative management for first-time traumatic anterior shoulder instability: a systematic review. Arthroscopy 2020.
6questions

Glenoid dysplasia & shoulder examination

Glenoid dysplasia, and the physical examination of the rotator cuff and instability.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2023 (x2), 2024F, 2025

  • Glenoid dysplasia (glenoid hypoplasia) is a developmental deficiency of the posteroinferior glenoid, producing increased retroversion, a rounded/'lazy J' or 'delta'-shaped posteroinferior glenoid, and a hypertrophied posterior labrum that partially compensates. It is often bilateral and frequently an incidental finding.
  • Clinically, most patients with glenoid dysplasia are asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic, but it predisposes to posterior instability and to early posterior glenohumeral arthritis (Walch C glenoid). Management is non-operative in the first instance; posterior bone block/glenoid osteotomy is reserved for symptomatic recurrent posterior instability and carries a high complication rate.
  • Subscapularis examination: the lift-off test (hand off the back, actively lift away) assesses the lower subscapularis and is the most specific; the belly-press test assesses the upper subscapularis and is used when internal rotation is limited; the bear-hug test is the most sensitive for an upper subscapularis tear. Increased passive external rotation is an indirect sign.
  • Supraspinatus: Jobe/empty can, drop-arm sign. Infraspinatus/teres minor: external rotation lag sign, Hornblower sign (inability to hold the arm in external rotation at 90° abduction — indicates teres minor deficiency). Biceps/SLAP: Speed, Yergason, O'Brien active compression, and the most sensitive combination is a positive O'Brien plus Speed/biceps load test — no single test is adequate, and combinations improve accuracy.
  • Shoulder imaging: a true AP (Grashey) shows the glenohumeral joint space in profile; an axillary lateral is essential to assess dislocation direction, glenoid version and posterior subluxation — it is the view most often omitted and the one that identifies a locked posterior dislocation. The scapular Y assesses acromial morphology; the Stryker notch view shows a Hill-Sachs lesion; the West Point view shows anteroinferior glenoid bone loss.
  • Subjective instability can be produced by pathology other than true glenohumeral instability: biceps tendinitis/SLAP lesions, rotator cuff pathology, suprascapular nerve impingement, and scapular dyskinesis/long thoracic nerve palsy — a patient can report a 'slipping' sensation without a structurally unstable joint.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder.
  • Harper KW et al. Glenoid dysplasia: incidence and association with posterior labral tears. AJR 2005.
  • Barth JRH, Burkhart SS, De Beer JF. The bear-hug test: a new and sensitive test for diagnosing a subscapularis tear. Arthroscopy 2006.
  • Hegedus EJ et al. Physical examination tests of the shoulder: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med 2012.
5questions

Acromioclavicular joint injury

Rockwood classification, the vertical stabilisers, and the evidence for operative treatment.

4 of 7 sittings2021, 2022, 2023 (x2), 2024S

  • Stabilisers: the AC ligaments (especially the superior/posterior AC capsule) are the primary restraints to anterior–posterior (horizontal) translation, while the coracoclavicular ligaments are the primary restraints to superior (vertical) translation. The conoid ligament (medial, originating from the posteromedial base of the coracoid, inserting on the conoid tubercle) is the principal restraint to superior/vertical displacement, and the trapezoid resists axial compression and contributes to horizontal stability.
  • Rockwood classification: I — AC sprain; II — AC torn, CC intact; III — both torn with 25–100% superior displacement; IV — posterior displacement into/through trapezius (the axillary lateral view makes the diagnosis); V — >100% displacement (>2× the normal CC distance) with deltotrapezial fascia disruption; VI — inferior/subcoracoid displacement (rare).
  • Types I and II are treated non-operatively. Types IV, V and VI are generally treated operatively. Type III is controversial. The Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society (COTS) multicentre RCT for acute complete AC dislocation (types III–V) found that hook plate fixation produced better radiographic alignment but no clinically important difference in DASH/Constant scores at one year compared with non-operative treatment, with more complications and reoperations (hardware removal) in the surgical group, and non-operative patients returned to work sooner.
  • Because of this, the modern approach to type III is initial non-operative treatment with delayed reconstruction for the minority who remain symptomatic — outcomes of delayed reconstruction are not compromised by an initial trial of non-operative care. Type IIIB (with scapular dyskinesis/persistent symptoms) is more likely to need surgery.
  • Surgical options: anatomic CC reconstruction with tendon graft (modified Weaver-Dunn, or free graft reconstruction of the conoid and trapezoid), cortical button/suspensory devices, and hook plate (temporary, requires removal, risk of acromial erosion/subacromial impingement). Address horizontal instability by reconstructing/imbricating the AC capsule — persistent horizontal instability is a common cause of a poor result.
  • Distal clavicle osteolysis (weightlifter's shoulder) is a distinct overuse entity treated with activity modification and, if refractory, distal clavicle excision. Distal clavicle excision must preserve the CC ligaments and the superior/posterior AC capsule (resect ≤1 cm, less from a direct superior approach).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma: AC Joint; Shoulder.
  • Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society (COTS). Multicenter randomized clinical trial of nonoperative versus operative treatment of acute acromioclavicular joint dislocation. J Orthop Trauma 2015.
  • Fukuda K, Craig EV, An KN, Cofield RH, Chao EY. Biomechanical study of the ligamentous system of the acromioclavicular joint. JBJS Am 1986.
  • Beitzel K et al. ISAKOS upper extremity committee consensus statement on the need for diversification of the Rockwood classification for AC joint injuries. Arthroscopy 2014.
5questions

Scapular winging & long thoracic/spinal accessory palsy

Medial versus lateral winging and its causes.

4 of 7 sittings2021, 2022, 2024S (x2), 2024F

  • Winging is defined by the direction the inferior angle/medial border of the scapula translates, and the standard exam definition is based on the position of the inferior angle of the scapula relative to the midline: medial winging — the inferior angle rotates medially (toward the spine); lateral winging — the inferior angle rotates laterally.
  • Medial winging = serratus anterior weakness = long thoracic nerve (C5-6-7) palsy — the commonest cause of winging. Accentuated by forward flexion/wall push-up. Causes: viral illness/Parsonage-Turner, traction injury, repetitive overhead activity, surgery (axillary node dissection, first rib resection), and blunt trauma.
  • Lateral winging = trapezius weakness = spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) palsy — accentuated by shoulder abduction/external rotation. It classically follows posterior triangle neck surgery (lymph node biopsy), and presents with drooping shoulder, weakness of abduction above 90°, and pain.
  • Timeline and treatment: most long thoracic nerve palsies are neurapraxic and recover spontaneously over 12–24 months — treat with observation, physiotherapy to maintain motion, and brace/scapular stabilisation. Serial EMG at 3–6 months guides prognosis. Failure to recover by 12–24 months → pectoralis major transfer (split sternal head, Eden-Lange for trapezius palsy) or scapulothoracic fusion.
  • The exam scenario: 'a man falls, has neck and shoulder pain, negative radiographs, and returns a month later with winging, weak abduction and lateral arm pain' — this is a traction injury to the brachial plexus/long thoracic nerve (Parsonage-Turner brachial neuritis is the classic mimic). Brachial neuritis (neuralgic amyotrophy) presents with severe pain that precedes profound patchy weakness and has a generally good but slow prognosis.
  • A 17-year-old with medial scapular winging 4 months after a football injury is a long thoracic nerve palsy — the treatment is continued observation with physiotherapy, since spontaneous recovery is the rule at this time point.
  • Pseudowinging can result from a scapular osteochondroma, scapulothoracic bursitis, or painful inhibition — always examine for a bony lesion.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder; Upper Extremity Nerve Pathology.
  • Martin RM, Fish DE. Scapular winging: anatomical review, diagnosis, and treatments. Curr Rev Musculoskelet Med 2008.
  • Kuhn JE et al. Scapular winging. JAAOS 1995.
  • Wiater JM, Flatow EL. Long thoracic nerve injury. CORR 1999.
4questions

Proximal humerus fracture: Management & outcomes

The evidence for non-operative treatment, fixation pitfalls, and arthroplasty.

3 of 7 sittings2024S, 2024F (x2), 2025

  • The evidence strongly supports non-operative treatment for most displaced proximal humerus fractures in older patients. The PROFHER trial (JAMA 2015) found no difference in Oxford Shoulder Score or quality of life at 2 years between surgery and sling treatment for displaced fractures involving the surgical neck in patients with a mean age of 66. This is one of the highest-yield trials in shoulder trauma.
  • Factors that reduce the risk of fixation failure in a 3-part fracture: restoration of the medial calcar/medial hinge support (an inferomedial 'calcar' screw), avoiding varus malreduction (anatomic or slight valgus reduction), repair of the tuberosities with heavy sutures through the rotator cuff to the plate, appropriate screw length avoiding intra-articular penetration, and augmentation (fibular strut allograft) in osteoporotic bone. Varus malreduction and loss of medial support are the strongest predictors of screw cut-out.
  • Bending rigidity of a proximal humerus locking plate construct is most influenced by the working length (distance between the most distal proximal screw and the most proximal diaphyseal screw) and screw configuration/number in the head, plus restoration of the medial column. Increasing plate length alone without changing screw density does not increase rigidity proportionally.
  • Reverse total shoulder arthroplasty is the arthroplasty of choice for a 4-part fracture in an elderly patient with poor bone quality or unreconstructible tuberosities — it is far less dependent on tuberosity healing than hemiarthroplasty. However, tuberosity healing in a reverse for fracture significantly improves external rotation and functional scores, so anatomic tuberosity repair remains worthwhile.
  • Tuberosity malunion after non-operative or operative treatment causes impingement, loss of motion (especially external rotation with a greater tuberosity malunion in >5 mm superior displacement) and pain. It is a difficult problem — options include arthroscopic acromioplasty/tuberoplasty, osteotomy (technically demanding, high complication rate) or conversion to reverse arthroplasty.
  • Axillary nerve injury occurs in up to 30–60% of fracture-dislocations (often subclinical). Deltoid weakness with lateral shoulder numbness after reduction of a proximal humerus fracture-dislocation is an axillary nerve palsy — observe, document, and obtain EMG at 6 weeks; most are neurapraxic and recover. Confirm reduction and rule out ongoing compression first.
  • Post-injury stiffness after a 4-part fracture treated non-operatively with a firm end-feel at 1 year suggests malunion with mechanical block ± post-traumatic arthritis/AVN, rather than simple capsular contracture — CT is required.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma: Proximal Humerus.
  • Rangan A et al. PROFHER Trial: surgical vs nonsurgical treatment of adults with displaced fractures of the proximal humerus. JAMA 2015.
  • Gardner MJ et al. The importance of medial support in locked plating of proximal humerus fractures. J Orthop Trauma 2007.
  • Boileau P et al. Tuberosity malposition and migration: reasons for poor outcomes after hemiarthroplasty for displaced fractures of the proximal humerus. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2002.
  • Handoll HHG, Brorson S. Interventions for treating proximal humeral fractures in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev.
4questions

Sternoclavicular joint injury & posterior dislocation

The posterior SC dislocation — a genuine emergency.

3 of 7 sittings2024S, 2024F (x2), 2025

  • The SC joint is the only true articulation between the axial skeleton and the upper limb, and it is inherently unstable bony architecture stabilised almost entirely by ligaments — the posterior sternoclavicular capsular ligament is the most important restraint to both anterior and posterior translation.
  • The medial clavicular physis is the last physis in the body to close (~23–25 years). Therefore, in anyone under about 25, an apparent 'SC dislocation' is usually a physeal (Salter-Harris I/II) fracture-separation, which has substantial remodelling potential — an important management distinction.
  • Posterior SC dislocation is a surgical emergency because of the retrosternal structures: trachea, oesophagus, great vessels (brachiocephalic/subclavian) and the brachial plexus. Symptoms include dysphagia, dyspnoea, stridor, venous congestion of the arm, or a diminished pulse. CT with contrast (CT angiogram) is the imaging study of choice — plain films (including the serendipity view) are unreliable.
  • Closed reduction of a posterior dislocation must be performed in the operating theatre with cardiothoracic surgery available, under general anaesthesia, using a bump between the scapulae, abduction/extension traction and a percutaneous towel clip on the medial clavicle. If closed reduction fails or the joint is unstable, open reduction with figure-of-eight semitendinosus graft reconstruction is performed. Never use K-wires or Steinmann pins across the SC joint — migration into the mediastinum has caused deaths.
  • Anterior SC dislocation is far more common and is usually treated non-operatively even when it remains subluxed — most patients have minimal functional deficit, and surgical stabilisation has a high complication rate. Recurrent instability is common but usually tolerated.
  • The 'snowboarder with shoulder pain and a posteriorly displaced distal clavicle relative to the acromion' is a posterior AC (Rockwood type IV) injury, not an SC injury — the axillary view is the discriminator. Read these stems carefully: a clavicle displaced posteriorly at the acromion is type IV AC; posteriorly at the sternum is a posterior SC dislocation.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma: Sternoclavicular Joint.
  • Spencer EE, Kuhn JE. Biomechanical analysis of reconstructions for sternoclavicular joint instability. JBJS Am 2004.
  • Groh GI, Wirth MA. Management of traumatic sternoclavicular joint injuries. JAAOS 2011.
  • Laffosse JM et al. Posterior dislocation of the sternoclavicular joint and epiphyseal disruption of the medial clavicle with posterior displacement in sports participants. JBJS Br 2010.
3questions

Clavicle fracture

Predictors of nonunion and the operative/non-operative debate.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2024S, 2025

  • Predictors of nonunion of a midshaft clavicle fracture: complete displacement (no cortical contact), comminution, shortening >2 cm, female sex, advanced age, and smoking. These are also the criteria that identify patients most likely to benefit from fixation.
  • The landmark Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society (COTS) RCT showed that plate fixation of a completely displaced midshaft clavicle fracture produced improved DASH and Constant scores, faster time to union, lower nonunion and symptomatic malunion rates, and higher patient satisfaction compared with sling treatment — at the cost of hardware irritation and the need for removal in a proportion of patients. This is one of the most cited Canadian orthopaedic trials.
  • Subsequent meta-analyses confirm a lower nonunion rate with surgery but show that functional differences narrow by 1 year, so shared decision-making based on displacement, shortening, occupation and patient preference is appropriate. Nonunion rates: ~15–20% for completely displaced fractures treated non-operatively versus ~1–3% with plating.
  • Distal (lateral third) clavicle fractures: Neer classification. Type II (fracture medial to the CC ligaments, with the medial fragment displaced superiorly by the trapezius and the lateral fragment held by the CC ligaments) has a high nonunion rate (up to 30%) and is the type most often fixed. Types I and III are usually treated non-operatively.
  • Fixation options: superior or anteroinferior plating (anteroinferior may reduce hardware prominence and protect the neurovascular structures during drilling), intramedullary devices, and hook plates (for distal fractures; requires removal). A figure-of-eight brace confers no advantage over a simple sling and is less comfortable.
  • Complications: hardware prominence/irritation is the commonest complication after plating (up to 30% request removal); supraclavicular nerve injury causes numbness inferior to the incision (warn patients pre-operatively); rare but serious pneumothorax and subclavian injury during drilling.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma: Clavicle.
  • Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society. Nonoperative treatment compared with plate fixation of displaced midshaft clavicular fractures. JBJS Am 2007.
  • Robinson CM et al. Estimating the risk of nonunion following nonoperative treatment of a clavicular fracture. JBJS Am 2004.
  • McKee RC, Whelan DB, Schemitsch EH, McKee MD (Canadian). Operative versus nonoperative care of displaced midshaft clavicular fractures: a meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials. JBJS Am 2012.
3questions

Shoulder periprosthetic fracture & infection

Periprosthetic humerus fractures and the peculiarities of shoulder PJI.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2024F (x2)

  • Periprosthetic humeral fracture classification (Wright & Cofield): Type A — centred at the stem tip with proximal extension; Type B — at or just distal to the stem tip; Type C — entirely distal to the stem tip. Management hinges on stem stability: a well-fixed stem with acceptable alignment → non-operative treatment (functional bracing) is reasonable for type C and many type B fractures, or ORIF with plate/cerclage; a loose stem → revision to a long-stem implant ± strut allograft.
  • Non-operative treatment of periprosthetic humeral fractures has a reasonable union rate but a prolonged course; ORIF with a long plate spanning the stem, using cerclage cables/locking screws proximally and bicortical screws distally, plus strut allograft in osteoporotic bone, is favoured for displaced fractures and in patients unable to tolerate prolonged bracing.
  • Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes is the defining organism of shoulder periprosthetic infection. It is a slow-growing, Gram-positive anaerobic rod that is a normal resident of the sebaceous glands of the dermis — which is why standard skin preparation does not eliminate it and why it is found in a substantial percentage of 'sterile' shoulder cases.
  • Key clinical points about C. acnes: it causes a low-grade, indolent infection with a normal or only mildly elevated ESR/CRP and no sinus tract, often presenting simply as unexplained pain and stiffness or early loosening. It is far more common in men (greater sebaceous gland density). Cultures must be held for 13–14 days — a 5-day culture will miss it. Multiple (≥5) deep tissue specimens should be taken.
  • Prevention: benzoyl peroxide skin preparation reduces the C. acnes burden; chlorhexidine–alcohol prep, changing the scalpel after the skin incision, and adding vancomycin to prophylaxis are used, though none eliminates the organism.
  • Management of shoulder PJI: coagulase-negative staphylococci and C. acnes are the commonest organisms. Acute infections may be managed with débridement and component/liner exchange with retention; chronic infections require single- or two-stage revision — the shoulder literature increasingly supports single-stage revision with prolonged antibiotics for low-virulence organisms with comparable eradication rates and better function than two-stage.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder.
  • Wright TW, Cofield RH. Humeral fractures after shoulder arthroplasty. JBJS Am 1995.
  • Pottinger P et al. Prognostic factors for bacterial cultures positive for Propionibacterium acnes and other organisms in a large series of revision shoulder arthroplasties. JBJS Am 2012.
  • Nelson GN, Davis DE, Namdari S. Outcomes in the treatment of periprosthetic joint infection after shoulder arthroplasty: a systematic review. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2016.
  • Athwal GS et al. (Canadian) Periprosthetic humeral fractures during shoulder arthroplasty. JBJS Am 2009.
3questions

Throwing shoulder, GIRD & internal impingement

The overhead athlete's shoulder and its adaptive changes.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2024F, 2025

  • The late cocking phase (maximal abduction and external rotation) is the most dangerous position for the throwing shoulder — it generates peak anterior capsular strain, internal impingement of the posterosuperior cuff between the greater tuberosity and posterosuperior glenoid, and peak valgus stress at the elbow.
  • GIRD (glenohumeral internal rotation deficit) is a loss of internal rotation in the throwing shoulder, generally defined as >20° loss compared with the contralateral side (or a loss exceeding the gain in external rotation, i.e. a reduced total arc of motion). It results from posteroinferior capsular contracture and, in part, from humeral retroversion adaptation.
  • Associated with GIRD: posterosuperior (internal) impingement, SLAP/posterosuperior labral tears, undersurface partial-thickness articular-sided cuff tears (PASTA), scapular dyskinesis, and the peel-back mechanism of the biceps anchor. Anterior capsular contracture is NOT associated with GIRD — the contracture is posteroinferior; likewise, a gain in internal rotation, or an anterior labral tear as the primary lesion, are the usual distractors.
  • Treatment of GIRD is non-operative first: sleeper stretches and cross-body adduction stretching of the posterior capsule, scapular stabilisation, and correction of kinetic-chain deficits. A large majority respond. Arthroscopic posteroinferior capsular release is rarely needed.
  • Total rotational motion (IR + ER) should be within ~5° of the contralateral side; loss of total arc is more predictive of injury than isolated IR loss. Humeral retroversion in the dominant arm (an adaptive bony change from repeated throwing during growth) accounts for part of the ER gain and is not pathologic.
  • Little League shoulder is a proximal humeral physeal stress injury (widened physis) in the skeletally immature thrower — treat with rest from throwing for 3 months and correction of mechanics/pitch counts.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports; Shoulder and Elbow.
  • Burkhart SS, Morgan CD, Kibler WB. The disabled throwing shoulder: spectrum of pathology. Part I: pathoanatomy and biomechanics. Arthroscopy 2003.
  • Wilk KE et al. Deficits in glenohumeral passive range of motion increase risk of shoulder injury in professional baseball pitchers. AJSM 2015.
  • Kibler WB et al. Scapular dyskinesis and its relation to shoulder injury. JAAOS 2012.
2questions

Adhesive capsulitis

The natural history, stages and evidence-based treatment of frozen shoulder.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2023

  • Adhesive capsulitis is a fibrotic contracture of the glenohumeral capsule, with the rotator interval and the coracohumeral ligament the primary sites of contracture (limiting external rotation first). Associations: diabetes mellitus (the strongest — up to 5× risk, more severe and refractory), thyroid disease, Dupuytren disease, cardiac disease, and prolonged immobilisation.
  • Histopathologic sequence (Neviaser stages) — the order is repeatedly tested: (1) inflammatory/hypervascular synovitis with capsular hypertrophy → (2) fibroblastic proliferation with synovitis and early adhesion formation ('freezing') → (3) maturation/fibrosis with dense capsular collagen and loss of synovitis ('frozen') → (4) chronic burnt-out fibrosis with resolving stiffness ('thawing'). The pattern is synovitis first, fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition second, then maturation and resolution.
  • Clinical hallmark: loss of PASSIVE external rotation with the arm at the side, in a patient with normal radiographs — this distinguishes it from cuff pathology (where passive motion is preserved) and from arthritis (where radiographs are abnormal).
  • Natural history is self-limiting in most patients over 1–3 years, but a meaningful minority (particularly diabetics) retain some restriction long-term. This is the fundamental counselling point.
  • Treatment: intra-articular corticosteroid injection combined with a home stretching programme provides the most rapid improvement in pain and motion in the early (painful/freezing) phase — the injection is most effective early. Physiotherapy alone is effective but slower; aggressive stretching during the inflammatory phase can worsen symptoms. Hydrodilatation is a reasonable adjunct.
  • For refractory cases after ~6 months of good non-operative treatment: manipulation under anaesthesia and/or arthroscopic capsular release (rotator interval, anterior capsule, ± posterior capsule), with immediate post-operative physiotherapy. Beware humeral fracture and dislocation with MUA in osteopenic bone.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder.
  • Neviaser AS, Hannafin JA. Adhesive capsulitis: a review of current treatment. AJSM 2010.
  • Hannafin JA, Chiaia TA. Adhesive capsulitis: a treatment approach. CORR 2000.
  • Rangan A et al. UK FROST randomised trial: physiotherapy with steroid injection, manipulation under anaesthetic, or arthroscopic capsular release. Lancet 2020.
2questions

Scapula fracture & scapulothoracic dissociation

Operative indications for scapular fractures and the closed forequarter amputation.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2024S

  • Most scapular body fractures are treated non-operatively; they are markers of high-energy trauma (associated rib fractures, pneumothorax, head injury, brachial plexus injury in up to 5–10%). Operative indications include glenopolar angle <22°, medialisation >20 mm, angulation >45°, glenoid articular step >4 mm, or an associated ipsilateral clavicle fracture producing a 'floating shoulder' with significant displacement.
  • The Judet (posterior) approach is the standard for scapular body/neck fractures: the interval develops between infraspinatus and teres minor, elevating the deltoid, with the suprascapular nerve at risk at the spinoglenoid notch (do not retract medially beyond ~2 cm from the glenoid rim) and the circumflex scapular artery at the lateral border. A modified/minimally invasive Judet approach uses the same intervals with less deltoid takedown.
  • Scapulothoracic dissociation is a closed forequarter amputation — a traction injury producing lateral displacement of the scapula with disruption of the musculature, and injury to the subclavian/axillary vessels and the brachial plexus. It is often accompanied by a clavicle fracture, AC or SC disruption.
  • Diagnostic clue: a non-rotated chest radiograph showing lateral displacement of the scapula — measured as an increased distance from the midline (spinous processes) to the medial border of the scapula compared with the opposite side (a ratio >1.29 is suggestive). Massive swelling with a flail, pulseless, insensate limb is the classic presentation.
  • Management: immediate vascular assessment (angiography) and repair of vascular injury, skeletal stabilisation, and neurological assessment. The neurologic injury determines the outcome — a complete preganglionic brachial plexus avulsion produces a flail, insensate limb, and above-elbow amputation with shoulder arthrodesis may ultimately give better function than a flail limb.
  • Mortality is roughly 10%, and complete plexus injury occurs in about half. Early recognition on the trauma chest radiograph is the key exam point.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Upper Extremity Trauma: Scapula; Scapulothoracic Dissociation.
  • Cole PA, Gauger EM, Schroder LK. Management of scapular fractures. JAAOS 2012.
  • Zelle BA, Pape HC et al. Functional outcome following scapulothoracic dissociation. JBJS Am 2004.
  • Oreck SL, Burgess A, Levine AM. Traumatic lateral displacement of the scapula: a radiographic sign of neurovascular disruption. JBJS Am 1984.
2questions

Scapulohumeral rhythm & shoulder biomechanics

Coordinated scapular and glenohumeral motion.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2024F

  • Scapulohumeral rhythm is the coordinated motion of the glenohumeral and scapulothoracic joints during elevation. Overall the ratio is approximately 2:1 (glenohumeral : scapulothoracic) — of 180° of elevation, ~120° occurs at the glenohumeral joint and ~60° at the scapulothoracic articulation.
  • The first ~30° of abduction (the 'setting phase') is predominantly glenohumeral; beyond that the ratio approaches 2:1 and, in the terminal range, the scapular contribution increases further.
  • At 150° of abduction compared with neutral, the scapula has undergone: upward rotation (~45–60°), posterior tilt, and external rotation, with clavicular elevation and retraction and posterior clavicular axial rotation. The scapula does not internally rotate or anteriorly tilt during normal elevation — anterior tilt and internal rotation define scapular dyskinesis, which is associated with impingement, cuff pathology and instability.
  • Muscle couples: the upper trapezius, lower trapezius and serratus anterior form the force couple producing scapular upward rotation and posterior tilt; the deltoid and rotator cuff form the glenohumeral force couple, with the cuff providing a compressive, depressing force that offsets the superiorly directed deltoid vector. Loss of the cuff (massive tear) breaks this couple and produces superior migration.
  • Supraspinatus insertion: it inserts on the superior facet of the greater tuberosity, and typically covers the entire superior facet plus a small portion of the highest part of the middle facet; contemporary anatomic studies show the supraspinatus footprint is smaller and more anterior than classically taught, with the infraspinatus covering more of the greater tuberosity (including part of the superior facet) than previously believed. The supraspinatus footprint does not normally extend onto the lesser tuberosity.
  • The coracoacromial arch provides static superior restraint; releasing the CA ligament in a cuff-deficient shoulder can precipitate anterosuperior escape.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder.
  • Inman VT, Saunders JB, Abbott LC. Observations on the function of the shoulder joint. JBJS 1944.
  • Ludewig PM et al. Motion of the shoulder complex during multiplanar humeral elevation. JBJS Am 2009.
  • Mochizuki T et al. Humeral insertion of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus: new anatomical findings regarding the footprint of the rotator cuff. JBJS Am 2008.
2questions

Shoulder arthroscopy: Complications & portals

Portal anatomy, structures at risk and the complication profile.

2 of 7 sittings2024F, 2025

  • The commonest complication of shoulder arthroscopy overall is transient neurapraxia related to positioning and traction (particularly in the lateral decubitus position with excessive traction, and in the beach-chair position). Brachial plexus traction injuries and, rarely, cerebral hypoperfusion events in the beach-chair position are the recognised positional risks.
  • Portals and structures at risk: posterior portal (2 cm inferior, 1 cm medial to the posterolateral acromion — the 'soft spot') risks the axillary nerve (inferiorly) and suprascapular nerve (medially) if placed too far inferior/medial; anterior portal (in the rotator interval, lateral to the coracoid) risks the musculocutaneous nerve and cephalic vein if placed medial to the coracoid — stay lateral to the coracoid; lateral portal risks the axillary nerve if placed >5 cm distal to the acromion; the 5 o'clock/anteroinferior portal is closest to the axillary nerve and artery.
  • The axillary nerve runs ~5 cm distal to the lateral acromion and passes closest to the inferior glenoid (as close as 10–15 mm at the 6 o'clock position) — this is the reason for care during inferior capsular release and anchor placement.
  • Fluid extravasation causing airway compromise, chondrolysis (historically from intra-articular pain pumps with local anaesthetic and from thermal devices), and infection (C. acnes) are other recognised complications.
  • Diabetes and arthroscopic shoulder surgery: hyperglycaemia is associated with infection, stiffness and adhesive capsulitis. Optimising perioperative glycaemic control (HbA1c and perioperative glucose) is the single most effective way to reduce post-operative complications in diabetic patients undergoing arthroscopic shoulder surgery.
  • Stiffness/adhesive capsulitis after arthroscopic cuff repair is common and is more likely in diabetics, in patients with pre-operative stiffness, and after small tear repairs with aggressive immobilisation — early passive motion protocols mitigate it.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder.
  • Meyer M et al. Anatomic risk of shoulder arthroscopy portals: anatomic cadaveric study of 12 portals. Arthroscopy 2007.
  • Weber SC, Abrams JS, Nottage WM. Complications associated with arthroscopic shoulder surgery. Arthroscopy 2002.
  • Cancienne JM et al. Perioperative hemoglobin A1c as a predictor of deep infection following shoulder arthroscopy. Arthroscopy 2018.
2questions

Suprascapular nerve entrapment

Compression at the suprascapular versus spinoglenoid notch.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2025

  • The suprascapular nerve (C5-6, from the upper trunk) passes through the suprascapular notch beneath the transverse (superior) scapular ligament — remember 'the Army goes over the bridge, the Navy goes under': the suprascapular artery passes over the ligament, the nerve passes under it.
  • Compression at the suprascapular notch affects BOTH the supraspinatus and infraspinatus (weak abduction initiation and external rotation, deep posterolateral shoulder pain).
  • Compression at the spinoglenoid notch (distal) affects ONLY the infraspinatus — isolated infraspinatus atrophy and external rotation weakness, typically painless or minimally painful because the sensory branches to the AC/glenohumeral joint have already departed. This is a repeatedly tested distinction.
  • Causes: a spinoglenoid (paralabral) cyst from a posterior labral/SLAP tear is the classic cause at the spinoglenoid notch; ganglia, traction (overhead athletes, volleyball players), a hypertrophied/ossified transverse scapular ligament, massive retracted rotator cuff tears (traction/tethering), and iatrogenic injury.
  • Diagnosis: MRI shows the cyst and the pattern of denervation oedema/fatty atrophy — which muscles are involved localises the lesion. EMG/NCS confirms and quantifies. Injection of local anaesthetic at the notch can be diagnostic.
  • Treatment: for a paralabral cyst, address the labral tear — arthroscopic labral repair with or without cyst decompression resolves the cyst in most cases; isolated cyst aspiration recurs. For idiopathic compression, arthroscopic or open release of the transverse scapular ligament. Massive cuff tear-associated neuropathy often improves with cuff repair.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder; Upper Extremity Nerve Pathology.
  • Moen TC et al. Suprascapular neuropathy: what does the literature show? J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2012.
  • Piatt BE et al. Clinical evaluation and treatment of spinoglenoid notch ganglion cysts. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2002.
  • Boykin RE, Friedman DJ, Higgins LD, Warner JJP. Suprascapular neuropathy. JBJS Am 2010.
1question

Biceps & SLAP pathology

Diagnosis of SLAP lesions and the tenotomy/tenodesis decision.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • No single physical examination test is adequate for a SLAP lesion. The most useful combination is the O'Brien active compression test plus a biceps-specific test (Speed's or the biceps load II test); combining tests improves specificity substantially. Isolated tests have poor specificity because of overlap with cuff, AC and instability pathology.
  • SLAP lesion types (Snyder): I — fraying with intact anchor (degenerative, usually débrided); II — detachment of the biceps anchor (the commonest surgically treated type); III — bucket-handle tear with an intact anchor; IV — bucket-handle extending into the biceps tendon.
  • The peel-back mechanism (Burkhart) describes posterior type II SLAP lesions in throwers: with the arm abducted and externally rotated, the biceps vector shifts posteriorly and peels the posterosuperior labrum off the glenoid. It is closely linked to GIRD and posterior capsular contracture.
  • Treatment: in patients over ~35–40 years, SLAP repair has less predictable results (persistent pain, stiffness, hardware complications) and biceps tenodesis is preferred for symptomatic type II lesions; SLAP repair is reserved for young athletes, especially overhead throwers (although return to elite throwing is only ~60–70%). Débridement alone is appropriate for type I and for degenerative fraying.
  • Tenotomy versus tenodesis of the long head of biceps: both relieve pain reliably. Tenotomy is faster, simpler, requires no rehabilitation protection, and is preferred in older, low-demand patients — but causes a 'Popeye' deformity in ~20–40%, cramping, and a small loss of supination/elbow flexion strength. Tenodesis avoids the deformity and cramping, and is preferred in younger, thinner or more cosmetically concerned patients and manual labourers.
  • Superior labral variants must be recognised and not 'repaired': a sublabral foramen, a Buford complex (cord-like middle glenohumeral ligament with an absent anterosuperior labrum) and a meniscoid superior labrum are normal variants — repairing a Buford complex causes severe loss of external rotation.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder; Sports.
  • Snyder SJ et al. SLAP lesions of the shoulder. Arthroscopy 1990.
  • O'Brien SJ et al. The active compression test: a new and effective test for diagnosing labral tears and acromioclavicular joint abnormality. AJSM 1998.
  • Provencher MT et al. A prospective analysis of 179 type 2 superior labrum anterior and posterior repairs: outcomes and factors associated with success and failure. AJSM 2013.
  • Burkhart SS, Morgan CD. The peel-back mechanism: its role in producing and extending posterior type II SLAP lesions. Arthroscopy 1998.
1question

Cervical vs shoulder pain differentiation

Sorting out referred neck pain from primary shoulder pathology.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • The single most useful discriminator is the effect of neck movement versus shoulder movement on the pain, combined with the location of the pain: pain distal to the elbow, in a dermatomal distribution, reproduced by neck extension/rotation (Spurling test) and relieved by shoulder abduction (the shoulder abduction relief sign) indicates a cervical source. Pain localised to the deltoid insertion, reproduced by shoulder-specific provocative tests and painful arc, with a normal neurologic examination, indicates a shoulder source.
  • Spurling's test (extension, ipsilateral rotation and axial compression reproducing radicular arm pain) has high specificity but low sensitivity for cervical radiculopathy — a positive test is meaningful, a negative test does not exclude it. It is the highest-yield single manoeuvre.
  • Neurologic findings favouring cervical pathology: dermatomal sensory loss, diminished reflexes (biceps C5-6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7), myotomal weakness that does not fit a single tendon, and symptoms below the elbow. Weakness confined to a specific rotator cuff tendon with a positive lag sign favours the shoulder.
  • Nocturnal pain lying on the shoulder and a painful arc with positive impingement signs favour the shoulder; pain worse with prolonged neck posture, coughing/Valsalva and relieved by the hand-on-head position favours the neck.
  • Both can coexist — the 'double crush' or dual-pathology patient is common in older adults. A diagnostic subacromial or glenohumeral injection is often the most practical way to separate the two: substantial temporary relief localises the pain to the shoulder.
  • Do not forget the red-flag mimics: suprascapular neuropathy, brachial neuritis (Parsonage-Turner), Pancoast tumour, cardiac referral, and cervical myelopathy (gait/balance disturbance, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow; Spine: Spinal Conditions.
  • Tong HC, Haig AJ, Yamakawa K. The Spurling test and cervical radiculopathy. Spine 2002.
  • Rubinstein SM et al. A systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of provocative tests of the neck for diagnosing cervical radiculopathy. Eur Spine J 2007.
  • Manifold SG, McCann PD. Cervical radiculitis and shoulder disorders. CORR 1999.
1question

Inflammatory (rheumatoid) shoulder arthropathy

Recognising the inflammatory glenohumeral joint and its arthroplasty implications.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • The classic radiographic appearance of an inflammatory (rheumatoid) shoulder is central/medial glenoid erosion with periarticular osteopenia, symmetric joint space narrowing, marginal erosions, and an absence of osteophytes — in contrast to primary osteoarthritis, which shows inferior humeral osteophytes ('goat's beard'), posterior glenoid wear, subchondral sclerosis and cysts, and preserved bone density.
  • Diffuse osteopenia with central glenoid wear in an older patient with lupus, rheumatoid arthritis or another connective tissue disease points to an inflammatory arthropathy. Associated rotator cuff tearing is common (up to 25–50% in long-standing rheumatoid disease), which strongly influences implant choice.
  • Arthroplasty considerations: central glenoid erosion with medialisation limits glenoid bone stock and may preclude a glenoid component in an anatomic TSA; rotator cuff deficiency mandates a reverse. Bone quality is poor, so periprosthetic fracture and glenoid baseplate failure are more likely. Infection risk is higher in rheumatoid patients (particularly on biologics).
  • Medication management: continue conventional synthetic DMARDs; hold biologics and schedule surgery at the end of the dosing interval, restarting ~14 days post-operatively once the wound is satisfactory (ACR/AAHKS guideline). Minimise glucocorticoids.
  • The cervical spine must be evaluated before general anaesthesia in a patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis — atlantoaxial instability is common and can cause catastrophic injury during intubation and positioning.
  • Other inflammatory shoulders to recognise: Milwaukee shoulder (rapidly destructive crystalline/basic calcium phosphate arthropathy in an elderly woman with a massive cuff tear and large bloody effusion), and septic arthritis, which must be excluded before attributing an effusion to inflammation.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder; Systemic Disease.
  • Sperling JW, Cofield RH, Schleck CD, Harmsen WS. Total shoulder arthroplasty versus hemiarthroplasty for rheumatoid arthritis of the shoulder. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 2007.
  • Goodman SM et al. 2022 ACR/AAHKS perioperative antirheumatic medication guideline. J Arthroplasty 2022.
  • McCarty DJ et al. 'Milwaukee shoulder' — association of microspheroids containing hydroxyapatite crystals. Arthritis Rheum 1981.
1question

Shoulder arthrodesis

The rare salvage operation, its indications and contraindications.

1 of 7 sittings2023

  • Modern indications for glenohumeral arthrodesis are limited and are largely salvage: complete brachial plexus palsy (particularly with a functioning trapezius/serratus/levator scapulae), paralytic deltoid AND rotator cuff loss, failed arthroplasty with irreparable deltoid or unreconstructible bone loss, chronic recalcitrant infection, and post-tumour resection. It also has a role in refractory instability in patients with neurologic or seizure disorders.
  • Critical prerequisite: functioning scapulothoracic musculature (trapezius, serratus anterior, levator scapulae). Because all post-fusion motion comes from the scapulothoracic articulation, paralysis of the periscapular muscles is the principal contraindication — as is an active infection (relative, staged), and (in most series) the presence of a functioning deltoid and cuff (in which case arthroplasty is better).
  • Optimal position of fusion: approximately 20–30° of abduction, 20–30° of forward flexion, and 30–45° of internal rotation (measured relative to the scapula) — the position must allow the hand to reach the mouth, the midline anteriorly, and the perineum. Excessive abduction causes periscapular pain and winging.
  • Technique: plate fixation (a contoured 4.5 mm pelvic reconstruction plate from the scapular spine across the acromion to the humerus) with compression screws across the glenohumeral joint and cancellous graft; alternatively external fixation or cast in specific circumstances.
  • Expected outcomes: reliable pain relief and stability at the cost of motion; residual elevation is roughly 90–110° and rotation is markedly limited. Patients cannot reach behind their back or overhead easily and cannot sleep prone.
  • Complications: nonunion (up to 10–15%), malposition, periprosthetic/peri-implant humeral fracture (a well-recognised late complication because the fused unit acts as a long lever arm), hardware prominence, and persistent periscapular pain.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Shoulder and Elbow: Shoulder.
  • Cofield RH, Briggs BT. Glenohumeral arthrodesis: operative and long-term functional results. JBJS Am 1979.
  • Rühmann O et al. Shoulder arthrodesis: indications, technique, results. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg.
  • Scalise JJ, Iannotti JP. Glenohumeral arthrodesis after failed prosthetic shoulder arthroplasty. JBJS Am 2008.
