9questions

Talus fracture & avascular necrosis

Talar neck fractures, the vascular supply, and the most-tested complications.

5 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2022 (x3), 2023, 2024S, 2025 (x2)

  • Blood supply: the artery of the tarsal canal (a branch of the posterior tibial artery) is the dominant supply to the talar body, supplemented by the artery of the sinus tarsi (from the peroneal and dorsalis pedis), the deltoid branch of the posterior tibial artery, and dorsal branches from the dorsalis pedis. The deltoid artery is the critical remaining supply after a talar neck fracture — never strip the deltoid ligament medially.
  • Hawkins classification and AVN risk: I (non-displaced) ~0–15%; II (subtalar subluxation/dislocation) ~20–50%; III (subtalar and tibiotalar dislocation) ~50–100%; IV (plus talonavicular dislocation) ~100%. The single most important determinant of AVN is the initial displacement/energy of injury, not the timing of surgery.
  • Anatomic reduction is the most important modifiable factor in preventing AVN and post-traumatic arthritis. Contemporary evidence (Vallier) shows that urgent (emergency) fixation does not reduce the rate of AVN — the vascular insult occurs at the moment of injury. What is urgent is reduction of a dislocation to relieve skin and neurovascular pressure. Definitive fixation can await soft-tissue readiness.
  • Surgical principles: dual (anteromedial and anterolateral) approaches to judge and correct the classic varus malreduction of the neck; a medial malleolar osteotomy if the body needs exposure; and fixation from anterior to posterior with lag or positional screws, or posterior-to-anterior screws which are biomechanically superior. Mini-fragment plates prevent shortening in comminuted necks.
  • The Hawkins sign — a subchondral lucency in the talar dome on the AP ankle radiograph at 6–8 weeks — indicates intact vascularity (revascularisation/subchondral atrophy requires perfusion) and is a good prognostic sign; its absence suggests AVN. MRI is definitive but titanium implants are preferred to allow it.
  • The most commonly associated fracture with a talar neck fracture is a medial malleolus fracture; the Canale view (foot in maximal equinus, pronated 15°, tube angled 75° cephalad) is the dedicated view to assess talar neck alignment and varus.
  • Pantalar dislocation (tibiotalar + subtalar + talonavicular) without fracture — the most common complication is AVN (and then post-traumatic arthritis); a substantial proportion are open injuries. Urgent reduction is required.
  • Lateral subtalar dislocation that is irreducible is most often blocked by the posterior tibial tendon (medial dislocations are blocked by the extensor digitorum brevis or the talonavicular capsule) — the classic pair. Open reduction is required.
  • Posterolateral ankle pain after a healed talar neck fracture suggests os trigonum/posterior impingement or FHL tenosynovitis, or a malunited posterior process.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Lower Extremity Trauma: Talus.
  • Vallier HA, Nork SE, Barei DP, Benirschke SK, Sangeorzan BJ. Talar neck fractures: results and outcomes. JBJS Am 2004; and Vallier HA et al. A new look at the Hawkins classification. JBJS Am 2014.
  • Gelberman RH, Mortensen WW. The arterial anatomy of the talus. Foot Ankle 1983.
  • Halvorson JJ, Winter SB, Teasdall RD, Scott AT. Talar neck fractures: a systematic review of the literature. J Foot Ankle Surg 2013.
  • Canale ST, Kelly FB. Fractures of the neck of the talus: long-term evaluation of seventy-one cases. JBJS Am 1978.
7questions

Ankle arthroscopy & impingement

Portal safety and the impingement syndromes.

5 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2022, 2024S, 2024F (x2), 2025

  • Anteromedial portal — made just medial to the tibialis anterior tendon at the joint line; the structure at greatest risk is the saphenous nerve and greater saphenous vein. Anterolateral portal — just lateral to peroneus tertius; the structure at risk is the superficial peroneal nerve (intermediate dorsal cutaneous branch), which can be identified pre-operatively by plantarflexing and inverting the foot.
  • Because the anteromedial portal is made first (under direct vision, with the anterolateral placed by transillumination/needle localisation), 'what is at risk with the first portal' is answered by the saphenous nerve/vein if the anteromedial is specified, and the superficial peroneal nerve if the anterolateral is specified. The superficial peroneal nerve is the most commonly injured nerve in ankle arthroscopy overall.
  • Posterior ankle impingement — pain in maximal plantarflexion in a dancer, footballer or downhill athlete, caused by an os trigonum or a prominent Stieda process (posterolateral talar process), with associated flexor hallucis longus tenosynovitis (the FHL runs immediately medial to the os trigonum between the posteromedial and posterolateral talar tubercles). Treat with rest, injection and, if refractory, posterior arthroscopic (or open) excision with FHL release.
  • Anterior ankle impingement — anterior ankle pain with dorsiflexion, from anterior tibial and talar neck osteophytes ('footballer's ankle'), soft-tissue/synovial impingement, and anterolateral (Bassett ligament/meniscoid lesion) impingement. Causes include repetitive dorsiflexion, previous ankle sprains and osteochondral injury. Chronic Achilles/gastrocsoleus contracture (equinus) is not a cause of anterior impingement — it limits dorsiflexion but does not create the bony impingement lesion; this is the usual 'which is not a cause' answer.
  • Traction (invasive or non-invasive) improves access to the posterior joint but increases neurologic complication risk; most anterior work is done with the ankle in dorsiflexion without traction.
  • The posterior (prone) two-portal hindfoot arthroscopy technique (van Dijk) accesses the os trigonum, FHL and subtalar joint; the structure at greatest risk is the tibial nerve/posterior tibial neurovascular bundle medially — stay lateral to the FHL, which is the medial 'safety' landmark.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Ferkel RD, Small HN, Gittins JE. Complications in foot and ankle arthroscopy. CORR 2001.
  • van Dijk CN, Scholten PE, Krips R. A 2-portal endoscopic approach for diagnosis and treatment of posterior ankle pathology. Arthroscopy 2000.
  • Talusan PG et al. Anterior ankle impingement: diagnosis and treatment. JAAOS 2014.
7questions

Calcaneus fracture: Approaches & outcomes

The extensile lateral versus sinus tarsi debate, Sanders classification and non-operative sequelae.

4 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2023 (x2), 2024S, 2025 (x2)

  • Sanders classification is based on the number and location of fracture lines through the posterior facet on a coronal CT: type I non-displaced; II two-part; III three-part; IV four-part/comminuted. The number of posterior facet fragments is the strongest predictor of outcome and of the need for later subtalar fusion.
  • Goals of fixation: restore posterior facet articular congruity, calcaneal height (Böhler angle), length, width (decompressing the lateral wall to relieve peroneal impingement) and hindfoot alignment (correct the varus). Restoring the articular surface of the posterior facet is the primary goal.
  • Extensile lateral approach gives the best articular visualisation but has a wound complication rate of 10–30% (higher in smokers, diabetics, open injuries and with early surgery). Sinus tarsi (limited lateral) approach has a markedly lower wound complication rate and allows earlier surgery, at the cost of less direct visualisation of the articular surface and less ability to correct severe comminution/lateral wall widening — the trade-off is the 'consequence' the exam asks about. Both give comparable functional outcomes for Sanders II–III fractures.
  • Timing: wait for the wrinkle sign (usually 10–21 days) with an extensile approach; a sinus tarsi approach permits earlier surgery. Never operate through swollen, blistered skin.
  • The Canadian-influenced literature (Buckley's multicentre RCT, JBJS Am 2002) showed no overall difference in outcome between operative and non-operative treatment of displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures, but identified subgroups who benefit from surgery: women, younger patients, those not receiving workers' compensation, patients with a Böhler angle 0–14°, a light workload, and simpler fracture patterns. Patients treated non-operatively were 5.5× more likely to require a late subtalar fusion.
  • The most common problem after non-operative treatment of a displaced intra-articular calcaneal fracture is post-traumatic subtalar arthritis requiring subtalar fusion, along with loss of heel height with anterior ankle impingement, heel widening with peroneal impingement/subluxation, and hindfoot varus. Late in-situ subtalar fusion of a malunited calcaneus is technically harder and gives worse results than fusion after anatomic ORIF — a distraction bone-block fusion may be needed to restore height.
  • Reported nonunion rate of subtalar fusion in a non-smoker after a non-operatively treated calcaneal fracture is roughly 5–15% (higher with smoking, AVN, prior infection or deformity).
  • The Broden view assesses the posterior facet; the Harris (axial) view assesses heel width, length and varus; the hindfoot alignment view (Saltzman) is the best plain radiograph for hindfoot alignment.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Lower Extremity Trauma: Calcaneus.
  • Buckley R, Tough S, McCormack R et al. (Canadian) Operative compared with nonoperative treatment of displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures: a prospective, randomized, controlled multicenter trial. JBJS Am 2002.
  • Sanders R et al. Operative treatment in 120 displaced intraarticular calcaneal fractures. CORR 1993.
  • Schepers T. The sinus tarsi approach in displaced intra-articular calcaneal fractures: a systematic review. Int Orthop 2011.
  • Griffin D et al. (UK HeFT) Operative versus non-operative treatment for closed, displaced, intra-articular fractures of the calcaneus. BMJ 2014.
7questions

Hallux valgus: Assessment & osteotomy selection

Radiographic parameters, choosing the osteotomy, and the complications of correction.

6 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022 (x2), 2023, 2024S, 2025

  • Radiographic parameters (weightbearing AP): hallux valgus angle (HVA) normal <15°; intermetatarsal angle (IMA) normal <9°; distal metatarsal articular angle (DMAA) normal <10°; and the presence of MTP congruency and sesamoid subluxation. Severity: mild HVA <20°/IMA <11°; moderate HVA 20–40°/IMA 11–16°; severe HVA >40°/IMA >16°.
  • Procedure selection by IMA: distal osteotomy (chevron/Austin) for mild–moderate deformity (IMA <13–15°); proximal or diaphyseal osteotomy (proximal crescentic, proximal chevron, scarf, Ludloff) for larger IMA; Lapidus (first TMT fusion) for hypermobility of the first ray, TMT arthritis, or recurrent deformity; first MTP arthrodesis for severe deformity with arthritis, in inflammatory arthritis, or in a neuromuscular foot. A distal soft-tissue (modified McBride) procedure is combined with bony correction.
  • Troughing is the classic complication of the scarf osteotomy — the dorsal fragment sinks into the plantar fragment, causing loss of correction, shortening and elevation of the first ray. It is minimised by cutting the osteotomy in the correct plane, avoiding excessive translation, and taking care in osteoporotic bone. (Chevron is associated with AVN of the head with an aggressive lateral release; proximal osteotomies with dorsal malunion/transfer metatarsalgia.)
  • Iatrogenic hallux varus is most commonly caused by over-resection of the medial eminence and over-aggressive lateral soft-tissue release (± excision of the fibular sesamoid) with over-tightening of the medial capsular plication — the most frequently cited single factor is excessive lateral release with lateral sesamoid excision/over-correction of the IMA. Over-resection of the medial eminence (violating the sagittal sulcus) is the other classic answer.
  • Risk factors for developing hallux valgus include female sex, positive family history/genetic predisposition (the strongest), constrictive/high-heeled footwear, pes planus and first-ray hypermobility, generalised ligamentous laxity, inflammatory arthropathy, and neuromuscular disease. Hallux rigidus is not a risk factor — it is a separate degenerative entity.
  • The most important determinant of patient outcome after hallux valgus surgery is patient satisfaction/expectation and pain relief with adequate correction of the IMA and restoration of sesamoid position — recurrence correlates with under-correction of the IMA, an uncorrected DMAA/incongruent joint, and failure to address first-ray hypermobility. Sesamoid position is a strong predictor of recurrence.
  • Juvenile/adolescent hallux valgus differs: there is a high recurrence rate (up to 50%) after surgery in the skeletally immature, a high familial incidence, frequently an increased DMAA with a congruent joint, and associated pes planus/metatarsus adductus. Delay surgery until skeletal maturity where possible, and reserve it for pain, not appearance.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Coughlin MJ, Jones CP. Hallux valgus: demographics, etiology, and radiographic assessment. Foot Ankle Int 2007.
  • Robinson AHN, Limbers JP. Modern concepts in the treatment of hallux valgus. JBJS Br 2005.
  • Deenik A et al. Scarf versus chevron osteotomy in hallux valgus: a randomized controlled trial. Foot Ankle Int 2007.
  • Belczyk R et al. Iatrogenic hallux varus: etiology and treatment. Clin Podiatr Med Surg.
6questions

Ankle fracture: Malleolar fixation & weightbearing

Medial malleolus fixation, the posterior malleolus, and post-operative weightbearing.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2023 (x2), 2024F, 2025

  • One screw versus two for the medial malleolus: biomechanical and clinical studies show that a single properly placed screw (particularly a bicortical or a larger-diameter screw with an anti-rotation K-wire) provides fixation comparable to two screws for most transverse medial malleolar fractures. Two screws (or a screw plus a K-wire) resist rotation better in comminuted or vertical shear patterns; a vertical shear (supination-adduction) medial malleolar fracture requires an antiglide/buttress plate, not lag screws alone.
  • Posterior malleolus: modern evidence favours direct fixation (usually via a posterolateral approach with an antiglide plate) of posterior malleolar fragments because it restores the incisura (improving syndesmotic reduction) and the articular surface. Fixing the posterior malleolus restores syndesmotic stability via the posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, and may obviate a syndesmotic screw. The historical '25–33% of the articular surface' threshold has been superseded by attention to fragment morphology (Haraguchi/Bartoníček), syndesmotic involvement and articular incongruity.
  • Fixing the posterior malleolus does not reliably reduce post-traumatic arthritis rates on its own, and it does not eliminate the need to assess syndesmotic reduction — the classic 'results in all of the following except'.
  • Early weightbearing after ankle fracture ORIF: multiple RCTs and meta-analyses show that early (≤2 weeks) protected weightbearing in a removable boot after stable fixation gives faster return to work and better early functional scores without increasing loss of fixation, malunion or complication rates in appropriately selected patients (stable fixation, good bone quality, compliant, non-diabetic). Diabetics with neuropathy, osteoporotic bone, and syndesmotic fixation are treated more conservatively.
  • Weber/Lauge-Hansen: the Weber classification is based on the level of the fibular fracture relative to the syndesmosis (A below, B at, C above). Stability is determined by the medial side — a Weber B fracture with an intact deltoid (no medial tenderness, negative gravity/external rotation stress view) is stable and can be treated non-operatively.
  • Diabetic ankle fractures deserve special caution: higher rates of infection, malunion, Charcot arthropathy and loss of fixation. Use robust fixation (longer plates, more screws, consider transarticular fixation/hindfoot nail in neuropathic patients) and prolonged protection (double the usual immobilisation).
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Lower Extremity Trauma: Ankle.
  • Ricci WM et al. Is after-hours fixation of ankle fractures... / Fowler TT et al. Medial malleolar fixation: a biomechanical comparison. J Orthop Trauma.
  • Smeeing DPJ et al. Weight-bearing or non-weight-bearing after surgical treatment of ankle fractures: a multicenter randomized controlled trial. Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg 2020.
  • Gardner MJ, Brodsky A, Briggs SM, Nielson JH, Lorich DG. Fixation of posterior malleolar fractures provides greater syndesmotic stability. CORR 2006.
  • Bartoníček J et al. Anatomy and classification of the posterior tibial fragment in ankle fractures. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg 2015.
6questions

Syndesmotic injury: Diagnosis, reduction & fixation

The syndesmotic ligaments, radiographic measures, and the malreduction problem.

4 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2022, 2023 (x2), 2024F

  • Syndesmotic ligaments: the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL), the posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (PITFL — the strongest component, contributing ~40–42% of syndesmotic strength), the interosseous ligament/membrane, and the inferior transverse ligament. The AITFL is the first and most commonly injured.
  • Radiographic measures on the mortise view, measured 1 cm above the plafond: tibiofibular clear space <6 mm (the most reliable measure, and the answer to 'what is normal'), tibiofibular overlap >1 mm on mortise (>6 mm on AP), and medial clear space ≤4 mm and not greater than the superior clear space.
  • Plain radiographs and intra-operative fluoroscopy are unreliable for judging syndesmotic reduction — this is the central modern message. CT studies show a malreduction rate of 15–52% after syndesmotic screw fixation, most commonly in the sagittal plane (anterior–posterior translation of the fibula), which fluoroscopy cannot detect. Bilateral CT comparison is the reference standard.
  • Strategies to improve reduction: direct open visualisation/reduction of the incisura, avoiding over-compression with a clamp (clamp obliquity causes malreduction), reducing and fixing the posterior malleolus (restoring the PITFL) when present, ensuring anatomic fibular length/rotation first, and considering intra-operative 3D imaging.
  • Screws versus suspensory (suture-button) fixation: suture-button devices allow physiologic micromotion, have lower rates of malreduction and hardware removal, and better functional scores in several RCTs and meta-analyses, with comparable maintenance of reduction. Screws remain acceptable; the number, size and number of cortices matter less than the accuracy of reduction. Routine screw removal is not mandatory.
  • Indication for fixation: a positive intra-operative external rotation or hook (Cotton) test after fibular fixation, a Maisonneuve pattern, and instability on stress imaging. A Weber C fracture does not automatically require syndesmotic fixation if it is stable after fibular fixation.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Lower Extremity Trauma: Ankle/Syndesmosis.
  • Gardner MJ, Demetrakopoulos D, Briggs SM, Helfet DL, Lorich DG. Malreduction of the tibiofibular syndesmosis in ankle fractures. Foot Ankle Int 2006.
  • Ogilvie-Harris DJ, Reed SC, Hedman TP. Disruption of the ankle syndesmosis: biomechanical study of the ligamentous restraints. Arthroscopy 1994.
  • Sanders D, Schneider P, Taylor M, Tieszer C, Lawendy AR (Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society). Improved reduction of the tibiofibular syndesmosis with TightRope compared with screw fixation: results of a randomized controlled study. J Orthop Trauma 2019.
5questions

Ankle arthritis: Fusion vs total ankle arthroplasty

Choosing between arthrodesis and arthroplasty, and the outcomes of each.

4 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2022, 2024F, 2025

  • Factors favouring total ankle arthroplasty (TAA): older, lower-demand patient; inflammatory arthritis (especially with multiple affected joints/bilateral disease); adjacent hindfoot (subtalar/talonavicular) arthritis or a prior hindfoot fusion (preserving ankle motion protects the remaining joints); good bone stock, neutral or correctable alignment (<10–15° of coronal deformity), and adequate soft tissue; and a patient who values motion.
  • Factors favouring arthrodesis: young, high-demand/manual labourer; neuropathy/Charcot (an absolute contraindication to TAA); active or prior infection; avascular necrosis of the talus; severe uncorrectable deformity; poor soft-tissue envelope; and significant bone loss.
  • Contraindications to TAA: active infection, Charcot neuroarthropathy, severe talar AVN, uncorrectable malalignment, neuromuscular disease, poor vascularity or soft tissue, and severe osteoporosis.
  • Outcomes: contemporary studies (including the Canadian COFAS cohorts) show comparable pain relief and functional improvement between TAA and arthrodesis at intermediate follow-up, with TAA offering better gait mechanics and less adjacent-joint arthritis, and arthrodesis offering greater durability. TAA has a higher reoperation rate but avoids the ~50% rate of subtalar/adjacent joint arthritis seen at 10–20 years after fusion.
  • Late TAA complications presenting as activity-related pain: aseptic loosening and periprosthetic cyst formation/osteolysis (the commonest cause of late pain and revision at 10 years), component subsidence, gutter impingement (medial or lateral — frequently the cause of pain with preserved implant position), polyethylene wear, and infection.
  • Ankle fusion technique: position in neutral dorsiflexion, 0–5° of hindfoot valgus, and 5–10° of external rotation, with the talus translated slightly posteriorly. Malposition (equinus or varus) is poorly tolerated and causes knee and foot pain and lateral column overload.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Daniels TR, Younger ASE, Penner M, Wing K, Dryden PJ, Wong H, Glazebrook M (Canadian, COFAS). Intermediate-term results of total ankle replacement and ankle arthrodesis: a COFAS multicenter study. JBJS Am 2014.
  • Saltzman CL et al. Prospective controlled trial of STAR total ankle replacement versus ankle fusion. Foot Ankle Int 2009.
  • Haddad SL et al. Intermediate and long-term outcomes of total ankle arthroplasty and ankle arthrodesis: a systematic review. JBJS Am 2007.
5questions

Diabetic foot: Ulceration, Charcot & infection

Ulcer healing, Charcot neuroarthropathy and the diabetic foot at risk.

4 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2022, 2024F, 2025

  • The single most important predictor of healing of a diabetic foot ulcer with non-operative treatment is adequate arterial perfusion — assessed by palpable pulses, ankle-brachial index (unreliable in calcified vessels — use toe pressures/TBI), transcutaneous oxygen tension (TcPO₂ >30–40 mmHg) and toe pressure (>30–45 mmHg). Without perfusion nothing heals; with perfusion, offloading heals most ulcers.
  • The other essentials: total contact casting is the gold standard for offloading a plantar neuropathic ulcer; débridement of callus and necrotic tissue; glycaemic control; treatment of infection; and nutritional optimisation (albumin, total lymphocyte count).
  • Probing to bone (positive probe-to-bone test) strongly predicts underlying osteomyelitis. In a recurrent ulcer over a bony prominence that has previously healed with total contact casting and has no exposed bone, the appropriate step is offloading surgery — exostectomy/resection of the bony prominence (or a tendo-Achilles lengthening if equinus is driving forefoot pressure), rather than repeated casting alone.
  • Charcot neuroarthropathy: a red, hot, swollen foot in a neuropathic patient — the great mimic of infection. Distinguishing features: it is usually not painful in proportion to the appearance, and the swelling and erythema resolve with elevation (the 'dependent rubor' test), whereas cellulitis does not. Inflammatory markers may be normal or mildly raised.
  • Eichenholtz stages: 0 (prodromal/inflammation with normal radiographs, MRI oedema), I fragmentation (debris, subluxation), II coalescence, III consolidation/remodelling. The midfoot (Lisfranc/tarsometatarsal, Brodsky type 1) is the commonest location, producing a rocker-bottom deformity with plantar ulceration.
  • Charcot treatment: immobilisation and total contact casting until the inflammatory phase resolves (skin temperature normalises, often 3–6 months), then bracing (CROW boot). Surgery is reserved for unstable/deformed feet with recurrent ulceration or instability — exostectomy for a plantar prominence, or realignment arthrodesis with superconstructs (extended fusion beyond the zone of injury, robust fixation, bone-beam/intramedullary screws) — expect prolonged healing and high complication rates. Bisphosphonates have not shown convincing benefit.
  • Charcot spine (in paraplegia/syringomyelia/tabes) presents with a painless progressive kyphosis or a new spinal deformity with gross destruction, and often requires long circumferential fusion.
  • A puncture wound through a running shoe presenting with a swollen, purulent foot days later must be treated for Pseudomonas aeruginosa — surgical débridement plus an antipseudomonal agent (ciprofloxacin or an antipseudomonal beta-lactam).
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle; Medical Conditions.
  • Rogers LC et al. The Charcot foot in diabetes. Diabetes Care 2011 (ADA/APMA task force).
  • Lavery LA, Armstrong DG et al. Probe-to-bone test for diagnosing diabetic foot osteomyelitis. Diabetes Care 2007.
  • Lipsky BA et al. IDSA clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of diabetic foot infections. Clin Infect Dis 2012.
  • Wukich DK, Sung W. Charcot arthropathy of the foot and ankle: modern concepts and management review. J Diabetes Complications 2009.
5questions

Lisfranc & midfoot injury

Diagnosing the subtle Lisfranc injury and choosing fixation.

3 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2023, 2024F (x2)

  • The Lisfranc ligament runs from the plantar-lateral aspect of the medial cuneiform to the plantar-medial base of the second metatarsal; there is no intermetatarsal ligament between the first and second metatarsals, making this the weak point. The recessed base of the second metatarsal in the mortise between the cuneiforms is the keystone of the midfoot arch.
  • Classic presentation of the subtle injury: midfoot pain and swelling after a twisting/axial load injury (soccer tackle, fall from a horse with the foot in the stirrup), inability to weightbear, and plantar ecchymosis — the pathognomonic sign. Non-weightbearing radiographs are frequently normal.
  • The best next step for a suspected Lisfranc injury with normal non-weightbearing radiographs is weightbearing (or stress) radiographs of both feet for comparison, with a weightbearing CT where available (increasingly the most sensitive practical test). Look for: diastasis >2 mm between the first and second metatarsal bases, the fleck sign (an avulsion of the Lisfranc ligament from the second metatarsal base), loss of alignment of the medial border of the second metatarsal with the medial border of the middle cuneiform on the AP, and loss of alignment of the medial border of the fourth metatarsal with the medial cuboid on the oblique. MRI is useful for a purely ligamentous injury.
  • Purely ligamentous Lisfranc injuries have worse outcomes than bony equivalents and are the group most likely to fail fixation — traditionally treated with primary arthrodesis of the medial two/three TMT joints, which several RCTs (Ly & Coetzee) suggest gives better outcomes and fewer reoperations than ORIF for purely ligamentous injuries. More recent evidence with modern fixation has narrowed this gap.
  • Bridge (dorsal) plating avoids violating the articular surface and provides stable fixation, useful for comminuted injuries; the plate typically requires later removal. Transarticular screws damage cartilage but are lower profile.
  • Anatomic reduction is the key determinant of outcome. Non-anatomic reduction, missed injuries and delayed diagnosis lead to painful post-traumatic midfoot arthritis and planovalgus collapse, requiring salvage arthrodesis.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Lower Extremity Trauma: Foot; Foot and Ankle.
  • Myerson MS et al. Fracture dislocations of the tarsometatarsal joints: end results correlated with pathology and treatment. Foot Ankle 1986.
  • Ly TV, Coetzee JC. Treatment of primarily ligamentous Lisfranc joint injuries: primary arthrodesis compared with open reduction and internal fixation. JBJS Am 2006.
  • Watson TS, Shurnas PS, Denker J. Treatment of Lisfranc joint injury: current concepts. JAAOS 2010.
4questions

Achilles tendon rupture & tendinopathy

The operative/non-operative debate, functional rehabilitation, and chronic ruptures.

4 of 7 sittings2022, 2023, 2024S, 2024F

  • Functional (accelerated) rehabilitation has transformed the management of acute Achilles rupture. The landmark Canadian multicentre RCT (Willits, JBJS Am 2010) showed that non-operative treatment with accelerated functional rehabilitation gives equivalent re-rupture rates, strength and functional outcomes to open repair, while avoiding the complications of surgery (wound problems, infection, sural nerve injury).
  • Key elements of a functional rehabilitation protocol: early protected weightbearing (within ~2 weeks) in a boot with heel wedges, early controlled range of motion (active plantarflexion and dorsiflexion to neutral), and progressive weaning of wedges over 6–8 weeks. Prolonged rigid cast immobilisation in equinus with non-weightbearing is NOT part of functional rehabilitation — that is the classic 'which is not part of functional rehab' answer.
  • Surgery is still considered for: elite athletes (some evidence of faster return to sport and higher plantarflexion strength), delayed presentation (>2–4 weeks), re-rupture, and large tendon gaps. Percutaneous/mini-open techniques reduce wound complications but increase the risk of sural nerve injury.
  • Meta-analyses show operative treatment reduces re-rupture by a few percentage points but at the cost of a significantly higher complication rate; with functional rehabilitation the difference in re-rupture largely disappears.
  • Chronic/neglected rupture management is guided by the gap size after maximal plantarflexion: <2 cm — end-to-end repair; 2–5 cm — V-Y advancement or turndown; >5 cm — FHL (flexor hallucis longus) transfer ± allograft or a combination. A 9-month-old rupture with a 6 cm gap in dorsiflexion and a 3 cm gap in maximum plantarflexion is not amenable to simple end-to-end repair — that is the 'least appropriate' option.
  • Insertional versus non-insertional tendinopathy: non-insertional (2–6 cm above the insertion, watershed zone) responds well to eccentric loading (Alfredson protocol); insertional tendinopathy responds poorly to full eccentric protocols (they aggravate impingement against the calcaneus) — use floor-level eccentrics, heel lifts, shockwave therapy, and consider débridement with Haglund resection and reattachment if refractory.
  • Never inject corticosteroid into the Achilles tendon — rupture risk. Fluoroquinolones are associated with tendinopathy and rupture.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Willits K, Amendola A, Bryant D, Mohtadi NG, Giffin JR, Fowler P, Kean CO, Kirkley A (Canadian). Operative versus nonoperative treatment of acute Achilles tendon ruptures: a multicenter randomized trial using accelerated functional rehabilitation. JBJS Am 2010.
  • Soroceanu A, Sidhwa F, Aarabi S, Kaufman A, Glazebrook M (Canadian). Surgical versus nonsurgical treatment of acute Achilles tendon rupture: a meta-analysis. JBJS Am 2012.
  • Alfredson H et al. Heavy-load eccentric calf muscle training for the treatment of chronic Achilles tendinosis. AJSM 1998.
  • Myerson MS. Achilles tendon ruptures. Instr Course Lect 1999.
4questions

Chronic lateral ankle instability & Broström repair

The modified Broström-Gould, augmentation, and hypermobility.

4 of 7 sittings2021, 2023, 2024S, 2025

  • The anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) is the weakest and most commonly injured lateral ligament, and is the primary restraint to anterior translation and internal rotation of the talus with the ankle in plantarflexion. The calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) restrains inversion with the ankle in dorsiflexion and also crosses the subtalar joint.
  • Modified Broström-Gould: anatomic imbrication/repair of the ATFL (± CFL) augmented with the inferior extensor retinaculum, which is mobilised and sutured over the repair — this is the classic augmentation and the answer to 'what do you use to augment your repair'. It improves strength and adds a proprioceptive/subtalar restraint.
  • Additional augmentation with suture tape/internal brace allows earlier rehabilitation and is used in high-demand athletes, revision, obesity and poor tissue. Non-anatomic tenodesis reconstructions (Chrisman-Snook, Evans, Watson-Jones) sacrifice the peroneus brevis and alter subtalar mechanics and are now reserved for salvage; anatomic allograft/autograft reconstruction is preferred for failed Broström.
  • Assess for hindfoot varus in every patient with recurrent ankle instability. Uncorrected cavovarus alignment is the commonest cause of failure of a lateral ligament reconstruction — a Coleman block test is essential. If the varus does not correct on the block, the deformity is hindfoot-driven and requires a lateralising (Dwyer) calcaneal osteotomy in addition to the ligament reconstruction. If it corrects, the deformity is forefoot-driven (plantarflexed first ray) and requires a dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal.
  • Beighton score (9 points) for generalised joint hypermobility: passive dorsiflexion of the fifth MCP >90° (1 each side), passive apposition of the thumb to the forearm (1 each side), elbow hyperextension >10° (1 each side), knee hyperextension >10° (1 each side), and forward flexion with palms flat on the floor with knees extended (1). A score ≥4–5 in adults indicates generalised hypermobility. Ankle dorsiflexion, shoulder or hip range, and the ability to touch the toes with knees bent are not part of the score — the typical distractors.
  • Hypermobility predicts higher failure rates of soft-tissue repair, favouring augmentation or reconstruction.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Gould N, Seligson D, Gassman J. Early and late repair of lateral ligament of the ankle. Foot Ankle 1980.
  • Beighton P, Solomon L, Soskolne CL. Articular mobility in an African population. Ann Rheum Dis 1973.
  • Vega J, Dalmau-Pastor M et al. Ligamentous ankle instability: current concepts. Foot Ankle Clin.
  • Maffulli N, Ferran NA. Management of acute and chronic ankle instability. JAAOS 2008.
4questions

Deltoid ligament injury

The medial-sided ankle injury and when to repair it.

3 of 7 sittings2023, 2024F, 2025 (x2)

  • Anatomy: the superficial deltoid (tibionavicular, tibiospring, tibiocalcaneal, superficial posterior tibiotalar) primarily resists eversion/valgus and external rotation of the talus; the deep deltoid (anterior and posterior tibiotalar) is the primary restraint to lateral talar translation and is the most important component for ankle stability.
  • Key clinical point: the physical examination is unreliable. Medial tenderness, swelling and ecchymosis have poor sensitivity and specificity for a competent versus incompetent deltoid — stress radiography (gravity stress or manual external rotation stress) is required to determine stability in a Weber B fracture. Medial tenderness alone should not drive the decision to operate.
  • Routine repair of the deltoid ligament in an acute ankle fracture is not required. If the fibula (and syndesmosis where indicated) is anatomically reduced and fixed, the deltoid heals reliably and the medial clear space normalises. Deltoid repair is indicated when the medial clear space remains widened after anatomic fibular fixation (suggesting interposed deltoid or posterior tibial tendon), in some Maisonneuve injuries, and in the chronically insufficient/valgus ankle.
  • Persistent medial clear space widening after fixation should prompt exploration — the deltoid ligament or posterior tibial tendon may be interposed in the joint, blocking reduction.
  • Chronic deltoid insufficiency produces valgus ankle instability and is a component of progressive collapsing foot deformity (adult acquired flatfoot) with a valgus talar tilt — it is treated with deltoid reconstruction combined with correction of the hindfoot deformity, not in isolation.
  • In an isolated deltoid injury without fracture (rare), non-operative treatment is standard. In a supination-external rotation IV equivalent (fibula fracture + medial ligament injury with medial clear space widening), the injury is unstable and requires fixation of the fibula.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Lower Extremity Trauma: Ankle.
  • Michelson JD et al. Examination of the pathologic anatomy of ankle fractures. J Trauma 1992.
  • McConnell T, Creevy W, Tornetta P. Stress examination of supination external rotation-type fibular fractures. JBJS Am 2004.
  • Stufkens SA et al. The role of the deltoid ligament in ankle fracture surgery. Injury 2012.
3questions

Cavovarus foot & Charcot-Marie-Tooth

The cavovarus foot, the Coleman block test and CMT.

3 of 7 sittings2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • Charcot-Marie-Tooth (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy) is the commonest inherited neuropathy; type 1A (autosomal dominant, PMP22 duplication on chromosome 17) is the most frequent. The characteristic muscle imbalance: weak tibialis anterior with a relatively strong peroneus longus (plantarflexing the first ray) and weak peroneus brevis with a strong tibialis posterior (driving hindfoot varus and forefoot adduction), plus intrinsic weakness producing clawtoes.
  • The result is a cavovarus foot: plantarflexed first ray, forefoot pronation (valgus) relative to the hindfoot, hindfoot varus, clawtoes and a high arch, with recurrent ankle sprains and lateral column overload (fifth metatarsal stress fracture/base fracture, peroneal tears).
  • Radiographic findings of cavovarus: increased Meary angle (talus–first metatarsal, apex dorsal), increased calcaneal pitch, a 'bullet hole' sinus tarsi on the lateral, a positive Hibbs angle, and the 'double density'/overlapping talus and calcaneus on the AP. A decreased calcaneal pitch is a flatfoot finding, not cavovarus — the standard distractor.
  • Coleman block test is the key clinical discriminator: standing on a 1-inch block with the first ray hanging free, if the hindfoot varus corrects, the deformity is forefoot-driven (flexible) and is treated by addressing the plantarflexed first ray (dorsiflexion osteotomy of the first metatarsal) ± soft-tissue procedures. If it does not correct, the hindfoot is rigid and requires a lateralising/valgus-producing (Dwyer) calcaneal osteotomy, or arthrodesis in severe rigid deformity.
  • Comprehensive surgical correction typically combines: plantar fascia release, first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy, calcaneal osteotomy, peroneus longus-to-brevis transfer (removes the deforming plantarflexion force on the first ray and augments eversion), posterior tibial tendon transfer to the dorsum for foot drop, Jones procedure for clawtoes, and lateral ligament reconstruction.
  • Bilateral, symmetric cavovarus in an adolescent should prompt a neurologic work-up (CMT, Friedreich ataxia, spinal dysraphism, tethered cord) — a unilateral cavovarus foot is a spinal cord lesion until proven otherwise (MRI of the neuraxis).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle; Pediatrics.
  • Coleman SS, Chesnut WJ. A simple test for hindfoot flexibility in the cavovarus foot. CORR 1977.
  • Guyton GP, Mann RA. The pathogenesis and surgical management of foot deformity in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Foot Ankle Clin 2000.
  • Younger ASE, Hansen ST (Canadian). Adult cavovarus foot. JAAOS 2005.
3questions

Peroneal tendon pathology

Tears, subluxation and the anatomic risk factors.

3 of 7 sittings2022, 2024F, 2025

  • Peroneus brevis lies anterior and deep to peroneus longus at the level of the fibula and inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal; peroneus longus passes under the cuboid to insert on the plantar base of the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform (it plantarflexes the first ray — important in cavovarus). Peroneus brevis is the more commonly torn because it is compressed between the longus and the fibula.
  • Anatomic risk factors for peroneal tendon tears: a shallow or convex retromalleolar (fibular) groove, a low-lying peroneus brevis muscle belly, the presence of a peroneus quartus (accessory muscle, ~10–20%), a hypertrophied peroneal tubercle, hindfoot varus/cavovarus alignment, and lateral ligament insufficiency/chronic instability. Pes planus/hindfoot valgus is not a risk factor for brevis tears — it is the classic 'all except' distractor (though it can cause peroneal spasm/impingement in a different pattern).
  • Peroneal tendon subluxation/dislocation results from injury to the superior peroneal retinaculum, classically a forced dorsiflexion with sudden reflex contraction (skiing). Look for a 'fleck sign' — an avulsion of the posterolateral fibular rim. Acute injuries in athletes and chronic subluxation are treated surgically with SPR repair, with fibular groove deepening where the groove is shallow or convex.
  • Distinguish from a lateral ankle sprain: peroneal pathology causes pain and swelling posterior to the fibula (rather than anterior over the ATFL), pain with resisted eversion, and a snapping sensation. Dynamic ultrasound is excellent for demonstrating subluxation.
  • Treatment of tears: débridement and tubularisation if <50% of the tendon is involved; tenodesis to the adjacent intact tendon if >50%; and allograft/tendon transfer if both tendons are unusable. Always correct hindfoot varus with a lateralising calcaneal osteotomy at the same time or the repair will fail.
  • Chronic pain over the lateral hindfoot after a calcaneal fracture is frequently peroneal tendon impingement/subluxation from lateral wall blowout — treated with lateral wall exostectomy and tendon débridement.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Dombek MF et al. Peroneal tendon tears: a retrospective review. J Foot Ankle Surg 2003.
  • Heckman DS, Reddy S, Pedowitz D, Wapner KL, Parekh SG. Operative treatment for peroneal tendon disorders. JBJS Am 2008.
  • Ogawa BK, Thordarson DB. Current concepts review: peroneal tendon subluxation and dislocation. Foot Ankle Int 2007.
3questions

Subtalar dislocation & subtalar fusion

Blocks to reduction and the anatomy of the subtalar joint.

3 of 7 sittings2023, 2024S, 2024F

  • Medial subtalar dislocation ('basketball foot') is the more common (~80–85%): the foot displaces medially, and the block to reduction is typically the extensor digitorum brevis, the talonavicular capsule, or the peroneal tendons draped over the talar head. Lateral subtalar dislocation is higher energy and the block to reduction is classically the posterior tibial tendon (or the FHL/flexor retinaculum) wrapped around the talar neck.
  • This pairing is repeatedly tested: lateral dislocation → posterior tibial tendon block; medial dislocation → EDB/talonavicular capsule/peroneal tendon block.
  • Attempt closed reduction under sedation/anaesthesia with the knee flexed (relaxing the gastrocnemius), accentuating the deformity, then applying longitudinal traction and reversing it. If irreducible, proceed to open reduction — never apply repeated forceful attempts (skin necrosis, talar neck fracture).
  • CT after reduction is mandatory — associated osteochondral fragments and occult fractures (talar, navicular, calcaneal) are present in a majority. Lateral dislocations, open injuries and associated fractures predict a worse outcome, with subtalar arthritis and AVN the main sequelae.
  • Subtalar fusion anatomy: when preparing the subtalar joint, especially with distraction, the structure most at risk at the posteromedial aspect is the FHL tendon and the neurovascular bundle (tibial nerve and posterior tibial artery) — the FHL runs immediately behind the sustentaculum tali and is the first structure encountered; the tibial nerve/posterior tibial artery lie just medial to it. Instruments plunging medially through the posterior facet endanger these structures.
  • Reported nonunion rates for isolated subtalar arthrodesis are ~5–15% in non-smokers, rising substantially with smoking, prior trauma, AVN and inadequate preparation. Position the hindfoot in ~5° of valgus.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Lower Extremity Trauma: Foot; Foot and Ankle.
  • DeLee JC, Curtis R. Subtalar dislocation of the foot. JBJS Am 1982.
  • Bibbo C, Anderson RB, Davis WH. Injury characteristics and the clinical outcome of subtalar dislocations. Foot Ankle Int 2003.
  • Easley ME et al. Isolated subtalar arthrodesis. JBJS Am 2000.
2questions

Fifth metatarsal & Jones fracture

Zone anatomy, the Jones fracture and fixation pitfalls.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2024S

  • Zone 1 (tuberosity/avulsion) — an avulsion at the base from the lateral band of the plantar fascia and the peroneus brevis insertion, from an inversion injury. It heals reliably with symptomatic treatment (hard-soled shoe, weightbearing as tolerated). Zone 2 (Jones fracture) — at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction extending into the fourth–fifth intermetatarsal articulation, in a watershed vascular zone with a high rate of delayed union/nonunion. Zone 3 — proximal diaphyseal stress fracture, with the highest nonunion rate.
  • Fixation of a Jones fracture: use the largest-diameter partially threaded intramedullary screw the canal will accept (usually 4.5–6.5 mm) — under-sizing is the commonest technical error and predicts failure. Do not over-tap or use an excessively long screw: a screw that is too long straightens the lateral bow of the metatarsal and distracts/gaps the fracture at the lateral cortex, and can penetrate the diaphysis. The screw should be short enough to remain within the proximal metaphysis/diaphysis.
  • The starting point is 'high and inside' — at the very proximal tip of the base, slightly medial and dorsal, aligned with the axis of the metatarsal. Avoid the sural nerve and the peroneus brevis insertion.
  • Indications for acute fixation: the competitive athlete (faster union and return to sport), a displaced fracture, an established delayed union/nonunion, and the recreational athlete who prefers to avoid 8–12 weeks of non-weightbearing. Non-operative treatment is 6–8 weeks non-weightbearing in a cast with a union rate of roughly 75–85%.
  • Always assess hindfoot alignment: a cavovarus foot causes lateral column overload and is a major risk factor for a proximal fifth metatarsal stress fracture, nonunion and refracture. A Jones nonunion with correctable hindfoot varus on the Coleman block test is treated with screw fixation plus bone grafting AND correction of the varus (first metatarsal dorsiflexion osteotomy if forefoot-driven, or a lateralising calcaneal osteotomy if hindfoot-driven).
  • Also evaluate for vitamin D deficiency and metabolic bone disease in a stress fracture, and for relative energy deficiency in female athletes.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Lower Extremity Trauma: Foot; Foot and Ankle.
  • Torg JS et al. Fractures of the base of the fifth metatarsal distal to the tuberosity. JBJS Am 1984.
  • Lawrence SJ, Botte MJ. Jones' fractures and related fractures of the proximal fifth metatarsal. Foot Ankle 1993.
  • Kelly IP, Glisson RR, Fink C, Easley ME, Nunley JA. Intramedullary screw fixation of Jones fractures. Foot Ankle Int 2001.
2questions

Navicular & other stress fractures of the foot

The high-risk navicular stress fracture.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2023

  • The tarsal navicular stress fracture is a 'high-risk' stress fracture because it occurs in the central third of the navicular — a relatively avascular watershed zone between the medial (dorsalis pedis) and lateral (medial plantar artery) supplies, in a bone under high shear. Nonunion, delayed union and progression to a complete fracture are common.
  • Typical patient: a running/jumping athlete (sprinter, basketball, ballet) with insidious dorsal midfoot pain, vague and poorly localised, with tenderness over the 'N spot' (the dorsal proximal navicular). Plain radiographs are usually normal — CT is the study of choice to define the fracture and assess healing; MRI/bone scan is the most sensitive for early detection.
  • Treatment of an acute non-displaced navicular stress fracture is strict non-weightbearing immobilisation in a cast for 6–8 weeks — this is the evidence-based answer and it markedly outperforms weightbearing treatment or activity modification alone. Return to sport is guided by CT evidence of healing and a pain-free examination, typically at 4–6 months.
  • Operative fixation (screws ± bone graft) is indicated for displaced fractures, complete fractures, delayed union/nonunion, and in elite athletes who cannot tolerate prolonged non-weightbearing.
  • Risk factors for navicular stress fracture: high-impact running/jumping sport and a rapid increase in training volume, restricted ankle dorsiflexion (equinus), metatarsus adductus, a short first metatarsal with a long second metatarsal, cavus foot, subtalar/midfoot stiffness, and metabolic bone disease/vitamin D deficiency/relative energy deficiency in sport. A flexible pes planus foot is not a recognised risk factor — the classic distractor.
  • Other high-risk (tension-side or watershed) stress fractures requiring aggressive treatment: femoral neck (tension/superolateral side), anterior tibial cortex ('dreaded black line'), medial malleolus, fifth metatarsal base (Jones), talar neck, sesamoid, and the base of the second metatarsal in dancers.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle; Sports.
  • Torg JS et al. Stress fractures of the tarsal navicular: a retrospective review of twenty-one cases. JBJS Am 1982.
  • Khan KM et al. Outcome of conservative and surgical management of navicular stress fracture in athletes: eighty-six cases proven with computerized tomography. AJSM 1992.
  • Boden BP, Osbahr DC. High-risk stress fractures: evaluation and treatment. JAAOS 2000.
2questions

Osteochondral lesions of the talus

Location, prognostic factors and the treatment algorithm.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2024F

  • Classic locations and mechanisms: posteromedial lesions are typically atraumatic/deeper and 'cup-shaped' (associated with inversion and plantarflexion, or spontaneous osteonecrosis), whereas anterolateral lesions are typically traumatic, shallower and 'wafer-shaped' (inversion with dorsiflexion). An atraumatic OLT is most likely posteromedial — a repeated stem.
  • Staging: Berndt and Harty (radiographic), Hepple (MRI), Ferkel (CT). MRI is the most sensitive investigation and demonstrates the subchondral bone marrow oedema and cyst formation that correlate with symptoms.
  • Prognostic factors: lesion size is the most important — lesions >150 mm² (roughly >15 mm diameter) do poorly with marrow-stimulation techniques; the presence of subchondral cysts, an uncontained (shoulder) lesion, chronicity, patient age, high BMI, and uncorrected hindfoot malalignment or lateral ligament instability all predict a worse outcome.
  • Treatment algorithm: symptomatic small (<10–15 mm) lesion → arthroscopic débridement and microfracture/marrow stimulation (good short-term results, but fibrocartilage deteriorates over time). Larger lesions, cystic lesions or failed microfracture → osteochondral autograft transfer (OATS/mosaicplasty), autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI/MACI), particulated juvenile cartilage, or fresh osteochondral allograft.
  • OATS restores hyaline cartilage with a bony base and is well suited to a medium-sized lesion with a subchondral cyst, but requires a medial malleolar osteotomy for posteromedial access and carries donor-site morbidity at the knee. Extracellular matrix/scaffold-based options avoid donor-site morbidity but have less mature evidence.
  • Always correct associated pathology — hindfoot varus, lateral ligament instability and anterior impingement — or the lesion will recur.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Chuckpaiwong B, Berkson EM, Theodore GH. Microfracture for osteochondral lesions of the ankle: outcome analysis and outcome predictors of 105 cases. Arthroscopy 2008.
  • Choi WJ, Park KK, Kim BS, Lee JW. Osteochondral lesion of the talus: is there a critical defect size for poor outcome? AJSM 2009.
  • Hannon CP et al. International consensus on cartilage repair of the ankle. Foot Ankle Int 2018.
1question

Calcaneal osteotomy & hindfoot realignment

Percutaneous versus open calcaneal osteotomy.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • A medialising (Koutsogiannis) calcaneal osteotomy shifts the tuberosity medially to move the Achilles vector medial to the subtalar axis, correcting hindfoot valgus in flexible flatfoot. A lateralising (Dwyer) osteotomy — with or without a closing wedge — corrects hindfoot varus in cavovarus.
  • Percutaneous (minimally invasive, burr-based) calcaneal osteotomy versus open: the percutaneous technique gives a significantly lower rate of wound complications and less soft-tissue stripping, with comparable correction and union. The principal risk of the percutaneous technique is injury to neurovascular structures — particularly the sural nerve laterally and the medial/lateral plantar nerves and posterior tibial neurovascular bundle medially — because the osteotomy is made without direct visualisation, plus thermal necrosis from the burr if irrigation is inadequate.
  • The sural nerve crosses the lateral hindfoot obliquely and is the structure most at risk with a lateral incision (open or percutaneous). Medially, the lateral plantar nerve and the tibial nerve branches are at risk when the saw or burr plunges through the medial cortex — this is the reason for careful depth control and for using a guarded saw in the open technique.
  • Union rates are high with either technique. Fixation is with one or two large partially threaded screws from the posteroinferior tuberosity, taking care to countersink the heads to avoid painful hardware in the heel pad.
  • A medial calcaneal osteotomy is contraindicated (or must be combined with additional procedures) in a rigid deformity — assess flexibility first. Combine with lateral column lengthening, spring ligament repair, FDL transfer or gastrocnemius recession as indicated by the deformity.
  • Always assess for equinus and perform a gastrocnemius recession where dorsiflexion is <5–10° with the knee extended — uncorrected equinus is a common cause of recurrence.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Guyton GP. Minimally invasive osteotomies of the calcaneus. Foot Ankle Clin.
  • Kheir E et al. Minimally invasive versus open calcaneal osteotomy: a comparison of complications. Foot Ankle Int.
  • Myerson MS, Badekas A, Schon LC. Treatment of stage II posterior tibial tendon deficiency with flexor digitorum longus tendon transfer and calcaneal osteotomy. Foot Ankle Int 2004.
1question

Foot & ankle soft-tissue coverage

Reconstructive options for the foot and ankle.

1 of 7 sittings2024F

  • Dorsal foot defects with exposed tendon/bone require thin, pliable coverage: a split-thickness skin graft works only over a vascularised bed (intact paratenon/periosteum); otherwise use a local flap (reverse sural artery flap, extensor digitorum brevis flap, dorsalis pedis flap) or a free flap (anterolateral thigh, radial forearm, gracilis with a skin graft — thin flaps preferred).
  • The medial plantar artery (instep) flap is not appropriate for dorsal foot coverage — its arc of rotation reaches the heel and plantar hindfoot, not the dorsum. It is the ideal flap for the weightbearing heel, providing glabrous, durable, sensate skin. This is the classic 'which does not work' item.
  • Weightbearing plantar heel: medial plantar artery flap (best), free muscle flap with a skin graft (gracilis, latissimus), or a reverse sural flap. The essential goal is durable, sensate, shear-resistant coverage — a simple skin graft on the weightbearing surface fails.
  • Distal third of the leg and ankle: local muscle flaps are inadequate (the gastrocnemius reaches the proximal third and the soleus the middle third), so this region generally requires a free tissue transfer or a reverse sural fasciocutaneous flap.
  • General principles: timing matters — early definitive coverage of an open fracture (ideally within 72 hours, certainly within 7 days) markedly reduces deep infection and flap failure. Assess vascular inflow before flap planning (angiography/CTA), and use negative pressure wound therapy only as a temporising measure.
  • In the diabetic/dysvascular foot, revascularisation must precede reconstruction, and a well-planned amputation may give better function and faster recovery than a marginal flap.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas; Foot and Ankle.
  • Attinger CE et al. Angiosomes of the foot and ankle and clinical implications for limb salvage. Plast Reconstr Surg 2006.
  • Hollenbeck ST et al. Perineal and lower extremity reconstruction. Plast Reconstr Surg.
  • Godina M. Early microsurgical reconstruction of complex trauma of the extremities. Plast Reconstr Surg 1986.
1question

Gastrocnemius contracture & equinus

The Silfverskiöld test and the consequences of equinus.

1 of 7 sittings2021

  • Equinus is defined as <10° (some authors <5°) of ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended and the hindfoot held in neutral/slight inversion (locking the midfoot so the motion measured is true ankle dorsiflexion, not midfoot sag).
  • Silfverskiöld test: measure dorsiflexion with the knee extended and then with the knee flexed to 90°. If dorsiflexion improves markedly with the knee flexed, the contracture is isolated to the gastrocnemius (which crosses the knee) → treat with a gastrocnemius recession (Strayer, Baumann or Vulpius). If dorsiflexion remains limited with the knee flexed, the soleus is also involved → tendo-Achilles lengthening is required.
  • Associations/consequences of a gastrocsoleus contracture: plantar fasciitis, metatarsalgia and forefoot overload, midfoot (Charcot/Lisfranc) collapse, diabetic forefoot ulceration, Achilles tendinopathy, progressive collapsing foot deformity, and anterior ankle pain — and it is a key contributor to recurrence after almost any foot reconstruction if not addressed. Posterior ankle impingement is not caused by equinus (it is caused by an os trigonum/Stieda process).
  • In cerebral palsy with equinus and toe walking, the same test guides treatment: an isolated gastrocnemius contracture (dorsiflexion −10° with the knee extended improving to 0° with the knee flexed) is treated with a gastrocnemius recession, whereas involvement of both heads requires a tendo-Achilles lengthening. Over-lengthening the Achilles causes a calcaneal (crouch) gait, which is far worse and largely irreversible — the cardinal error in CP surgery.
  • Tendo-Achilles lengthening reduces forefoot plantar pressures and is an evidence-based adjunct in the treatment and prevention of recurrent diabetic forefoot ulceration.
  • Non-operative treatment (dedicated gastrocnemius stretching with the knee extended, night splints, serial casting) should be attempted first in most non-neurologic patients.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle; Pediatrics.
  • DiGiovanni CW et al. Isolated gastrocnemius tightness. JBJS Am 2002.
  • Silfverskiöld N. Reduction of the uncrossed two-joint muscles of the leg to one-joint muscles in spastic conditions. Acta Chir Scand 1924.
  • Mueller MJ et al. Effect of Achilles tendon lengthening on neuropathic plantar ulcers: a randomized clinical trial. JBJS Am 2003.
1question

Hallux rigidus & first MTP arthritis

Grading and choosing between cheilectomy and fusion.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • Hallux rigidus is degenerative arthritis of the first MTP joint with characteristic dorsal osteophyte formation and progressive loss of dorsiflexion. Classic examination: dorsal joint-line tenderness with pain at the extremes of dorsiflexion but a relatively pain-free mid-range, and a negative or mildly positive grind test in early disease.
  • Coughlin & Shurnas grading: 0 — stiffness only; 1 — mild dorsal osteophyte, dorsiflexion 40–60°; 2 — dorsiflexion 30–40° with mild-moderate joint narrowing and pain only at terminal dorsiflexion; 3 — dorsiflexion <30°, substantial narrowing/osteophyte, with pain at terminal range but NOT mid-range; 4 — as grade 3 but with pain throughout the mid-range of motion.
  • Cheilectomy (dorsal osteophyte and 25–30% of the dorsal metatarsal head resection) is appropriate for grades 1–3 — where pain is at the extremes of motion and the plantar/mid-range articular cartilage is preserved. Mid-range pain (grade 4) means the whole joint surface is involved and cheilectomy will fail — this is the key discriminator.
  • First MTP arthrodesis is the gold-standard operation for grade 3–4 disease with mid-range pain: it is durable and reliably relieves pain. Fusion position: 10–15° of dorsiflexion relative to the ground (about 20–25° to the first metatarsal shaft), 10–15° of valgus and neutral rotation — the pulp of the toe should just clear the ground and allow footwear.
  • The stem describing a middle-aged patient with dorsal AND plantar (sesamoid) tenderness, 5° of dorsiflexion and 10° of plantarflexion who has failed injections and orthotics has grade 4 disease with mid-range/plantar pain → first MTP arthrodesis, not cheilectomy.
  • Alternatives: interpositional arthroplasty, synthetic cartilage implant (Cartiva — comparable to fusion in the pivotal trial but with mixed longer-term data), Moberg dorsiflexion osteotomy of the proximal phalanx (adjunct to cheilectomy in the young), and hemiarthroplasty (historically poor results).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Coughlin MJ, Shurnas PS. Hallux rigidus: grading and long-term results of operative treatment. JBJS Am 2003.
  • Deland JT, Williams BR. Surgical management of hallux rigidus. JAAOS 2012.
  • Baumhauer JF et al. Prospective randomized multi-centered clinical trial assessing safety and efficacy of a synthetic cartilage implant versus first metatarsophalangeal arthrodesis. Foot Ankle Int 2016.
1question

Metatarsalgia, lesser toe deformity & Weil osteotomy

Treating transfer metatarsalgia and the Weil osteotomy's characteristic complication.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • Metatarsalgia results from abnormal load distribution across the lesser metatarsal heads — from a long or plantarflexed metatarsal, first-ray insufficiency (after hallux valgus surgery or in hallux rigidus), equinus contracture, claw/hammer toe with plantar plate attenuation, or a plantar fat pad atrophy.
  • The Weil osteotomy is an intra-articular, oblique, distal metatarsal shortening osteotomy that translates the metatarsal head proximally to offload it. The most common complication of a Weil osteotomy is 'floating toe' — the toe fails to touch the ground (loss of MTP plantarflexion/toe purchase), reported in up to 15–50% of cases.
  • The mechanism of floating toe is plantar translation of the metatarsal head axis relative to the intrinsic muscles: the interossei, whose line of pull now passes dorsal to the new (proximally translated) centre of rotation, become extensors rather than flexors of the MTP joint. Modifying the osteotomy by removing a dorsal slice of bone to prevent plantar displacement of the head reduces the incidence. Post-operative stiffness and transfer metatarsalgia to the adjacent ray are the other common problems.
  • Always address the plantar plate — attenuation/tear causes MTP instability with a positive drawer (Lachman) test of the MTP joint. Modern practice frequently repairs the plantar plate at the time of the Weil osteotomy.
  • Consider gastrocnemius recession where equinus contributes to forefoot overload — this is increasingly recognised as an important adjunct.
  • Non-operative treatment (metatarsal pads/bars placed proximal to the metatarsal head, stiff-soled rocker shoes, callus care and activity modification) should be exhausted first, and is often sufficient.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Highlander P et al. Complications of the Weil osteotomy. Foot Ankle Spec.
  • Migues A et al. Floating-toe deformity as a complication of the Weil osteotomy. Foot Ankle Int 2004.
  • Coughlin MJ. Common causes of pain in the forefoot in adults. JBJS Br 2000.
1question

Plantar fasciitis & heel pain

Risk factors, natural history and treatment.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: obesity/increased BMI (the strongest in the non-athletic population), limited ankle dorsiflexion/gastrocnemius-soleus contracture (the strongest modifiable factor), prolonged weightbearing occupations, pes planus and pes cavus, sudden increases in running volume, and inappropriate footwear. A calcaneal (plantar) heel spur is a radiographic association, not a cause — spurs occur in ~15–20% of asymptomatic people and lie within the flexor digitorum brevis origin, not the fascia; spur excision is not required.
  • Classic history: pain with the first steps in the morning or after rest, improving with a few minutes of walking, and worsening again at the end of the day. Tenderness at the medial calcaneal tuberosity, worse with passive dorsiflexion of the toes (windlass mechanism).
  • The natural history is favourable: >90% resolve within 10–12 months with non-operative treatment. First-line treatment is plantar fascia-specific stretching (Digiovanni protocol — dorsiflexing the toes) plus gastrocnemius/Achilles stretching, which outperforms generic Achilles stretching alone; add heel cups/orthoses, activity modification, weight loss and night splints.
  • Second-line: corticosteroid injection (short-term relief only, with a small risk of plantar fascia rupture and fat-pad atrophy), extracorporeal shockwave therapy, PRP (evidence mixed). Surgery — partial (medial one third) plantar fascia release ± gastrocnemius recession — is reserved for symptoms lasting >9–12 months. Complete fascia release causes lateral column overload and arch collapse.
  • Isolated gastrocnemius recession has emerging evidence as an effective operation for recalcitrant plantar fasciitis with an equinus contracture.
  • Differential diagnosis: Baxter's neuritis (entrapment of the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve — pain more medial and proximal, no morning-start pattern, occasional ADM atrophy), calcaneal stress fracture (positive squeeze test, night pain, MRI), fat pad atrophy, tarsal tunnel syndrome, and S1 radiculopathy.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • DiGiovanni BF et al. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain. JBJS Am 2003/2006.
  • Riddle DL et al. Risk factors for plantar fasciitis: a matched case-control study. JBJS Am 2003.
  • Buchbinder R. Plantar fasciitis. NEJM 2004.
1question

Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction & adult flatfoot

Progressive collapsing foot deformity: staging and treatment.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • Johnson & Strom staging (modified by Myerson), now increasingly described as progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD): Stage I — tenosynovitis with a normally aligned foot, intact single-leg heel rise; Stage II — flexible deformity with hindfoot valgus, forefoot abduction ('too many toes' sign) and inability to perform a single-leg heel rise; Stage III — rigid hindfoot valgus with subtalar arthritis; Stage IV — valgus talar tilt at the ankle from deltoid ligament failure.
  • The posterior tibial tendon is the dynamic stabiliser of the medial longitudinal arch and the primary invertor; its failure allows the spring (calcaneonavicular) ligament — the key static stabiliser — to attenuate. Both must be considered.
  • Treatment: Stage I — immobilisation/orthosis, NSAIDs, tenosynovectomy if refractory. Stage II — joint-preserving reconstruction: FDL transfer to the navicular + medialising calcaneal osteotomy ± lateral column lengthening (for forefoot abduction) ± Cotton osteotomy or first TMT fusion (for forefoot varus) ± gastrocnemius recession ± spring ligament repair. Stage III — hindfoot (triple or double) arthrodesis. Stage IV — deltoid reconstruction with hindfoot correction, or tibiotalocalcaneal fusion/TAA in selected cases.
  • Always assess and correct equinus — a gastrocnemius contracture is present in the majority and drives recurrence if untreated (Silfverskiöld test to distinguish isolated gastrocnemius from gastrocsoleus contracture).
  • A young athlete with a symptomatic posterior tibial tendon insertional avulsion/accessory navicular but normal, symmetric arches and full dorsiflexion does not have PCFD — treatment is excision of the accessory navicular with advancement/reattachment of the posterior tibial tendon (modified Kidner procedure), not a flatfoot reconstruction.
  • The too-many-toes sign (viewed from behind, more lateral toes visible because of forefoot abduction) and the single-limb heel rise (failure to invert the hindfoot) are the two key examination findings.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle.
  • Johnson KA, Strom DE. Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction. CORR 1989.
  • Myerson MS et al. Classification and nomenclature: progressive collapsing foot deformity. Foot Ankle Int 2020 (consensus).
  • Deland JT. Adult-acquired flatfoot deformity. JAAOS 2008.
1question

Puncture wound of the foot & Pseudomonas osteomyelitis

The classic nail-through-a-shoe injury.

1 of 7 sittings2024F

  • A puncture wound through the sole of a running/athletic shoe that develops infection is classically caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which colonises the moist foam rubber of the shoe insole and is inoculated directly into the deep tissues, including bone and cartilage. Staphylococcus aureus remains the commonest organism in puncture wounds overall, but the shoe-associated deep infection/osteomyelitis is Pseudomonas until proven otherwise.
  • Presentation: increasing pain and swelling 3–7 days after the puncture (in contrast to simple cellulitis, which appears within 1–2 days), with purulent drainage and often a benign initial appearance.
  • Management: surgical débridement/exploration of the puncture tract with removal of the foreign body (shoe/sock material), plus antipseudomonal antibiotic coverage — ciprofloxacin (in adults) or an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, cefepime). Tetracycline, cephalexin (Keflex) and clindamycin do not cover Pseudomonas and are the standard distractors.
  • Imaging: radiographs for retained foreign body and later bony change; MRI is the study of choice for osteomyelitis and abscess. Deep puncture wounds over the metatarsal heads and calcaneus are the most likely to produce osteomyelitis or septic arthritis.
  • Tetanus prophylaxis must be addressed in every puncture wound. Prophylactic antibiotics for a simple, clean, superficial puncture are not routinely indicated in an immunocompetent patient; the diabetic and immunocompromised patient warrants a lower threshold.
  • Note the fluoroquinolone caveat in children (cartilage toxicity concerns) — ceftazidime or another antipseudomonal beta-lactam is generally preferred in the paediatric population, though ciprofloxacin is used when needed.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle; Medical Conditions.
  • Jacobs RF et al. Pseudomonas osteochondritis complicating puncture wounds of the foot in children. Pediatrics 1989.
  • Fisher MC, Goldsmith JF, Gilligan PH. Sneakers as a source of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in children with osteomyelitis following puncture wounds. J Pediatr 1985.
  • Racette S et al. Puncture wounds to the foot. J Am Podiatr Med Assoc.
1question

Supramalleolar osteotomy & distal tibial malunion

Realigning the distal tibia to offload asymmetric ankle arthritis.

1 of 7 sittings2023

  • A supramalleolar osteotomy (SMO) realigns the distal tibial articular surface to redistribute load in asymmetric (varus or valgus) ankle arthritis — most commonly after a malunited pilon, distal tibial or ankle fracture, or in primary varus ankle osteoarthritis.
  • The ideal candidate has: asymmetric/eccentric ankle arthritis with a preserved (congruent) portion of the joint to offload onto, a mobile ankle with a reasonable arc of motion, a correctable deformity, and adequate vascularity and soft tissue. It is a joint-preserving alternative to fusion or arthroplasty in a younger, active patient.
  • Contraindications/poor candidates: concentric/global (end-stage) ankle arthritis (there is nowhere to shift the load to), severe stiffness, neuropathy/Charcot, active infection, and significant talar tilt with instability that cannot be corrected.
  • Planning must define the centre of rotation of angulation (CORA) and correct in all planes — coronal (varus/valgus), sagittal (recurvatum/procurvatum) and rotation. Medial opening-wedge osteotomy for varus (adds length, may need graft, risks wound problems over the thin medial skin) and lateral opening or medial closing wedge for valgus. A concomitant fibular osteotomy is often required for larger corrections.
  • Adjunctive procedures are frequently needed: calcaneal osteotomy for a compensatory hindfoot deformity, lateral ligament reconstruction, and débridement/microfracture of an osteochondral lesion.
  • Outcomes are good in properly selected patients, with pain relief and delay/avoidance of fusion; results deteriorate with more advanced arthritis, and conversion to fusion or arthroplasty later remains possible.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle; Lower Extremity Trauma.
  • Pagenstert GI, Hintermann B et al. Realignment surgery as alternative treatment of varus and valgus ankle osteoarthritis. CORR 2007.
  • Knupp M et al. Supramalleolar osteotomies for the treatment of ankle arthritis. JAAOS 2011.
  • Stufkens SA et al. Long-term outcome after supramalleolar osteotomy. Foot Ankle Int.
1question

Turf toe & first MTP injuries

The plantar plate injury of the great toe.

1 of 7 sittings2024F

  • Turf toe is a hyperextension injury of the first MTP joint that disrupts the plantar plate/capsuloligamentous complex, classically on artificial turf with flexible footwear. Grade I — stretch/sprain; Grade II — partial tear with moderate pain, ecchymosis and restricted motion; Grade III — complete tear of the plantar plate, with marked swelling, ecchymosis, inability to push off, and often sesamoid retraction/diastasis.
  • Radiographic sign of a complete (grade III) injury: proximal migration of the sesamoids on a lateral or axial view (comparison with the contralateral foot), or an increased sesamoid–joint distance; a bipartite sesamoid may show diastasis. MRI is the definitive study and shows the plantar plate disruption.
  • Grade III injuries in a collegiate/professional athlete are the group considered for surgical repair — direct repair of the plantar plate ± sesamoid fixation or excision of a fragmented sesamoid. Grade I and II injuries are treated non-operatively with taping, a stiff/rigid-soled shoe or carbon-fibre insert, and progressive return to play (grade I ~days, grade II ~2 weeks, grade III 8–10 weeks or surgery).
  • Loss of push-off power and persistent pain are the hallmarks of an inadequately treated turf toe, and chronic injury leads to hallux valgus/varus deformity, cock-up deformity, sesamoid problems and first MTP arthritis. This is a career-affecting injury in football and is a leading cause of missed games.
  • Sesamoid excision should be avoided where possible (removing both sesamoids causes a cock-up deformity; removing the tibial sesamoid predisposes to hallux valgus, and the fibular sesamoid to hallux varus).
  • Distinguish from a plantar plate/sesamoid stress injury and from hallux rigidus (dorsal pain, dorsal osteophyte, limited dorsiflexion with a grind test).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Foot and Ankle; Sports.
  • Anderson RB, McCormick JJ. Turf toe injuries of the hallux metatarsophalangeal joint. Sports Med Arthrosc Rev / JAAOS 2010.
  • Clanton TO, Ford JJ. Turf toe injury. Clin Sports Med 1994.
  • McCormick JJ, Anderson RB. Rehabilitation following turf toe injury and plantar plate repair. Clin Sports Med 2010.
