9questions

Amputation: Level selection, technique & outcomes

Level selection, energy cost, and the specific amputation levels tested.

6 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022 (x2), 2023 (x2), 2024S, 2025 (x2)

  • Energy expenditure above baseline walking rises with more proximal amputation and is a repeatedly tested list: traumatic transtibial ~25%; dysvascular transtibial ~40%; through-knee ~50%; traumatic transfemoral ~65%; dysvascular transfemoral ~100%; bilateral transtibial ~40%; bilateral transfemoral >200%. Walking velocity falls as the level ascends, but oxygen consumption per unit distance rises — patients self-select a slower speed to keep oxygen consumption per minute near normal.
  • Preserving the knee joint is the single most important functional goal — a transtibial amputee uses far less energy and has far better prosthetic function than a transfemoral amputee. Ideal transtibial length is 12–15 cm (a hand's breadth) below the joint line, with a long posterior myofasciocutaneous flap.
  • Healing potential in peripheral vascular disease: ankle-brachial index >0.5 (unreliable if calcified — use toe pressures), toe pressure >30–45 mmHg, TcPO₂ >30–40 mmHg, serum albumin >3.0 g/dL, and total lymphocyte count >1500/mm³. Nutrition and immunocompetence are as important as perfusion.
  • Above-knee (transfemoral) amputation for critical ischaemia: healing rates are high (>90%) because of the excellent proximal blood supply, but functional prosthetic ambulation in the dysvascular elderly population is poor — only a minority (roughly 25–40%) become community ambulators, and mortality at 1–2 years is high (30–50%). Retain as much femoral length as possible and perform a myodesis of the adductor magnus to prevent the abduction/flexion deformity from unopposed abductors and hip flexors.
  • Through-knee (knee disarticulation) preserves a long, end-bearing lever arm with excellent muscle balance and does not violate the medullary canal; it is particularly useful in non-ambulatory patients (better sitting balance and transfer) and in children (preserves the distal femoral physis). Drawbacks are the bulbous end, a cosmetically poor and functionally limited prosthetic knee (the knee centre sits distal to the contralateral knee), and difficulty fitting.
  • Syme amputation (ankle disarticulation with a durable heel pad): preserves an end-bearing residual limb allowing short-distance walking without a prosthesis, and has a low energy cost (~15%). Requires an intact, well-perfused heel pad and secure fixation of the pad to the tibia (heel pad migration is the classic complication). It leaves a bulbous stump with cosmetic prosthetic limitations.
  • Paediatric amputations: disarticulation is preferred over transosseous amputation wherever possible, because a transosseous amputation in a growing child produces terminal bony overgrowth (appositional new bone formation at the cut end) requiring revision in up to 15–30%. Children have excellent healing, adaptability and lower energy costs than adults, rarely develop phantom pain, and revision for overgrowth (rather than for prosthetic fitting) is the commonest reason to reoperate.
  • Upper extremity amputation: preserve every millimetre of length; rejection rates for upper limb prostheses are high, and function is often better with a well-preserved partial hand than with a prosthesis. Wrist disarticulation preserves forearm pronation/supination and is preferred to transradial when feasible.
  • Mangled extremity: the MESS score has poor positive predictive value and should not be used alone to decide on amputation; the LEAP study showed that 2-year functional outcomes were similar for reconstruction and amputation, and that the strongest predictors of outcome were psychosocial factors — self-efficacy, education, poverty, smoking and social support — not the injury characteristics. Insensate plantar skin is NOT an absolute indication for amputation (sensation frequently recovers).
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas: Amputation; Pediatrics.
  • Waters RL, Perry J, Antonelli D, Hislop H. Energy cost of walking of amputees: the influence of level of amputation. JBJS Am 1976.
  • Bosse MJ et al. (LEAP Study Group) An analysis of outcomes of reconstruction or amputation after leg-threatening injuries. NEJM 2002.
  • Pinzur MS et al. Controversies in lower-extremity amputation. JBJS Am 2007.
  • Krajbich JI, Bochmann D. Amputations in children. In Atlas of Amputations and Limb Deficiencies (AAOS).
9questions

Periprosthetic joint infection: Diagnosis & management

MSIS/ICM criteria, modern diagnostic tests, and the DAIR-versus-revision decision.

6 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2022, 2023, 2024S (x2), 2024F, 2025 (x2)

  • Diagnostic criteria (MSIS/ICM 2018) — a major criterion is definitive: (1) two positive periprosthetic cultures with the same organism, or (2) a sinus tract communicating with the prosthesis. Minor criteria are scored: elevated serum CRP and D-dimer, elevated ESR, elevated synovial WBC count, elevated synovial polymorphonuclear percentage, positive alpha-defensin, elevated synovial CRP, and positive histology (>5 neutrophils/high-power field).
  • Synovial fluid thresholds differ acutely and chronically: acute (<6 weeks) — WBC >10,000/µL with >90% PMN; chronic — WBC >3,000/µL with >80% PMN (far lower than the >50,000 used for a native joint). Do not apply native-joint thresholds to a prosthesis.
  • Synovial fluid aspiration with cell count, differential and culture has the highest diagnostic value for suspected PJI — the single most useful test. Alpha-defensin has high specificity and is not affected by antibiotics or inflammatory arthropathy, but it is expensive and has false positives with metallosis. Serum D-dimer is a newer adjunct. Next-generation sequencing is promising for culture-negative infection.
  • Hold antibiotics before aspiration and before intra-operative cultures (ideally ≥2 weeks) unless the patient is septic; take ≥3–5 tissue samples; and hold cultures for 13–14 days to capture Cutibacterium acnes (especially in the shoulder). Sonication of the explanted implant increases yield in biofilm infection.
  • Highest risk of PJI: previous PJI/revision surgery, rheumatoid arthritis and immunosuppression, obesity (BMI >40), poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c >7.5–8%), malnutrition, IV drug use, prolonged operative time, and a wound with persistent drainage. Prior septic arthritis of the same joint is a major risk.
  • DAIR (débridement, antibiotics and implant retention) is appropriate for an acute (<3–4 weeks from implantation, or <3 weeks of symptoms in an acute haematogenous infection) infection with a well-fixed implant, an intact soft-tissue envelope, no sinus tract, and a susceptible organism. It requires a modular component (liner/head) exchange to be effective. Success rates are roughly 30–70%, being worst with S. aureus, delayed presentation and a sinus tract.
  • A sinus tract, a chronic infection, a loose implant, or a resistant organism mandates implant removal — the classic scenario of a TKA 6 months post-operatively with a sinus tract and sepsis requires two-stage revision with an antibiotic spacer, not DAIR. Two-stage revision remains the gold standard in North America with ~85–95% eradication; single-stage revision is increasingly used in Europe for selected patients with a known susceptible organism and good soft tissue.
  • A patient 4 years post-THA attending for a dental extraction of an infected tooth: current AAOS/ADA guidance is that routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated for most patients; it is considered case-by-case in the immunocompromised. Treating the dental infection itself is the priority.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: General; Orthopaedic Dilemmas.
  • Parvizi J, Tan TL, Goswami K et al. The 2018 definition of periprosthetic hip and knee infection: an evidence-based and validated criteria. J Arthroplasty 2018.
  • Deirmengian C et al. Combined measurement of synovial fluid α-defensin and C-reactive protein levels. JBJS Am 2014.
  • Osmon DR et al. IDSA clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of prosthetic joint infection. Clin Infect Dis 2013.
  • Kunutsor SK et al. Debridement, antibiotics and implant retention for periprosthetic joint infections: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Infect 2018.
8questions

Hip arthroscopy, FAI & labral pathology

FAI morphology, radiographic assessment, outcomes and nerve injury.

6 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021 (x2), 2022, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • FAI morphology: cam (an aspherical femoral head-neck junction, alpha angle >55°, more common in young athletic men) and pincer (acetabular over-coverage — global coxa profunda/protrusio, or focal anterior over-coverage/retroversion, more common in middle-aged women). Most are mixed.
  • Radiographic signs of acetabular retroversion on an AP pelvis: the crossover sign, the posterior wall sign (the posterior wall lies medial to the centre of the femoral head), and the ischial spine sign (the ischial spine projects into the pelvic inlet). The ischial spine sign is the most useful sign for distinguishing true acetabular retroversion (a rotational abnormality of the whole hemipelvis) from focal anterior over-coverage, because it reflects the position of the entire hemipelvis. A crossover sign alone can be produced by focal anterior over-coverage or by pelvic tilt/rotation on the radiograph.
  • Evidence for hip arthroscopy in FAI: the UK FASHIoN RCT and the Canadian/Australian trials show that arthroscopic FAI surgery gives a modest but statistically significant improvement in hip-related quality of life over best conservative care at 12 months, though the difference may not exceed the MCID for all patients. It is not a benign or universally successful procedure.
  • Outcomes of hip arthroscopy for a labral tear in a patient over ~45–50 or with arthritis: results are markedly worse. Reoperation/conversion to THA is common — roughly 15–20% or more within 2 years in patients over 50, and higher with Tönnis grade ≥2 arthritis or joint space <2 mm. Arthritis is the strongest predictor of failure and is a relative contraindication.
  • Nerve injury in hip arthroscopy relates chiefly to traction and the perineal post: the pudendal nerve is the most commonly injured (neuropraxia from perineal post pressure — genital/perineal numbness), followed by the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (from the anterolateral portal), and the sciatic and femoral nerves (traction). Most are transient neuropraxias that resolve, and they are minimised by limiting traction time (<2 hours), using the least traction force necessary, a well-padded or post-less table, and careful portal placement.
  • Labral repair is preferred to débridement where the tissue is repairable, and the capsule should be closed/plicated — capsular deficiency is a recognised cause of iatrogenic instability and revision. Femoral neck fracture after over-resection of the head-neck junction (>30% of the neck diameter) is a serious complication.
  • Do not perform arthroscopy in dysplasia without addressing the coverage — isolated labral surgery in a dysplastic hip can worsen instability; a periacetabular osteotomy is the correct operation.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Approaches; Sports.
  • Griffin DR et al. (UK FASHIoN) Hip arthroscopy versus best conservative care for the treatment of femoroacetabular impingement syndrome. Lancet 2018.
  • Kalore NV, Jiranek WA et al. / Kappe T. Ischial spine sign. CORR / Arch Orthop Trauma Surg.
  • Reiman MP et al. Hip arthroscopy outcomes with respect to patient acceptable symptomatic state and minimal clinically important difference. Arthroscopy 2018.
  • Nakano N, Khanduja V et al. Complications following arthroscopic surgery of the hip: a systematic review of 36,761 cases. Bone Joint J 2017.
8questions

THA bearing surfaces, fixation & implant survivorship

Fixation choice, bearing selection and the commonest modes of failure.

5 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021 (x2), 2022, 2023 (x2), 2025

  • Aseptic loosening remains the commonest long-term cause of THA failure overall, though registry data show that in the first years instability/dislocation and infection dominate early revision, and periprosthetic fracture is increasingly common in the elderly. In cemented stems, debonding at the stem–cement interface with cement mantle fracture is the classic failure sequence.
  • Cemented versus cementless in the elderly: registry data (including the UK NJR and Canadian/Nordic registries) consistently show that cemented femoral fixation has a lower revision rate for periprosthetic fracture in patients over ~75, especially women, whereas cementless stems have a higher early periprosthetic fracture risk in osteoporotic bone. Hybrid fixation (cementless cup, cemented stem) has an excellent registry track record in the elderly and is the usual answer for an 86-year-old.
  • Grit-blasted (rough surface) vs polished tapered cemented stems: polished, tapered, collarless (force-closed) stems are designed to subside slightly within the cement mantle, converting shear to compressive hoop stress, and have excellent survivorship. Rough/grit-blasted (composite-beam) stems, if they debond, generate abrasive metal and cement debris, causing accelerated osteolysis and higher failure rates — this is the recurring exam point.
  • Improving cemented stem longevity: modern (3rd/4th generation) technique — pulsatile lavage, distal canal plug, retrograde cement delivery with a gun, pressurisation, vacuum mixing to reduce porosity, a stem centraliser, and a uniform mantle ≥2 mm. Pressurisation and a clean, dry interface are the critical steps.
  • Bearing selection: highly cross-linked polyethylene against a metal or ceramic head is the workhorse and has dramatically reduced wear-related osteolysis. Ceramic-on-ceramic has the lowest wear but risks fracture (rare with modern delta ceramic) and squeaking. Metal-on-metal has been abandoned for THA because of ALTR/pseudotumour, and metal-on-metal resurfacing is now used only in selected young men by experienced surgeons.
  • Volumetric wear increases with the square of the head radius; linear wear does not. This is why the wear advantage of highly cross-linked polyethylene is what permits the routine use of larger (36 mm) heads for stability.
  • Modularity adds versatility (independent adjustment of offset, length and version) but introduces taper corrosion (trunnionosis) and the risk of component dissociation and fretting. Modular-neck stems have a poor track record. Minimise unnecessary modularity.
  • Uncemented hemiarthroplasty for femoral neck fracture — the commonest reason for revision is periprosthetic fracture (and then acetabular erosion/protrusio and infection); this is a key argument for cemented hemiarthroplasty in the elderly, supported by the WHiTE 5 trial.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • National Joint Registry (UK) and Canadian Joint Replacement Registry (CIHI) annual reports.
  • Howie DW et al. Loosening of matt and polished cemented femoral stems. JBJS Br 1998.
  • Fernandez MA et al. (WHiTE 5) Cemented or uncemented hemiarthroplasty for intracapsular hip fracture. NEJM 2022.
  • Kurtz SM et al. Advances in highly crosslinked UHMWPE. CORR 2011.
8questions

THA instability: Component position, spinopelvic motion & prevention

Component position, the safe zone, spinopelvic pathology and strategies to prevent dislocation.

5 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2022 (x2), 2023, 2025 (x2)

  • Classic 'safe zone' (Lewinnek): acetabular inclination 40° ± 10° and anteversion 15° ± 10°. Modern data show that a substantial proportion of dislocating hips have components within this zone — there is no single universal safe zone, and target position must be individualised to spinopelvic mechanics.
  • A retroverted acetabular component predisposes to POSTERIOR instability (particularly in flexion — sitting, bending, rising from a chair) and to anterior impingement. Excessive anteversion predisposes to anterior instability in extension and external rotation.
  • Spinopelvic mechanics is the highest-yield modern concept: normally, when a patient sits, the pelvis rotates posteriorly (posterior pelvic tilt), which functionally increases acetabular anteversion and inclination, creating clearance for the flexing femur. In a patient with a stiff, degenerative or fused lumbar spine (especially a long fusion to the sacrum, or flatback deformity), the pelvis cannot rotate posteriorly when sitting — the cup remains relatively retroverted/under-anteverted in flexion, the femoral neck impinges on the posterior rim, and the hip levers out posteriorly.
  • The corollary: a stiff spine in a patient who stands with abnormal posterior pelvic tilt produces functional cup retroversion in standing and anterior instability. Decreased spinopelvic motion (a 'stiff spine') is the key risk factor — patients with lumbar fusion have a several-fold increased dislocation rate. Assess with standing and seated lateral radiographs measuring pelvic incidence, sacral slope and the change in sacral slope (ΔSS <10° = stiff).
  • Jump distance = the lateral displacement required for the head to dislocate = a function of head diameter (larger head = greater jump distance) and head coverage/cup design. Increasing femoral head size is the single most effective implant-based strategy for increasing jump distance, range of motion before impingement, and stability; increasing offset also improves soft-tissue tension without increasing leg length.
  • Primary arc of motion (motion before neck-on-liner impingement) is increased by a larger head-to-neck ratio — a bigger head, a thinner/trapezoidal neck, and a skirtless head. A skirted head reduces the head-neck ratio and reduces the arc.
  • Other prevention strategies: restoring offset and leg length, avoiding elevated-rim liners in the wrong orientation, repairing the posterior capsule and short external rotators in a posterior approach (this alone reduces dislocation several-fold), and using dual-mobility or constrained components in high-risk patients (neuromuscular disease, cognitive impairment, abductor deficiency, spinal fusion, revision).
  • Hip ankylosis converted to THA: the commonest reason for later revision is instability/dislocation and abductor insufficiency — the abductors have been non-functional for years and do not recover; consider a dual-mobility or constrained liner.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • Lewinnek GE et al. Dislocations after total hip-replacement arthroplasties. JBJS Am 1978.
  • Vigdorchik JM, Dorr LD et al. Spinopelvic motion and the hip-spine relationship. Bone Joint J / J Arthroplasty 2017–2021.
  • Buckland AJ et al. Dislocation of a primary total hip arthroplasty is more common in patients with a lumbar spinal fusion. Bone Joint J 2017.
  • Berry DJ et al. Effect of femoral head diameter and operative approach on risk of dislocation after primary total hip arthroplasty. JBJS Am 2005.
6questions

THA approaches & perioperative considerations

Approach selection, and the modifiable risk factors that matter.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2023, 2024F, 2025 (x2)

  • Direct anterior approach: internervous between sartorius/rectus femoris (femoral nerve) and tensor fascia lata (superior gluteal nerve). Advantages: lower early dislocation rate, faster early recovery in some series. Disadvantages: lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injury is very common (up to 15–80% report some numbness), a steep learning curve with higher early periprosthetic femoral fracture and wound complication rates (particularly in the obese), and difficult femoral exposure. It is not a 'muscle-sparing' approach in the sense of avoiding all muscle damage — the TFL is frequently injured.
  • Posterior approach: the workhorse; extensile, excellent femoral exposure, but historically higher dislocation rates — largely mitigated by posterior capsular and short external rotator repair, which reduces dislocation several-fold. Sciatic nerve is at risk.
  • Direct lateral (Hardinge): lower dislocation rate but risk of superior gluteal nerve injury and abductor deficiency/Trendelenburg gait — keep the split within 5 cm of the tip of the greater trochanter.
  • Smoking: the single most important modifiable risk factor. Smoking increases wound complications, deep infection, periprosthetic joint infection, delayed/nonunion, medical complications and revision after both TKA and THA. Cessation for at least 4–8 weeks pre-operatively measurably reduces complications — this is one of the most valuable interventions a surgeon can make.
  • Obesity: BMI >40 is associated with higher rates of infection, wound complications, dislocation, component malposition and reoperation, and lower absolute functional scores — but obese patients still achieve substantial improvement in pain and function, so obesity is not an absolute contraindication. Most guidelines recommend optimisation and shared decision-making rather than an arbitrary BMI cut-off.
  • Return to driving after lower extremity arthroplasty: the dominant determinant is restoration of brake reaction time, which is influenced most by the side operated on (right-sided procedures take longer), pain, and the use of opioid analgesia. Most patients recover baseline brake reaction time by ~4 weeks after THA and 4–6 weeks after TKA (right side); left-sided procedures in an automatic vehicle allow earlier return.
  • Geriatric THA: age alone is not a contraindication. Elderly patients report excellent pain relief and satisfaction; the priorities are medical optimisation, choosing fixation appropriate to bone quality (cemented stem), and minimising dislocation risk (larger head/dual mobility).
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Approaches; Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • Higgins BT et al. Anterior vs posterior approach for total hip arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Arthroplasty 2015.
  • Duchman KR et al. The effect of smoking on short-term complications following total hip and knee arthroplasty. JBJS Am 2015.
  • Marks R, Allegrante JP / Kandil A et al. Obesity and total joint arthroplasty. J Arthroplasty.
  • van der Velden CA et al. Return to driving after hip and knee arthroplasty: a systematic review. Bone Joint J.
6questions

TKA: Alignment philosophy & gap balancing

Alignment philosophies and the systematic correction of gap imbalance.

3 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2022 (x2), 2024S (x2)

  • Mechanical alignment targets a neutral hip-knee-ankle axis (0° ± 3°) with a femoral component perpendicular to the femoral mechanical axis and a tibial cut perpendicular to the tibial mechanical axis. Kinematic alignment reproduces the patient's pre-arthritic joint lines and obliquity. Anatomic alignment sets the joint line in ~3° of varus. Evidence to date shows comparable or modestly better early patient-reported outcomes with kinematic alignment, with no proven difference in survivorship — mechanical alignment remains the reference standard with the longest track record, and outliers (>3° varus) are associated with higher failure in some series.
  • Measured resection sets bone cuts from anatomic landmarks (transepicondylar axis, posterior condylar axis, Whiteside's line) and then balances soft tissue; gap balancing sets femoral rotation from the tension of the ligaments in flexion. Measured resection better restores the joint line and patellofemoral tracking; gap balancing more reliably produces a rectangular, balanced flexion gap but risks joint line elevation and femoral component malrotation if the ligaments are unbalanced.
  • Systematic approach to gap imbalance (memorise this grid):
  • • Tight in flexion, loose in extension → the femoral component is too anterior/small, or the distal femoral cut is excessive. Correct by upsizing the femoral component and/or translating it posteriorly, or by augmenting the distal femur.
    • Tight in extension, loose in flexion → resect more distal femur (raises the joint line) and/or downsize/translate the femur anteriorly; release posterior osteophytes and posterior capsule.
    • Tight in both → cut more tibia (a tibial cut affects both gaps equally).
    • Loose in both → increase polyethylene thickness (a thicker insert affects both gaps equally).
    • Balanced in extension, loose in flexion → upsize the femoral component and translate it posteriorly (or use a posterior-augmented femur). Increasing the polyethylene thickness alone would over-tighten extension; increasing tibial slope worsens flexion laxity.
  • Tight in flexion and loose in extension in a varus knee after the cuts → the classic answer is to downsize/anteriorly translate is wrong; instead upsize the femur and shift it posteriorly, or increase tibial slope to open the flexion gap. Be explicit about which gap you are changing and which structure controls it.
  • Release of the popliteus tendon significantly increases the LATERAL FLEXION gap — this is the classic 'which structure controls the lateral flexion gap' answer. The LCL controls the lateral gap in both flexion and extension; the posterolateral capsule and iliotibial band control the lateral extension gap; the superficial MCL controls the medial gap in flexion and extension, and the posteromedial capsule/posterior oblique ligament the medial extension gap.
  • Increasing tibial slope opens the flexion gap and increases posterior femoral rollback; excessive slope in a cruciate-retaining knee causes flexion instability and anterior tibial subluxation.
  • In a varus knee, the sequence of medial release is: osteophyte removal → deep MCL and anteromedial capsule → posteromedial capsule/semimembranosus (for extension tightness) → superficial MCL posterior fibres (for extension) or anterior fibres (for flexion). Remove osteophytes first — they are frequently the cause of the apparent contracture.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Knee Arthroplasty.
  • Whiteside LA. Soft tissue balancing: the knee. J Arthroplasty 2002.
  • Dossett HG et al. Kinematically versus mechanically aligned total knee arthroplasty: a randomized controlled trial. Bone Joint J 2014.
  • Bellemans J et al. The Chitranjan Ranawat Award: is neutral mechanical alignment normal for all patients? CORR 2012.
  • Griffin FM, Insall JN, Scuderi GR. Accuracy of soft tissue balancing in total knee arthroplasty. J Arthroplasty 2000.
5questions

Periprosthetic fracture around hip & knee

Vancouver and Rorabeck classifications, and the fundamental question of implant stability.

4 of 7 sittings2021, 2023, 2024S, 2024F (x2)

  • Vancouver classification (femur around a THA): A — trochanteric (AG greater, AL lesser); B — around the stem: B1 well-fixed stem, B2 loose stem with adequate bone stock, B3 loose stem with poor/deficient bone stock; C — distal to the stem tip.
  • Treatment: B1 → ORIF (locking plate with cables ± strut allograft); B2 → revision to a long, distally fixed (usually tapered fluted modular) stem ± ORIF; B3 → revision with proximal femoral replacement, allograft-prosthetic composite, or an extensively porous-coated long stem in the younger patient; C → ORIF with a plate spanning the stem (overlap the stem to avoid a stress riser); A → usually non-operative unless displaced with abductor dysfunction or associated osteolysis.
  • The single most important determination is whether the stem is loose. A stem that appears well fixed on plain films may be loose — assess pre-operative radiographs for subsidence and lucency, and test the stem intra-operatively. Misclassifying a B2 as a B1 and plating a loose stem is the classic error and leads to failure.
  • Periprosthetic fracture around a TKA (distal femur — Rorabeck): type I undisplaced with an intact prosthesis; type II displaced with an intact prosthesis; type III fracture with a loose or failed prosthesis. Types I/II → ORIF with a lateral locking plate or a retrograde intramedullary nail (confirm the femoral component is 'nail-compatible' with an open box); type III → revision arthroplasty, usually with a distal femoral replacement in the elderly.
  • 'Vancouver B2' terminology applied to a knee is a misuse but is used colloquially in exam stems to mean a periprosthetic fracture with a loose component — the answer is revision arthroplasty, not fixation.
  • Geriatric distal femur periprosthetic fracture: dual plating/nail-plate combination versus distal femoral replacement (DFR) — DFR allows immediate weightbearing and avoids nonunion, and is favoured for a loose component, severe comminution/bone loss, or very poor bone; but it has higher infection and extensor mechanism complication rates and is a bigger operation. Fixation preserves bone stock. Recent comparative data show similar mortality with faster mobilisation after DFR.
  • Periprosthetic patella fracture: most are treated non-operatively if the extensor mechanism is intact and the component is well fixed (results of fixation are poor, with high complication rates). Surgery is for extensor mechanism disruption or a loose patellar component (usually with component removal and patelloplasty rather than revision).
  • Nonunion of a distal femur periprosthetic ORIF (a painful, mobile fracture at 4 months with negative infection work-up) → revision fixation with bone graft, or conversion to a distal femoral replacement in an elderly, low-demand patient.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty; Lower Extremity Trauma.
  • Duncan CP, Masri BA (Canadian). Fractures of the femur after hip replacement. Instr Course Lect 1995.
  • Rorabeck CH, Taylor JW (Canadian). Periprosthetic fractures of the femur complicating total knee arthroplasty. Orthop Clin North Am 1999.
  • Abdel MP et al. Periprosthetic femur fractures treated with modular fluted, tapered stems. Bone Joint J 2014.
  • Hoellwarth JS et al. Equivalent mortality and complication rates following periprosthetic distal femur fractures managed with either lateral locked plating or distal femoral replacement. Injury 2018.
5questions

Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty & conversion to TKA

UKA indications, failure modes, and what conversion to TKA involves.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2021 (x2), 2023, 2025

  • Classic indications (Kozinn & Scott, now liberalised): isolated medial (or lateral) compartment arthritis, an intact ACL, a correctable deformity <10–15° of varus, a flexion contracture <10–15°, and a functional range of motion. Modern practice (Oxford group) has relaxed age, weight and patellofemoral criteria — anteromedial osteoarthritis with a functionally intact ACL is the key indication. Inflammatory arthritis and ACL deficiency remain contraindications (ACL deficiency is a contraindication for mobile-bearing designs in particular).
  • The commonest cause of EARLY failure (<5 years) of a mobile-bearing medial UKA is bearing dislocation, followed by progression of arthritis in the other compartments, aseptic loosening and unexplained pain. In fixed-bearing designs, early failure is more often from aseptic loosening and progression of disease. Later failures across designs are dominated by progression of arthritis in the lateral/patellofemoral compartment and aseptic loosening.
  • Conversion of UKA to TKA: results are generally worse than a primary TKA but better than a revision TKA, with the need for augments, stems or bone graft in ~25–75% of cases depending on the failure mode. The tibial side is the problem — tibial bone loss beneath the component often requires a metal augment or graft and a stemmed component.
  • Comparison of HTO-to-TKA versus UKA-to-TKA: conversion of a high tibial osteotomy to TKA is more technically demanding — patella baja, altered proximal tibial anatomy and metaphyseal deformity, retained hardware, scarring and a compromised lateral soft-tissue sleeve — and is associated with worse outcomes and higher complication rates than conversion of a UKA to TKA. This is a repeated comparison; UKA is generally the easier conversion.
  • Registry data show UKA has a higher revision rate than TKA but better function, faster recovery, lower perioperative morbidity and mortality, and lower complication rates — much of the revision-rate difference is attributable to a lower threshold for revising a UKA. High-volume surgeons achieve markedly better UKA survivorship (the 'usage effect' — surgeons doing >20% of their knees as UKA have better results).
  • Lateral UKA is technically different (the lateral compartment kinematics differ; a fixed bearing is preferred because of a high mobile-bearing dislocation rate) and is less commonly performed.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Knee Arthroplasty.
  • Kozinn SC, Scott R. Unicondylar knee arthroplasty. JBJS Am 1989.
  • Goodfellow J, Murray D et al. Oxford unicompartmental knee arthroplasty outcomes and bearing dislocation. JBJS Br.
  • Liddle AD, Judge A, Pandit H, Murray DW. Adverse outcomes after total and unicompartmental knee replacement in 101,330 matched patients. Lancet 2014.
  • Chen JY et al. Conversion of failed unicompartmental knee arthroplasty and high tibial osteotomy to total knee arthroplasty: a comparison. J Arthroplasty.
4questions

THA complications: Nerve injury, HO & psoas impingement

Nerve injury, iliopsoas impingement, screw safe zones and liner exchange.

3 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2022, 2024F

  • Nerve injury after THA (~1% primary, higher in revision, DDH and lengthening): the sciatic nerve is the most commonly injured, and the peroneal division is the most vulnerable (it is more lateral, more tethered at the sciatic notch and fibular neck, and has less protective connective tissue). Risk factors: developmental dysplasia, revision surgery, posterior approach, lengthening >2–4 cm, female sex, and direct retractor pressure. The femoral nerve is injured with anterior retractors over the acetabular rim, and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve with the direct anterior approach. A post-operative nerve palsy of unknown cause with the hip flexed and knee extended should be treated by flexing the knee and observing — most are neurapraxic and recover partially; explore only if there is a suspected haematoma or an intra-operative event.
  • Acetabular screw safe zones (Wasielewski quadrant system): divide the acetabulum by a line from the ASIS through the centre of the acetabulum and a perpendicular line. The posterosuperior quadrant is the safest (thickest bone, no major structures); the posteroinferior is safe with short screws (sciatic nerve, inferior gluteal vessels). The ANTEROSUPERIOR quadrant is the most dangerous — the external iliac artery and vein lie immediately adjacent; the anteroinferior quadrant risks the obturator neurovascular bundle.
  • Iliopsoas impingement/tendonitis after THA: anterior groin pain worse with resisted hip flexion, active straight-leg raise and rising from a chair or climbing stairs, months to years after surgery, with radiographs showing an anteriorly prominent/uncovered acetabular component rim (or a prominent screw or extruded cement). Diagnosis is supported by a CT measurement of anterior cup prominence and confirmed by an image-guided local anaesthetic injection into the iliopsoas sheath.
  • Treatment of psoas impingement: physiotherapy and injection first; then either arthroscopic or open iliopsoas tenotomy/release (simpler, but causes measurable hip flexion weakness) or acetabular component revision (addresses the cause; preferred where the cup is malpositioned or the patient is young). Tenotomy has good results when the cup is otherwise well positioned.
  • Isolated liner and head exchange for eccentric polyethylene wear with osteolysis: the shell is retained if well fixed and well positioned. The most likely complication is instability/dislocation — because the new liner may not restore jump distance/offset, the capsule has been re-opened, and soft-tissue tension may be altered. Also consider incomplete débridement of the osteolytic lesion and locking-mechanism damage.
  • Heterotopic ossification after THA is common radiographically (up to 30%) but is usually asymptomatic; only a minority (~5–10%) have functionally significant stiffness. Risk factors: male sex, ankylosing spondylitis, DISH, previous HO, hypertrophic OA, extensive muscle dissection. Prophylaxis with single-dose radiation or indomethacin is reserved for high-risk patients. It does not reliably resolve within 6 months — the classic false statement.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • Wasielewski RC, Cooperstein LA, Kruger MP, Rubash HE. Acetabular anatomy and the transacetabular fixation of screws in total hip arthroplasty. JBJS Am 1990.
  • Schmalzried TP, Amstutz HC, Dorey FJ. Nerve palsy associated with total hip replacement: risk factors and prognosis. JBJS Am 1991.
  • Chalmers BP et al. Iliopsoas impingement after primary total hip arthroplasty. J Arthroplasty / Bone Joint J 2017.
  • Board TN, Karva A, Board RE, Gambhir AK, Porter ML. The prophylaxis and treatment of heterotopic ossification following lower limb arthroplasty. JBJS Br 2007.
2questions

TKA outcomes, indications & obesity

Expectations, satisfaction and the influence of BMI.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2024F

  • Approximately 15–20% of TKA patients are not satisfied with their outcome — a substantially higher dissatisfaction rate than THA. The strongest predictors of dissatisfaction are unmet expectations, pre-operative pain catastrophising/depression, minimal radiographic arthritis, and persistent pain from a non-knee source. Managing expectations pre-operatively is the highest-yield intervention.
  • Obesity (BMI 40–45) and TKA: obese patients have higher rates of infection, wound complications, medical complications, component malposition and revision, and lower absolute post-operative scores — but they achieve similar or greater absolute improvement in pain and function from their (worse) baseline. Obesity is therefore not an absolute contraindication; guidelines favour optimisation and shared decision-making rather than a hard BMI cut-off, and bariatric surgery before TKA has not consistently improved arthroplasty outcomes.
  • Small varus deformity with a BMI of 45: proceed with a standard primary TKA using careful soft-tissue balancing — the small varus is easily corrected, and the BMI increases perioperative risk that requires optimisation (glycaemic control, smoking cessation, nutritional assessment, weight loss counselling), not a different implant.
  • Radiographic severity correlates poorly with symptoms; operating on a patient with minimal radiographic arthritis is one of the strongest predictors of a poor outcome.
  • Patients should be counselled that: pain relief is excellent, but a 'forgotten knee' is uncommon; kneeling is difficult for most; expected implant survivorship is >90–95% at 15 years; and full recovery takes up to a year.
  • Extensor mechanism disruption after TKA (patellar tendon rupture) is a devastating complication, particularly in a rheumatoid patient — primary repair alone fails at a high rate, and reconstruction with allograft (extensor mechanism allograft) or synthetic mesh with a gastrocnemius flap is generally required.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Knee Arthroplasty.
  • Bourne RB, Chesworth BM, Davis AM, Mahomed NN, Charron KDJ (Canadian). Patient satisfaction after total knee arthroplasty: who is satisfied and who is not? CORR 2010.
  • Kerkhoffs GMMJ et al. The influence of obesity on the complication rate and outcome of total knee arthroplasty: a meta-analysis. JBJS Am 2012.
  • Dowsey MM, Choong PFM. Obesity is a major risk factor for prosthetic infection after primary hip arthroplasty. CORR 2008.
1question

Hip osteoarthritis: Aetiology & natural history

What causes hip arthritis and what does not.

1 of 7 sittings2022

  • Primary hip osteoarthritis is now understood to be substantially secondary to subtle morphologic abnormality — cam and pincer femoroacetabular impingement, acetabular dysplasia, and post-slip/Perthes deformity account for the majority of 'idiopathic' hip OA in younger patients.
  • Established causes: developmental dysplasia of the hip, FAI (cam more strongly than pincer), SCFE, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, osteonecrosis, post-traumatic incongruity (acetabular fracture), inflammatory arthropathy, septic arthritis, haemochromatosis, and epiphyseal dysplasias.
  • Obesity, age and female sex are risk factors for symptomatic hip OA, though the relationship of obesity with hip OA is weaker than for knee OA. Occupational heavy lifting and farming are recognised occupational associations.
  • Recreational running is NOT associated with an increased risk of hip osteoarthritis — and several cohort studies suggest recreational runners have a lower prevalence than sedentary controls; elite/competitive running at very high volumes may increase risk. This is the classic 'all lead to hip OA except' answer.
  • Radiographic OA and symptoms correlate imperfectly; the presence of hip pain with radiographic changes, not the radiograph alone, drives management.
  • Non-operative management: activity modification, weight loss, physiotherapy, NSAIDs and intra-articular injection. Intra-articular corticosteroid injection into the hip has been associated in some series with rapidly progressive osteoarthritis/osteonecrosis and with increased infection risk if arthroplasty follows within ~3 months — a point worth counselling.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • Ganz R, Leunig M, Leunig-Ganz K, Harris WH. The etiology of osteoarthritis of the hip: an integrated mechanical concept. CORR 2008.
  • Alentorn-Geli E et al. The association of recreational and competitive running with hip and knee osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2017.
  • Agricola R et al. Cam impingement causes osteoarthritis of the hip: a nationwide prospective cohort study (CHECK). Ann Rheum Dis 2013.
1question

Inflammatory arthritis & the arthritic joint

Managing the inflamed joint in inflammatory arthropathy.

1 of 7 sittings2020

  • A patient with known rheumatoid arthritis and a persistently painful, swollen knee that has failed high-dose oral corticosteroids and intra-articular injection, with only mild radiographic changes, has persistent proliferative synovitis. The next step is synovectomy (arthroscopic or open) after optimising medical therapy — and, critically, after excluding septic arthritis, which must always be ruled out in a single inflamed joint.
  • Always aspirate a single acutely inflamed joint in an immunosuppressed patient on biologics: cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals. Inflammatory arthritis and infection can coexist, and biologic therapy blunts the systemic inflammatory response.
  • Synovectomy provides good short-to-medium-term pain relief and reduces synovitis but does not alter the progression of joint destruction; symptoms recur in a substantial proportion by 5 years. Radiosynovectomy is an alternative in some centres. It is a temporising measure in a joint with preserved cartilage.
  • Medical management dominates modern outcomes: early aggressive DMARD and biologic therapy has dramatically reduced the need for rheumatoid joint surgery. Perioperative management — continue conventional synthetic DMARDs; hold biologics, scheduling surgery at the end of the dosing cycle and restarting ~14 days post-operatively.
  • Special considerations in inflammatory arthritis: cervical spine instability (screen before general anaesthesia), poor bone quality and skin, higher infection risk, multiple joint involvement requiring a staged surgical plan (generally lower limb before upper limb; hip before knee; and address the joint causing most disability first).
  • When arthroplasty is indicated, outcomes in inflammatory arthritis are good, but with higher rates of infection, periprosthetic fracture and (in the shoulder/elbow) component loosening.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Systemic Disease; Arthroplasty.
  • Goodman SM et al. 2022 ACR/AAHKS guideline for the perioperative management of antirheumatic medication. J Arthroplasty 2022.
  • Chalmers PN, Sherman SL, Raphael BS, Su EP. Rheumatoid synovectomy: does the surgical approach matter? CORR 2011.
  • Singh JA et al. ACR guideline for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. Arthritis Rheumatol.
1question

Mechanical axis, limb alignment & deformity planning

Definitions of the mechanical and anatomic axes.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • The mechanical axis of the femur is the line from the CENTRE OF THE FEMORAL HEAD to the CENTRE OF THE KNEE (the centre of the intercondylar notch/femoral condyles). This is the standard definition and a recurring single-best-answer item — it is not a line down the shaft, and it is not from the greater trochanter.
  • The anatomic axis of the femur is the line down the mid-diaphysis. The angle between the mechanical and anatomic axes of the femur is ~5–7° (the basis for the 5–6° valgus distal femoral cut in TKA). In the tibia the mechanical and anatomic axes are essentially the same.
  • The overall mechanical axis of the limb (hip–knee–ankle axis) runs from the centre of the femoral head to the centre of the ankle; normally it passes just medial to the centre of the knee (~1.2° of varus). The mechanical axis deviation is measured from this line to the centre of the knee.
  • Key joint orientation angles for deformity planning: mLDFA (mechanical lateral distal femoral angle) ~85–90°; MPTA (medial proximal tibial angle) ~85–90°; LDTA ~86–92°; joint line convergence angle ~0–2°. Deviations localise the deformity to the femur, tibia or joint line.
  • CORA (centre of rotation of angulation) is the intersection of the proximal and distal axis lines; an osteotomy performed at the CORA corrects the angulation without creating translation. An osteotomy away from the CORA requires translation to avoid a secondary deformity.
  • Long-standing (hip-to-ankle) weightbearing radiographs are required for accurate assessment; rotation and flexion of the limb substantially alter the apparent alignment.
References3
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Principles of Orthopaedics; Arthroplasty.
  • Paley D. Principles of Deformity Correction. Springer, 2002.
  • Moreland JR, Bassett LW, Hanker GJ. Radiographic analysis of the axial alignment of the lower extremity. JBJS Am 1987.
1question

Metal-on-metal bearings & adverse local tissue reaction

Investigating and managing the painful metal-on-metal hip.

1 of 7 sittings2023

  • Metal-on-metal (MoM) bearings generate nanometre-sized wear particles and cobalt/chromium ions that produce an adverse local tissue reaction (ALTR/ALVAL) — a lymphocyte-dominated immune response with tissue necrosis, effusion and pseudotumour formation, which can destroy the abductors and bone. Volumetric wear is low but particle number is enormous, which is the mechanistic point.
  • Risk factors for ALTR: small component/head size (<50 mm) in resurfacing, high acetabular inclination (>50–55°) with edge loading, female sex, dysplasia, and specific implant designs (large-head MoM THA). Modular taper corrosion produces an identical picture even with a non-MoM bearing.
  • Work-up of a painful MoM hip: first exclude infection (ESR, CRP, aspiration with cell count — note that a MoM effusion can give falsely elevated automated cell counts, so a manual count is needed), then serum cobalt and chromium levels and MARS (metal artefact reduction sequence) MRI or ultrasound to identify a pseudotumour and assess the abductors. Plain films to assess component position and osteolysis.
  • Thresholds are guidance rather than absolutes: cobalt or chromium >7 µg/L (ppb) is widely used as a concerning level (UK MHRA), with higher levels and rising trends more significant. Metal levels alone do not mandate revision; symptoms plus a soft-tissue reaction do.
  • Indications for revision: pain with a pseudotumour/ALTR on imaging, progressive soft-tissue or bone destruction, abductor compromise, markedly elevated and rising metal ions, and component malposition. Revision should not be delayed once soft-tissue destruction is evident, because abductor loss produces a poor outcome and instability.
  • At revision: excise the pseudotumour and necrotic tissue, convert to a ceramic-on-polyethylene bearing, and be prepared for abductor deficiency (consider dual mobility or constrained components). Outcomes are worse than a routine revision, with high rates of dislocation and persistent weakness.
  • Asymptomatic patients with MoM implants require ongoing surveillance (symptoms, examination, radiographs and — for higher-risk designs — metal ions and cross-sectional imaging).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • Kwon YM, Lombardi AV, Jacobs JJ, Fehring TK, Lewis CG, Cabanela ME. Risk stratification algorithm for management of patients with metal-on-metal hip arthroplasty. JBJS Am 2014.
  • Langton DJ et al. Early failure of metal-on-metal bearings in hip resurfacing and large-diameter total hip replacement. JBJS Br 2010.
  • MHRA Medical Device Alert: All metal-on-metal hip replacements (updated guidance).
1question

Osteonecrosis & hip preservation

Femoral head osteonecrosis: causes, staging and treatment.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • Causes: corticosteroids and alcohol are the two commonest atraumatic causes; also sickle cell disease, Gaucher disease, caisson disease/dysbarism, systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV/antiretrovirals, chemotherapy/radiation, and post-traumatic (femoral neck fracture, hip dislocation, SCFE). A substantial proportion are idiopathic.
  • MRI is the most sensitive and specific investigation and detects disease long before radiographic change. The classic MRI finding is the 'double-line sign' on T2 (a hyperintense inner granulation line and a hypointense outer sclerotic line) with a serpiginous margin.
  • Ficat/ARCO staging: stage I — normal radiograph, abnormal MRI; stage II — sclerosis/cysts without collapse; stage III — subchondral collapse ('crescent sign') with a preserved spherical head; stage IV — femoral head flattening with acetabular involvement/arthritis. The crescent sign marks the transition to irreversible disease and is the key prognostic threshold.
  • Treatment: pre-collapse (stage I–II) with a small lesion → joint-preserving surgery, most commonly core decompression (± bone graft, bone marrow aspirate concentrate, or a vascularised fibular graft). Results are best for small, medial lesions in young patients. Bisphosphonates and other pharmacologic therapies have not shown consistent benefit. Protected weightbearing alone does not prevent collapse.
  • Post-collapse (stage III–IV) → total hip arthroplasty, which gives reliable results in modern series (historically worse in patients with sickle cell disease, renal transplant and ongoing steroid use). Hemiarthroplasty and resurfacing are generally avoided in osteonecrosis because of the involvement of the head.
  • A healthy 55-year-old with 2 months of severe groin pain, normal radiographs and increased uptake on bone scan — the differential is early osteonecrosis, a subchondral insufficiency fracture, and transient osteoporosis/bone marrow oedema syndrome (self-limiting, diffuse marrow oedema without a serpiginous line, treated with protected weightbearing) — MRI distinguishes them.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Hip Arthroplasty; Orthopaedic Dilemmas.
  • Mont MA, Hungerford DS. Non-traumatic avascular necrosis of the femoral head. JBJS Am 1995 / JBJS Am 2020 update.
  • Ficat RP. Idiopathic bone necrosis of the femoral head: early diagnosis and treatment. JBJS Br 1985.
  • Zalavras CG, Lieberman JR. Osteonecrosis of the femoral head: evaluation and treatment. JAAOS 2014.
1question

Revision arthroplasty: Bone loss, extensile exposure & constraint

Exposure options and managing bone loss in revision.

1 of 7 sittings2024F

  • Extended trochanteric osteotomy (ETO) is the workhorse extensile exposure for revision THA: it gives access to a well-fixed cemented or extensively porous-coated stem and to the femoral canal, and it corrects varus remodelling. It is typically ~12–15 cm long, taken laterally and hinged on the vastus lateralis/abductor sleeve to preserve the blood supply, and repaired with cables.
  • Trochanteric osteotomy complications: the classic problems are nonunion, trochanteric escape/migration with abductor weakness, and painful hardware (cable/wire irritation and breakage). A standard (Charnley) trochanteric osteotomy has a higher nonunion rate than an ETO or a trochanteric slide, because the slide/ETO preserves the vastus lateralis in continuity, neutralising the proximal pull of the abductors. The claim that a trochanteric osteotomy does not affect abductor function is false — the standard 'all are true except' item.
  • Femoral bone loss (Paprosky): types I–II are managed with a proximally or extensively porous-coated stem; type IIIA (>4 cm of intact diaphysis) with a long, extensively coated or modular tapered fluted titanium stem; type IIIB (<4 cm of diaphysis) and type IV (non-supportive diaphysis) require modular tapered stems, impaction grafting, allograft-prosthetic composite, or a proximal femoral replacement.
  • Acetabular bone loss (Paprosky): type I/II defects are usually managed with a hemispherical porous cup ± screws (highly porous metals such as tantalum have improved results with a supportive rim); type IIIA ('up and out') with a jumbo cup, augment or structural graft; type IIIB ('up and in') and pelvic discontinuity with a cup-cage construct, custom triflange, or distraction technique.
  • Constraint should be the last resort: a constrained liner transmits high stress to the bone-implant interface and has a high failure rate; correct the underlying cause (component position, offset, abductor function) first. Dual mobility is the preferred first-line option for recurrent instability with functioning abductors.
  • Always exclude infection before revising for aseptic loosening — ESR/CRP and aspiration are mandatory.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Arthroplasty: Total Hip Arthroplasty.
  • Paprosky WG, Perona PG, Lawrence JM. Acetabular defect classification and surgical reconstruction in revision arthroplasty. J Arthroplasty 1994.
  • Della Valle CJ, Paprosky WG. Classification and an algorithmic approach to the reconstruction of femoral deficiency in revision total hip arthroplasty. JBJS Am 2003.
  • Miner TM, Momberger NG, Chong D, Paprosky WL. The extended trochanteric osteotomy in revision hip arthroplasty. J Arthroplasty 2001.

15questions

Cerebral palsy: Classification, hip surveillance & management

GMFCS, hip surveillance, spasticity management and the specific surgical decisions tested.

7 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021 (x3), 2022 (x2), 2023 (x2), 2024S (x2), 2024F, 2025 (x3)

  • GMFCS (Gross Motor Function Classification System) — the single most important prognostic and communication tool: I walks without limitation; II walks with limitations (no assistive device, difficulty on uneven ground/stairs); III walks using a hand-held mobility device; IV self-mobility with limitations, may use powered mobility (sits with support, does not walk functionally); V transported in a manual wheelchair, no independent mobility, no head/trunk control. It is valid from age 2 and is generally stable over time.
  • The described child who 'walks independently with a walker, sits independently but needs trunk support when using the hands, and climbs stairs with assistance' is GMFCS III. A child with GMFCS I walks and climbs stairs without a railing and runs/jumps with reduced speed and coordination — importantly, GMFCS I children can usually be expected to walk into adulthood and are managed largely non-operatively with selective procedures.
  • Hip displacement risk is directly proportional to GMFCS level: roughly GMFCS I ~0%, II ~15%, III ~40%, IV ~70%, V ~90%. This is why GMFCS level is the strongest predictor of hip subluxation/dislocation — not age, not spasticity severity, not limb tone. Formal hip surveillance programmes with serial AP pelvis radiographs and measurement of the migration percentage (Reimers index) are standard of care.
  • Migration percentage (Reimers): the percentage of the femoral head lying lateral to Perkin's line. >30% = subluxation requiring intervention; >50% = significant displacement; >100% = dislocation. A migration percentage >50% with pain or difficulty with perineal care is an indication for reconstruction.
  • Reconstruction of the displaced hip in a non-ambulatory child (GMFCS IV–V) with migration >50%: the answer is varus derotation osteotomy of the proximal femur COMBINED with a pelvic (acetabular) osteotomy and soft-tissue releases (adductor ± psoas). Adding the pelvic osteotomy to the femoral VDRO is what most significantly improves the outcome and reduces recurrence — acetabular dysplasia is always present and does not remodel adequately in a non-ambulator. Soft-tissue release alone is inadequate once migration exceeds 40–50%.
  • For a 10-year-old GMFCS V (spastic quadriplegic, non-ambulatory) with bilateral migration of 50% and coxa valga, definitive management is bilateral VDRO with pelvic osteotomy and adductor releases — not observation, not adductor tenotomy alone, and not salvage (resection/interposition), which is reserved for the painful, arthritic, unreconstructible hip.
  • Botulinum toxin A: blocks acetylcholine release at the presynaptic neuromuscular junction by cleaving SNAP-25 (a SNARE protein), producing a temporary, reversible chemodenervation lasting 3–6 months. Evidence points: botox plus serial casting is superior to casting alone for dynamic equinus in the short term, but botox alone is comparable to serial casting alone; it does not prevent or delay the need for eventual surgery for a fixed contracture, and it is ineffective for a fixed (static) contracture — it treats dynamic tone only. Repeated injections can cause muscle atrophy/fibrosis and antibody formation.
  • Equinus and toe-walking in spastic diplegia: use the Silfverskiöld test. Dorsiflexion of −10° with the knee extended improving to 0° with the knee flexed indicates an isolated gastrocnemius contracture → gastrocnemius recession (Strayer). Over-lengthening the Achilles produces a calcaneal/crouch gait, which is far worse and largely irreversible — the cardinal error.
  • Jump gait (hip flexion contracture, knee flexion contracture, equinus) in an ambulatory GMFCS III adolescent: single-event multilevel surgery is standard, and the knee component of a 35° fixed knee flexion contracture is best treated by distal femoral extension osteotomy with patellar tendon advancement — isolated hamstring lengthening is inadequate for a fixed contracture and risks crouch.
  • Upper extremity surgery in CP: the strongest predictor of a good outcome is preserved sensation — specifically proprioception and stereognosis (and adequate voluntary control/selective motor control), not the degree of spasticity, contracture or age. A child with poor stereognosis will not use the hand regardless of how well it is positioned.
  • A 45° elbow flexion contracture in a child with good hand function is a relative contraindication to aggressive release — the contracture may be functionally useful, and release risks losing hand-to-mouth function; the classic 'what is contraindicated' answer relates to operating on a functional limb where the deformity aids function.
  • Scoliosis in CP correlates with GMFCS level and non-ambulatory status (up to 70–90% in GMFCS V); curves are long, C-shaped, with pelvic obliquity, progress after skeletal maturity, and bracing does not prevent progression (it may aid sitting). Surgery is posterior instrumented fusion to the pelvis for pelvic obliquity.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Cerebral Palsy.
  • Palisano R, Rosenbaum P, Walter S, Russell D, Wood E, Galuppi B (Canadian, CanChild/McMaster). Development and reliability of a system to classify gross motor function in children with cerebral palsy. Dev Med Child Neurol 1997.
  • Soo B, Howard JJ, Boyd RN, Reid SM, Lanigan A, Wolfe R, Reddihough D, Graham HK. Hip displacement in cerebral palsy. JBJS Am 2006.
  • Reimers J. The stability of the hip in children: a radiological study of the results of muscle surgery in cerebral palsy. Acta Orthop Scand Suppl 1980.
  • Shore BJ, Graham HK et al. Adductor surgery to prevent hip displacement in children with cerebral palsy. JBJS Am 2012.
  • Novak I et al. State of the evidence traffic light 2019: systematic review of interventions for preventing and treating children with cerebral palsy. Curr Neurol Neurosci Rep 2020.
15questions

DDH: Screening, Pavlik & surgical management

Screening, ultrasound parameters, Pavlik harness use and failure, and the surgical algorithm by age.

7 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022 (x3), 2023, 2024S (x3), 2024F (x3), 2025 (x3)

  • Risk factors: breech presentation (the strongest — especially frank breech), female sex, family history, firstborn, oligohydramnios and left hip predominance (the left hip lies against the maternal sacrum). Associated packaging disorders: congenital muscular torticollis, metatarsus adductus, and congenital knee dislocation.
  • Physical examination by age: Ortolani (reduction of a dislocated hip) and Barlow (dislocation of a reducible hip) are reliable only in the first ~3 months — after that the hip becomes fixed and these tests become negative. After 3 months the most useful and reliable examination finding is LIMITED HIP ABDUCTION (with asymmetric thigh folds, apparent femoral shortening/Galeazzi sign, and a limp/Trendelenburg in the walking child). For a 7-month-old with a family history and frank breech, limited abduction is the most reliable examination finding — Ortolani/Barlow will be negative.
  • Ultrasound is the imaging of choice until the femoral head ossifies (~4–6 months), after which an AP pelvis radiograph is used. Graf alpha angle (bony acetabular roof) normal >60°; 50–59° immature/mild dysplasia; <50° dysplastic. Beta angle (cartilaginous roof) normal <55°. Femoral head coverage (D/d ratio) should be >50%. Ultrasound before 6 weeks over-diagnoses physiologic immaturity.
  • Pavlik harness: the mainstay under ~6 months. Position the hips in flexion of 90–100° and abduction (not forced) — 'flexion and gentle abduction'. Follow with ultrasound at 3 weeks; if the hip is not reduced by 3–4 weeks, abandon the harness and proceed to closed reduction.
  • Pavlik complications — the exam favourites: femoral nerve palsy (from excessive hip FLEXION — usually >120°; presents as absent quadriceps function/inability to actively extend the knee; management is to discontinue the harness until the palsy resolves, then reapply with less flexion — it is a marker of higher failure risk); and avascular necrosis of the femoral head (from excessive ABDUCTION, which is caused by over-tightening the POSTERIOR strap — the classic 'over-tighten the posterior strap' stem; the posterior strap controls abduction, the anterior strap controls flexion). Inferior/posterior dislocation and 'Pavlik harness disease' (posterolateral acetabular erosion from persistent harness use on an unreduced hip) also occur.
  • Predictors of Pavlik failure: an irreducible (Ortolani-negative, dislocated) hip is the strongest predictor; also bilateral dislocation, an initially dislocated (rather than subluxed/dysplastic) hip, absent femoral head coverage, older age at initiation (>7 weeks), development of femoral nerve palsy, and low initial alpha angle. A large baby is not a recognised predictor of failure — a common distractor.
  • A 6-month-old treated for 4 weeks in a well-fitted Pavlik whose ultrasound shows alpha angle 30° and coverage 25% has failed harness treatment — the appropriate next step is to abandon the Pavlik and proceed to closed reduction with arthrogram under anaesthesia and spica casting (with adductor tenotomy as needed), not to continue or tighten the harness.
  • Treatment algorithm by age: 0–6 months — Pavlik harness. 6–18 months — closed reduction with arthrogram ± adductor tenotomy and spica cast; open reduction if closed reduction fails or the reduction is not concentric/stable in the 'safe zone' (Ramsey). 18 months–2 years — open reduction (± femoral shortening). >2–3 years — open reduction with femoral shortening derotational osteotomy ± pelvic osteotomy. Femoral shortening is preferred to traction to reduce AVN.
  • Blocks to reduction (from the arthrogram/open reduction): inverted limbus (infolded labrum), hypertrophied ligamentum teres, pulvinar, transverse acetabular ligament, capsular constriction (hourglass), and the iliopsoas tendon. An inverted limbus is a block to concentric reduction and is an indication for open reduction; a 2-month-old with an inverted limbus should not be assumed to need immediate open reduction — a Pavlik trial is still reasonable at that age, and many limbi evert with reduction.
  • Medial (Ludloff) approach for open reduction in the infant: gives direct access to the inferomedial block (transverse acetabular ligament, iliopsoas, ligamentum teres) with less blood loss, but you cannot perform a capsulorrhaphy, cannot address the superior/lateral acetabulum, and cannot perform a concurrent femoral or pelvic osteotomy through it — these are the limitations tested. It also carries a higher reported rate of AVN (medial femoral circumflex artery at risk). The structure most at risk during an iliopsoas tenotomy from a medial approach in an infant is the medial femoral circumflex artery (with the lesser trochanter apophysis and the femoral nerve also at risk).
  • The primary femoral deformity in DDH is excessive femoral anteversion (with coxa valga); the acetabular deformity is deficient anterolateral coverage. Trisomy 21 produces a characteristic posterior/posterolateral acetabular deficiency (with generalised ligamentous laxity), which is why standard anterior-coverage osteotomies may be inadequate.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: DDH.
  • Graf R. Fundamentals of sonographic diagnosis of infant hip dysplasia. J Pediatr Orthop 1984.
  • Mubarak S, Garfin S, Vance R, McKinnon B, Sutherland D. Pitfalls in the use of the Pavlik harness for treatment of congenital dysplastic hip. JBJS Am 1981.
  • Murnaghan ML, Browne RH, Sucato DJ, Birch J. Femoral nerve palsy in Pavlik harness treatment for developmental dysplasia of the hip. JBJS Am 2011.
  • Lerman JA, Emans JB, Millis MB, Share J, Zurakowski D, Kasser JR. Early failure of Pavlik harness treatment for developmental hip dysplasia: clinical and ultrasound predictors. J Pediatr Orthop 2001.
  • Weinstein SL, Mubarak SJ, Wenger DR. Developmental hip dysplasia and dislocation. Instr Course Lect 2004.
13questions

Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: Natural history, bracing & surgery

Progression risk, skeletal maturity staging, the BrAIST trial, MRI indications and surgical planning.

6 of 7 sittings2020, 2021 (x3), 2022, 2023 (x3), 2024F (x3), 2025 (x2)

  • Risk factors for curve progression: remaining skeletal growth (the dominant factor — quantified by Risser stage, Sanders stage, triradiate cartilage status and menarchal status), larger curve magnitude at presentation, female sex, thoracic curve location, and double curves. A curve >25–30° in a skeletally immature patient (Risser 0–1, premenarchal) has a very high risk of progression; a curve <30° at skeletal maturity rarely progresses. Curves >50° at maturity progress ~1°/year into adulthood.
  • Sanders skeletal maturity staging (based on the hand/wrist digital physes) is more precise than Risser for predicting the peak growth velocity and progression risk. Sanders 1–2 = pre-peak growth velocity (highest risk); Sanders 3–4 = peak; Sanders 5–8 = declining/closed growth (low risk). Therefore the highest risk of progression on non-operative treatment is a young patient at Sanders 1–2 with a curve already in the 30–39° range — combining maximum remaining growth with a large curve. A Sanders 5–8 patient with a 30–39° curve has little growth left and much lower progression risk.
  • BrAIST (Weinstein, NEJM 2013) — the landmark trial: bracing significantly decreased progression to the surgical threshold (50°) compared with observation (72% vs 48% success), with a clear dose-response relationship — the benefit increased with hours of wear, with >12–13 hours/day giving ~90% success. The trial was stopped early for efficacy. Bracing is indicated for curves 25–40° in a skeletally immature patient (Risser 0–2).
  • Bracing does not correct the curve — it prevents progression. It is ineffective at skeletal maturity, in curves >45–50°, and (traditionally) in hypokyphotic/thoracic lordotic curves; compliance is the dominant determinant of success.
  • Indications for MRI of the neuraxis in AIS — this is a high-yield list: atypical curve pattern (LEFT thoracic curve), rapid progression, age <10 years (juvenile/infantile onset), abnormal neurologic examination (absent abdominal reflexes is a classic sign), pain that is significant or nocturnal, associated foot deformity (cavovarus), and excessive thoracic kyphosis or a short sharp curve. These raise concern for syringomyelia, Chiari malformation, tethered cord or an intraspinal tumour.
  • A 10-year-old with a LEFT thoracic curve, wedge vertebrae at T8–10 and a compensatory right lumbar curve is not idiopathic — the best first test is an MRI of the whole spine (and this pattern also suggests congenital scoliosis, requiring assessment for the VACTERL associations: renal ultrasound and cardiac echo).
  • The radiographic measure most predictive of curve correction for main thoracic and thoracolumbar curves is curve flexibility as measured on side-bending (or fulcrum-bending/traction) films — flexibility, not the standing Cobb angle, predicts the achievable correction. (Fulcrum-bending radiographs correlate best for thoracic curves.)
  • Surgical indications: curves >45–50° in the skeletally immature, >50–55° at maturity, progressive curves despite bracing, significant deformity/truncal imbalance, and pain. Standard treatment is posterior spinal instrumented fusion with pedicle screws; selective thoracic fusion is used for Lenke 1 curves with a compensatory lumbar curve that will correct spontaneously.
  • Intraoperative neuromonitoring: a >50% drop in motor evoked potentials (MEPs) is the alert criterion. In a paediatric deformity correction, the commonest cause of a significant MEP drop after instrumentation and correction is HYPOTENSION/relative spinal cord ischaemia and the correction manoeuvre itself (distraction/derotation), rather than direct screw malposition — the immediate response is a stepwise protocol: raise the mean arterial pressure (to >80–85 mmHg), confirm normothermia/haemoglobin/anaesthetic technique, remove the correction (release the rods/distraction), check implant position, and perform a wake-up test if signals do not return. Cord ischaemia from distraction and hypotension is the mechanism.
  • Post-operative complications of AIS surgery: the commonest cause of low urine output with normal haemodynamics after AIS correction is SIADH (a well-described post-operative phenomenon in adolescent spine surgery) — treat with fluid restriction, not with a fluid bolus. VTE risk in an adolescent with AIS is very low, and the best prophylaxis is mechanical (early mobilisation and sequential compression devices), not chemical anticoagulation.
  • Superior mesenteric artery (cast) syndrome occurs after significant lengthening/correction in a thin patient (post-prandial vomiting and abdominal pain) — treat with nasogastric decompression, positioning and nutritional support.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Scoliosis.
  • Weinstein SL, Dolan LA, Wright JG (Canadian co-author), Dobbs MB. Effects of bracing in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis (BrAIST). NEJM 2013.
  • Sanders JO et al. Predicting scoliosis progression from skeletal maturity: a simplified classification during adolescence. JBJS Am 2008.
  • Lonstein JE, Carlson JM. The prediction of curve progression in untreated idiopathic scoliosis during growth. JBJS Am 1984.
  • Lenke LG et al. Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: a new classification to determine extent of spinal arthrodesis. JBJS Am 2001.
  • Vitale MG et al. Best practices in intraoperative neuromonitoring in spine deformity surgery. Spine Deform 2014.
11questions

Paediatric Monteggia & radial neck fractures

The Bado classification, causes of failed radial head reduction, and radial neck fracture management.

5 of 7 sittings2021, 2023, 2024S (x3), 2024F (x3), 2025 (x3)

  • Bado classification is defined by the direction of radial head dislocation: type I — anterior (the commonest, ~70%, with an apex-anterior ulnar fracture); type II — posterior/posterolateral (the commonest in adults, rare in children); type III — lateral (common in children, associated with an olecranon/proximal metaphyseal ulna greenstick fracture); type IV — anterior dislocation with fractures of both the radius and ulna.
  • The cardinal principle: anatomic reduction of the ULNA reduces the radial head. In a child, this usually means correcting the ulnar length and angulation — closed reduction and casting for a plastic/greenstick ulnar deformity, and intramedullary nailing or plating for a complete or unstable ulnar fracture. If the radial head will not stay reduced, the ulnar reduction is inadequate until proven otherwise.
  • Causes of a radial head remaining unreduced/failure of reduction: residual ulnar deformity (plastic deformation, malreduction, shortening — the commonest and the most important), interposition of the annular ligament (buttonholed over the radial head), interposition of the capsule or the biceps tendon, a delayed/chronic presentation (>3–4 weeks) with soft-tissue contracture and a deformed radial head, and an osteochondral fragment. A PIN palsy is NOT a cause of failed reduction — it is a consequence of the injury and the usual 'all contribute EXCEPT' answer.
  • PIN palsy with a paediatric Monteggia: occurs in up to ~10–20% of type I and III injuries. It is almost always a neurapraxia that resolves spontaneously once the radial head is reduced. The correct next step is anatomic reduction of the ulna/radial head and observation, with EMG at ~6 weeks and exploration only if there is no recovery by ~3 months. Do not explore the nerve acutely.
  • Bado type II (posterior) in an elderly adult is a different animal — it is usually a transolecranon/proximal ulna fracture-dislocation with a comminuted proximal ulna, a coronoid fragment and a radial head fracture. The essential steps are anatomic restoration of the proximal ulna (trochlear notch) with a dorsal plate, and fixation or replacement of the radial head; a small coronoid tip fragment is the structure least likely to require fixation once the ulna and radial head are restored.
  • Chronic/missed Monteggia (presenting weeks to months later) is a difficult problem: treatment requires ulnar osteotomy (usually opening-wedge with over-correction into extension/lengthening) with or without annular ligament reconstruction and open reduction of the radial head. Results deteriorate with time; a chronically dislocated radial head with a deformed, dome-shaped head may be best left alone in an older child.
  • Radial neck fractures: acceptable alignment in a child is <30° of angulation and <3–4 mm of translation (some accept up to 45° in very young children, given remodelling potential). Closed reduction techniques include the Patterson manoeuvre (traction with varus and direct pressure), the Israeli technique (thumb pressure with forearm pronation/supination), and percutaneous joystick (Métaizeau intramedullary nail) reduction, which is the workhorse for a fracture that cannot be reduced closed.
  • Factors associated with a failed/difficult closed reduction of a radial neck fracture: greater initial angulation (>60°), greater translation/complete displacement, delayed presentation, associated elbow injuries (olecranon fracture, elbow dislocation), and older age. A small degree of angulation (e.g. <30°) is NOT associated with decreased odds of successful reduction — it simply does not need reduction, and this is the standard 'which is not associated' answer.
  • Open reduction of a radial neck fracture carries a substantially higher rate of AVN of the radial head, stiffness, synostosis and premature physeal closure, and should be a last resort. Never remove the radial head in a child.
  • The radiocapitellar line (a line drawn down the radial neck must pass through the capitellum on every view) is the diagnostic tool — any paediatric ulna fracture demands scrutiny of this line.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatric Trauma: Upper Extremity.
  • Bado JL. The Monteggia lesion. CORR 1967.
  • Ring D, Waters PM. Operative fixation of Monteggia fractures in children. JBJS Br 1996.
  • Métaizeau JP. Reduction and osteosynthesis of radial neck fractures in children by centromedullary pinning. Injury 2005.
  • Kim HT et al. Management of displaced radial neck fractures in children. J Pediatr Orthop.
  • Rodgers WB, Waters PM, Hall JE. Chronic Monteggia lesions in children. JBJS Am 1996.
11questions

Supracondylar humerus fracture

Gartland classification, the pulseless hand, nerve injury patterns and predictors of loss of reduction.

6 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2022 (x2), 2023 (x3), 2024S (x2), 2024F, 2025

  • Gartland classification (extension type): I non-displaced; II displaced with an intact posterior cortex/hinge (IIA angulation only, IIB with rotation/translation); III completely displaced with no cortical contact (posteromedial displacement is more common, ~75%); IV complete instability in both flexion and extension (multidirectional, diagnosed intra-operatively).
  • Nerve injury patterns — memorise the pairing: in the common EXTENSION type with posteromedial displacement, the ANTERIOR INTEROSSEOUS NERVE (a branch of the median) is the most commonly injured (inability to make an 'OK' sign, no sensory loss); the radial nerve is injured with posterolateral displacement. In the uncommon FLEXION type, the ULNAR NERVE is the most commonly injured. Iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury is the commonest nerve complication of treatment, related to medial pin placement.
  • Block to reduction of a FLEXION-type supracondylar fracture: the proximal fragment buttonholes anteriorly through the brachialis, and the structure most commonly blocking closed reduction is the ULNAR NERVE (entrapped at the fracture site as it passes posteromedially) — in the extension type the classic block is the brachialis muscle (the 'brachialis sign'/pucker sign) and the anterior neurovascular bundle. Flexion-type fractures are more often irreducible and require open reduction.
