  • The 'brachialis sign' (anterior skin puckering/dimpling) indicates the proximal fragment has penetrated the brachialis and is tenting the skin — it is associated with an irreducible fracture, higher rates of open reduction, neurovascular injury and compartment syndrome. It is not associated with a benign course, and 'milking' the fracture free is required.
  • Prognostic factors for loss of reduction after CRPP: the strongest is failure to achieve/maintain an adequate pin configuration (inadequate pin spread at the fracture site, fewer than the required number of pins, or pins that do not engage both cortices), and residual sagittal or coronal malreduction — of the radiographic features, sagittal obliquity of the fracture (an oblique fracture line in the sagittal plane) is the most cited single predictor of loss of reduction, followed by coronal obliquity and comminution. Age itself is not a strong predictor.
  • Pin configuration: two or three lateral divergent pins provide adequate stability for most fractures and avoid the risk of ulnar nerve injury. A medial pin adds torsional stability and is used for medial comminution or type IV instability, but must be placed with the elbow extended (to allow the ulnar nerve to fall posteriorly) or through a mini-open incision. Crossed pinning has a several-fold higher rate of iatrogenic ulnar nerve injury (~4–6%).
  • Post-operative ulnar nerve palsy after crossed pinning: the appropriate management is to remove the medial pin (and explore/decompress if the palsy does not recover). The palsy is usually a neurapraxia and recovers over weeks to months; exploration is not required immediately but is indicated for a palsy that appeared after pinning and does not improve.
  • The pulseless supracondylar fracture — the highest-yield algorithm: pulseless but WELL-PERFUSED hand (pink, warm, capillary refill <3 s) → urgent reduction and pinning, then reassess. If the hand remains pink and perfused after reduction even without a palpable pulse, the accepted management is close observation in hospital for 24–48 hours — collateral circulation is usually adequate and the pulse commonly returns; routine exploration or angiography is not required. Pulseless AND poorly perfused (white, cold) hand → immediate reduction and pinning; if perfusion does not return, urgent vascular exploration (with vascular surgery) — do not delay for angiography.
  • In a 5-year-old with a supracondylar fracture, an AIN palsy and a cold, pulseless hand, the next step is immediate closed reduction and percutaneous pinning in theatre — reduction alone frequently restores perfusion.
  • Compartment syndrome risk is increased by: a floating elbow (ipsilateral forearm fracture), vascular injury with reperfusion, high-energy injury, delayed presentation, and hyperflexion of the elbow >90° in a cast. In children, the 3 A's — increasing Analgesia requirement, Anxiety and Agitation — precede the classic signs.
  • Cubitus varus (gunstock deformity) is the classic malunion — a cosmetic deformity from a malreduced fracture (coronal tilt/medial column collapse and internal rotation), not from growth arrest. It is associated with an increased risk of later posterolateral rotatory instability and lateral condyle fracture, and is treated with a lateral closing wedge (or dome) osteotomy when symptomatic.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatric Trauma: Upper Extremity.
  • Gartland JJ. Management of supracondylar fractures of the humerus in children. Surg Gynecol Obstet 1959.
  • AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: The Treatment of Pediatric Supracondylar Humerus Fractures, 2011.
  • Skaggs DL et al. Operative treatment of supracondylar fractures of the humerus in children: the consequences of pin placement. JBJS Am 2001.
  • Blakey CM, Biant LC, Birch R. Ischaemia and the pink, pulseless hand complicating supracondylar fractures of the humerus in childhood. JBJS Br 2009.
  • Bashyal RK et al. Complications after pinning of supracondylar distal humerus fractures. J Pediatr Orthop 2009.
9questions

Paediatric septic arthritis & osteomyelitis

Kocher criteria, distinguishing septic arthritis from transient synovitis, and the neonatal hip.

5 of 7 sittings2022 (x3), 2023 (x2), 2024S, 2024F (x2), 2025

  • Kocher criteria for septic arthritis of the hip versus transient synovitis: (1) non-weightbearing, (2) fever >38.5 °C, (3) ESR >40 mm/h, (4) WBC >12,000/mm³. Probability of septic arthritis: 1 predictor ~3%, 2 ~40%, 3 ~93%, 4 ~99%. CRP >2.0 mg/dL is an independent predictor and, in Caird's modification, fever is the strongest single predictor.
  • Definitive diagnosis requires joint aspiration — the criteria are a probability tool, not a substitute. The best test to rule out septic arthritis in an equivocal case is aspiration with synovial fluid analysis (cell count, Gram stain, culture); a synovial WBC >50,000/mm³ with >90% neutrophils supports septic arthritis (though lower counts occur in early or partially treated cases). Aspirate before starting antibiotics wherever possible. A 4-year-old with borderline inflammatory markers, an effusion on ultrasound and refusal to weightbear needs aspiration, not empirical treatment or MRI first.
  • Ultrasound detects an effusion but cannot distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis — this is a repeatedly tested limitation.
  • Organisms: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest at all ages (including MRSA in endemic areas). Age-specific additions: neonates — group B Streptococcus, S. aureus, gram-negative bacilli; 6 months–5 years — Kingella kingae (an increasingly recognised cause of subacute, indolent septic arthritis/osteomyelitis in toddlers, often with normal or minimally elevated inflammatory markers, and it grows poorly on standard media — inoculate into blood culture bottles and use PCR); adolescents — Neisseria gonorrhoeae; sickle cell disease — Salmonella and S. aureus; puncture wound through a shoe — Pseudomonas.
  • A 2-week-old neonate with elbow swelling, fever and refusal to move the arm — the expected organism is Staphylococcus aureus, with group B Streptococcus and gram-negative organisms also in the differential. Neonates require broad empirical cover.
  • Neonatal septic arthritis of the hip is a surgical emergency and behaves differently: neonates are often afebrile with normal or minimally elevated inflammatory markers (an immature immune response), the presentation is pseudoparalysis and irritability with hip/knee motion, and the transphyseal vessels present until ~18 months allow rapid spread between metaphysis and joint, so concomitant osteomyelitis is the rule rather than the exception. Delay causes catastrophic destruction of the capital femoral epiphysis (Tom Smith arthritis).
  • Suspect concomitant osteomyelitis with septic arthritis when: symptoms have been present >3–4 days, CRP >13–15 mg/L and persistently elevated after drainage, age <1 year (transphyseal vessels), platelet count <310,000, positive blood cultures, and failure to improve after adequate joint drainage. MRI is the study of choice to identify adjacent osteomyelitis, subperiosteal abscess and pyomyositis. Roughly a third of children with septic arthritis have adjacent osteomyelitis.
  • The most common finding in paediatric osteomyelitis is metaphyseal involvement of a long bone (the distal femur and proximal tibia are the commonest sites) — the sluggish flow in the metaphyseal sinusoidal loops adjacent to the physis is the classic pathophysiology. Radiographs are normal for the first 7–14 days (until 30–50% of bone mineral is lost); MRI is the most sensitive early imaging, and bone scan is useful when the site is unclear or for multifocal disease. Blood cultures are positive in ~50%.
  • Treatment: urgent surgical drainage/irrigation of the septic joint (arthrotomy for the hip — a septic hip is a surgical emergency because of the intracapsular blood supply to the femoral head) plus IV antibiotics. For osteomyelitis without abscess, antibiotics alone frequently suffice; surgical drainage is indicated for a subperiosteal or intraosseous abscess, sequestrum, or failure to respond in 48–72 hours. Modern practice uses a short IV course transitioning to oral antibiotics once clinically improving and CRP is falling, for a total of 3–4 weeks (longer for MRSA/complicated disease).
  • Special situations: MRSA (particularly PVL-positive) causes more severe disease with multifocal involvement, DVT, septic emboli and pyomyositis — obtain an MRI of the whole limb and consider a Doppler. Chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis (CRMO) is a sterile, culture-negative inflammatory mimic with multiple symmetric metaphyseal lesions, treated with NSAIDs.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Infection.
  • Kocher MS, Zurakowski D, Kasser JR. Differentiating between septic arthritis and transient synovitis of the hip in children. JBJS Am 1999; and Kocher MS et al. Validation. JBJS Am 2004.
  • Caird MS et al. Factors distinguishing septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip in children. JBJS Am 2006.
  • Montgomery NI, Rosenfeld S. Pediatric osteoarticular infection update. J Pediatr Orthop 2015.
  • Yagupsky P. Kingella kingae: from medical rarity to an emerging paediatric pathogen. Lancet Infect Dis 2004.
  • Peltola H, Pääkkönen M. Acute osteomyelitis in children. NEJM 2014.
8questions

Paediatric ACL & tibial spine injury

Physeal-sparing techniques, graft failure risk, and tibial eminence fractures.

5 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2022, 2023 (x2), 2024S (x2)

  • Paediatric ACL tears do NOT do well non-operatively. Delayed reconstruction is associated with higher rates of meniscal tears (particularly medial meniscus), chondral damage and instability episodes — multiple studies and a Canadian/international consensus support early reconstruction in the skeletally immature athlete rather than bracing until maturity. This is the central management point.
  • Technique selection is by skeletal age, not chronological age: prepubescent/Tanner 1–2 (large amount of growth remaining) → physeal-sparing techniques — the iliotibial band (Micheli/Kocher) combined intra-/extra-articular reconstruction or an all-epiphyseal reconstruction. Adolescent/Tanner 3 with modest growth remaining → transphyseal reconstruction with a soft-tissue (hamstring) graft using vertical, centrally placed, small-diameter tunnels, avoiding bone blocks across the physis and avoiding hardware/tensioned fixation across the physis. Skeletally mature → standard adult reconstruction.
  • Growth disturbance after paediatric ACL reconstruction is uncommon but well described: distal femoral valgus/leg-length discrepancy and tibial recurvatum from a bone block or a large/oblique tunnel across the physis, or from hardware crossing the physis. A BTB graft with bone blocks across an open physis is contraindicated — the classic 'most appropriate technique' question for a 10-year-old competitive soccer player is an all-epiphyseal or IT-band physeal-sparing reconstruction, not BTB.
  • Risk factors for graft failure in adolescents: young age at reconstruction, return to high-level pivoting sport, allograft use (markedly higher failure in this population), non-anatomic tunnel placement, increased posterior tibial slope, generalised ligamentous laxity, and early return to sport before achieving strength symmetry. Female sex is a risk factor for primary ACL injury but is not a consistent risk factor for graft failure — the standard 'all except' distractor.
  • Differences between adult and paediatric knee ligament injuries: children more often sustain tibial eminence (spine) avulsion fractures than mid-substance ACL tears (though mid-substance tears now predominate even in children because of early sport specialisation), and physeal injuries occur in place of some ligament injuries. A physeal fracture is more common than a collateral ligament rupture in a skeletally immature knee — always stress-test and consider stress views.
  • Tibial spine (eminence) fracture — Meyers & McKeever: type I non-displaced; type II hinged anteriorly (posterior cortex intact); type III completely displaced; type IV comminuted/rotated. Types I and reducible II → closed reduction in extension and immobilisation. Types II (irreducible), III and IV → arthroscopic reduction and fixation (suture or screw).
  • The block to reduction of a displaced tibial eminence fracture is the anterior horn of the medial meniscus (and the intermeniscal ligament) entrapped under the fragment — this must be recognised and extracted at arthroscopy.
  • The most common complication after surgical treatment of a tibial spine fracture is ARTHROFIBROSIS/loss of motion (particularly loss of extension), reported in up to 10–20%. Early range of motion is therefore emphasised. Residual anterior laxity (a positive Lachman without symptomatic instability) is very common but usually well tolerated; nonunion and growth arrest are rare.
  • A 14-year-old with a skeletally immature knee, an effusion, positive Lachman and a visible eminence fracture on radiograph should have arthroscopic assessment and fixation — the options that are inappropriate are non-operative treatment of a displaced fragment and adult-style transphyseal BTB reconstruction.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics; Sports.
  • Kocher MS, Garg S, Micheli LJ. Physeal-sparing reconstruction of the anterior cruciate ligament in skeletally immature prepubescent children and adolescents. JBJS Am 2005.
  • Ramski DE et al. Anterior cruciate ligament tears in children and adolescents: a meta-analysis of nonoperative versus operative treatment. AJSM 2014.
  • Kocher MS et al. Tibial eminence fractures in children: prevalence of meniscal entrapment. AJSM 2003.
  • Frosch KH et al. Outcomes and risks of operative treatment of rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament in children and adolescents. Arthroscopy 2010.
8questions

Paediatric femoral shaft fracture & spica casting

Treatment by age, contraindications to early spica, and fixation options.

5 of 7 sittings2021, 2022 (x2), 2024S, 2024F (x2), 2025 (x2)

  • Treatment algorithm by age (AAOS CPG): 0–6 months — Pavlik harness or a simple splint. 6 months–5 years — early spica casting (with >2–3 cm of shortening being the main limit); flexible intramedullary nails are an alternative in the older end of this range. 5–11 years — flexible (titanium elastic) intramedullary nails are the workhorse; submuscular bridge plating for length-unstable or comminuted fractures. >11 years/adolescent — rigid locked intramedullary nail using a lateral trochanteric or piriformis-sparing entry (avoid the piriformis fossa entry because of the risk of AVN of the femoral head), or submuscular plating.
  • Contraindications to early (immediate) spica casting — high-yield: shortening >2–3 cm or unacceptable angulation, age over ~5–6 years or weight >~50 lb (spica becomes impractical and remodelling less reliable), an associated abdominal/thoracic injury or polytrauma requiring access and monitoring, head injury, an open fracture, vascular injury, and suspected non-accidental injury requiring investigation. An 18-month-old polytrauma patient with a possible abdominal injury should NOT go into an early spica — the abdominal injury is the contraindication (access, monitoring and the risk of a compartment/abdominal problem).
  • Acceptable alignment in a spica (by age, using remodelling potential): shortening <2 cm (some accept 1.5–2 cm; overgrowth of ~1 cm typically occurs after femoral shaft fracture in children aged 2–10 years), varus/valgus <10–15°, anterior/posterior angulation <20–30°, and rotation <10°. Remodelling is greatest closest to the physis, in the plane of joint motion, and in the youngest children.
  • Overgrowth after paediatric femoral shaft fracture averages ~1 cm (0.7–2 cm) in children aged 2–10 years, driven by physeal hyperaemia, and is maximal in the first 2 years after injury. The best predictor of final leg length is serial measurement over time (the multiplier method or a Moseley/Green-Anderson chart applied to serial data) — a single early measurement is unreliable. For a 4-year-old with a 2 cm discrepancy 24 months post-injury, serial follow-up with the multiplier method is the answer, since overgrowth has largely occurred and the discrepancy usually stabilises.
  • Flexible (elastic) intramedullary nails: use two nails of equal diameter, each filling ~40% of the canal at the isthmus (so a combined ~80% canal fill) — the classic number. They work by three-point elastic fixation and are ideal for length-stable, transverse or short-oblique mid-diaphyseal fractures. They are relatively contraindicated in length-unstable (long spiral or comminuted) fractures and in children over ~50 kg, where they have a high rate of malunion and shortening — use submuscular plating or a rigid nail instead. Titanium nails have a lower modulus and are more elastic than stainless steel nails.
  • Retrograde flexible nailing of the femur uses entry points ~2 cm proximal to the distal femoral physis medially and laterally; the physis must be avoided. For a radius, the dorsal entry point is just proximal to the distal radial physis, between the second and third dorsal compartments, avoiding the EPL — a common paired question.
  • Submuscular bridge plating with NON-locking screws in a spiral/oblique femoral shaft fracture: this is relative stability (bridge plating) and healing occurs by secondary bone healing with abundant callus — the classic answer. The plate acts as an internal splint over a long working length; no attempt is made at anatomic reduction of the intercalary fragments.
  • Complications: flexible nails — symptomatic hardware at the entry site (the commonest), malunion, shortening in length-unstable patterns. Rigid nails via the piriformis fossa in the young — AVN of the femoral head (the disaster complication, hence lateral trochanteric entry in patients under ~14–16 years). Spica — skin breakdown, compartment syndrome of the leg (particularly with 90/90 casting and excessive traction/leg positioning), and loss of reduction.
  • Femoral shaft fracture in a child under walking age (<1 year) is a red flag for non-accidental injury and mandates a full evaluation.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatric Trauma: Lower Extremity.
  • AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Treatment of Pediatric Diaphyseal Femur Fractures, 2015.
  • Flynn JM et al. Titanium elastic nails for pediatric femur fractures: a multicenter study of early results with analysis of complications. J Pediatr Orthop 2001.
  • Sink EL et al. Results and technique of unstable pediatric femoral fractures treated with submuscular bridge plating. J Pediatr Orthop 2006.
  • Paley D, Bhave A, Herzenberg JE, Bowen JR. Multiplier method for predicting limb-length discrepancy. JBJS Am 2000.
  • Mubarak SJ et al. Volkmann contracture and compartment syndromes after femur fractures in children treated with 90/90 spica casts. J Pediatr Orthop 2006.
7questions

Non-accidental injury (child abuse)

Recognising the fracture patterns of abuse and the physician's legal duty.

6 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024S, 2025 (x2)

  • Fracture patterns highly specific for non-accidental injury: classic metaphyseal lesions (CML — the 'corner' or 'bucket-handle' fracture), posterior rib fractures (from anteroposterior chest compression — squeezing), scapular, spinous process and sternal fractures, and bilateral/multiple fractures of differing ages. The CML is the single most specific fracture for abuse and results from a shearing/torsional force applied to the limb — violent pulling, twisting or shaking, most often the distal femur, proximal/distal tibia and proximal humerus.
  • Moderate specificity: multiple fractures, fractures of different ages, epiphyseal separations, vertebral body fractures, digital fractures, and complex skull fractures. Low specificity (common in accidents): clavicle fractures, long bone diaphyseal fractures, and linear skull fractures. A spiral femur fracture in an ambulatory toddler is NOT in itself diagnostic of abuse — a spiral fracture in a non-ambulatory infant is highly concerning.
  • The single strongest red flag is a history inconsistent with the injury, or inconsistent with the child's developmental stage — the classic 'no history of trauma at all' with multiple healing fractures, or a stated mechanism that could not generate the observed force. Other red flags: delay in seeking care, changing history, inappropriate affect, and prior injuries.
  • Any fracture in a non-ambulatory child (<1 year, or a child who is not yet cruising/walking) must be considered abuse until proven otherwise and mandates a full work-up.
  • Investigation: a skeletal survey is mandatory in every child under 2 years with suspected abuse (and is considered up to age 5 depending on the circumstances), often repeated at 2 weeks to identify healing injuries not initially visible. Add a head CT/MRI (for subdural haematoma) and ophthalmologic examination for retinal haemorrhages in infants, plus a bone profile (calcium, phosphate, ALP, PTH, vitamin D) and consideration of osteogenesis imperfecta in the differential.
  • The duty to report is legal and mandatory in every Canadian province and territory. The threshold is reasonable grounds to suspect, not proof. The correct answer to 'what should you do' is report to child protection services (and admit the child if the home is unsafe) — you do not need to be certain, you do not need to confirm the diagnosis first, and you do not confront or investigate the family yourself. Reporting in good faith carries statutory protection from liability. Failure to report is an offence.
  • For a 9-month-old with a 'strange fracture' and a vague history in which you believe an accident is plausible but are not certain — the answer is still to report/consult child protection. Uncertainty is precisely the situation the reporting threshold is designed for.
  • Differential diagnosis must be considered and documented: osteogenesis imperfecta (family history, blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, wormian bones, low bone density), rickets/nutritional deficiency, Menkes disease, osteopenia of prematurity, congenital insensitivity to pain, and birth trauma (clavicle, humerus).
  • A distal femoral metaphyseal corner fracture in an infant is the archetypal abusive injury; the most common association is other occult injuries — additional fractures of differing ages and intracranial injury — which is precisely why the skeletal survey and head imaging are required.
  • The mortality of missed abuse is high: roughly a third of children returned to an abusive environment are re-injured, and a proportion die. Recognition is a genuine life-saving intervention.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatric Trauma: General.
  • Kleinman PK. Diagnostic Imaging of Child Abuse, 3rd ed.
  • Flaherty EG, Perez-Rossello JM et al. American Academy of Pediatrics Clinical Report: Evaluating children with fractures for child physical abuse. Pediatrics 2014.
  • Kocher MS, Kasser JR. Orthopaedic aspects of child abuse. JAAOS 2000.
  • Canadian Paediatric Society position statement — Multidisciplinary guidelines on the identification, investigation and management of suspected abusive head trauma.
7questions

Paediatric forearm & distal radius fractures

Acceptable alignment, the cast index, refracture and physeal arrest.

5 of 7 sittings2021, 2022, 2023, 2024F, 2025 (x3)

  • Acceptable angulation in a paediatric both-bone forearm fracture depends on age and location: in a child under 9 years, up to 15° of angulation, 45° of malrotation and complete (bayonet) apposition with <1 cm of shortening may remodel acceptably; in a child over 10 years, accept <10° of angulation and minimal malrotation. Rotational malalignment does NOT remodel and is the least forgiving deformity. Fractures nearer the physis remodel best.
  • Cast index = the internal cast width on the lateral view ÷ the internal width on the AP view, measured at the fracture. >0.8 predicts loss of reduction. Good three-point moulding with an appropriate cast index is more important than cast material or the number of layers. Other predictors of redisplacement: complete initial displacement, an associated ulna fracture, poor initial reduction, and an older child.
  • A 7-year-old with a both-bone forearm fracture that remains 100% displaced and bayonetted after casting — a repeat closed reduction under anaesthesia is reasonable, but persistent complete displacement with shortening in a child of this age (particularly with a mid-diaphyseal fracture) generally warrants operative treatment with flexible intramedullary nailing rather than accepting bayonet apposition; the older the child and the more proximal the fracture, the lower the tolerance.
  • Refracture after paediatric forearm fracture is a well-recognised problem: the overall risk is roughly 5%, but after open reduction and plating the risk of refracture at ~1 year is approximately 5–10%, often occurring after plate removal (through the screw holes) or at the plate ends. Refracture risk is highest in the first 6–12 months, and diaphyseal (particularly mid-diaphyseal) fractures with plate fixation carry the highest rate. Protecting the arm for a period after plate removal is standard.
  • Flexible nailing of the radius: the dorsal entry point is just proximal to the distal radial physis, between the second and third dorsal compartments (radial to Lister's tubercle), taking care to protect the EPL tendon and the superficial radial nerve. The physis must not be crossed.
  • Distal radius physeal (Salter-Harris) fractures: SH II is the commonest. Growth arrest occurs in roughly 4–7% and is associated with repeated/late (after 7–10 days) reduction attempts, high-energy injury, and SH III/IV patterns. Repeated forceful manipulation after 7 days should be avoided — accept the deformity and allow remodelling rather than risk iatrogenic physeal injury.
  • Adolescent 'transitional' distal radius fractures: injuries occurring as the physis closes. The pattern LEAST associated with growth arrest is the classic Salter-Harris II fracture in a young child treated with a single early gentle reduction — whereas SH III/IV patterns, crush (SH V), open injuries, and late/repeated manipulations are strongly associated with arrest. Ask specifically which pattern the stem describes.
  • Distal radius physeal arrest produces progressive ulnar positive variance with ulnocarpal impaction and a radial deviation deformity; treatment options include epiphysiodesis of the distal ulna (in a growing child), ulnar shortening osteotomy, or bar resection with fat interposition if the bar is <50% of the physeal area and >2 years of growth remain.
  • Galeazzi and Monteggia equivalents are easy to miss — image the elbow and wrist in every forearm fracture, and check the radiocapitellar line and DRUJ.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatric Trauma: Upper Extremity.
  • Chess DG, Hyndman JC, Leahey JL, Brown DC, Sinclair AM (Canadian, Dalhousie). Short arm plaster cast for distal pediatric forearm fractures. J Pediatr Orthop 1994.
  • Webb GR, Galpin RD, Armstrong DG. Comparison of short and long arm plaster casts for displaced fractures in the distal third of the forearm in children. JBJS Am 2006.
  • Bould M, Bannister GC. Refractures of the radius and ulna in children. Injury 1999.
  • Cannata G et al. Physeal fractures of the distal radius and ulna: long-term prognosis. J Orthop Trauma 2003.
7questions

Paediatric lateral condyle & medial epicondyle fractures

Two very different elbow fractures with very different management thresholds.

5 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2024S, 2024F (x2), 2025

  • Lateral condyle fractures are intra-articular Salter-Harris IV injuries with a high propensity to displace and go on to nonunion. Displacement is the key: <2 mm — cast immobilisation with weekly radiographs (they can displace late, so follow closely); 2–4 mm with an intact articular cartilage hinge — closed reduction and percutaneous pinning, or arthrogram-assisted assessment; >4 mm or an incongruent articular surface — open reduction and internal fixation.
  • Imaging: the internal oblique view is the most accurate radiograph for assessing displacement of a lateral condyle fracture and is the answer to 'what x-rays should you obtain' — standard AP and lateral views underestimate displacement. An arthrogram at the time of surgery defines articular congruity.
  • Complications: nonunion (the most feared, from the intra-articular location, the pull of the extensor origin, and the tenuous blood supply), cubitus valgus with a late tardy ulnar nerve palsy, lateral spur formation (very common, usually cosmetic and benign), stiffness, AVN of the lateral condyle (associated with aggressive posterior dissection — never strip posteriorly, where the blood supply enters), and fishtail deformity.
  • Fishtail deformity is a central defect of the distal humeral trochlea, resulting from osteonecrosis of the lateral aspect of the medial crista of the trochlea after a lateral condyle, supracondylar or T-condylar fracture (or physeal separation). It is usually asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic and often an incidental radiographic finding; it does not routinely progress to major dysfunction and is not a cause of progressive cubitus varus. Some patients develop later pain, locking and loose bodies.
  • Medial epicondyle fractures are extra-articular apophyseal avulsions pulled by the flexor-pronator origin and the ulnar collateral ligament. They occur with elbow dislocation in ~50% and in the throwing athlete. The controversy is the displacement threshold for surgery — historically 5 mm, but measurements on plain films are unreliable and CT is more accurate.
  • Absolute indications for ORIF of a medial epicondyle fracture: an INCARCERATED (intra-articular) fragment, an open fracture, and ulnar nerve dysfunction with an entrapped fragment. Relative indications: significant displacement (variously 5–15 mm) in a high-demand throwing athlete or gymnast, and valgus instability.
  • A 4-year-old with a NON-incarcerated, displaced medial epicondyle fracture with a congruent joint — the definitive treatment is non-operative immobilisation in a long-arm cast (the classic answer). Non-operative treatment reliably produces a fibrous union that is functionally asymptomatic in the great majority; multiple studies show equivalent functional outcomes to surgery for non-incarcerated fractures, with the main difference being a higher rate of radiographic nonunion that is clinically irrelevant.
  • Recognising an incarcerated fragment is the critical skill: after reduction of an elbow dislocation, look for the medial epicondyle ossification centre in the joint (it may be mistaken for the trochlear ossification centre — remember CRITOE: Capitellum ~1 yr, Radial head ~3, Internal (medial) epicondyle ~5, Trochlea ~7, Olecranon ~9, External (lateral) epicondyle ~11). If the trochlea appears ossified but the medial epicondyle is absent from its normal position, the epicondyle is in the joint.
  • Ulnar nerve symptoms occur in 10–15% acutely; routine transposition is not required, but the nerve should be identified and protected during ORIF.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatric Trauma: Upper Extremity.
  • Song KS et al. Internal oblique radiographs for diagnosis of nondisplaced or minimally displaced lateral condylar fractures of the humerus in children. JBJS Am 2007.
  • Kamath AF, Baldwin K, Horneff J, Hosalkar HS. Operative versus non-operative management of pediatric medial epicondyle fractures: a systematic review. J Child Orthop 2009.
  • Weiss JM et al. A new classification system predictive of complications in surgically treated pediatric humeral lateral condyle fractures. J Pediatr Orthop 2009.
  • Glotzbecker MP et al. Fishtail deformity of the distal humerus. J Pediatr Orthop.
6questions

Clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) & Ponseti method

Deformity components, the Ponseti sequence, and recurrence.

6 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • Components of the deformity — CAVE: Cavus (forefoot, from first-ray plantarflexion/forefoot pronation relative to the hindfoot), Adductus (forefoot), Varus (hindfoot), Equinus (hindfoot). The correction sequence follows the same order — CAVE — and the cavus must be corrected FIRST.
  • The first and most commonly tested technical point: the cavus is corrected by SUPINATING the forefoot and elevating (dorsiflexing) the first ray to align it with the hindfoot — bringing the forefoot into line with the hindfoot. Pronating the forefoot is WRONG and worsens the cavus. The whole foot is then abducted around the head of the talus as a fulcrum, with counter-pressure on the lateral aspect of the talar head (NOT the calcaneocuboid joint — that is the Kite error, which blocks the calcaneus from rotating and prevents correction). The foot is never pronated at any stage.
  • Equinus is corrected LAST, after abduction of ~60–70° has been achieved. Approximately 70–90% require a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy to correct residual equinus, followed by 3 weeks in a cast.
  • Bracing (foot abduction orthosis — Denis Browne bar with the affected foot in 60–70° of external rotation) is mandatory: 23 hours/day for 3 months, then night-time and nap-time until age 4–5 years.
  • Non-compliance with the foot abduction orthosis is BY FAR the greatest risk factor for recurrence after successful Ponseti casting — it increases the recurrence risk roughly five- to seventeen-fold and is the single most important thing to discuss with the family. This is the answer to 'the highest risk of failure following successful Ponseti casting' and to 'the most important thing to counsel a family about recurrence'. Other risk factors: lower parental education/socioeconomic status, a more severe initial deformity (higher Pirani/Dimeglio score), and an atypical/syndromic (non-idiopathic) clubfoot.
  • Ponseti has replaced extensive surgical release, which produces a stiff, painful, weak foot in adulthood. The Ponseti method achieves initial correction in >90% of idiopathic clubfeet and is effective even in older infants and in delayed presentations.
  • Recurrence (~20–40%) usually presents first as recurrent equinus and hindfoot varus. Management: repeat Ponseti casting, then a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy if needed; for a dynamic supination/adduction deformity in a walking child (typically >2.5–3 years), transfer the tibialis anterior tendon to the lateral cuneiform. Bony procedures are reserved for older children with rigid deformity.
  • A 3-year-old previously treated with Ponseti who walks on the lateral border of the foot with hindfoot varus should be treated with repeat serial casting first to regain correction, followed by a tibialis anterior tendon transfer if the deformity is dynamic and the child is old enough (the lateral cuneiform must be ossified).
  • The commonest residual/most common deformity in clubfoot is EQUINUS (with hindfoot varus), and the commonest presenting deformity component overall is equinovarus. Associated features: a smaller foot and calf, a shorter limb, and internal tibial torsion.
  • Non-idiopathic clubfoot (arthrogryposis, myelomeningocele, amniotic band syndrome, Möbius) is stiffer, responds less well, and recurs more — but Ponseti is still the first-line treatment.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Foot.
  • Ponseti IV. Congenital Clubfoot: Fundamentals of Treatment. Oxford University Press, 1996.
  • Dobbs MB, Rudzki JR, Purcell DB, Walton T, Porter KR, Gurnett CA. Factors predictive of outcome after use of the Ponseti method for the treatment of idiopathic clubfeet. JBJS Am 2004.
  • Morcuende JA, Dolan LA, Dietz FR, Ponseti IV. Radical reduction in the rate of extensive corrective surgery for clubfoot using the Ponseti method. Pediatrics 2004.
  • Zionts LE, Dietz FR. Bracing following correction of idiopathic clubfoot using the Ponseti method. JAAOS 2010.
6questions

Paediatric ankle fractures: Tillaux & triplane

The transitional fractures of the closing distal tibial physis.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2023 (x3), 2024S

  • Transitional fractures occur in adolescents (12–15 years) during the ~18-month window of asymmetric physeal closure. The distal tibial physis closes in a predictable pattern: CENTRAL first, then MEDIAL (anteromedial), then LATERAL last — the mnemonic is that closure proceeds from central to medial to lateral. The still-open anterolateral portion is therefore the last to close and is the part avulsed.
  • Juvenile Tillaux fracture = a Salter-Harris III fracture of the anterolateral distal tibial epiphysis, avulsed by the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament with an external rotation mechanism. It is a two-fragment, purely epiphyseal injury.
  • Triplane fracture = a fracture with components in all three planes: a sagittal plane fracture through the epiphysis, a transverse plane fracture through the physis, and a coronal plane fracture through the metaphysis — hence it appears as a Salter-Harris III on the AP and a Salter-Harris II on the lateral. It may be 2-, 3- or 4-part, and can be lateral (more common) or medial.
  • CT is essential for both — it defines the number of fragments, the plane of the fracture and, critically, the degree of articular displacement, which plain films consistently underestimate.
  • Treatment threshold: <2 mm of articular displacement → closed reduction and cast immobilisation (reduction by internal rotation for a Tillaux, and internal rotation with the foot in a long-leg cast for a lateral triplane). ≥2 mm of displacement → closed or open reduction and fixation with epiphyseal (and/or metaphyseal) screws, taking care to place screws parallel to and not across the physis where growth remains.
  • Growth arrest is generally NOT a concern in true transitional fractures — this is the key conceptual point and the standard 'all are true except' distractor. Because these injuries occur as the physis is closing, there is minimal remaining growth, so the priority is anatomic restoration of the articular surface to prevent post-traumatic arthritis, not the physis. Growth disturbance is a concern in the younger child with a SH III/IV distal tibial fracture, not in the classic 15-year-old Tillaux.
  • In contrast, a Salter-Harris III or IV medial malleolar fracture in a YOUNGER child (e.g. a 10-year-old) carries a high risk of medial physeal bar formation and progressive VARUS deformity — these require anatomic reduction and close follow-up with serial radiographs (and a CT/MRI to map any bar). The mechanism of a SH III/IV medial malleolar fracture with a distal fibular injury is supination-inversion (supination-adduction).
  • A 10-year-old with a SH III medial malleolar fracture treated non-operatively who develops a small medial physeal bar on CT at 6 months — if the bar is <50% of the physeal area with >2 years of growth remaining, bar resection with interposition (fat, cranioplast) is indicated; larger bars or minimal remaining growth are managed with completion epiphysiodesis ± contralateral epiphysiodesis and deformity correction.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatric Trauma: Lower Extremity.
  • Kling TF, Bright RW, Hensinger RN. Distal tibial physeal fractures in children that may require open reduction. JBJS Am 1984.
  • Ertl JP et al. Triplane fracture of the distal tibial epiphysis: long-term follow-up. JBJS Am 1988.
  • Schnetzler KA, Hoernschemeyer D. The pediatric triplane ankle fracture. JAAOS 2007.
  • Peterson HA. Epiphyseal Growth Plate Fractures. Springer, 2007.
6questions

Paediatric polytrauma & resuscitation

How the injured child differs from the injured adult.

4 of 7 sittings2022, 2023 (x2), 2024S, 2024F (x2)

  • Physiologic differences: children have greater physiologic reserve and maintain blood pressure until ~30–45% of blood volume is lost — hypotension is a LATE and pre-terminal sign. Tachycardia is the earliest and most reliable sign of hypovolaemia, followed by decreased peripheral perfusion, narrowed pulse pressure and altered mental state. Never wait for hypotension.
  • Resuscitation: the fluid bolus in paediatric trauma is 20 mL/kg of warmed isotonic crystalloid, repeated once if needed; if the child remains unstable after 2 boluses (40 mL/kg), give blood — 10–20 mL/kg of packed red cells (many centres now move to blood earlier, after the first bolus, in haemorrhagic shock). Maintenance fluid uses the 4-2-1 rule.
  • Anatomic differences: a relatively larger head (higher incidence of head injury and a larger surface area for heat loss), a more compliant, cartilaginous skeleton (so significant internal injury occurs without fracture — the classic 'pulmonary contusion without rib fractures' and 'solid organ injury without lower rib fractures'), a higher surface-area-to-mass ratio (rapid hypothermia), a mobile mediastinum, and a more elastic cervical spine with a higher fulcrum (see SCIWORA and paediatric c-spine).
  • Injury patterns: head injury is the leading cause of death in paediatric trauma; solid organ (liver/spleen) injury is more common and is more often managed non-operatively than in adults; pelvic fractures in children are less often associated with catastrophic haemorrhage because of the elastic pelvis and the ability to absorb energy without disruption (but a paediatric pelvic fracture still signifies a high-energy mechanism with a high rate of associated injuries and mortality).
  • Paediatric pelvic ring fractures: the majority are stable and treated non-operatively, healing rapidly with a high remodelling potential. They are NOT usually associated with massive haemorrhage requiring angioembolisation (unlike adults) — the classic 'what is false' item. However, associated intra-abdominal, genitourinary and head injuries are common, and displaced triradiate cartilage injuries risk acetabular growth arrest with progressive dysplasia.
  • Outcome: children generally have better outcomes and lower mortality than adults for an equivalent Injury Severity Score, with faster fracture healing, greater remodelling capacity and a much lower incidence of nonunion, fat embolism and ARDS. However, children have a higher rate of long-term neurologic disability after head injury and worse functional outcomes from severe TBI relative to the initial physiologic picture.
  • Non-accidental injury must be considered in every injured child, especially where the history does not match the injury or the child's developmental stage.
  • Practical resuscitation points: use a length-based (Broselow) tape for weights and drug/tube sizes; intraosseous access is the fallback after two failed IV attempts; children desaturate rapidly (higher oxygen consumption, lower functional residual capacity); and aggressively prevent hypothermia.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatric Trauma: General.
  • American College of Surgeons. Advanced Trauma Life Support, 10th ed — Pediatric Trauma chapter.
  • Silber JS, Flynn JM. Changing patterns of pediatric pelvic fractures with skeletal maturation. J Pediatr Orthop 2002.
  • Chia JPY et al. Pelvic fractures and associated injuries in children. J Trauma 2004.
  • Kissoon N, Dreyer J, Walia M. Pediatric trauma: differences in pathophysiology, injury patterns and treatment compared with adult trauma. CMAJ 1990.
5questions

Congenital muscular torticollis & atlantoaxial rotatory displacement

Two causes of the tilted, rotated head in a child — with very different management.

4 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2022, 2024S, 2025

  • Congenital muscular torticollis (CMT): fibrosis/contracture of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM). The SCM's action is ipsilateral side-bending and CONTRALATERAL rotation, so a contracted right SCM produces the head TILTED TOWARD the affected (right) side with the chin ROTATED AWAY (to the left). So a child with the head tilted to the right and chin rotated to the left has a RIGHT SCM contracture — the standard question and the answer to 'which muscle is involved'.
  • Presentation: typically noted in the first 2–3 months, often with a palpable, non-tender SCM 'pseudotumour' (a fibrous mass) in the first weeks that resolves. Associated 'packaging' conditions must be sought: DDH (up to 10–20% — examine the hips and obtain ultrasound/radiograph), metatarsus adductus, and plagiocephaly.
  • Treatment of CMT: passive stretching and physiotherapy is highly effective (>90%) if started early (before 1 year). Failure of conservative treatment by ~12–18 months, or presentation after 1 year with a fixed deformity, warrants surgical release (unipolar or bipolar SCM release) — best done between 1 and 4 years, before permanent facial and skull asymmetry develops. Persistent deformity beyond ~6–12 years causes irreversible facial hemihypoplasia.
  • A child who presents with torticollis and does NOT have a tight SCM, or who develops torticollis acutely, does not have CMT — the differential includes atlantoaxial rotatory displacement, ocular torticollis (superior oblique palsy), Klippel-Feil, posterior fossa/spinal cord tumour, syringomyelia, and Sandifer syndrome (reflux). Non-CMT torticollis warrants imaging of the neuraxis.
  • Atlantoaxial rotatory displacement (AARD) is the acute, painful 'cock-robin' posture — head tilted to one side with the chin rotated to the OPPOSITE side, and the SCM on the side of the chin rotation is in spasm (the opposite pattern of muscle involvement to CMT — the SCM contracts to try to correct, not to cause, the deformity). It follows minor trauma, upper respiratory infection or retropharyngeal inflammation (Grisel syndrome), or ENT surgery.
  • Fielding & Hawkins classification: I — rotatory fixation without anterior displacement (ADI normal, transverse ligament intact — the commonest); II — rotatory fixation with 3–5 mm anterior displacement (unilateral facet subluxation); III — >5 mm anterior displacement (both facets subluxed); IV — posterior displacement.
  • Diagnosis: plain films (open-mouth odontoid view showing asymmetry of the lateral masses with one appearing wider/closer) are suggestive but are confounded by the child's rotated position. Dynamic CT (imaging with the head in maximal rotation to each side) is the definitive investigation and demonstrates that the C1-C2 relationship does not change with rotation — the diagnosis of fixation.
  • Management by duration is the key clinical point: acute presentation (<1 week) → soft collar, analgesia/anti-inflammatories and observation — the majority resolve spontaneously; this is the answer for a 'healthy child with 3 days of AARD and normal radiographs'. 1 week–1 month → halter traction, muscle relaxants and analgesia. >1 month (chronic) → halo traction, and consider C1-C2 fusion for irreducible or recurrent deformity or for types III/IV with instability. Prompt treatment prevents the fixed deformity.
  • A child with a c-spine injury, fixed rotated head, normal neurologic examination, no fracture on plain films, and asymmetry of the lateral masses on the open-mouth view should have a dynamic CT as the next investigation.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Cervical Spine.
  • Fielding JW, Hawkins RJ (Canadian). Atlanto-axial rotatory fixation. JBJS Am 1977.
  • Cheng JCY et al. Clinical determinants of the outcome of manual stretching in the treatment of congenital muscular torticollis in infants. JBJS Am 2001.
  • Pang D, Li V. Atlantoaxial rotatory fixation. Neurosurgery 2004/2005.
  • Do TT. Congenital muscular torticollis: current concepts and review of treatment. Curr Opin Pediatr 2006.
5questions

Congenital vertical talus & paediatric flatfoot

Distinguishing the rigid rocker-bottom foot from the common flexible flatfoot.

4 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2022, 2023, 2024S

  • Congenital vertical talus (CVT) is a rigid rocker-bottom flatfoot with a fixed dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talar head. The talus is vertical and 'points at the floor'; the hindfoot is in equinus and valgus and the forefoot is dorsiflexed and abducted — the opposite of clubfoot in the forefoot but sharing hindfoot equinus.
  • The diagnostic radiograph is the FORCED PLANTARFLEXION LATERAL view: in CVT the talo-first metatarsal alignment does NOT correct (the navicular remains dorsally dislocated); in the much more common oblique talus or a flexible flatfoot, the alignment reduces. A forced dorsiflexion lateral confirms the fixed hindfoot equinus.
  • CVT is associated with an underlying condition in ~50% — neuromuscular disease (myelomeningocele, arthrogryposis), chromosomal abnormalities (trisomy 13/15/18), and syndromes — so every child with CVT needs a neurologic and genetic evaluation, including spinal imaging.
  • Treatment of CVT: the modern approach is the reverse Ponseti (Dobbs) method — serial manipulation and casting with the foot in plantarflexion and inversion (the reverse of clubfoot casting), followed by percutaneous reduction and pinning of the talonavicular joint with a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy. This has largely replaced the historical extensive soft-tissue release, which produced stiff, painful feet.
  • Flexible paediatric flatfoot (pes planovalgus) is normal in young children (the arch develops by ~5–10 years), is usually asymptomatic and requires no treatment, and orthotics do NOT change the natural history or create an arch — they may relieve symptoms. The key clinical test is flexibility: the arch reconstitutes on toe standing (heel rise) and with the Jack toe-raise test, and the hindfoot inverts.
  • A RIGID flatfoot in a child or adolescent is pathological until proven otherwise — the differential is tarsal coalition (the commonest), congenital vertical talus, an accessory navicular with posterior tibial dysfunction, and a neurologic cause.
  • Tarsal coalition presents in adolescence (as the coalition ossifies): calcaneonavicular (ossifies 8–12 years, seen on the 45° internal oblique view as the 'anteater nose' sign) and talocalcaneal/middle facet (ossifies 12–16 years, seen on the lateral as the 'C sign' and 'talar beak'; CT is the best study). Treat symptomatic coalitions with immobilisation first; then resection with interposition (extensor digitorum brevis for calcaneonavicular, fat/tendon for talocalcaneal) if the coalition involves <50% of the joint with no arthritis or significant hindfoot valgus, and arthrodesis for larger coalitions/degenerative change.
  • Symptomatic accessory navicular in an adolescent with normal foot alignment and full dorsiflexion: treat non-operatively first; if refractory, excision of the accessory navicular with advancement/reattachment of the posterior tibial tendon (modified Kidner) — a flatfoot reconstruction is NOT indicated when the arch is normal.
  • Symptomatic flexible flatfoot in an adolescent that fails orthotics may be treated with lateral column (calcaneal) lengthening (Evans) for forefoot abduction, medial displacement calcaneal osteotomy for hindfoot valgus, ± medial cuneiform (Cotton) osteotomy for forefoot supination, plus gastrocnemius recession for equinus. Always assess for equinus.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Foot.
  • Dobbs MB, Purcell DB, Nunley R, Morcuende JA. Early results of a new method of treatment for idiopathic congenital vertical talus. JBJS Am 2006.
  • Mosca VS. Flexible flatfoot in children and adolescents. J Child Orthop 2010.
  • Vincent KA. Tarsal coalition and painful flatfoot. JAAOS 1998.
  • Alaee F, Boehm S, Dobbs MB. A new approach to congenital vertical talus. J Child Orthop 2007.
5questions

Paediatric cervical spine: Pseudosubluxation & normal variants

Normal paediatric radiographic variants that mimic injury.

4 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2022, 2024S

  • Anatomic differences of the immature cervical spine: a relatively larger head, horizontally oriented and shallower facet joints, incompletely ossified, wedge-shaped vertebral bodies, increased ligamentous laxity and more elastic soft tissues, underdeveloped uncinate processes, and weaker neck musculature. The consequence is that the fulcrum of motion is HIGHER (at C2-C3) in the young child, migrating to C5-C6 by adolescence — hence upper cervical injuries dominate in children under 8 and subaxial injuries thereafter.
  • Pseudosubluxation is the commonest normal variant: physiologic anterior displacement of C2 on C3 (and to a lesser extent C3 on C4) of up to 3–4 mm, present in up to 40% of children under 8 years, and accentuated by flexion. Swischuk's (posterior cervical/spinolaminar) line distinguishes it from a true injury: a line drawn from the anterior cortex of the spinous process of C1 to that of C3 should pass within 1.5–2 mm of the anterior cortex of the C2 spinous process. If it does, the finding is pseudosubluxation; if C2 is displaced posteriorly from this line by >2 mm, suspect a true injury (hangman's fracture).
  • Other normal paediatric variants: increased atlanto-dens interval (up to 4–5 mm in children versus 3 mm in adults), absence of cervical lordosis in up to 15%, anterior wedging of the vertebral bodies, incomplete ossification/synchondroses (the dens synchondrosis fuses at ~6 years and can be mistaken for a fracture), widened prevertebral soft tissues with crying/expiration, and overriding of the anterior arch of C1 on the odontoid in extension.
  • SCIWORA (spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormality) occurs almost exclusively in children under 8, because the elastic column can stretch and rebound while the cord cannot (the cord tolerates ~5 mm of stretch, the column ~5 cm). Normal radiographs and CT do not exclude a cord injury — MRI is required in any child with neurologic symptoms. Delayed onset of deficit hours after injury is characteristic.
  • Practical implications: immobilise the small child on a spine board with an occipital recess or a thoracic elevation pad, because a standard board forces the large head into flexion. Use paediatric-specific clearance rules (e.g. PECARN/the paediatric adaptation of NEXUS) — adult Canadian C-Spine Rules were not validated for children under 16.
  • Traumatic occipitocervical (atlanto-occipital) dissociation is proportionally more common in children because of the horizontal occipital condyles and ligamentous laxity, and it is frequently fatal or devastating. It is NOT a stable injury and must never be managed with a collar alone; treatment is occipitocervical fusion. Traction is contraindicated. The BAI/BDI and the condylar-C1 interval on CT are used for diagnosis, with MRI to assess the ligaments.
  • In a child, the commonest cervical spine injuries are in the upper cervical spine (occiput to C2) and include atlanto-occipital dissociation, odontoid synchondrosis fractures, and atlantoaxial rotatory displacement.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Cervical Spine.
  • Swischuk LE. Anterior displacement of C2 in children: physiologic or pathologic? Radiology 1977.
  • Pang D, Wilberger JE. Spinal cord injury without radiographic abnormalities in children. J Neurosurg 1982.
  • Copley PC et al. Management of cervical spine trauma in children. Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg 2019.
  • Herman MJ, Pizzutillo PD. Cervical spine disorders in children. Orthop Clin North Am.
5questions

Physeal injury, growth arrest & angular deformity

Physeal anatomy, the Salter-Harris classification, and post-traumatic deformity.

3 of 7 sittings2022, 2024S (x2), 2024F (x2)

  • Physeal zones (from epiphysis to metaphysis): reserve/resting → proliferative (the zone of longitudinal growth, with the highest rate of cell division and where the physeal blood supply enters) → hypertrophic (subdivided into maturation, degeneration and provisional calcification — this is the WEAKEST zone and where Salter-Harris fractures propagate) → metaphysis (primary spongiosa).
  • Zone-specific disease: achondroplasia — proliferative zone (FGFR3 inhibits chondrocyte proliferation); SCFE, rickets and most fractures — hypertrophic zone; mucopolysaccharidoses — reserve zone; scurvy and metaphyseal dysplasia — primary spongiosa/metaphysis.
  • Salter-Harris: I — through the physis; II — physis + metaphyseal (Thurston-Holland) fragment (the commonest); III — physis + epiphysis (intra-articular); IV — across the metaphysis, physis and epiphysis (intra-articular); V — crush. Growth arrest risk rises with grade (III–V), with high-energy mechanisms, with repeated or late reduction attempts, and with physeal location (distal femur is the highest-risk physis).
  • Cozen phenomenon: a proximal tibial metaphyseal fracture in a young child (2–6 years) treated non-operatively, developing progressive VALGUS deformity 12–18 months later. The mechanism is thought to be relative overgrowth/asymmetric stimulation of the medial proximal tibial physis (with contributions from tethering by the intact fibula and soft-tissue interposition). The critical management point is that it usually corrects spontaneously over 2–4 years — the answer is observation and parental reassurance, NOT osteotomy or guided growth, which risks over-correction and recurrence.
  • Distal femoral fracture with fixation that did NOT bridge the physis, developing valgus a year later — this is a growth disturbance from a partial physeal bar (the distal femoral physis is the most commonly injured physis for growth arrest, and asymmetric arrest produces angular deformity). Evaluate with MRI or CT mapping of the bar.
  • Physeal bar management: if the bar is <50% of the physeal cross-sectional area with >2 years (or >2 cm) of growth remaining → bar resection with interposition (fat graft, cranioplast/PMMA, silicone), ± concurrent deformity correction. If the bar is >50%, or minimal growth remains → completion epiphysiodesis of the affected physis ± contralateral epiphysiodesis, with corrective osteotomy or guided growth for the deformity, and limb-length equalisation as needed.
  • Remodelling potential is greatest in the youngest child, closest to the physis, and in the plane of motion of the adjacent joint. Rotational deformity does not remodel. The distal radius and proximal humerus have the greatest remodelling potential (they contribute ~80% of the growth of their bones); the distal femur and proximal tibia contribute most to lower limb length (~70% combined).
  • Growth contributions to remember: distal femur ~9 mm/year (38% of limb), proximal tibia ~6 mm/year (27%), proximal humerus ~80% of humeral growth, distal radius ~75–80% of forearm growth.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Physis; Pediatric Trauma.
  • Salter RB, Harris WR (Canadian, Toronto). Injuries involving the epiphyseal plate. JBJS Am 1963.
  • Cozen L. Fracture of the proximal portion of the tibia in children followed by valgus deformity. Surg Gynecol Obstet 1953.
  • Peterson HA. Physeal fractures: Part 3. Classification. J Pediatr Orthop 1994.
  • Birch JG. Surgical technique of physeal bar resection. Instr Course Lect 1992.
5questions

Skeletal dysplasias: Achondroplasia & others

Achondroplasia and the dysplasias that recur on the exam.

4 of 7 sittings2022, 2023, 2024F, 2025 (x2)

  • Achondroplasia: FGFR3 gain-of-function mutation, autosomal dominant, >80% sporadic (associated with advanced paternal age). It is the commonest skeletal dysplasia. Features: rhizomelic (proximal) shortening, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, trident hands, genu varum, thoracolumbar kyphosis, lumbar hyperlordosis, and spinal stenosis from short pedicles and decreased interpedicular distance caudally.
  • The limb deformity of achondroplasia is RHIZOMELIC shortening — the proximal segments (humerus and femur) are disproportionately short. (Contrast: mesomelic = middle segment, as in dyschondrosteosis/Léri-Weill; acromelic = distal segment/hands and feet.)
  • Pre-operative anaesthetic consultation in achondroplasia is warranted for: foramen magnum stenosis with cervicomedullary compression (the most important — it causes central sleep apnoea, hypotonia, and sudden death in infancy), obstructive sleep apnoea, restrictive lung disease from a small thoracic cage, difficult airway (midface hypoplasia, large tongue), difficult neuraxial anaesthesia (spinal stenosis, short pedicles), and cervical instability. A history of sleep apnoea, snoring, or any neurologic sign is the trigger for a formal work-up. Atlantoaxial instability is a feature of Down syndrome, Morquio and SED, not classically of achondroplasia.
  • Thoracolumbar kyphosis in achondroplasia is present in infancy and resolves in the majority once the child begins ambulating and trunk strength develops. Persistent kyphosis is associated with apical vertebral wedging, apical vertebral translation, thoracolumbar hyperkyphosis >30° persisting past ambulation, and delayed motor development/prolonged unsupported sitting. Hydrocephalus/foramen magnum stenosis is not a cause of persistent thoracolumbar kyphosis — the classic 'all except'. Prevent it by avoiding unsupported sitting in infancy (counsel families to avoid slouching seats); bracing for progressive curves; fusion for curves >50–60° that persist.
  • Genu varum in achondroplasia results from fibular overgrowth relative to the tibia with lateral ligamentous laxity; correct with proximal tibia/fibula osteotomy or guided growth if symptomatic. Limb lengthening is possible but controversial.
  • Other dysplasias worth recognising: Pseudoachondroplasia (COMP; normal facies, normal at birth, presents at 2–3 years, ligamentous laxity, C1-2 instability). Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia (SED) (COL2A1; short trunk, odontoid hypoplasia with atlantoaxial instability, coxa vara, myopia/retinal detachment). Morquio (MPS IV) (GALNS; odontoid hypoplasia with atlantoaxial instability — screen everyone, corneal clouding, normal intelligence, genu valgum). Diastrophic dysplasia (DTDST, autosomal recessive; 'hitchhiker thumb', cauliflower ear, rigid clubfoot, cervical kyphosis). Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (COMP/COL9; irregular epiphyses, early-onset arthritis, normal spine — the differential for bilateral Perthes).
  • Cleidocranial dysplasia (RUNX2/CBFA1): absent or hypoplastic clavicles, delayed skull suture closure, coxa vara, and dental anomalies.
  • A red flag in any short-statured child undergoing anaesthesia is cervical spine instability — obtain flexion-extension cervical radiographs in Down syndrome, Morquio, SED and pseudoachondroplasia before general anaesthesia.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Skeletal Dysplasias.
  • Horton WA, Hall JG, Hecht JT. Achondroplasia. Lancet 2007.
  • Ain MC et al. Progression of low back and lower extremity pain in a cohort of patients with achondroplasia. J Neurosurg Spine / J Pediatr Orthop.
  • White KK et al. Best practices in peri-operative management of patients with skeletal dysplasias. Am J Med Genet A 2017.
  • Pauli RM. Achondroplasia: a comprehensive clinical review. Orphanet J Rare Dis 2019.
5questions

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

Classification, associated conditions, AVN risk and contralateral slip prediction.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2023, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • SCFE is a Salter-Harris I fracture through the hypertrophic zone of the proximal femoral physis, with the epiphysis remaining in the acetabulum and the metaphysis displacing anteriorly and externally rotating — so the deformity is described as the epiphysis slipping posteriorly and inferiorly relative to the neck. Typical patient: an obese adolescent (10–16 years) presenting with hip, thigh or knee pain and an externally rotated, shortened limb with obligate external rotation on hip flexion.
  • The stability classification (Loder) is the most important prognostic factor: stable = able to weightbear (with or without crutches) → AVN risk <10% (very low); unstable = unable to weightbear even with crutches → AVN risk 20–60%. Chronicity (acute <3 weeks, chronic, acute-on-chronic) and severity (Southwick angle: mild <30°, moderate 30–50°, severe >50°) are secondary.
  • Risk factors for AVN in an unstable SCFE: instability itself (the dominant factor), severity of the slip, attempted forceful/complete closed reduction of an unstable slip, delay to decompression/fixation, and pin/screw penetration or placement in the posterosuperior quadrant of the epiphysis (where the retinacular vessels enter). Gentle incidental reduction from positioning is accepted; deliberate aggressive reduction is not.
  • Treatment is in-situ fixation with a single central screw perpendicular to the physis, aiming for the centre of the epiphysis on both views. Avoid the posterosuperior quadrant. For unstable slips, urgent (within 24 hours) fixation with capsular decompression is favoured by many. Severe slips may be treated with a modified Dunn procedure (surgical hip dislocation with subcapital realignment) — this achieves excellent correction but carries a meaningful AVN risk even in expert hands.
  • Associated endocrine and metabolic conditions — screen when SCFE occurs outside the typical age range (<10 or >16 years), in a child of normal or low weight, or bilaterally at presentation: hypothyroidism, growth hormone therapy/deficiency, hypogonadism, panhypopituitarism, renal osteodystrophy/chronic renal failure, and prior radiation therapy. Hyperthyroidism and hyperparathyroidism are NOT classically associated — hypothyroidism is the association, and hyperthyroidism is the usual distractor.
  • An 8-year-old with a history of leukaemia treated with chemotherapy and PANCORPORAL RADIATION presenting with SCFE — this is a radiation-associated (and endocrinopathy-associated) SCFE; the appropriate management still involves in-situ fixation, and the child requires an endocrine work-up and screening of the contralateral side.
  • Predicting a contralateral slip: the risk of a subsequent contralateral slip is roughly 20–40%, and most occur within 18 months. The posterior sloping angle (PSA) of the contralateral proximal femoral physis on the frog-leg lateral is the radiographic measure most predictive of a contralateral slip — a PSA >14° carries a markedly increased risk (and >12–14° is the commonly quoted threshold). The modified Oxford bone age score is the other validated predictor (a lower/less mature score predicts higher risk).
  • Prophylactic contralateral pinning is indicated for an endocrinopathy/renal disease, an open triradiate cartilage with a young age at presentation, a PSA >14°, and where reliable follow-up is doubtful — otherwise close surveillance is acceptable.
  • Following surgical hip dislocation for a chronic SCFE, risk factors for post-operative hip instability/dislocation include capsular insufficiency, an incompetent posterior capsule/labral repair, and neuromuscular compromise; a well-performed trochanteric flip osteotomy with careful capsular closure is protective, not a risk factor — read these stems carefully.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Hip.
  • Loder RT et al. Acute slipped capital femoral epiphysis: the importance of physeal stability. JBJS Am 1993.
  • Barrios C, Blasco MA et al. / Phillips PM, Phadnis J, Willoughby R, Hunt L. Posterior sloping angle as a predictor of contralateral slipped capital femoral epiphysis. JBJS Am 2013.
  • Loder RT, Starnes T, Dikos G. Atypical and typical (idiopathic) slipped capital femoral epiphysis. JBJS Am 2006.
  • Ziebarth K, Leunig M, Slongo T, Kim YJ, Ganz R. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis: relevant pathophysiological findings with open surgery. CORR 2013.
4questions

Arthrogryposis & congenital knee dislocation

The stiff newborn and the hyperextended knee.

3 of 7 sittings2022, 2024S, 2024F (x2)

  • Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (AMC) is a non-progressive syndrome of multiple congenital joint contractures present at birth, resulting from fetal akinesia (decreased intrauterine movement from any cause). The classic form is amyoplasia: symmetric, featureless cylindrical limbs with absent skin creases, internally rotated shoulders, extended elbows, flexed wrists, and severe rigid clubfeet or knee contractures, with a characteristic midline facial haemangioma.
  • Key facts: intelligence is normal in amyoplasia, sensation is preserved, and it is NOT progressive — this distinguishes it from muscular dystrophy and neurologic disease. It is usually sporadic and NOT inherited in the amyoplasia form (though some syndromic forms are genetic), which is what families need to know. Distal arthrogryposis is autosomal dominant.
  • Management: aggressive early physiotherapy and serial casting in the first months (the joints are most responsive early), then surgery for residual deformity. The goal is FUNCTION, not normal anatomy — the priorities are a plantigrade foot for walking, at least one elbow that flexes for hand-to-mouth function (and one that extends for perineal care/crutch use), and hips that are located enough to sit and stand.
  • Hips in arthrogryposis: a unilateral dislocation should generally be reduced (open reduction); bilateral dislocations are more controversial and many are left alone, because the surgery risks stiffness — and a stiff, reduced hip is worse than a mobile, dislocated one in a patient whose problem is stiffness. Motion matters more than reduction.
  • Clubfoot in arthrogryposis is rigid, recurrent and difficult; Ponseti casting is still first-line but requires more casts, more frequent tenotomy and has a much higher recurrence rate; talectomy may be required for the resistant foot.
  • Congenital knee dislocation/hyperextension presents as a hyperextended knee with the tibia anterior to the femur, and is associated with arthrogryposis, Larsen syndrome, myelomeningocele, DDH (in ~50% — always examine the hips), clubfoot, and breech position (a packaging disorder). It is NOT associated with cerebral palsy, which is a common distractor.
  • Larsen syndrome (FLNB) is the classic syndromic association with multiple congenital joint dislocations (knees, hips, elbows), a flattened facies with a depressed nasal bridge and hypertelorism, and — critically — CERVICAL KYPHOSIS AND INSTABILITY, which can cause myelopathy and must be screened for before any anaesthetic.
  • Treatment of congenital knee dislocation: early serial casting/splinting into progressive flexion in the first weeks of life is successful in the majority; surgery (quadriceps V-Y lengthening, anterior capsular release) is reserved for failures. Treat the knee BEFORE the hip — the hip cannot be reduced or braced in a Pavlik while the knee is hyperextended.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Neuromuscular.
  • Bevan WP, Hall JG, Bamshad M, Staheli LT, Jaffe KM, Song K. Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (amyoplasia): an orthopaedic perspective. J Pediatr Orthop 2007.
  • Hall JG. Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita: etiology, genetics, classification, diagnostic approach, and general aspects. J Pediatr Orthop B 1997.
  • Ko JY, Shih CH, Wenger DR. Congenital dislocation of the knee. J Pediatr Orthop 1999.
  • Mahirogullari M et al. Congenital dislocation of the knee: results of treatment. J Child Orthop.
4questions

Congenital scoliosis & vertebral anomalies

Failures of formation and segmentation, progression risk, and the mandatory work-up.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2023, 2024S, 2024F

  • Congenital scoliosis results from a defect in vertebral formation or segmentation occurring in the 4th–6th week of gestation. Two categories: failures of FORMATION (hemivertebra — fully segmented, semi-segmented, incarcerated; wedge vertebra) and failures of SEGMENTATION (unilateral unsegmented bar, block vertebra), or mixed.
  • Progression risk (highest to lowest) — the key list: unilateral unsegmented bar WITH a contralateral hemivertebra (the worst — >10°/year, virtually 100% progression) > unilateral unsegmented bar > fully segmented hemivertebra > semi-segmented hemivertebra > wedge vertebra > block vertebra (essentially non-progressive). Thoracic curves progress faster than lumbar. Progression is fastest during the growth spurts (<5 years and adolescence).
  • Because the deformity is structural, bracing does NOT work for the congenital curve itself — it may be used to control a flexible compensatory curve. This is a central management point.
  • Mandatory work-up — the associations are the highest-yield component: the deformity arises at a time when the spinal cord, heart, kidneys and other organs are forming, so ~30–40% have intraspinal anomalies and 20–40% have extraspinal anomalies (VACTERL). Every child with congenital scoliosis requires: MRI of the whole neuraxis (tethered cord, diastematomyelia, syringomyelia, Chiari — present in ~20–40%), renal ultrasound (~20–33% have renal anomalies, including unilateral renal agenesis), cardiac echocardiography (~10–25% have congenital heart disease), and clinical examination for anal atresia, limb and rib anomalies.
  • A 10-year-old presenting for the first time with a LEFT thoracic curve, wedge vertebrae around T8–T10 and a compensatory right lumbar curve is congenital/atypical — the best first test is MRI of the entire spine, and the child needs renal and cardiac screening.
  • Surgical options: hemivertebra excision with short-segment fusion (best for a lumbosacral or thoracolumbar fully segmented hemivertebra causing progressive trunk imbalance, ideally performed young — 2–5 years — with a short fusion); in-situ fusion (for a slowly progressive curve without significant deformity); convex hemiepiphysiodesis (limited indications); growth-friendly instrumentation/VEPTR (for early-onset curves with thoracic insufficiency, particularly with rib fusions); and vertebral column resection for severe rigid deformity.
  • Early, short fusion in a young child with a progressive curve beats a long fusion later — the surgical philosophy is to intervene early while the curve is short and flexible.
  • Neuromonitoring is essential, and the risk of neurologic injury is higher than in idiopathic scoliosis because of the anomalous anatomy and associated cord pathology — always image the cord first.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Spine.
  • McMaster MJ, Ohtsuka K. The natural history of congenital scoliosis: a study of two hundred and fifty-one patients. JBJS Am 1982.
  • Hedequist D, Emans J. Congenital scoliosis: a review and update. J Pediatr Orthop 2007.
  • Basu PS, Elsebaie H, Noordeen MHH. Congenital spinal deformity: a comprehensive assessment at presentation. Spine 2002.
  • Ruf M, Harms J. Hemivertebra resection by a posterior approach. Spine 2002.
4questions

Early-onset & infantile scoliosis, growing rods

Scoliosis before age 10 — natural history and growth-friendly surgery.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2025 (x3)

  • Early-onset scoliosis (EOS) is any spinal deformity presenting before age 10. Its defining problem is not the curve itself but the effect on pulmonary development — thoracic insufficiency syndrome: the alveoli multiply until ~age 8 and the thoracic volume until ~age 10, so an untreated severe EOS produces irreversible restrictive lung disease and early mortality. Preserving thoracic growth, not achieving a straight spine, is the goal.
  • Infantile idiopathic scoliosis (<3 years) is unique in that a substantial proportion resolve spontaneously. The rib-vertebral angle difference (RVAD, Mehta angle) predicts behaviour: RVAD <20° → likely to resolve (observation); RVAD >20° or a phase II rib (rib head overlapping the vertebral body) → likely to progress and requires treatment. It is more common in boys, is usually a left thoracic curve, and is associated with plagiocephaly, DDH and intraspinal anomalies — so MRI of the neuraxis is indicated.
  • Serial Mehta (elongation-derotation-flexion) casting is the first-line treatment for progressive infantile idiopathic scoliosis and can be curative if started early (before age 2 and with curves <60°), avoiding surgery altogether — a major advance.
  • Growth-friendly surgery for progressive EOS: traditional growing rods (requiring repeated lengthening surgeries every 6 months), magnetically controlled growing rods (MCGR — lengthened non-invasively in clinic), vertical expandable prosthetic titanium rib (VEPTR — for rib fusions/thoracic insufficiency), and guided growth (Shilla/Luqué trolley) systems.
  • Complications of growing-rod constructs are the rule rather than the exception — roughly half of patients experience at least one complication. The commonest are implant-related: rod breakage, anchor/hook pull-out and proximal anchor failure, along with infection (rates rise with each repeat procedure), proximal junctional kyphosis, and the 'law of diminishing returns' (progressively less lengthening achieved with each procedure due to autofusion). For magnetically controlled growing rods specifically, the commonest complications are implant/rod-related — rod failure or failure of the lengthening mechanism, plus proximal anchor failure.
  • Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) in growing-rod constructs is increased by: hyperkyphosis (preoperative thoracic kyphosis >40°), a proximal anchor ending in the mid-thoracic apex rather than the upper thoracic spine, disruption of the posterior ligamentous complex/facet violation at the upper instrumented vertebra, hook rather than screw fixation in some series, and excessive correction/distraction force. Ending the construct more proximally (e.g. at T2 rather than T5–6) and preserving the posterior soft tissues reduces PJK — so 'a more proximal upper instrumented vertebra' is generally the answer that does NOT increase PJK.
  • Definitive fusion is deferred until adequate thoracic growth is achieved (typically Risser 4–5 / around 10–12 years or later), though some children achieve autofusion and do not need a final fusion.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Scoliosis.
  • Mehta MH. Growth as a corrective force in the early treatment of progressive infantile scoliosis. JBJS Br 2005.
  • Campbell RM et al. The characteristics of thoracic insufficiency syndrome associated with fused ribs and congenital scoliosis. JBJS Am 2003.
  • Bess S, Akbarnia BA et al. Complications of growing-rod treatment for early-onset scoliosis. JBJS Am 2010.
  • Cheung KMC et al. Magnetically controlled growing rods for severe spinal curvature in young children. Lancet 2012.
  • Sankar WN et al. Sequential derotational lengthening: the law of diminishing returns. Spine 2011.
4questions

Osteochondritis dissecans (capitellum & knee) in the young

Prognostic factors and treatment of OCD.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2024S

  • Osteochondritis dissecans is a focal idiopathic lesion of subchondral bone with secondary effects on the overlying articular cartilage. The classic knee location is the LATERAL aspect of the MEDIAL femoral condyle (~70%); in the elbow it is the capitellum (in throwers and gymnasts); in the ankle, the talar dome.
  • The single most important prognostic factor is SKELETAL MATURITY: juvenile OCD (open physes) has a much better prognosis and a high rate of healing with non-operative treatment, whereas adult OCD (closed physes) heals poorly. Other favourable factors: a stable lesion with intact overlying cartilage, smaller lesion size, and the classic (medial femoral condyle) location.
