Unfavourable: an unstable lesion, larger size, an atypical/weightbearing location, and mechanical symptoms (locking, effusion).
  • Treatment algorithm: stable juvenile OCD → non-operative (activity restriction, protected weightbearing ± immobilisation for 3–6 months) with healing in ~50–75%. Failure of non-operative treatment or a stable lesion in a nearly mature patient → transarticular or retroarticular drilling to stimulate vascular ingrowth. Unstable lesion (fluid signal beneath the fragment on MRI, a displaced fragment or a loose body) → fixation (compression screws, bioabsorbable implants) with bone grafting of the crater, or, if the fragment is unsalvageable, cartilage restoration (microfracture for small lesions, OATS/osteochondral allograft for larger ones).
  • Capitellar OCD (in the dominant elbow of a thrower or gymnast, 11–15 years) must be distinguished from Panner disease (a self-limiting osteochondrosis of the entire capitellar ossific nucleus in a younger child, 5–10 years, which resolves with rest and has an excellent prognosis).
  • Poor prognostic signs for capitellar OCD: open vs closed physis (a CLOSED physis is a poor prognostic sign), lateral extension of the lesion beyond the lateral border of the capitellum, an unstable lesion/loose body, large lesion size, and restricted elbow range of motion at presentation. Conversely, an open capitellar physis with a small, stable, contained lesion and full range of motion is a GOOD prognostic sign — the answer to 'which is NOT a poor prognostic sign'.
  • MRI is the key investigation: signs of instability include a high-signal (fluid) line between the fragment and the parent bone on T2, surrounding cysts, a fluid-filled defect, and a displaced fragment.
  • Return to sport after successful treatment of an elbow OCD requires healing on imaging, painless full motion and a graduated throwing programme; a permanent change in sport or position may be required in the gymnast.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics; Sports.
  • Kocher MS, Tucker R, Ganley TJ, Flynn JM. Management of osteochondritis dissecans of the knee: current concepts review. AJSM 2006.
  • Takahara M et al. Classification, treatment, and outcome of osteochondritis dissecans of the humeral capitellum. JBJS Am 2007.
  • Edmonds EW, Polousky J. A review of knowledge in osteochondritis dissecans: 123 years of minimal evolution from König to the ROCK study group. CORR 2013.
  • Churchill RW et al. Osteochondritis dissecans of the elbow. Curr Rev Musculoskelet Med 2016.
4questions

Paediatric discitis & spine infection

The toddler who refuses to walk or sit.

4 of 7 sittings2021, 2023, 2024S, 2025

  • Paediatric discitis is a low-grade infection (or inflammatory process) of the intervertebral disc and adjacent endplates, occurring predominantly in children under 5 years (peak 6 months to 4 years). It is possible because the child's disc retains a vascular supply from the vertebral endplates until ~age 8–10, which regresses thereafter — hence in older children and adults the infection is vertebral osteomyelitis rather than discitis.
  • Presentation is non-specific and often subtle: refusal to walk or sit, irritability, back or abdominal pain, a limp, and loss of normal lumbar lordosis with refusal to flex the spine. Most children are AFEBRILE or have only a low-grade fever, with a normal or mildly elevated WBC and a raised ESR — the ESR is the most consistently abnormal marker, and CRP is useful for monitoring. The lumbar spine (L4-5) is the commonest site.
  • Imaging: radiographs are normal for the first 2–4 weeks, then show disc space narrowing with endplate irregularity. MRI is the study of choice and is diagnostic much earlier. Bone scan is an alternative when the site is unclear.
  • Staphylococcus aureus is the most commonly identified organism, though cultures and blood cultures are frequently negative (up to 50–70%) — which is why routine biopsy is NOT required for a typical presentation responding to empirical treatment.
  • Treatment is empirical intravenous antistaphylococcal antibiotics followed by oral therapy, with immobilisation/bracing for comfort. The prognosis is excellent, with most children recovering fully; spontaneous interbody fusion of the affected level occurs in a proportion and is generally asymptomatic. Surgery is reserved for abscess formation, neurologic compromise, failure to respond to appropriate antibiotics, or diagnostic uncertainty requiring biopsy.
  • Biopsy is indicated when: the child fails to improve on antibiotics, the presentation is atypical (older child, marked systemic illness, immunocompromise), there is a paraspinal or epidural collection, or tuberculosis or malignancy is a possibility.
  • The differential must always include tumour — Langerhans cell histiocytosis (vertebra plana), Ewing sarcoma, leukaemia and neuroblastoma metastasis — and tuberculous spondylitis (which classically spares the disc, involves multiple contiguous levels with large paravertebral abscesses, and produces anterior vertebral body destruction with kyphosis).
  • Epidural abscess in a child is rarer but far more dangerous — presenting with back pain, fever and neurologic deficit; it requires urgent MRI and, in the presence of neurologic compromise or a large collection, surgical decompression with antibiotics.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Spine Infection.
  • Fernandez M, Carrol CL, Baker CJ. Discitis and vertebral osteomyelitis in children: an 18-year review. Pediatrics 2000.
  • Early SD, Kay RM, Tolo VT. Childhood diskitis. JAAOS 2003.
  • Chandrasenan J et al. Spondylodiscitis in children: a retrospective series. J Bone Joint Surg Br 2011.
4questions

Spondylolysis & spondylolisthesis in the young

Pars defects, slip grading and the surgical decision.

3 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2024S, 2024F

  • Spondylolysis is a defect (usually a stress fracture) of the pars interarticularis, most commonly at L5, present in ~4–6% of the population and much higher in athletes performing repetitive hyperextension and rotation (gymnastics, football linemen, divers, cricket bowlers, dancers). Isthmic spondylolisthesis is the forward slip that follows a bilateral pars defect.
  • Wiltse classification: I dysplastic (congenital, with a dysplastic L5-S1 facet and a high risk of progression); II isthmic (the commonest in the young — IIA lytic/stress fracture, IIB elongated pars, IIC acute fracture); III degenerative (older adults, L4-5, female, with an intact pars); IV traumatic; V pathologic.
  • Meyerding grading by percentage slip: I <25%, II 25–50%, III 50–75%, IV 75–100%, V spondyloptosis. The slip angle (lumbosacral kyphosis) is a better predictor of progression and outcome than the percentage slip.
  • A lytic L5-S1 spondylolisthesis with radicular pain typically produces an L5 radiculopathy — the L5 nerve root is compressed in the foramen by the fibrocartilaginous pars mass and the downward-migrating pedicle. So a patient with a lytic L5-S1 slip and pain radiating below the knee has an L5 pattern (dorsum of the foot, great toe, weak EHL/dorsiflexion), not S1.
  • Treatment: non-operative is the mainstay — activity restriction/rest from the provoking sport, bracing (for acute lesions), and core/hamstring rehabilitation — with good results in the majority. Acute pars stress reactions (marrow oedema on MRI, positive SPECT) have the best chance of bony healing with rest and bracing.
  • Surgical indications: persistent pain despite ≥6 months of non-operative treatment, progressive slip, a high-grade slip (>50%), neurologic deficit, or significant deformity/gait disturbance. Options are direct pars repair (for a young patient with an L1–L4 defect, minimal disc degeneration and no slip) or posterolateral fusion at L5-S1 (± instrumentation and reduction).
  • Adding posterior spinal instrumented fusion to a direct pars repair improves fusion rates and provides immediate stability, but sacrifices the motion segment — the trade-off is fusion reliability versus preserved motion, and instrumentation is favoured in higher-grade slips, older adolescents and where the disc is degenerate.
  • Reduction of a high-grade slip is controversial — it improves sagittal alignment and lumbosacral kyphosis but carries a significant risk of L5 nerve root injury (up to 20–30%); in-situ fusion has a lower neurologic risk but a higher pseudarthrosis rate and does not correct deformity.
  • Scoliosis and spondylolisthesis coexist in adolescents. Key points: the scoliosis is often a sciatic/antalgic (olisthetic) curve that resolves when the spondylolisthesis is treated; a true idiopathic curve co-existing with a spondylolisthesis is treated on its own merits; the presence of a spondylolisthesis does not, by itself, mandate extending an idiopathic scoliosis fusion to the sacrum; and the incidence of spondylolysis is higher in patients with scoliosis than in the general population.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Spine; Spine: Spinal Conditions.
  • Wiltse LL, Newman PH, Macnab I (Canadian). Classification of spondylolisis and spondylolisthesis. CORR 1976.
  • Beutler WJ et al. The natural history of spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis: 45-year follow-up evaluation. Spine 2003.
  • Cavalier R, Herman MJ, Cheung EV, Pizzutillo PD. Spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis in children and adolescents. JAAOS 2006.
  • Lonstein JE. Spondylolisthesis in children: cause, natural history, and management. Spine 1999.
3questions

Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia & anterolateral bowing

The serious bow, and its relationship to neurofibromatosis.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2023

  • Anterolateral bowing of the tibia is the harbinger of congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia (CPT) and must be distinguished from benign posteromedial bowing. Approximately 50–60% of children with CPT have neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), and conversely a small percentage of NF1 patients develop CPT. Fibrous dysplasia is the other association.
  • Clinical examination findings that support NF1 in a child presenting with anterolateral bowing: café-au-lait macules (≥6, >5 mm prepubertal), axillary/inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), cutaneous neurofibromas, optic glioma, and a first-degree relative with NF1. Look for these in every child with an anterolateral bow.
  • Natural history: the bow is present at birth or develops in infancy, the tibia fractures (often with minimal trauma) and then fails to heal, producing a pseudarthrosis with a tapered, sclerotic, atrophic bone end and a hamartomatous fibrous tissue at the site. The tibia does NOT correct spontaneously — this is the fundamental difference from posteromedial bowing.
  • Boyd/Crawford classification describes the appearance (cystic, sclerotic, dysplastic, frank pseudarthrosis). Management before fracture is PROTECTION — a total-contact clamshell orthosis/KAFO worn full time to prevent fracture — and this is the single most important early intervention. Prophylactic bone grafting is not standard.
  • Once a pseudarthrosis is established, treatment is difficult and often requires multiple operations. Options: resection of the hamartomatous tissue with intramedullary rodding and autologous bone grafting (± BMP), vascularised free fibular transfer, Ilizarov bone transport/compression, and combined techniques. Union rates have improved but refracture is common (up to 50%) and the limb often ends up short and deformed. Amputation (Syme/Boyd) with prosthetic fitting remains a legitimate and sometimes superior option after multiple failures.
  • Never perform an osteotomy through or near an anterolaterally bowed tibia — it will not heal and creates the pseudarthrosis you were trying to avoid.
  • Dystrophic scoliosis in NF1 is a related manifestation: a short, sharply angulated curve (fewer than 6 segments) with vertebral scalloping, rib penciling, dural ectasia, foraminal enlargement, apical vertebral rotation and paraspinal masses. It is rapidly progressive, does NOT respond to bracing, has a high pseudarthrosis rate after fusion, and requires circumferential (anterior and posterior) fusion with instrumentation and careful pre-operative MRI for dural ectasia and intraspinal lesions.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Tibia; Systemic Disease.
  • Crawford AH, Schorry EK. Neurofibromatosis in children: the role of the orthopaedist. JAAOS 1999.
  • Pannier S. Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia. Orthop Traumatol Surg Res 2011.
  • Vander Have KL et al. Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia. JAAOS 2008.
  • Hsu LC, Lee PC, Leong JC. Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia: treatment with free vascularised fibular grafting. JBJS Br.
3questions

Fibular hemimelia & proximal focal femoral deficiency

Congenital longitudinal deficiencies and the reconstruction-versus-amputation decision.

3 of 7 sittings2023, 2024F, 2025

  • Fibular hemimelia is the commonest congenital long bone deficiency. Features: partial or complete absence of the fibula, ANTEROMEDIAL bowing of the tibia with a skin dimple, a valgus ankle with a ball-and-socket or sloped tibial plafond, absent lateral rays of the foot, tarsal coalition, equinovalgus foot, a shortened femur with a hypoplastic lateral femoral condyle and genu valgum, and a cruciate-deficient knee. The apex of the tibial bow is ANTERIOR (anteromedial).
  • The critical decision is driven by the FOOT, not the fibula: the classic teaching is that the number of functional rays and the stability/plantigrade potential of the foot determine whether reconstruction or amputation is appropriate. A foot with ≥3–4 functional rays, a stable ankle and a manageable projected discrepancy can be reconstructed and lengthened; a severely deformed, non-plantigrade foot with fewer rays and a large projected discrepancy is best served by early Syme or Boyd amputation with prosthetic fitting, which produces excellent function.
  • An 8-year-old with fibular hemimelia, a projected 4 cm discrepancy, a 4-ray foot and a valgus ankle is a RECONSTRUCTION candidate — a projected discrepancy of only 4 cm with a functional foot is readily managed by contralateral epiphysiodesis or ipsilateral lengthening plus correction of the ankle valgus. Amputation would be inappropriate in this scenario — the classic 'what is most inappropriate at this time' answer.
  • Proximal focal femoral deficiency (PFFD) is a spectrum of proximal femoral deficiency (Aitken A–D) with a short, externally rotated, flexed and abducted femur, a bulbous thigh, hip instability/coxa vara or an absent proximal femur, knee flexion contracture with cruciate deficiency, and a significant limb-length discrepancy. Fibular hemimelia coexists in ~50–70% — always look for it.
  • Orthopaedic manifestations of PFFD include: coxa vara or a pseudarthrosis of the femoral neck, acetabular dysplasia, hip instability, knee instability with absent cruciate ligaments, knee flexion contracture, a foot at the level of the contralateral knee, and profound shortening. A normal, stable knee with intact cruciates is NOT a manifestation of PFFD — cruciate deficiency is characteristic, and this is the standard 'which is not a manifestation' item.
  • Management of PFFD depends on the severity and the projected discrepancy: for a mild deficiency with a stable hip — lengthening with contralateral epiphysiodesis; for severe deficiency — prosthetic fitting with a Syme/Boyd amputation to convert the limb to a functional above- or below-knee prosthetic level, and/or a Van Nes rotationplasty (rotating the limb 180° so the ankle functions as a knee), or knee fusion to create a single functional lever arm.
  • Tibial hemimelia (much rarer) is distinguished by an absent tibia, a VARUS foot, and an association with hand anomalies and autosomal dominant inheritance — it may require knee disarticulation when the quadriceps mechanism is absent.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Limb Deficiency.
  • Achterman C, Kalamchi A. Congenital deficiency of the fibula. JBJS Br 1979.
  • Birch JG, Lincoln TL, Mack PW, Birch CM. Congenital fibular deficiency: a review of thirty years' experience at one institution. JBJS Am 2011.
  • Aitken GT. Proximal femoral focal deficiency: definition, classification and management. In Proximal Femoral Focal Deficiency: A Congenital Anomaly, 1969.
  • Paley D. Surgical reconstruction for fibular hemimelia. J Child Orthop 2016.
3questions

Genu varum/valgum & guided growth

Normal physiologic alignment and when to intervene.

3 of 7 sittings2021, 2022, 2024S

  • Normal developmental alignment sequence: infants are in physiologic VARUS (~15°) at birth, correcting to neutral at ~18–24 months, then progressing to maximal physiologic VALGUS (~10–12°) at approximately 3–4 years of age, and settling to the adult value of ~5–7° of valgus by 7–8 years. Maximum physiologic valgus occurs at about 3–4 years — the answer to 'at approximately what age does a patient have normal maximum physiologic valgus'.
  • Red flags that a bowleg is NOT physiologic: unilateral or asymmetric deformity, progression after age 2, a deformity that is severe (>15–20°) or worsening, short stature, a lateral thrust on gait, a family history, or focal metaphyseal changes on radiograph. These mandate radiographs and consideration of Blount disease, rickets, skeletal dysplasia, physeal injury or focal fibrocartilaginous dysplasia.
  • Guided growth (hemiepiphysiodesis) with a tension-band plate or staples is the modern first-line correction for angular deformity in a growing child — it is minimally invasive, reversible, and corrects gradually. It requires SUFFICIENT REMAINING GROWTH — this is the essential prerequisite.
  • Hemiepiphysiodesis is unlikely to succeed when: there is inadequate remaining growth (skeletal maturity approaching, closed or closing physes), the physis is already damaged/tethered (a physeal bar), the deformity is intra-articular or from bone loss rather than physeal, or in the presence of severe obesity with high mechanical loads causing implant failure. The scenario where it IS likely to succeed is an open physis with substantial growth remaining and a purely physeal (metaphyseal-based) angular deformity — the answer to 'in which scenario is hemiepiphysiodesis likely to be successful'.
  • Monitor closely and remove the implant once alignment is corrected — over-correction is common and occurs quickly, particularly in young children. Rebound deformity after implant removal is well described in the very young.
  • Blount disease (see separate topic) must be excluded in a bowlegged child over 2 years — measure the metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle (Drennan): >16° is abnormal and suggests Blount; <11° is likely physiologic.
  • Adolescent genu varum requires evaluation for adolescent (late-onset) Blount disease, which is associated with obesity, is often unilateral or asymmetric, and may require osteotomy rather than guided growth because of the limited remaining growth.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Lower Extremity Alignment.
  • Salenius P, Vankka E. The development of the tibiofemoral angle in children. JBJS Am 1975.
  • Stevens PM. Guided growth for angular correction: a preliminary series using a tension band plate. J Pediatr Orthop 2007.
  • Levine AM, Drennan JC. Physiological bowing and tibia vara: the metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle. JBJS Am 1982.
  • Ballal MS, Bruce CE, Nayagam S. Correcting genu varum and genu valgum in children by guided growth. JBJS Br 2010.
3questions

Neuromuscular & syndromic spine deformity

Myelomeningocele kyphosis and neuromuscular curves.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022

  • Neuromuscular scoliosis differs fundamentally from idiopathic: the curves are long, C-shaped, involve the sacrum with PELVIC OBLIQUITY, present earlier, progress relentlessly (including after skeletal maturity), and are associated with poor sitting balance, skin breakdown and pulmonary compromise. Bracing does not prevent progression (it may improve sitting balance as a temporising measure).
  • Surgical indications: loss of sitting balance, progressive curve, pelvic obliquity causing skin breakdown, and pain. Fusion is typically LONG — from the upper thoracic spine TO THE PELVIS when there is significant pelvic obliquity, using iliac or S2-alar-iliac screws. Complication rates are high (infection, pulmonary, pseudarthrosis, blood loss), and nutritional and pulmonary optimisation is essential.
  • Myelomeningocele kyphosis is a distinct and severe problem: a rigid, congenital, progressive thoracolumbar kyphosis (a 'gibbus') present at birth in ~10–20% of children with myelomeningocele. It is NOT flexible and does not respond to bracing.
  • Key features of myelomeningocele kyphosis: it produces skin breakdown over the apex (recurrent ulceration is the commonest indication for surgery), impairs sitting balance, and compromises respiratory function by reducing abdominal domain. Surgery involves kyphectomy (vertebral resection) with long posterior instrumentation to the pelvis, and carries a high complication rate (wound problems, infection, hardware failure). The dural sac may be ligated below the level of the neurologic lesion during kyphectomy, since function below the level is already absent.
  • A 4-month-old with an L1 myelomeningocele and bilateral Ortolani-positive (dislocated) hips: the correct management is observation/non-operative treatment. In myelomeningocele, hip reduction does NOT improve function or ambulatory potential, and surgery carries a high rate of stiffness, recurrent dislocation, AVN and fracture. A supple, painless, dislocated hip is preferable to a stiff, reduced hip. The exceptions are a unilateral dislocation causing significant pelvic obliquity in a functional ambulator (low lesion, L4 or below), where reduction may be considered. This is a repeatedly tested management question.
  • Level-based function in myelomeningocele: L4 (quadriceps function) is the key threshold for community ambulation; thoracic-level lesions are wheelchair users; sacral-level lesions ambulate with minimal support. Predict function by the motor level, and set orthopaedic goals accordingly.
  • Latex allergy is very common in myelomeningocele (up to 20–70%) and can cause intra-operative anaphylaxis — all care must be latex-free. Also watch for tethered cord (progressive scoliosis, new weakness, changing urologic function, back pain) and shunt malfunction, both of which present as a change in the orthopaedic picture.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Neuromuscular; Spine.
  • Sarwark JF. Spina bifida. Pediatr Clin North Am 1996.
  • Guille JT, Sarwark JF, Sherk HH, Kumar SJ. Congenital and developmental deformities of the spine in children with myelomeningocele. JAAOS 2006.
  • Swaroop VT, Dias L. Orthopaedic management of spina bifida — part I: hip, knee, and rotational deformities. J Child Orthop 2009.
  • Sponseller PD et al. Pelvic fixation in neuromuscular scoliosis. Spine.
3questions

Obstetrical brachial plexus palsy

Prognosis, natural history and the sequelae.

3 of 7 sittings2023, 2024S, 2025

  • Occurs in ~0.5–3 per 1000 live births. Risk factors: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, breech delivery, instrumented (forceps/vacuum) delivery, prolonged labour, maternal diabetes and a previous affected child. Most involve the upper trunk (C5-6, Erb palsy) producing the 'waiter's tip' posture — shoulder adduction and internal rotation, elbow extension, forearm pronation, with the hand spared.
  • Prognosis is determined chiefly by the level and extent of injury and by the timing of recovery of biceps function — the classic prognostic rule is that failure to recover ANTIGRAVITY BICEPS FUNCTION (elbow flexion) by 3–6 months predicts a poor outcome and is the standard indication for microsurgical exploration/nerve reconstruction.
  • Poor prognostic factors: total plexus (C5-T1) involvement, preganglionic root avulsion — signalled by HORNER SYNDROME (ptosis, miosis, anhydrosis, indicating T1 root avulsion), an associated phrenic nerve palsy (elevated hemidiaphragm), absent hand function/flail limb, failure of biceps recovery by 3 months, and an associated fracture/vascular injury. Isolated upper trunk (Erb) involvement with early return of biceps function is a GOOD prognostic sign — the usual 'all are poor prognostic factors EXCEPT' answer.
  • Natural history: roughly 70–90% recover spontaneously and completely, mostly within the first few months. Klumpke (lower trunk, C8-T1) palsy alone is rare and has a worse prognosis; total plexus palsy has the worst.
  • Sequelae of an incompletely recovered upper trunk palsy — the muscle imbalance is strong internal rotators/adductors (pectoralis major, subscapularis, latissimus) versus weak external rotators/abductors, producing an internal rotation and adduction contracture with progressive glenohumeral dysplasia — a retroverted, flattened, biconcave glenoid with posterior humeral head subluxation.
  • Management of sequelae: early physiotherapy and passive range of motion to prevent contracture; botulinum toxin to the internal rotators; anterior release (subscapularis and pectoralis major lengthening) with capsular release for a contracture with a reducible joint; tendon transfers (latissimus dorsi and teres major to the rotator cuff) to restore external rotation; and humeral derotational osteotomy for a fixed deformity with an incongruent joint.
  • Key nuance: an external rotation (derotational) humeral osteotomy improves function in a fixed internal rotation contracture but does NOT treat glenohumeral dysplasia or anterior instability — and it can worsen anterior instability by rotating the humeral head out of the (posteriorly deficient) glenoid. Joint-preserving release/transfer is preferred where the joint can be reduced; osteotomy is a salvage for the incongruent joint.
  • Always distinguish from a pseudoparalysis of the newborn caused by a clavicle or proximal humerus fracture, or by septic arthritis/osteomyelitis — an infant not moving an arm needs radiographs and an infection screen, not just a plexus diagnosis.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Brachial Plexus.
  • Waters PM. Update on management of pediatric brachial plexus palsy. J Pediatr Orthop 2005.
  • Gilbert A, Tassin JL. Surgical repair of the brachial plexus in obstetric paralysis. Chirurgie 1984.
  • Pearl ML. Shoulder problems in children with brachial plexus birth palsy: evaluation and management. JAAOS 2009.
  • Waters PM, Smith GR, Jaramillo D. Glenohumeral deformity secondary to brachial plexus birth palsy. JBJS Am 1998.
3questions

Paediatric amputation & limb deficiency

How the amputee child differs from the adult.

3 of 7 sittings2021, 2022, 2024F

  • Disarticulation is preferred over transosseous amputation in the growing child. The reason is terminal bony overgrowth — appositional new bone formation at the cut end of a transected long bone (NOT physeal growth), which occurs in up to 8–30% of transosseous amputations and is the commonest reason for reoperation in paediatric amputees. The humerus, fibula, tibia and femur are most affected, in that rough order.
  • Disarticulation also preserves the distal physis (maintaining limb length and the residual limb's growth), provides an end-bearing surface, and avoids overgrowth entirely.
  • Energy expenditure in children is lower than in adults for an equivalent amputation level, and children adapt remarkably well. Nonetheless the same principle holds: preserving the knee joint matters most. Oxygen consumption is NOT the same regardless of amputation level — the classic false statement. Approximate figures: paediatric transtibial adds ~25–30% and transfemoral ~50–65% to the energy cost of walking, though children compensate by self-selecting a slower speed.
  • Phantom limb sensation and pain are uncommon in congenital limb deficiency (children born without a limb rarely experience it) but do occur after acquired/traumatic amputation, particularly in older children and adolescents.
  • Prosthetic fitting milestones: fit an upper limb prosthesis when the child begins to sit independently (~6 months), and a lower limb prosthesis when the child begins to pull to stand (~9–12 months) — matching the prosthesis to developmental milestones rather than chronological age. Early fitting improves acceptance.
  • Children outgrow prostheses rapidly and need frequent replacement (roughly annually in the young child), which is a major cost and access issue and should be planned for.
  • Revision is usually needed for overgrowth or for prosthetic fitting problems, not for phantom pain or neuroma — and revision for overgrowth involves stump revision with resection of the overgrown spike, or capping with an autologous osteochondral (Marquardt) cap, which reduces recurrence.
  • For congenital deficiencies, the decision between reconstruction/lengthening and early amputation with prosthetic fitting should be made with the family early, weighing the number of operations, the years of treatment, the projected discrepancy and the functional prognosis of the foot.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Limb Deficiency.
  • Krajbich JI (Canadian), Bochmann D. Amputations in children. In Atlas of Amputations and Limb Deficiencies, 4th ed (AAOS).
  • Abraham E, Pellicore RJ, Hamilton RC, Hallman BW, Ghosh L. Stump overgrowth in juvenile amputees. J Pediatr Orthop 1986.
  • Herring JA. Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics — Limb Deficiencies.
  • Wilk B, Karol L et al. Energy cost of walking in children with limb deficiencies.
3questions

Paediatric pelvic osteotomies

The menu of acetabular osteotomies and how each works.

3 of 7 sittings2021, 2023, 2025

  • Redirectional osteotomies (reorient the acetabulum, requiring a congruent, concentrically reduced hip and a mobile joint): Salter (innominate) — a single cut through the innominate hinging on the pubic symphysis; triple innominate (Steel/Tönnis); periacetabular osteotomy (Ganz PAO) — requires a closed triradiate cartilage (skeletal maturity), preserves the posterior column, and is the workhorse for the adolescent/young adult dysplastic hip.
  • Reshaping/volume-reducing osteotomies (change the shape of the acetabulum, requiring an open triradiate cartilage which acts as the hinge): Pemberton (pericapsular) — hinges on the triradiate cartilage and decreases acetabular volume; Dega — an incomplete transiliac osteotomy hinging on the medial cortex, useful for posterior/posterolateral deficiency in cerebral palsy.
  • Salvage osteotomies (create coverage with non-articular tissue where the joint is incongruent/subluxed and cannot be reduced): Chiari (medial displacement osteotomy) — displaces the distal fragment medially, with the joint capsule interposed, which undergoes fibrocartilaginous metaplasia (so the covering surface is fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage); shelf (augmentation) procedure — adds a bone graft laterally over the capsule.
  • The classic exam distinction: which osteotomies provide coverage with HYALINE cartilage? The redirectional osteotomies (Salter, triple, PAO) and reshaping osteotomies (Pemberton, Dega) all reorient/reshape the native acetabulum and therefore provide HYALINE cartilage coverage. The SALVAGE osteotomies (Chiari and shelf) provide coverage by FIBROCARTILAGE metaplasia of the interposed capsule — so 'all have hyaline cartilage except' = Chiari (or shelf).
  • Common false statements to recognise: the Chiari MEDIALISES the hip (it does not lateralise it), and the shelf procedure adds bone LATERALLY and does NOT medialise the hip — a shelf described as 'medialising the acetabulum' is false. The Pemberton decreases acetabular volume, and the Salter redirects rather than reshapes (it does not change acetabular volume).
  • A Salter innominate osteotomy provides approximately 15–25° of additional anterolateral coverage (correcting the acetabular index by roughly 10–15°) — it is a modest correction and is inadequate for severe dysplasia, where a triple or PAO is needed. It also lengthens the limb slightly and requires a concentrically reducible hip.
  • Femoral osteotomy (varus derotation) is combined with a pelvic osteotomy when there is excessive anteversion/coxa valga; in older children with DDH, a femoral shortening osteotomy is used to reduce the pressure on the femoral head and lower the AVN risk during open reduction.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Hip.
  • Salter RB (Canadian, Toronto). Innominate osteotomy in the treatment of congenital dislocation and subluxation of the hip. JBJS Br 1961.
  • Ganz R, Klaue K, Vinh TS, Mast JW. A new periacetabular osteotomy for the treatment of hip dysplasias. CORR 1988.
  • Pemberton PA. Pericapsular osteotomy of the ilium for treatment of congenital subluxation and dislocation of the hip. JBJS Am 1965.
  • Chiari K. Medial displacement osteotomy of the pelvis. CORR 1974.
3questions

Posteromedial tibial bowing & limb length discrepancy

The benign congenital bow, and predicting limb length.

3 of 7 sittings2022, 2024S, 2025

  • Posteromedial bowing of the tibia is a benign congenital condition, present at birth, associated with a CALCANEOVALGUS FOOT (the foot is dorsiflexed against the anterior tibia, sometimes touching it). It results from intrauterine positioning/packaging.
  • The critical distinction is from ANTEROLATERAL bowing — the two must never be confused: posteromedial bowing = benign, spontaneously corrects, associated with calcaneovalgus foot and a LIMB-LENGTH DISCREPANCY; anterolateral bowing = congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia and neurofibromatosis type 1 — a serious problem that does not spontaneously correct and progresses to fracture and nonunion.
  • Natural history of posteromedial bowing: the angular deformity corrects spontaneously and substantially over the first 5–7 years (usually to a clinically acceptable degree, though some residual bow persists). The lasting problem is a limb-length discrepancy, which averages 3–4 cm at maturity and correlates with the initial severity of the bow. This is why the child needs long-term follow-up.
  • Management: observation and stretching/orthotics for the calcaneovalgus foot in infancy (it resolves), with serial monitoring of limb length. Treat the discrepancy at the appropriate time with contralateral epiphysiodesis (for discrepancies of ~2–5 cm) or lengthening (for larger discrepancies). Osteotomy for residual angular deformity is rarely needed.
  • The multiplier method (Paley) predicts the discrepancy at maturity from a single measurement in congenital (proportionate) discrepancies, by multiplying the current discrepancy by an age- and sex-specific multiplier. It works for CONGENITAL discrepancies that grow proportionately (fibular hemimelia, posteromedial bowing, hemihypertrophy).
  • The multiplier method does NOT apply to acquired/developmental discrepancies where growth is not proportionate — specifically after trauma with growth arrest, infection, or a physeal injury, and it does not predict overgrowth after a femoral shaft fracture. For these, serial measurements plotted on a Green-Anderson or Moseley straight-line graph are required. This is the classic 'the multiplier method can be used in all of the following except' item.
  • Assessment of limb length: standing block test, scanogram/EOS imaging for the true discrepancy, and a bone age (hand/wrist radiograph) for skeletal maturity, which must be plotted rather than assumed from chronological age.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Limb Deficiency and Length.
  • Paley D, Bhave A, Herzenberg JE, Bowen JR. Multiplier method for predicting limb-length discrepancy. JBJS Am 2000.
  • Pappas AM. Congenital posteromedial bowing of the tibia and fibula. J Pediatr Orthop 1984.
  • Moseley CF. A straight line graph for leg length discrepancies. JBJS Am 1977.
  • Shapiro F. Developmental patterns in lower-extremity length discrepancies. JBJS Am 1982.
2questions

Blount disease & paediatric tibia vara

Distinguishing pathologic from physiologic bowing.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2022

  • Blount disease (tibia vara) is a growth disturbance of the posteromedial proximal tibial physis producing progressive varus, internal tibial torsion and procurvatum. Two forms: infantile (early-onset, <4 years — often bilateral, associated with early walking and obesity) and adolescent (late-onset, >10 years — usually unilateral, strongly associated with obesity).
  • The metaphyseal-diaphyseal (Drennan) angle distinguishes it from physiologic bowing: >16° is likely Blount; <11° is likely physiologic; 11–16° is indeterminate and requires follow-up. Radiographs additionally show medial metaphyseal beaking, depression of the medial tibial plateau, and physeal widening/irregularity medially.
  • Langenskiöld staging (I–VI) describes progressive medial physeal changes, from metaphyseal beaking (I–II) through to a physeal bar with a bony bridge (V–VI). Stages V–VI have an established physeal bar and require bar resection or completion epiphysiodesis in addition to correction.
  • Treatment by age and stage: under 3 years with Langenskiöld I–II → bracing (KAFO) may be tried, though its efficacy is debated. Over 3–4 years, or progressive/advanced disease → proximal tibial (and fibular) valgus-producing osteotomy with correction of internal torsion, ideally before age 4 to reduce the risk of recurrence and physeal bar formation. Guided growth (lateral tension-band plating) is an option in early disease with sufficient remaining growth, but is less reliable in the obese adolescent because of implant failure and limited growth.
  • Focal fibrocartilaginous dysplasia (FFCD) is the key differential for a young child with unilateral tibia vara: a benign, self-limiting fibrocartilaginous lesion at the pes anserinus insertion on the MEDIAL proximal tibial metaphysis, producing abrupt varus with a well-defined radiolucent lesion (cortical defect) with sclerotic margins at the medial metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction. Key distinguishing features: it produces a sharp, focal varus, the physis is NORMAL (no medial physeal depression, no beaking, no widening), and it resolves SPONTANEOUSLY in the majority over 1–2 years — treatment is observation. Medial physeal depression/beaking is a Blount finding, not an FFCD finding — the standard 'all are radiographic findings of tibia vara secondary to FFCD except'.
  • Other causes of pathologic tibia vara: rickets/metabolic bone disease, skeletal dysplasia (particularly metaphyseal chondrodysplasia), physeal injury from trauma or infection, and osteogenesis imperfecta.
  • In the adolescent (late-onset) form, the deformity is often multiplanar with a distal femoral component, so full-length standing radiographs are essential to localise the deformity before planning correction.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Lower Extremity.
  • Levine AM, Drennan JC. Physiological bowing and tibia vara: the metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle. JBJS Am 1982.
  • Langenskiöld A. Tibia vara: osteochondrosis deformans tibiae. CORR 1981.
  • Bell SN, Campbell PE, Cole WG, Menelaus MB. Tibia vara caused by focal fibrocartilaginous dysplasia. JBJS Br 1985.
  • Sabharwal S. Blount disease. JBJS Am 2009.
2questions

Congenital radioulnar synostosis & upper limb anomalies

The stiff forearm and other congenital upper limb differences.

2 of 7 sittings2024S, 2024F

  • Congenital radioulnar synostosis is a failure of longitudinal segmentation of the proximal radius and ulna at ~5–7 weeks of gestation, producing a bony or fibrous bridge with a FIXED forearm position — most often in PRONATION. It is bilateral in ~60%, often autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, and associated with other anomalies (Apert, Klinefelter, arthrogryposis, thrombocytopenia-absent radius, Poland).
  • Diagnosis is frequently DELAYED (often until age 3–6 years or later) because children compensate remarkably well with shoulder and wrist motion, and the deformity is not visually obvious. The presenting complaint is difficulty with tasks requiring supination — receiving change, holding a bowl, or eating with a spoon.
  • Elbow flexion and extension are usually preserved; it is forearm rotation that is absent. Radiographs show the proximal fusion with a hypoplastic radial head, often posteriorly dislocated.
  • Management is based on the FIXED POSITION and the functional impairment, not the presence of the synostosis. Mild to moderate pronation (up to ~30–60°) is usually well tolerated and requires NO treatment — this is the key management point. Surgery (derotational osteotomy through the synostosis mass) is indicated for severe fixed hyperpronation (>60°), especially when bilateral, repositioning the forearm to neutral or slight pronation (~10–20°) for a unilateral case, and asymmetric positions (one in slight pronation, one in slight supination) for bilateral cases.
  • Attempts to RESTORE rotation (excision of the synostosis with interposition) have historically had poor and unpredictable results with recurrence, and are not standard; the goal is repositioning, not motion restoration. Neurovascular compromise from acute derotation is the main surgical risk — gradual correction with an external fixator is used for large corrections.
  • Other congenital upper limb anomalies to recognise: radial longitudinal deficiency (radial club hand) — associated with VACTERL, Fanconi anaemia (obtain a chromosomal breakage test — it is fatal if missed), Holt-Oram (cardiac), and TAR syndrome; ulnar longitudinal deficiency (less common, associated with musculoskeletal rather than visceral anomalies); syndactyly (the commonest congenital hand anomaly; release the border digits early — thumb-index and ring-small — to prevent deviation as they grow at different rates); polydactyly; and congenital trigger thumb.
  • Congenital hallux varus (the foot equivalent question) is associated with a short/duplicated first metatarsal, a medial longitudinal bracket epiphysis (delta phalanx), and preaxial polydactyly; treatment is surgical realignment with excision of the accessory ray and soft-tissue release.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Upper Extremity.
  • Cleary JE, Omer GE. Congenital proximal radio-ulnar synostosis: natural history and functional assessment. JBJS Am 1985.
  • Bauer AS, Bae DS. Congenital radioulnar synostosis. J Hand Surg Am 2011.
  • Kozin SH. Upper-extremity congenital anomalies. JBJS Am 2003.
2questions

Discoid meniscus

The congenital meniscal variant of childhood.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2022

  • A discoid meniscus is a congenital variant in which the meniscus is abnormally thick and disc-shaped rather than semilunar, covering more of the tibial plateau. It is almost always LATERAL (~3–5% of the population; medial discoid is very rare, <0.3%), and is bilateral in ~20%.
  • Watanabe classification: type I complete (covers the entire lateral plateau, with normal posterior meniscotibial attachments); type II incomplete (partial coverage, normal attachments); type III Wrisberg variant (lacks the normal posterior tibial attachment, being anchored only by the Wrisberg ligament — this is the hypermobile, unstable type that produces the classic snapping knee).
  • Presentation: the Wrisberg type presents in a young child with a painless 'snapping knee' on extension. Complete and incomplete types are often asymptomatic until they tear, presenting in older children/adolescents with pain, locking, effusion, loss of terminal extension, and a lateral joint-line bulge. A 5-year-old whose parents note the knee 'looks odd' with a snapping/clunking sensation is the classic discoid presentation.
  • Imaging: on plain radiographs — widened lateral joint space, squaring of the lateral femoral condyle, cupping of the lateral tibial plateau, and a high fibular head. On MRI, the diagnostic criteria are three or more contiguous 5 mm sagittal slices showing meniscal continuity ('bow-tie sign'), or a meniscal width >15 mm (or >20% of the tibial width) on a coronal image.
  • Treatment: an incidentally discovered ASYMPTOMATIC discoid meniscus requires NO treatment — this is the key management point. Symptomatic lesions are treated with arthroscopic saucerisation (partial central meniscectomy) to create a stable 6–8 mm peripheral rim, with repair of any peripheral instability or tear and stabilisation of the Wrisberg variant.
  • Total meniscectomy must be avoided — it reliably produces early lateral compartment arthritis (Fairbank changes) in a young patient and creates a candidate for a meniscal allograft transplant decades later.
  • Discoid menisci are more prone to tearing because of abnormal collagen orientation and increased thickness with relative hypovascularity centrally, so they tear with lower-energy mechanisms than a normal meniscus.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics; Sports.
  • Kocher MS, Klingele K, Rassman SO. Meniscal disorders: normal, discoid, and cysts. Orthop Clin North Am 2003.
  • Watanabe M, Takada S, Ikeuchi H. Atlas of Arthroscopy, 1969.
  • Kramer DE, Micheli LJ. Meniscal tears and discoid meniscus in children: diagnosis and treatment. JAAOS 2009.
2questions

Duchenne muscular dystrophy & Friedreich ataxia

Two progressive neuromuscular diseases with characteristic orthopaedic patterns.

1 of 7 sittings2020 (x2)

  • Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD): X-linked recessive, dystrophin gene mutation (absent dystrophin) — affects boys, presenting at 3–6 years with a waddling gait, toe walking, calf pseudohypertrophy, a positive Gowers sign (climbing up the legs to stand), proximal weakness that progresses distally, and markedly elevated creatine kinase (10–100×). Diagnosis is by genetic testing (muscle biopsy shows absent dystrophin). Becker muscular dystrophy is the milder allelic variant with reduced but present dystrophin.
  • Natural history: loss of independent ambulation at ~10–12 years (later with corticosteroids), followed by rapidly progressive scoliosis once wheelchair-bound, and death from cardiorespiratory failure in the second-to-third decade. Corticosteroids (prednisone/deflazacort) prolong ambulation, delay scoliosis and preserve pulmonary function and are standard of care.
  • Orthopaedic management priorities in DMD: maintain ambulation as long as possible (stretching, night splints, KAFOs, selective contracture releases), and — critically — operate on the SPINE EARLY. Scoliosis develops in ~90% after ambulation is lost and progresses rapidly. Fusion is recommended once the curve reaches ~20–30° AND while forced vital capacity is still >30–40% predicted — waiting risks an inoperable respiratory state. Fusion typically extends from the upper thoracic spine to the pelvis (or to L5 in selected patients).
  • Anaesthetic risk in DMD is a critical safety point: patients are at risk of malignant hyperthermia-like reactions, rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest with succinylcholine and volatile agents — avoid succinylcholine and inhalational agents; use total intravenous anaesthesia. Cardiomyopathy requires pre-operative echocardiography.
  • Friedreich ataxia: autosomal recessive, GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin (FXN) gene, presenting at 8–15 years with progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, loss of proprioception and vibration sense (posterior column), absent deep tendon reflexes with UPPER motor neuron signs (extensor plantars), muscle weakness, and — the orthopaedic signature — BILATERAL CAVOVARUS FEET and SCOLIOSIS. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the usual cause of death and diabetes is common.
  • The described patient with ataxia, dysarthria, diminished proprioception, absent reflexes, bilateral cavus feet and scoliosis is Friedreich ataxia — the combination of cerebellar signs plus cavovarus feet plus areflexia is pathognomonic.
  • Orthopaedic care in Friedreich ataxia: scoliosis behaves more like idiopathic scoliosis than a typical neuromuscular curve (bracing may be tried in flexible curves) and is treated with posterior fusion for progressive curves; cavovarus feet are managed with orthoses, tendon transfers and osteotomies, avoiding triple arthrodesis where possible in an ataxic patient who needs a flexible foot for balance. Cardiac assessment is mandatory before any surgery.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Neuromuscular.
  • Birnkrant DJ et al. Diagnosis and management of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD Care Considerations Working Group). Lancet Neurol 2018.
  • Bushby K et al. Diagnosis and management of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Lancet Neurol 2010.
  • Delatycki MB, Corben LA. Clinical features of Friedreich ataxia. J Child Neurol 2012.
  • Milbrandt TA, Kunes JR, Karol LA. Friedreich's ataxia and scoliosis: the experience at two institutions. J Pediatr Orthop 2008.
2questions

Klippel-Feil & congenital cervical anomalies

The short-necked child with fused cervical vertebrae.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2023

  • Klippel-Feil syndrome is the congenital fusion of two or more cervical vertebrae from a failure of segmentation of the cervical somites in the 3rd–8th week. The classic clinical triad — a short neck, a low posterior hairline, and limited cervical range of motion — is present in fewer than 50% of patients, so the diagnosis is often radiographic.
  • The associations are the high-yield content and are the reason a diagnosis matters — every child with Klippel-Feil requires a systematic screen: Sprengel deformity (the most common musculoskeletal association, ~20–30%, with an omovertebral bone in about a third), scoliosis/congenital vertebral anomalies (~60%, the most common overall association), renal anomalies (~30% — including unilateral renal agenesis; obtain a renal ultrasound), congenital heart disease (~4–15% — VSD is the commonest; obtain an echocardiogram), deafness/hearing loss (~30% — obtain audiology), and cranial nerve/brainstem anomalies including synkinesis (mirror movements) and Chiari malformation/syringomyelia.
  • The single most common association depends on how the question is framed: scoliosis/congenital spine deformity is the most frequent overall, and Sprengel deformity is the most frequent extraspinal musculoskeletal association. Renal anomalies are the most important 'silent' association to screen for.
  • The key orthopaedic concern is instability and degeneration at the mobile segments ADJACENT to the fused blocks, which bear increased stress. Patients with long fusion masses, occipitocervical fusion, C2-3 fusion with occipitalisation of C1, and associated basilar invagination or stenosis are at highest risk of neurologic injury, including from minor trauma.
  • Counselling: patients with high-risk patterns should avoid contact and collision sports, and should have flexion-extension radiographs before general anaesthesia. Most patients with a single-level fusion and no instability are asymptomatic and lead normal lives.
  • Sprengel deformity (congenital undescended scapula) presents with a small, high, medially rotated scapula limiting abduction, often with an omovertebral bone tethering the scapula to the cervical spine. Treatment for functional/cosmetic impairment is surgical scapular repositioning (Woodward or Green procedure) before age 6–8, with resection of the omovertebral bone and the superomedial scapular angle; the brachial plexus is at risk with aggressive caudal translation (a clavicular osteotomy may be performed to reduce this risk).
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Cervical Spine.
  • Hensinger RN, Lang JE, MacEwen GD. Klippel-Feil syndrome: a constellation of associated anomalies. JBJS Am 1974.
  • Samartzis DD et al. Classification of congenitally fused cervical patterns in Klippel-Feil patients. Spine 2006.
  • Tracy MR, Dormans JP, Kusumi K. Klippel-Feil syndrome: clinical features and current understanding of etiology. CORR 2004.
2questions

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease

Idiopathic osteonecrosis of the immature femoral head.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2023

  • Perthes disease is idiopathic osteonecrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis in a child, typically 4–8 years old (range 2–12), boys 4–5:1, often small for age with delayed bone age, presenting with a painless or minimally painful limp of insidious onset and restricted abduction and internal rotation. Bilateral in ~10–15% (but characteristically asymmetric/at different stages — symmetric bilateral disease suggests a dysplasia).
  • Features that argue AGAINST Perthes and for an alternative diagnosis: symmetric bilateral involvement at the same stage (suggests multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia or hypothyroidism), age outside the typical range, a positive family history of dysplasia, short stature with other epiphyseal changes, and systemic features. Also exclude sickle cell disease, Gaucher disease and steroid-induced osteonecrosis. In a 5-year-old with bilateral lateral pillar B/C hips, the finding that would most point away from Perthes is symmetric, simultaneous bilateral involvement with other epiphyseal abnormalities.
  • Herring lateral pillar classification (assessed at the fragmentation stage, the most reliable prognostic tool): A — no loss of height of the lateral pillar (good outcome); B — >50% of lateral pillar height maintained; B/C border — ~50% with a narrow pillar; C — <50% of lateral pillar height maintained (worst outcome).
  • The two most important prognostic factors are AGE AT ONSET and the lateral pillar classification. Children under 6 (some say under 8) at onset do well regardless of treatment; children over 8 with lateral pillar B/C or C do poorly and benefit most from containment surgery. Loss of containment/subluxation, decreased range of motion, and 'head at risk' signs (Catterall) also predict a worse result.
  • Treatment principle is CONTAINMENT — keeping the femoral head within the acetabulum during the biologically plastic phase so that it remodels into a spherical shape. Achieved non-operatively (activity restriction, physiotherapy to maintain abduction, brief traction/casting for a painful stiff hip) or operatively (femoral varus derotation osteotomy, or a pelvic/Salter osteotomy, or a combination).
  • For a 4-year-old with lateral pillar B disease and mild extrusion, the appropriate management is non-operative — physiotherapy to maintain motion and observation. For a child over 8 with lateral pillar B or B/C, containment surgery (femoral or pelvic osteotomy) improves outcomes in the Herring multicentre study.
  • Late sequelae are coxa magna, coxa breva, a short femoral neck with trochanteric overgrowth, femoroacetabular impingement, hinge abduction, and early osteoarthritis. Salvage procedures include trochanteric advancement, valgus osteotomy for hinge abduction, and femoral head-neck osteochondroplasty for impingement.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Hip.
  • Herring JA, Kim HT, Browne R. Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease. Part II: prospective multicenter study of the effect of treatment on outcome. JBJS Am 2004.
  • Catterall A. The natural history of Perthes' disease. JBJS Br 1971.
  • Stulberg SD, Cooperman DR, Wallensten R. The natural history of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease. JBJS Am 1981.
  • Kim HKW. Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease. JAAOS 2010.
2questions

Paediatric hallux valgus

Juvenile/adolescent hallux valgus and why it behaves differently.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2022

  • Juvenile/adolescent hallux valgus differs from the adult form in several important ways: there is a strong family history (particularly maternal) in the majority, it is frequently bilateral, there is often an increased distal metatarsal articular angle (DMAA) with a CONGRUENT joint, there is a higher incidence of metatarsus primus varus and pes planus/first-ray hypermobility, and the deformity is often more of a cosmetic than a painful complaint.
  • The single most important management point is that surgery in the skeletally immature has a HIGH RECURRENCE RATE (up to 30–50%, higher in the very young and with an uncorrected DMAA or open physis) — so surgery should be deferred until skeletal maturity wherever possible, and should be performed for PAIN, not appearance. Reassurance, footwear modification and orthoses (particularly if there is associated pes planus) are first-line.
  • Because the joint is often congruent with an increased DMAA, a standard distal soft-tissue procedure that realigns an incongruent joint is inappropriate — it creates an incongruent joint. A distal metatarsal (biplanar chevron) osteotomy that corrects the DMAA, or a double/triple osteotomy (proximal for the IMA plus distal for the DMAA), is required. Failure to address the DMAA is a leading cause of recurrence.
  • Beware the physis: the proximal first metatarsal physis is open in the growing child, so a proximal metatarsal osteotomy risks physeal injury — a Lapidus (first TMT fusion) is contraindicated with an open physis, and osteotomy planning must respect the growth plate.
  • Congenital hallux VARUS is a different entity: the great toe deviates medially at birth, and it is associated with a short/duplicated first metatarsal, a longitudinal epiphyseal bracket (delta phalanx), preaxial polydactyly, and a tight abductor hallucis. Treatment is surgical — excision of the accessory ray/duplicated structures, release of the medial soft tissues, and correction of the bracket — and it does not resolve spontaneously.
  • Iatrogenic hallux varus after hallux valgus surgery is caused by over-correction: excessive lateral release with fibular sesamoid excision, over-resection of the medial eminence, over-tightening of the medial capsule, and over-correction of the IMA — always the first thing to look for in a post-operative varus toe.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Foot; Foot and Ankle.
  • Coughlin MJ. Juvenile hallux valgus: etiology and treatment. Foot Ankle Int 1995.
  • Chell J, Dhar S. Pediatric hallux valgus. Foot Ankle Clin 2014.
  • Farrar NG, Duncan N, Ahmed N, Rajan RA. Adolescent hallux valgus: advances in management. Indian J Orthop 2012.
2questions

Paediatric hip fracture & femoral neck fracture in children

A rare, high-stakes injury.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2024F

  • Paediatric femoral neck fractures are rare (<1% of paediatric fractures) and result from HIGH-ENERGY trauma in a child (unlike the low-energy fragility fracture of the elderly) — so they are frequently accompanied by other injuries. A femoral neck fracture in a child from low-energy trauma should raise suspicion of a pathologic lesion (unicameral bone cyst, fibrous dysplasia) or metabolic bone disease.
  • Delbet classification and the corresponding AVN risk — the key list: type I transepiphyseal (~90–100% AVN, worst; often associated with dislocation of the epiphysis); type II transcervical (the commonest, ~50% AVN); type III cervicotrochanteric/basicervical (~25%); type IV intertrochanteric (~10%, best prognosis). AVN is the most common and most devastating complication overall (~20–40% across all types) and is directly related to the fracture level.
  • The blood supply is the reason: the lateral epiphyseal (posterosuperior retinacular) vessels from the medial femoral circumflex artery are the sole supply to the capital femoral epiphysis after age ~4 years, because the physis is a barrier and the artery of the ligamentum teres contributes almost nothing until adolescence.
  • Management principles: urgent anatomic reduction and stable internal fixation, with capsular decompression (aspiration or capsulotomy) to relieve the tamponade effect of the intracapsular haematoma — which some evidence suggests reduces AVN. Even non-displaced fractures should generally be fixed because of the high rate of late displacement in a cast/spica.
  • Implant choice: cannulated screws, crossing the physis if necessary to achieve stability in a young child with a proximal fracture (stability takes priority over the physis — a growth arrest is a lesser problem than a nonunion or AVN), and stopping short of the physis in the older child. Supplement with a spica cast in the young child.
  • Other complications: coxa vara (from malreduction or growth disturbance, ~20–30%), premature physeal closure, and nonunion (~5–10%). Nonunion requires valgus osteotomy with bone grafting.
  • Femoral neck stress fracture in an adolescent/young athlete or military recruit: distinguish the compression (inferomedial) side — which is stable and can be treated with protected weightbearing and close follow-up — from the tension (superolateral) side, which is unstable and requires prophylactic in-situ screw fixation because of the risk of displacement and catastrophic AVN. A large (>50%) inferomedial lesion with a joint effusion, or any tension-sided lesion, warrants fixation.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatric Trauma: Lower Extremity.
  • Delbet P (per Colonna). Fractures of the neck of the femur in children. Am J Surg 1929.
  • Moon ES, Mehlman CT. Risk factors for avascular necrosis after femoral neck fractures in children: 25 Cincinnati cases and meta-analysis of 360 cases. J Orthop Trauma 2006.
  • Ratliff AHC. Fractures of the neck of the femur in children. JBJS Br 1962.
  • Boardman MJ, Herman MJ, Buck B, Pizzutillo PD. Hip fractures in children. JAAOS 2009.
2questions

Paediatric humeral shaft & proximal humerus fractures

Remodelling potential and the limits of non-operative treatment.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2024S

  • The proximal humeral physis contributes ~80% of the growth of the humerus, giving the proximal humerus enormous remodelling capacity. Combined with the wide range of shoulder motion (which forgives residual angulation), this means the great majority of paediatric proximal humerus fractures are treated non-operatively with excellent results.
  • Acceptable angulation by age: <5 years — up to 70° of angulation and complete displacement; 5–12 years — up to 40–60°; >12 years — up to 20–30° and <50% displacement. Beyond skeletal maturity, adult parameters apply.
  • Operative indications: an open fracture, neurovascular injury, an irreducible fracture with interposed soft tissue, unacceptable alignment in an adolescent near skeletal maturity, a floating elbow, polytrauma, and a pathologic fracture requiring stabilisation. Fixation is usually percutaneous smooth pins or flexible intramedullary nails.
  • The most common cause of failure of closed reduction of a completely displaced proximal humeral physeal separation is INTERPOSITION OF THE BICEPS TENDON (long head) between the fragments — the classic answer. The periosteum, the deltoid and (rarely) the joint capsule can also block reduction. Recognising this avoids repeated futile manipulations, which risk physeal injury.
  • Flexible intramedullary nails for paediatric HUMERAL SHAFT fractures work well: they are inserted retrograde (or antegrade) with two nails, provide relative stability with callus healing, and have high union rates. Points to know: the radial nerve is at risk (particularly with a lateral entry or with distal third fractures), entry-site irritation is the commonest complication, and the nails do NOT provide rotational control in comminuted/length-unstable patterns. They are not indicated for most paediatric humeral shaft fractures, which heal readily in a sling or functional brace — 'all are true except' items often hinge on over-stating their necessity.
  • A 10-year-old with a pathologic proximal humerus fracture through a unicameral bone cyst (with a fallen-leaf sign) should be treated non-operatively in a sling initially — allow the fracture to heal, then address the cyst if it persists. Immediate curettage of a fractured cyst is not the first step.
  • Radial nerve palsy with a paediatric humeral shaft fracture is uncommon and, as in adults, is usually a neurapraxia that recovers; observation with EMG at 6 weeks is appropriate unless there is an open fracture or the palsy appears after manipulation.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatric Trauma: Upper Extremity.
  • Beringer DC et al. Severely displaced proximal humeral epiphyseal fractures: a follow-up study. J Pediatr Orthop 1998.
  • Pahlavan S, Baldwin KD, Pandya NK, Namdari S, Hosalkar H. Proximal humerus fractures in the pediatric population: a systematic review. J Child Orthop 2011.
  • Canavese F et al. Displaced proximal humerus fractures in children and adolescents. J Pediatr Orthop.
2questions

Paediatric obesity & orthopaedic implications

The musculoskeletal consequences of childhood obesity.

2 of 7 sittings2024F, 2025

  • Childhood obesity is associated with a specific and testable set of orthopaedic conditions: slipped capital femoral epiphysis, Blount disease (both infantile and adolescent tibia vara), genu valgum, flatfoot, fractures (a higher fracture rate overall, particularly of the forearm and lower limb), and vitamin D deficiency.
  • Obesity increases complications across paediatric orthopaedic care: higher rates of fracture reduction failure and loss of reduction, more complications after supracondylar fracture fixation, higher infection and wound complication rates, more difficult imaging and casting, longer operative times, and higher complication rates after spine surgery and after guided growth (implant failure from mechanical load).
  • In fracture care, obese children have more severe fracture patterns for the same mechanism, higher rates of operative treatment, and higher rates of complications including compartment syndrome and loss of reduction in casts — a cast on an obese limb is harder to mould effectively.
  • Vitamin D deficiency is common in obese children (sequestration in adipose tissue) and should be measured and corrected, particularly before elective surgery and in fracture patients.
  • Obesity is NOT protective against fracture — the classic false statement. Despite greater bone mass, obese children have a higher fracture rate, attributed to greater force at impact, poorer balance and postural stability, lower physical activity and vitamin D deficiency.
  • Blount disease in the obese adolescent (late-onset tibia vara) is often unilateral, less responsive to guided growth (because of high mechanical loads causing implant failure and limited remaining growth), and frequently requires osteotomy.
  • Practical points: counsel about weight management as part of orthopaedic care, screen for SCFE symptoms (hip/knee pain, limp) in the obese adolescent, screen the contralateral hip in a child presenting with SCFE, check vitamin D, and anticipate technical difficulty and higher complication rates when planning surgery.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics.
  • Taylor ED et al. Orthopedic complications of overweight in children and adolescents. Pediatrics 2006.
  • Sabharwal S, Root MZ. Impact of obesity on orthopaedics. JBJS Am 2012.
  • Kessler J et al. Childhood obesity is associated with increased risk of most lower extremity fractures. CORR 2013.
2questions

Rickets & metabolic bone disease of childhood

Recognising the bowed, short child with metabolic bone disease.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2025

  • Radiographic hallmarks of rickets: physeal WIDENING with metaphyseal FLARING, CUPPING and FRAYING, particularly at the knees, wrists and costochondral junctions ('rachitic rosary'), plus generalised osteopenia, bowing of the long bones (genu varum), and, in older children, Looser zones/pseudofractures. A child presenting with progressive bilateral femoral and tibial varus with widened physes and metaphyseal flaring in the 25th percentile for height and weight has rickets — not Blount disease (which is unilateral or asymmetric with a depressed medial tibial plateau and no physeal widening) and not physiologic bowing (which has normal physes).
  • Nutritional (vitamin D deficiency) rickets is the commonest form worldwide and is re-emerging: risk factors are exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D supplementation, darker skin pigmentation, limited sun exposure, northern latitude (highly relevant in Canada), maternal deficiency, and malabsorption. Biochemistry: low or normal calcium, LOW phosphate, HIGH alkaline phosphatase, HIGH PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), and low 25-OH vitamin D. Treatment is vitamin D and calcium replacement, which corrects the biochemistry and, in the young child, the deformity.
  • X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (vitamin D-resistant rickets) — the commonest inherited form: X-linked dominant, PHEX mutation, causing renal phosphate wasting via elevated FGF23. Biochemistry: LOW phosphate, NORMAL calcium, HIGH ALP, NORMAL or low-normal PTH, and normal 25-OH vitamin D (distinguishing it from nutritional rickets, where PTH is high). Treatment is oral phosphate and calcitriol, and now burosumab (an anti-FGF23 antibody), which is transformative.
  • Renal osteodystrophy (chronic kidney disease): high phosphate, low calcium, high PTH, and a mixture of osteomalacia and hyperparathyroid bone disease; associated with SCFE and severe deformity.
  • Distinguishing from other bowing causes: physiologic bowing (symmetric, corrects by age 2, normal physes and normal biochemistry); Blount disease (metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle >16°, medial physeal depression, often obese and often unilateral); skeletal dysplasia (short stature with characteristic epiphyseal/metaphyseal changes); hypophosphatasia (LOW alkaline phosphatase — the biochemical opposite, with premature loss of teeth).
  • Orthopaedic management: treat the metabolic disease FIRST — correcting the biochemistry allows remodelling and often corrects the deformity in the young child, and operating on untreated metabolic bone disease leads to recurrence, delayed union and hardware failure. Guided growth or osteotomy is reserved for residual deformity after medical optimisation, and osteotomies should be performed close to skeletal maturity to reduce recurrence.
  • In an adolescent with unexplained bowing, always check calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, 25-OH vitamin D, PTH, and renal function.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics; Systemic Disease.
  • Carpenter TO et al. A clinician's guide to X-linked hypophosphatemia. J Bone Miner Res 2011.
  • Munns CF et al. Global consensus recommendations on prevention and management of nutritional rickets. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016.
  • Ward LM (Canadian, CHEO). Vitamin D deficiency in the 21st century: a persistent problem among Canadian infants and mothers. CMAJ 2005.
  • Novais E, Stevens PM. Hypophosphatemic rickets: the role of hemiepiphysiodesis. J Pediatr Orthop 2006.
1question

Congenital coxa vara

Developmental coxa vara and the Hilgenreiner-epiphyseal angle.

1 of 7 sittings2022

  • Congenital (developmental) coxa vara is a primary defect in endochondral ossification of the femoral neck, producing a progressive decrease in the neck-shaft angle with a vertically oriented physis, a short femoral neck, trochanteric overgrowth and a Trendelenburg gait. It presents in early childhood (2–6 years) as a painless limp with limited abduction and internal rotation. Bilateral in ~30–50%.
  • The Hilgenreiner-epiphyseal (HE) angle is the key measurement — the angle between Hilgenreiner's line and the femoral capital physis: normal <25°; 45–60° is the indeterminate/watch zone; >60° indicates a high risk of PROGRESSION and is an indication for surgery. An HE angle >60° is the single measurement most associated with radiographic progression — the standard answer.
  • A neck-shaft angle <90–100° and a progressive deformity are the other indications for corrective surgery, along with a Trendelenburg gait and a significant limb-length discrepancy.
  • Treatment is a valgus-producing proximal femoral osteotomy (with derotation as needed), aiming to reduce the HE angle to <38° and restore the neck-shaft angle to ~140–150°. Slight over-correction is desirable because some recurrence is expected. Concurrent adductor release and, in the older child, trochanteric epiphysiodesis or advancement to address trochanteric overgrowth.
  • Premature physeal closure of the proximal femur occurs in up to 90% after osteotomy, so limb length must be monitored. Recurrence occurs in up to 30%, particularly in the young child and with inadequate initial correction.
  • The differential for coxa vara: developmental/congenital, acquired (SCFE, Perthes, post-traumatic malunion or physeal injury, post-infectious), and dysplastic (osteogenesis imperfecta, fibrous dysplasia, cleidocranial dysplasia, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, metaphyseal chondrodysplasia). Bilateral coxa vara with short stature should prompt a skeletal survey for a dysplasia.
  • Female sex and age <5 years are not the strongest predictors of progression — the HE angle is; these demographic factors are the usual distractors in this question.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics: Hip.
  • Weinstein JN, Kuo KN, Millar EA. Congenital coxa vara: a retrospective review. J Pediatr Orthop 1984.
  • Beals RK. Coxa vara in childhood: evaluation and management. JAAOS 1998.
  • Carroll K, Coleman S, Stevens PM. Coxa vara: surgical outcomes of valgus osteotomies. J Pediatr Orthop 1997.
1question

Hemihypertrophy & overgrowth syndromes

Asymmetric overgrowth and the tumour surveillance imperative.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • Isolated hemihypertrophy (hemihyperplasia) is asymmetric overgrowth of one side of the body. The single most important clinical implication is the markedly increased risk of embryonal tumours — particularly WILMS TUMOUR (nephroblastoma) and hepatoblastoma — requiring a surveillance protocol: abdominal ultrasound every 3 months until age 7–8 years, and serum alpha-fetoprotein every 3 months until age 4 for hepatoblastoma.
  • Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (11p15 imprinting defect) is the classic overgrowth syndrome: macrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele/abdominal wall defect, hemihypertrophy, neonatal hypoglycaemia, ear creases/pits, and a substantially increased embryonal tumour risk — the same surveillance applies.
  • Other overgrowth conditions to distinguish: Klippel-Trenaunay-Weber syndrome (capillary/port-wine stain, venous and lymphatic malformations, and limb overgrowth — the vascular malformation is the defining feature); Proteus syndrome (AKT1, progressive, disproportionate, asymmetric overgrowth with cerebriform connective tissue naevi); neurofibromatosis type 1 (localised overgrowth, plexiform neurofibroma); and macrodystrophia lipomatosa (localised digital overgrowth).
  • Conditions NOT associated with hemihypertrophy — the usual distractors: Turner syndrome (short stature, not overgrowth), achondroplasia, and Marfan syndrome (tall but symmetric).
  • Orthopaedic management centres on the limb-length discrepancy: measure serially with scanograms and bone age, predict the discrepancy at maturity (the multiplier method works here because the overgrowth is proportionate/congenital), and treat with contralateral epiphysiodesis timed to skeletal maturity for discrepancies of ~2–5 cm, or lengthening/shortening for larger differences. Scoliosis and foot size discrepancy also require attention.
  • Refer to genetics — establishing the underlying diagnosis determines the tumour surveillance protocol, which is the intervention that saves lives.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics.
  • Clericuzio CL, Martin RA. Diagnostic criteria and tumor screening for individuals with isolated hemihyperplasia. Genet Med 2009.
  • Kalish JM et al. Surveillance recommendations for children with overgrowth syndromes and predisposition to Wilms tumors and hepatoblastoma. Clin Cancer Res 2017.
  • Ballock RT, Wiesner GL, Myers MT, Thompson GH. Hemihypertrophy: concepts and controversies. JBJS Am 1997.
1question

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

Classification and orthopaedic implications of JIA.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • JIA is defined as arthritis of unknown cause beginning before the 16th birthday and persisting for at least 6 weeks, after exclusion of other causes. Subtypes (ILAR): oligoarticular (≤4 joints — the commonest, ~50%), polyarticular (≥5 joints, RF-positive or RF-negative), systemic (Still disease), psoriatic, enthesitis-related, and undifferentiated.
  • Oligoarticular JIA is the commonest subtype: a young girl (2–4 years) with a swollen knee, ANA-positive, and — the critical association — CHRONIC ANTERIOR UVEITIS, which is ASYMPTOMATIC and can cause blindness. All children with JIA require regular slit-lamp ophthalmologic screening, most frequently in the young, ANA-positive, oligoarticular group. This is the single most important non-orthopaedic point.
  • Systemic JIA (Still disease) presents with quotidian spiking fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink rash, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, serositis and markedly elevated inflammatory markers/ferritin, with arthritis that may appear later. It mimics infection and malignancy — leukaemia must be excluded before starting steroids. It carries the risk of macrophage activation syndrome, a life-threatening complication.
  • Orthopaedic manifestations: local growth disturbance — chronic hyperaemia around an inflamed joint causes overgrowth (limb-length discrepancy, an enlarged epiphysis, a valgus knee) early, and premature physeal closure with shortening late. Micrognathia from TMJ involvement, leg-length discrepancy, flexion contractures, cervical spine fusion and atlantoaxial instability (screen before anaesthesia), and osteoporosis from disease and steroids.
  • Modern medical therapy (methotrexate and biologics — TNF inhibitors, IL-1 and IL-6 blockade) has transformed the disease and dramatically reduced the need for joint surgery. The orthopaedic surgeon's role is now largely: intra-articular corticosteroid injection (highly effective in oligoarticular disease), synovectomy for refractory monoarticular synovitis, contracture management, limb-length equalisation, and arthroplasty in the young adult with end-stage joint destruction.
  • Always exclude septic arthritis and malignancy in a child with a single swollen joint — a positive ANA and a chronic course do not exclude sepsis, and leukaemia commonly presents with joint pain.
  • Perioperative management follows the ACR/AAHKS principles: continue conventional DMARDs, hold biologics and time surgery at the end of the dosing cycle, and screen the cervical spine before general anaesthesia.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics; Systemic Disease.
  • Petty RE et al. International League of Associations for Rheumatology classification of juvenile idiopathic arthritis. J Rheumatol 2004.
  • Ravelli A, Martini A. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Lancet 2007.
  • Cassidy J et al. Ophthalmologic examinations in children with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (AAP clinical report). Pediatrics 2006.
1question

Paediatric compartment syndrome

How compartment syndrome differs in children.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • The classic adult sign — pain out of proportion — is unreliable in a child, who may be too young, too frightened or too distracted to report it, and who may have received analgesia or regional anaesthesia.
