The paediatric presentation is therefore based on the '3 A's': increasing ANALGESIA requirement, ANXIETY and AGITATION. An escalating analgesic requirement is the earliest and most reliable warning sign and should trigger immediate assessment.
  • Highest-risk paediatric injuries: tibial shaft fractures (particularly with a concomitant fibular fracture and high-energy mechanism), supracondylar humerus fractures (especially with a floating elbow, vascular injury, or excessive elbow flexion in a cast), forearm fractures, and femoral shaft fractures treated in a 90/90 spica cast (which can cause compartment syndrome of the LEG from excessive traction and calf pressure).
  • A floating elbow (ipsilateral supracondylar and forearm fracture) markedly increases the risk and is an indication for fixation of both fractures rather than casting.
  • Measurement: compartment pressures are used when the examination is unreliable (obtunded, very young, regional block) — the ΔP (diastolic pressure − compartment pressure) <30 mmHg threshold applies as in adults. Children often have a higher baseline compartment pressure (13–16 mmHg) than adults, so absolute values must be interpreted with care.
  • Prevention: avoid circumferential casts on high-risk injuries (use a splint with room to swell), release the padding and split the cast to skin (which relieves more pressure than splitting the cast alone), avoid elevating the limb above the heart (this reduces perfusion pressure), and avoid hyperflexion of the elbow after supracondylar reduction.
  • Treatment is emergent fasciotomy of all involved compartments. The outcome in children after timely fasciotomy is generally good, with a better capacity for recovery than adults; delayed diagnosis leads to Volkmann ischaemic contracture.
  • Neonatal compartment syndrome of the forearm is a rare, distinct entity presenting at birth with a swollen, discoloured forearm and a sentinel skin lesion — it is usually diagnosed late, and the consequence is a Volkmann contracture.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics; Orthopaedic Dilemmas.
  • Bae DS, Kadiyala RK, Waters PM. Acute compartment syndrome in children: contemporary diagnosis, treatment, and outcome. J Pediatr Orthop 2001.
  • Noonan KJ, McCarthy JJ. Compartment syndromes in the pediatric patient. J Pediatr Orthop 2010.
  • Mubarak SJ et al. Volkmann contracture and compartment syndromes after femur fractures in children treated with 90/90 spica casts. J Pediatr Orthop 2006.

14questions

Odontoid & upper cervical fractures

Odontoid fracture classification, treatment by type and age, and C1-C2 fixation options.

7 of 7 sittings2020, 2021 (x4), 2022 (x2), 2023, 2024S (x2), 2024F (x3), 2025

  • Anderson & D'Alonzo classification: type I — an avulsion of the tip at the alar ligament insertion (rare; may indicate occipitocervical instability — always assess the craniocervical junction); type II — through the base of the dens at the junction with the body (the commonest and the problem fracture — a watershed vascular zone with a small cross-sectional area of cancellous bone, hence a high nonunion rate); type III — extending into the cancellous body of C2 (heals well in a collar/halo because of the large cancellous surface).
  • Risk factors for nonunion of a type II fracture: displacement >4–6 mm, angulation >10°, POSTERIOR displacement, age >50 (and especially >65), comminution at the fracture site, delayed presentation/treatment, and smoking. Nonunion rates in the elderly treated non-operatively approach 30–60%.
  • Elderly type II odontoid fracture — this is now a well-defined evidence area. Non-operative treatment in a hard collar is a legitimate and commonly chosen option in the elderly, accepting a high rate of stable fibrous nonunion, which is usually asymptomatic and does not require further treatment. Surgery (posterior C1-C2 fusion) gives higher union rates but carries substantial perioperative morbidity in this population. A HALO VEST IS A POOR OPTION IN THE ELDERLY — it is associated with markedly increased mortality, pneumonia, dysphagia, pin complications and poor tolerance — this is the classic 'all are good treatment options EXCEPT' answer for an elderly type II odontoid fracture.
  • Anterior odontoid screw fixation: preserves C1-C2 rotation (~50% of cervical rotation) and is attractive in the younger patient. Contraindications — the high-yield list: an OBLIQUE FRACTURE LINE running anterosuperior to posteroinferior (i.e. parallel to the intended screw path — an 'anterior oblique' pattern), comminution of the dens or the C2 body, osteoporosis (poor screw purchase), a disrupted transverse atlantal ligament (which makes the C1-C2 complex unstable regardless of dens union), chronic nonunion (>6 months), a barrel chest/short neck or fixed thoracic kyphosis preventing the necessary screw trajectory, and pathologic bone.
  • Posterior C1-C2 fixation options: Magerl transarticular screws with a posterior wiring/graft construct (biomechanically excellent) versus Harms/Goel C1 lateral mass–C2 pedicle screw-rod constructs (more forgiving, allows reduction). The principal contraindication to transarticular screws is an aberrant/high-riding vertebral artery in the C2 isthmus (present in ~20% of patients — a CT angiogram or careful CT assessment is mandatory before planning), plus an irreducible C1-C2 subluxation (the transarticular screw cannot reduce the joint) and severe osteoporosis. The vertebral artery is the answer to 'what is a contraindication to C1-C2 transarticular screw fixation'.
  • Injury from anterior perforation with a C1 lateral mass screw: the internal carotid artery lies immediately anterior to the C1 lateral mass (as does the hypoglossal nerve) — this is the structure at risk with ventral penetration, and a repeated question.
  • Atlas (C1/Jefferson) fractures: stability depends on the transverse atlantal ligament. The rule of Spence — combined lateral mass overhang >6.9 mm on the open-mouth odontoid view — implies a transverse ligament rupture and instability. An atlanto-dens interval >3 mm in adults (>5 mm in children) also indicates transverse ligament insufficiency. A bony avulsion (Dickman type II) can heal in a halo/collar; a mid-substance ligamentous rupture (type I) will not and requires C1-C2 fusion.
  • Hangman's fracture (traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2) — Levine & Edwards: type I (<3 mm translation, no angulation — stable, treat in a collar); type II (>3 mm translation with significant angulation — from flexion-distraction, treat with reduction and halo/collar, or surgery if reduction fails); type IIA (severe angulation with minimal translation — TRACTION IS CONTRAINDICATED as it distracts and worsens the deformity; treat with compression/extension); type III (with bilateral facet dislocation — unstable, requires open reduction and fusion). Most hangman's fractures heal non-operatively.
  • A 14-year-old with a displaced type II odontoid fracture who has been non-compliant with a hard collar and shows displacement and nonunion at 12 weeks requires surgical stabilisation — posterior C1-C2 fusion. In children under ~7, odontoid fractures typically occur through the dens synchondrosis and heal readily with closed reduction (usually in extension) and halo/Minerva immobilisation.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spine Trauma.
  • Anderson LD, D'Alonzo RT. Fractures of the odontoid process of the axis. JBJS Am 1974.
  • Vaccaro AR et al. / Chapman J et al. The AOSpine upper cervical injury classification system. Global Spine J 2020.
  • Harrop JS et al. / Smith HE et al. Complications of anterior odontoid screw fixation. Spine J.
  • Fehlings MG (Canadian, Toronto) et al. Geriatric odontoid fracture management: a systematic review. Spine 2013.
  • Harms J, Melcher RP. Posterior C1-C2 fusion with polyaxial screw and rod fixation. Spine 2001.
13questions

Spinal cord injury: Classification (ASIA) & incomplete syndromes

The ASIA examination, incomplete cord syndromes and their prognosis, plus steroids and shock.

7 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 (x3), 2024S (x2), 2024F (x3), 2025 (x2)

  • ASIA Impairment Scale: A — complete, no motor or sensory function preserved in the sacral segments S4-S5; B — sensory incomplete (sensory but not motor function below the level, including S4-S5); C — motor incomplete, with more than half of the key muscles below the neurologic level having a grade LESS than 3; D — motor incomplete, with at least half of the key muscles below the level graded 3 or MORE; E — normal.
  • Sacral sparing is the defining feature of an incomplete injury — voluntary anal contraction, perianal sensation (S4-S5 light touch or pinprick), or deep anal pressure. The rectal examination is mandatory and is what separates ASIA A from B.
  • Motor scoring: 10 key muscles on each side (5 upper limb, 5 lower limb), each graded 0–5, giving a maximum total motor score of 100 (50 upper limb + 50 lower limb). So a motor score of exactly 50 is achieved by a patient with full (grade 5) power in all upper limb myotomes and no power in the lower limbs — the classic complete cervical (C8/T1-level) tetraplegic. To score greater than 50, the patient must have some preserved lower limb motor function in addition to full upper limb power.
  • Zone of partial preservation (ZPP) applies only to ASIA A (complete) injuries and describes the dermatomes and myotomes caudal to the neurologic level that retain some innervation.
  • Spinal shock must resolve before the injury can be accurately classified. Return of the bulbocavernosus reflex (typically at 24–48 hours) marks the end of spinal shock. Distinguish this from neurogenic shock — hypotension WITH BRADYCARDIA from loss of sympathetic outflow (T6 and above), warm and well-perfused peripheries. A young patient with a complete cervical cord injury and a closed femur fracture who is hypotensive (BP 87/50) with a HEART RATE OF 110 after 2 L of crystalloid has HAEMORRHAGIC shock, not neurogenic shock — the tachycardia is the discriminator. Neurogenic shock is a diagnosis of exclusion after haemorrhage is ruled out.
  • Incomplete syndromes and their prognosis (best to worst): Brown-Séquard > Central cord > Posterior cord > Anterior cord > Conus/Cauda — the classic ordering. Brown-Séquard has the best prognosis (~75–90% ambulate); anterior cord syndrome has the worst (~10–20% recovery).
  • Central cord syndrome is the most common incomplete spinal cord syndrome. Classic scenario: an elderly patient with cervical spondylosis who falls and sustains a HYPEREXTENSION injury without fracture. Findings: upper extremity weakness GREATER than lower extremity weakness (especially the hands), with variable sensory loss and sacral sparing, and bladder dysfunction. The anatomic basis is the somatotopic arrangement of the lateral corticospinal tract, with cervical/upper limb fibres most MEDIAL. Most recover to ambulate, but hand function often remains impaired. Recovery order is typically: lower extremities → bladder → proximal upper extremity → hand intrinsics (last and least).
  • Brown-Séquard (cord hemisection — a stab wound 2 cm from midline): IPSILATERAL motor weakness (corticospinal), ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration (dorsal columns), and CONTRALATERAL loss of pain and temperature beginning 1–2 levels below the lesion (spinothalamic, which decussates near its entry).
  • Anterior cord syndrome: loss of motor function and pain/temperature with preserved proprioception, vibration and deep touch (dorsal columns spared) — from anterior spinal artery injury or a retropulsed fragment. Worst prognosis.
  • Methylprednisolone in acute SCI: high-dose steroid (the NASCIS II/III protocols) is NO LONGER RECOMMENDED as standard of care. The evidence of benefit rests on post-hoc subgroup analysis, and the trials demonstrated increased rates of pneumonia, sepsis, GI bleeding and wound complications. Current AANS/CNS guidelines state that steroids are not recommended; some guidelines describe a 24-hour infusion within 8 hours as a option with the harms explicitly discussed. Steroids are contraindicated in penetrating SCI.
  • A patient with a thoracic fracture, altered sensation from the groin to the sacrum, no voluntary rectal contraction, and motor grades of 2–3/5 in multiple lower limb myotomes is ASIA C (motor incomplete but with more than half the key muscles below the level graded <3) — but note that absent voluntary anal contraction with preserved perianal sensation makes this sensory-incomplete/ASIA B unless motor function is voluntary and below the level; read the stem carefully for whether the sacral motor function is present.
  • MAP support: maintaining a mean arterial pressure of 85–90 mmHg for the first 7 days after acute SCI is recommended to optimise cord perfusion, and early (<24 hour) surgical decompression improves neurologic recovery (STASCIS).
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spine Trauma.
  • ASIA/ISCoS International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI), 2019 revision.
  • Fehlings MG (Canadian, Toronto) et al. (STASCIS) Early versus delayed decompression for traumatic cervical spinal cord injury. PLoS One 2012.
  • Hurlbert RJ (Canadian, Calgary) et al. Pharmacological therapy for acute spinal cord injury (AANS/CNS guidelines). Neurosurgery 2013.
  • Bracken MB et al. NASCIS II and III. NEJM 1990 / JAMA 1997.
  • Schneider RC et al. The syndrome of acute central cervical spinal cord injury. J Neurosurg 1954.
10questions

Lumbar disc herniation & sciatica

Nomenclature, the nerve root affected, natural history, and the evidence for surgery.

6 of 7 sittings2020, 2021 (x3), 2022 (x2), 2023, 2024F (x2), 2025

  • Nomenclature (essential and frequently tested): BULGE — a generalised, circumferential extension of the disc margin beyond the endplate involving >25% (90–360°) of the circumference, without focal displacement of nucleus pulposus — 'a generalised prominence/outpouching of the annulus without focal nucleus displacement' is the definition of a disc bulge. PROTRUSION — a focal herniation where the base is wider than the dome. EXTRUSION — the dome is wider than the base (it has herniated through the annulus). SEQUESTRATION — a free fragment with no continuity with the parent disc.
  • Which nerve root is affected — the single most tested concept: a PARAMEDIAN/POSTEROLATERAL herniation (the commonest) compresses the TRAVERSING (descending, lower-numbered-level) root — so an L4-5 paramedian herniation compresses the L5 root. A FAR LATERAL/FORAMINAL herniation compresses the EXITING root — so an L4-5 far lateral herniation compresses the L4 root (producing quadriceps weakness, a diminished patellar reflex, and anteromedial thigh/leg pain).
  • Root findings: L4 — anteromedial thigh/leg pain, weak quadriceps and tibialis anterior, diminished patellar reflex, positive femoral stretch test; L5 — lateral leg and dorsum of foot, weak EHL and tibialis anterior (foot drop), weak hip abduction, no reliable reflex; S1 — posterior leg and lateral foot, weak plantarflexion, diminished Achilles reflex.
  • A 50-year-old with leg pain and a foot drop has an L5 radiculopathy — most commonly from a paramedian L4-5 disc herniation. A patient with pain radiating from the posterior thigh to the foot with BOTH a positive straight leg raise AND a positive femoral nerve stretch test has involvement of both upper and lower lumbar roots, suggesting an upper lumbar (L3-4 or a large L4-5 far-lateral) lesion.
  • Natural history is favourable: the majority of radicular symptoms from a disc herniation improve substantially within 6–12 weeks with non-operative care, and large extruded/sequestered herniations resorb more readily than small contained protrusions. This is the key counselling point.
  • SPORT (Weinstein, JAMA 2006): comparing discectomy with non-operative care for lumbar disc herniation, as-treated analyses showed surgery produced greater and faster improvement in pain and function, but intention-to-treat analyses showed no statistically significant difference because of substantial crossover. By 2–4 years both groups improved substantially, and the honest summary is that surgery produces faster relief; the long-term difference narrows.
  • Surgical indications: cauda equina syndrome (an emergency), a progressive or severe motor deficit, and persistent, disabling radicular pain that has failed 6–12 weeks of appropriate non-operative treatment with a concordant MRI finding. A patient with 8 months of chronic, debilitating sciatica with poor quality of life who has failed conservative treatment is an appropriate candidate for discectomy — waiting longer does not improve the outcome and prolonged symptom duration (>6–12 months) is associated with a worse surgical result.
  • Cauda equina syndrome — saddle anaesthesia, bowel/bladder dysfunction (urinary retention with overflow incontinence is the most consistent finding), bilateral leg pain and weakness, and decreased anal tone. It requires urgent MRI and decompression — outcomes are better with earlier surgery (traditionally within 48 hours, and sooner is better).
  • Epidural steroid injection provides short-term (weeks to a few months) relief of radicular pain but does not alter the long-term course or the eventual need for surgery.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spinal Conditions.
  • Weinstein JN et al. (SPORT) Surgical vs nonoperative treatment for lumbar disk herniation. JAMA 2006.
  • Fardon DF, Milette PC et al. Lumbar disc nomenclature: version 2.0 — recommendations of the combined task forces of the NASS, ASSR and ASNR. Spine J 2014.
  • Peul WC et al. Surgery versus prolonged conservative treatment for sciatica. NEJM 2007.
  • Ahn UM et al. Cauda equina syndrome secondary to lumbar disc herniation: a meta-analysis of surgical outcomes. Spine 2000.
7questions

Anterior cervical discectomy & fusion / disc arthroplasty

ACDF technique, complications, and the arthroplasty comparison.

6 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024S (x2), 2025

  • Structures at risk in the anterior (Smith-Robinson) approach (see also the Anatomy section): the recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness — the left has a longer, more predictable course, hence a left-sided approach is often preferred at low levels), the superior laryngeal nerve (external branch, at C3-4 — loss of high-pitch phonation, the 'professional singer cannot hit high notes' stem), the hypoglossal nerve (C2-3), the sympathetic chain on the longus colli (Horner syndrome), the oesophagus (perforation — devastating), the vertebral artery (lateral to the uncovertebral joints), and the thoracic duct on the left at the cervicothoracic junction.
  • Dysphagia is the commonest post-operative complaint after ACDF (up to 50% early, most resolving by 6–12 months), and is related to retraction time, the number of levels, plate profile and prevertebral swelling.
  • Multi-level versus single-level ACDF: with each additional level, the pseudarthrosis rate rises substantially (single level ~5–10%; two-level ~15–20%; three-level ~25–30%+), and dysphagia, swallowing complications and airway compromise increase. Fusion rates fall and complication rates rise with each added level — this is the essential comparison. Three-level and above ACDF is where a posterior or combined approach, or a corpectomy, is considered.
  • Relative contraindications to ACDF at C5-6 for a flexion-distraction injury — the key concept is that an ACDF provides anterior column support and tension-band function only if the posterior elements are able to resist, and if the vertebral body itself can hold the graft: the classic answer is a fracture of the vertebral body/endplate (particularly a comminuted or 'teardrop' body fracture) or a laminar/posterior element fracture at the same level, and significant posterior ligamentous complex disruption with facet fractures, which make an isolated anterior construct inadequate. A posterior fracture (lamina or facet) at the level to be fused is the classic relative contraindication — an anterior-only construct will fail, and a posterior or combined approach is needed.
  • Cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA): multiple FDA IDE trials and their long-term follow-ups show CDA is at least equivalent, and in several trials superior, to ACDF for 1- and 2-level degenerative disease at 7–10 years, with lower rates of subsequent surgery at the index and adjacent levels.
  • Contraindications to cervical disc replacement — the high-yield list: facet arthropathy at the index level (the single most cited contraindication — the arthroplasty preserves motion through a degenerate, painful facet), significant segmental kyphosis or instability, osteoporosis, ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament, ankylosing spondylitis or other inflammatory arthropathy, severe spondylosis with loss of disc height/autofusion, active infection, severe axial neck pain as the primary complaint, and known metal allergy.
  • Lumbar total disc arthroplasty follows the same logic — the best predictor of a good outcome is a young patient with single-level discogenic pain, preserved facet joints, no instability or spondylolisthesis, no significant osteoporosis, and a BMI within normal limits. Facet arthropathy is the principal contraindication and the strongest predictor of a poor outcome.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Surgical Techniques.
  • Smith GW, Robinson RA. The treatment of certain cervical spine disorders by anterior removal of the intervertebral disc. JBJS Am 1958.
  • Burkus JK et al. Long-term clinical and radiographic outcomes of cervical disc replacement versus ACDF: 10-year results. J Neurosurg Spine 2018.
  • Fountas KN et al. Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion associated complications. Spine 2007.
  • Bono CM et al. NASS clinical guidelines: cervical degenerative disease.
7questions

Cervical myelopathy: Diagnosis & surgical decision-making

Recognising myelopathy and choosing between anterior and posterior approaches.

5 of 7 sittings2021, 2023, 2024S, 2024F (x3), 2025

  • Degenerative cervical myelopathy is the commonest cause of spinal cord dysfunction in adults over 55. Presentation: gait disturbance and loss of balance (often the earliest symptom), hand clumsiness and loss of fine motor control (difficulty with buttons, handwriting), diffuse numbness, and — late — bowel and bladder dysfunction. Neck pain is variable and often absent.
  • Upper motor neuron signs: hyperreflexia, clonus, a positive Babinski (extensor plantar), a positive Hoffmann sign, the finger escape sign (Wartenberg), the inverted radial reflex, a positive Lhermitte sign, and a broad-based unsteady gait. The Spurling test is a test for RADICULOPATHY, not myelopathy — and a positive Spurling sign is the classic 'which is NOT an upper motor neuron sign of myelopathy' answer. Similarly, atrophy and fasciculation are lower motor neuron findings.
  • Natural history: myelopathy is generally progressive in a stepwise fashion, and neurologic function lost is not reliably regained — the goal of surgery is to halt progression, with variable recovery. This is why surgery is recommended for moderate-to-severe or progressive myelopathy rather than watching. Mild, non-progressive myelopathy may be observed with close follow-up.
  • A 60–72-year-old with neck pain, hand weakness and poor balance has cervical myelopathy until proven otherwise — the next step is MRI of the cervical spine to define the level, degree of compression and cord signal change.
  • Choosing the approach: anterior (ACDF/corpectomy) is favoured for 1–2 level disease, kyphotic or straight alignment (an anterior approach can restore lordosis; a posterior decompression relies on the cord drifting backwards, which cannot occur in kyphosis), and anterior/ventral compression (disc-osteophyte complex, focal OPLL). Posterior (laminoplasty or laminectomy and fusion) is favoured for multilevel (≥3 levels) disease with preserved lordosis, congenital stenosis, and posterior compression.
  • The advantage of the anterior approach that the posterior approach does not have is the ability to DIRECTLY remove ventral compressive pathology and to restore/correct cervical lordosis (sagittal alignment) — this is the answer to 'what does the anterior approach have that the posterior does not'.
  • OPLL (ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament) with myelopathy and preserved lordosis (no kyphosis) is best treated with a POSTERIOR approach — laminoplasty or laminectomy and fusion — because an anterior approach in the setting of extensive OPLL carries a high risk of dural tear and CSF leak (the ossified ligament is frequently adherent to or has replaced the dura) and the cord can drift posteriorly when lordosis is preserved. A multilevel ACDF is the wrong answer for multilevel OPLL with preserved lordosis.
  • Laminoplasty complications: the commonest specific neurologic complication is a C5 nerve root palsy (~5–10%), presenting with deltoid and biceps weakness with lateral shoulder numbness, typically 2–5 days post-operatively. The mechanism is tethering/traction of the C5 root as the cord drifts posteriorly (the C5 root is short, exits most horizontally and is at the apex of the lordosis). Most recover over weeks to months with observation and therapy; this is the answer to 'the most common nerve root injury with laminoplasty' and to the post-operative deltoid weakness scenario after a posterior C2-T1 decompression and fusion.
  • Modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score grades severity: mild ≥15, moderate 12–14, severe <12 — a useful framework for surgical decision-making and for the AO Spine guidelines.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spinal Conditions.
  • Fehlings MG (Canadian, Toronto) et al. A clinical practice guideline for the management of patients with degenerative cervical myelopathy. Global Spine J 2017.
  • Fehlings MG et al. (AOSpine North America) Efficacy and safety of surgical decompression in patients with cervical spondylotic myelopathy. JBJS Am 2013.
  • Sakaura H et al. C5 palsy after decompression surgery for cervical myelopathy: review of the literature. Spine 2003.
  • Matsunaga S, Sakou T. OPLL: disease entity, incidence, literature search, and natural history. Spine 2012.
6questions

Spine infection: Osteomyelitis, discitis & epidural abscess

Vertebral osteomyelitis, tuberculosis, and epidural abscess.

6 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2023, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • Adult vertebral osteomyelitis is typically haematogenous, seeding the anterior vertebral body adjacent to the endplate (via segmental arteries), then spreading across the disc to the adjacent vertebra — hence the classic MRI pattern of two adjacent vertebral bodies with DESTRUCTION OF THE INTERVENING DISC and endplate erosion, with high T2/STIR signal and enhancement. Disc space involvement is the hallmark of PYOGENIC infection.
  • Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism (~50%), followed by streptococci, coagulase-negative staphylococci and gram-negative organisms. In an intravenous drug user, consider S. aureus (still the commonest) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa — the classic pairing. Sickle cell disease → Salmonella; genitourinary source → E. coli and gram-negatives; post-procedural → S. aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci.
  • Distinguishing infection from tumour on imaging is a repeated exam task: infection crosses the disc space and destroys it, and typically involves TWO CONTIGUOUS vertebrae with an adjacent paraspinal/epidural collection. Metastasis SPARES the disc, often involves the PEDICLE (the 'winking owl' sign), and can be multilevel and non-contiguous. A CT showing a lytic L4 body lesion with a follow-up MRI showing disc involvement and endplate destruction in a septic patient with a UTI is INFECTION; the same lesion sparing the disc with pedicle involvement is metastasis.
  • Spinal tuberculosis (Pott disease) is the important exception: TB characteristically SPARES the disc (it lacks proteolytic enzymes), spreads subligamentously to involve MULTIPLE CONTIGUOUS levels, produces large, well-defined paravertebral/psoas abscesses with calcification and thin rim enhancement, causes anterior vertebral body destruction with progressive KYPHOSIS (gibbus), and follows an indolent course. A patient with HIV and a vertebral body lesion with a large prevertebral abscess and preserved disc height is TB.
  • TB treatment is primarily MEDICAL — prolonged multi-drug antitubercular chemotherapy (typically 4 drugs initially, 9–18 months total). Surgery is indicated for neurologic deficit, significant kyphotic deformity/instability, a large abscess requiring drainage, failure of medical therapy, or the need for diagnostic tissue. Chemotherapy is not optional and is the mainstay — 'surgery alone' or 'short-course antibiotics' are the standard wrong answers.
  • Diagnosis: ESR and CRP are elevated in the great majority and are the most useful screening and monitoring tests (CRP falls first and tracks response). Blood cultures are positive in ~50–70%; obtain them before antibiotics. MRI with gadolinium is the imaging study of choice. CT-guided biopsy is indicated when blood cultures are negative — and antibiotics should be held before biopsy unless the patient is septic.
  • Treatment of pyogenic spinal infection: organism-directed IV antibiotics for ~6 weeks (followed by oral therapy) with bracing, in a neurologically intact patient with a stable spine. Surgical indications: neurologic deficit, epidural abscess with compression, instability or progressive deformity, failure of medical management, and the need for tissue diagnosis.
  • Spinal epidural abscess presents with the classic (but frequently incomplete) triad of back pain, fever and neurologic deficit, progressing through radicular pain to weakness, then paralysis. It is a neurosurgical emergency — urgent MRI of the whole spine (skip lesions are common) and decompression with antibiotics. Delay to decompression after the onset of deficit is the strongest predictor of a poor outcome. Non-operative management with antibiotics alone may be considered only in a neurologically intact patient with a small abscess, a known organism and the ability to monitor closely.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spinal Conditions; Spine Oncology.
  • Berbari EF et al. IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Native Vertebral Osteomyelitis in Adults. Clin Infect Dis 2015.
  • Zimmerli W. Vertebral osteomyelitis. NEJM 2010.
  • Reihsaus E, Waldbaur H, Seeling W. Spinal epidural abscess: a meta-analysis of 915 patients. Neurosurg Rev 2000.
  • Moon MS. Tuberculosis of the spine: controversies and a new challenge. Spine 1997.
5questions

Adult spinal deformity & sagittal balance

Spinopelvic parameters, the realignment targets, and choosing an osteotomy.

4 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2023, 2024S, 2024F

  • Key parameters: Pelvic incidence (PI) is a fixed, morphologic parameter (the angle between a line perpendicular to the sacral endplate at its midpoint and a line from that midpoint to the femoral head centre) — it does not change with position. PI = PT + SS (pelvic tilt + sacral slope), and PT and SS are positional — the pelvis compensates for sagittal imbalance by retroverting (increasing PT and decreasing SS).
  • Realignment targets (Schwab/SRS): PI − LL (lumbar lordosis mismatch) within ±10°, pelvic tilt <20°, and sagittal vertical axis (SVA) <5 cm. These correlate strongly with health-related quality of life — PI−LL mismatch and PT are the parameters most associated with disability.
  • A patient with PI 50, LL 25 and SVA 10 cm has a PI−LL mismatch of 25° with severe positive sagittal imbalance — this requires approximately 25–30° of lordosis restoration to reach target.
  • Osteotomy selection — the correction achieved per level is the exam content: Smith-Petersen osteotomy (SPO, posterior column/Ponte) — resection of the posterior elements and facets, hinging on the disc, giving ~10° per level (and requiring a mobile anterior disc); performing SPOs at multiple levels is additive — so 4 levels of SPO (e.g. L2–L5) gives ~40° with less morbidity per level. Pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO) — a three-column wedge resection through the pedicle and vertebral body, giving ~30° at a single level, but with substantially greater blood loss, longer operative time, and higher neurologic and pseudarthrosis risk. Vertebral column resection (VCR) — the most powerful and the most morbid.
  • For a patient with a previous L3-S1 fusion, PI 50, LL 25 and SVA 10 cm, the LEAST INVASIVE option that restores sagittal balance is multi-level Smith-Petersen (Ponte) osteotomies through the mobile segments above the fusion — the answer to 'which is least invasive with the least complications'. A PSO achieves the same correction at one level but with much greater morbidity; a laminectomy achieves no correction; a vertebrectomy is far more invasive.
  • Proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) and failure (PJF) are the commonest complications of long fusions: risk factors include over-correction, a large PI−LL correction, fusion to the sacrum/pelvis, older age, osteoporosis, disruption of the posterior ligamentous complex at the upper instrumented vertebra, and a UIV in the thoracolumbar junction. Mitigation: preserve the supraspinous/interspinous ligaments at the UIV, avoid over-correction in the elderly, use transitional rods/cement augmentation, and consider a UIV above T5 or below the thoracolumbar junction.
  • Fusion to the sacrum requires pelvic fixation to protect the S1 screws and reduce lumbosacral pseudarthrosis. S2-alar-iliac (S2AI) screws versus conventional iliac screws: S2AI screws start more medially and caudally, allowing a lower-profile construct in line with the S1 screws, requiring less soft-tissue dissection, with a lower rate of symptomatic implant prominence and reoperation for hardware removal, and comparable or better biomechanical performance and lower rates of screw loosening.
  • Flatback syndrome after Harrington rod instrumentation (which distracted the lumbar spine and abolished lordosis) is the classic historical cause of iatrogenic sagittal imbalance, presenting decades later with back pain and an inability to stand upright; treatment is a lordosing osteotomy.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spinal Conditions.
  • Schwab F, Lafage V et al. Scoliosis Research Society-Schwab adult spinal deformity classification: a validation study. Spine 2012.
  • Lafage V, Schwab F, Patel A, Hawkinson N, Farcy JP. Pelvic tilt and truncal inclination: two key radiographic parameters in the setting of adults with spinal deformity. Spine 2009.
  • Bridwell KH. Decision making regarding Smith-Petersen vs pedicle subtraction osteotomy vs vertebral column resection for spinal deformity. Spine 2006.
  • Elias E, Bess S et al. Outcomes of operative treatment for adult spinal deformity. J Neurosurg Spine 2022.
4questions

Lumbar spinal stenosis & degenerative spondylolisthesis

Natural history, the evidence for decompression, and when to add a fusion.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2024S (x2)

  • Neurogenic claudication is the hallmark: bilateral buttock and leg pain, heaviness and paraesthesia, worse with standing and walking (extension), relieved by sitting or forward flexion (the 'shopping cart sign'). Distinguish from vascular claudication (relieved by standing still, reproducible walking distance, absent pulses, worse walking uphill) — the flexion relief is the discriminator.
  • Natural history of lumbar stenosis is relatively benign — most patients remain stable or improve, and rapid deterioration is uncommon; there is no urgency to operate in the absence of a progressive deficit or cauda equina. This supports an initial trial of non-operative care.
  • SPORT (Weinstein, NEJM 2008) for spinal stenosis and degenerative spondylolisthesis: surgical decompression produced significantly greater improvement in pain and function than non-operative care, maintained at 2 and 4 years, with the benefit particularly evident in degenerative spondylolisthesis. Symptom duration matters — better results in those operated on before very prolonged symptoms.
  • When to add a fusion to a decompression — the highest-yield question. The classic indication is DEGENERATIVE SPONDYLOLISTHESIS with stenosis — the accepted answer to 'a common reason to perform a fusion when doing a lumbar stenosis decompression'. Other indications: radiographic instability on dynamic films (>4–5 mm translation or >10° angulation), a degenerative scoliosis with coronal/sagittal imbalance, recurrent stenosis at a previously decompressed level, and iatrogenic instability created by the decompression (removal of >50% of the facets bilaterally or complete removal of one facet, or resection of the pars).
  • Central canal stenosis alone, without instability or spondylolisthesis, is NOT an indication for fusion — decompression alone is appropriate, and this is the usual distractor. Similarly, a mild degenerative lumbar curve (~20°) without imbalance does not by itself mandate fusion.
  • The fusion evidence is nuanced: the Swedish Ghogawala trial found fusion added benefit for degenerative spondylolisthesis, while Försth's Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study found no added benefit of fusion over decompression alone (including in the spondylolisthesis subgroup), at greater cost and morbidity. The modern position is that decompression alone is appropriate for many stable, low-grade degenerative spondylolistheses, with fusion reserved for demonstrable instability, deformity or predominant back pain.
  • Non-operative management of a degenerative spondylolisthesis (e.g. a 20% L4-5 slip) with back pain and no leg pain: the natural history is favourable, progression of the slip is uncommon and does not correlate with symptoms, and treatment is physiotherapy, core strengthening, activity modification and analgesia. Bracing is not effective, and prophylactic fusion is not indicated. The slip magnitude does not predict symptoms or outcome.
  • Degenerative spondylolisthesis characteristically occurs at L4-5, in women over 50, is associated with sagittally oriented facets, and — critically — has an intact pars (distinguishing it from isthmic spondylolisthesis), which is why the stenosis is severe (the whole vertebra translates with an intact ring).
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spinal Conditions.
  • Weinstein JN et al. (SPORT) Surgical versus nonsurgical therapy for lumbar spinal stenosis / degenerative spondylolisthesis. NEJM 2007/2008.
  • Ghogawala Z et al. Laminectomy plus fusion versus laminectomy alone for lumbar spondylolisthesis. NEJM 2016.
  • Försth P et al. A randomized, controlled trial of fusion surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis. NEJM 2016.
  • Matsunaga S et al. Natural history of degenerative spondylolisthesis. Spine 2000.
3questions

Occipitocervical dissociation & craniocervical injury

A frequently fatal, frequently missed injury.

3 of 7 sittings2021, 2024F, 2025

  • Atlanto-occipital/occipitocervical dissociation (AOD) is a highly unstable ligamentous injury of the craniocervical junction, resulting from a high-energy hyperextension/distraction mechanism. It is proportionally more common in children (horizontally oriented occipital condyles, ligamentous laxity, a large head), is often immediately fatal, and survivors frequently have cranial nerve (particularly lower cranial nerve) deficits, brainstem injury and vascular injury.
  • It is missed on plain radiographs in a large proportion of cases, so a high index of suspicion is essential in any high-energy injury, particularly with an unexplained neurologic deficit, cranial nerve palsy, or a large prevertebral soft-tissue shadow.
  • Radiographic and CT measurements: Basion-Dens Interval (BDI) >12 mm and Basion-Axial Interval (BAI) >12 mm (Harris' rule of 12s) suggest AOD; the Powers ratio >1.0 indicates ANTERIOR dissociation; the condylar-C1 interval (CCI) >2 mm on CT is the most sensitive measurement. An anterior occipitocervical dissociation is suggested by a Powers ratio >1.0 (the basion translating anteriorly relative to the posterior arch of C1) and an increased BDI — the classic finding to identify. MRI demonstrates the ligamentous injury (tectorial membrane, alar ligaments) and is the confirmatory study.
  • Management principles: AOD is grossly unstable and requires occipitocervical fusion. Crucially, TRACTION IS ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED — it will distract the already-dissociated joint and can cause catastrophic neurologic deterioration or death. Immobilise in a rigid collar/halo with meticulous attention to alignment and avoid any distraction while awaiting definitive fixation.
  • In the polytrauma patient with an OC dissociation requiring surgery who has been resuscitated in the ICU, the next step before surgery is to complete the assessment — specifically MRI of the craniocervical junction and cervical spine (to define the ligamentous injury and cord status) and a CT angiogram to assess the vertebral arteries — and to maintain rigid immobilisation without traction. Early stabilisation improves outcomes and facilitates nursing and mobilisation.
  • Occipital condyle fractures (Anderson & Montesano): type I impaction (stable), type II basilar skull extension (usually stable), type III alar ligament avulsion (potentially unstable — assess for AOD). Most are treated in a collar; type III with craniocervical instability requires fusion.
  • Vertebral artery injury is common with craniocervical and cervical spine fracture patterns — screen with CT angiography for: fractures through the transverse foramen, subluxation/dislocation, fractures of C1-C3, and any unexplained neurologic deficit. Most are asymptomatic (the contralateral vertebral artery compensates); antithrombotic therapy (antiplatelet or anticoagulation) is the mainstay of treatment, balanced against other injuries. Bilateral injury or a dominant vessel occlusion risks posterior circulation stroke.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spine Trauma.
  • Harris JH et al. Radiologic diagnosis of traumatic occipitovertebral dissociation. AJR 1994.
  • Bellabarba C, Mirza SK, Chapman JR et al. Diagnosis and treatment of craniocervical dislocation in a series of 17 consecutive survivors. Spine J 2006.
  • Horn EM et al. Survivors of occipitoatlantal dislocation injuries: imaging and clinical correlates. J Neurosurg Spine 2007.
  • Biffl WL et al. Blunt cerebrovascular injuries: screening and treatment. Ann Surg.
3questions

Rheumatoid & inflammatory cervical spine

Cervical instability in rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2023

  • Three patterns of rheumatoid cervical involvement, in order of frequency: (1) atlantoaxial instability (~65%) — from pannus destroying the transverse ligament; (2) basilar invagination/cranial settling (~20%) — the odontoid migrating superiorly through the foramen magnum, the most dangerous; (3) subaxial subluxation (~15%) — often multilevel, producing a 'staircase' deformity.
  • Radiographic measurements: anterior atlanto-dens interval (AADI) >3 mm is abnormal; >10 mm suggests complete ligamentous disruption. The POSTERIOR atlanto-dens interval (PADI) — the space available for the cord — is the more important prognostic measure: a PADI <14 mm predicts neurologic compromise and is a strong indication for surgery. For basilar invagination, use the Ranawat, Redlund-Johnell and Clark station measurements.
  • Critically, RA patients are frequently ASYMPTOMATIC despite severe instability, because their limited mobility masks myelopathic symptoms and pain is attributed to their joints. Flexion-extension cervical radiographs are mandatory before any general anaesthetic in a patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis — catastrophic cord injury has occurred during intubation and positioning. This is one of the most important practical safety points in the exam.
  • Indications for surgery: neurologic deficit/myelopathy, PADI <14 mm, basilar invagination, subaxial subluxation with canal compromise, and intractable pain. Treatment is C1-C2 fusion for atlantoaxial instability, and occipitocervical fusion for basilar invagination (± transoral or posterior odontoid resection). Pannus regresses after successful fusion — resection of the pannus is usually unnecessary once motion is eliminated.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis transforms the spine into a long, rigid, osteoporotic lever arm, so that even trivial trauma produces a highly unstable, three-column fracture — usually a transverse fracture through the ankylosed disc space, most commonly at the cervicothoracic junction. Neurologic injury and epidural haematoma are common, and delayed diagnosis is frequent because the fracture is difficult to see on plain films of a fused, deformed spine — CT of the whole spine is mandatory in any AS patient with new pain after trauma, and MRI if there is a deficit.
  • Management of the AS spine fracture: immobilise in the patient's PRE-INJURY DEFORMED POSITION — never force the neck into a 'neutral' collar or lay the patient flat, as this will displace the fracture and injure the cord. Fixation requires long, multilevel posterior instrumentation (short constructs fail in the long lever arm), and traction is dangerous.
  • Cervicothoracic osteotomy for AS kyphosis (usually a C7 pedicle subtraction osteotomy performed awake) has a well-described complication of bilateral C8 nerve root palsy — presenting as numbness and pain along the ulnar border of both hands with intrinsic weakness — from foraminal narrowing/root traction during correction. It is the classic post-operative finding after cervicothoracic osteotomy and usually improves with time.
  • DISH (diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis) produces similar fracture behaviour to AS (flowing anterior ossification of ≥4 contiguous vertebrae with preserved disc spaces and no sacroiliac involvement) and requires the same caution.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spinal Conditions; Systemic Disease.
  • Boden SD, Dodge LD, Bohlman HH, Rechtine GR. Rheumatoid arthritis of the cervical spine: a long-term analysis with predictors of paralysis and recovery. JBJS Am 1993.
  • Casey ATH, Crockard HA et al. Surgery on the rheumatoid cervical spine for the non-ambulant myelopathic patient. JBJS Br.
  • Westerveld LA, Verlaan JJ, Oner FC. Spinal fractures in patients with ankylosing spinal disorders: a systematic review. Eur Spine J 2009.
  • Caron T et al. Spine fractures in patients with ankylosing spinal disorders. Spine 2010.
3questions

Subaxial cervical trauma: Facet injuries & flexion-distraction

Unilateral and bilateral facet injuries, reduction and treatment.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2023

  • Unilateral facet dislocation produces approximately 25% anterolisthesis of the vertebral body and typically causes a nerve ROOT deficit at the level of the dislocated facet (the exiting root is compressed in the foramen) — commonly with preserved spinal cord function. Bilateral facet dislocation produces ~50% anterolisthesis and is far more likely to cause a spinal cord injury.
  • A C6-C7 unilateral locked facet dislocation causes a C7 radiculopathy — weak triceps and wrist flexors/finger extensors, diminished triceps reflex, and numbness of the middle finger. The stem asking for 'expected upper extremity findings' in a C6-C7 facet dislocation is asking for the C7 root pattern.
  • In a C6-C7 dislocation, the LOWEST nerve root that may retain function is C6 (the root exiting above the level of injury) — roots at and below the level are at risk.
  • Closed reduction with awake traction is safe and effective in the awake, alert, cooperative, examinable patient — allowing serial neurologic examination during progressive weight application. A pre-reduction MRI is mandatory in the obtunded or non-examinable patient, and in any patient who cannot be examined during reduction, to exclude a disc herniation that could be driven into the canal by reduction. In the awake, examinable patient, prompt reduction should not be delayed for MRI.
  • Definitive treatment for the best long-term functional outcome after a reduced unilateral facet fracture-dislocation is SURGICAL STABILISATION AND FUSION — most commonly a single-level ACDF (which allows discectomy, restores alignment and lordosis, and has a high fusion rate) or posterior fusion. Halo immobilisation alone has an unacceptably high rate of late instability, loss of reduction and recurrent deformity (up to 20–60% failure), and is not the best option for long-term function.
  • When ACDF is inadequate for a subaxial injury: significant posterior element fracture (lamina/facet fractures), severe posterior ligamentous disruption with a need for posterior tension-band reconstruction, an irreducible dislocation, multi-level injury, and poor bone quality — these favour a posterior or combined (360°) approach. A laminar or facet fracture at the intended fusion level is the classic relative contraindication to an isolated ACDF.
  • A 63-year-old with a hyperextension injury, 0/5 hand strength, 2/5 proximal arm and 3/5 leg strength, no fracture on CT, and MRI showing multilevel cord compression with no improvement at 24 hours is a central cord syndrome with underlying spondylotic compression, not improving — the appropriate treatment is surgical decompression, and where the compression is multilevel with a straight/lordotic alignment and too many levels for an ACDF, posterior laminectomy and instrumented fusion within 24 hours is the answer. Early (<24 h) decompression improves outcomes (STASCIS).
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spine Trauma.
  • Vaccaro AR et al. The subaxial cervical spine injury classification system (SLIC). Spine 2007.
  • Grant GA, Mirza SK, Chapman JR et al. Risk of early closed reduction in cervical spine subluxation injuries. J Neurosurg 1999.
  • Dvorak MF, Fisher CG, Fehlings MG et al. (Canadian) The surgical approach to subaxial cervical spine injuries. Spine 2007.
  • Fehlings MG et al. (STASCIS) Early versus delayed decompression for traumatic cervical spinal cord injury. PLoS One 2012.
3questions

Thoracolumbar burst & flexion-distraction (chance) fractures

Classification, the brace-versus-no-brace evidence, and the flexion-distraction injury.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2024F

  • Thoracolumbar burst fractures involve the anterior and middle columns with retropulsion. The single most important determination is the integrity of the POSTERIOR LIGAMENTOUS COMPLEX (PLC) — supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum and facet capsules — best assessed on MRI (STIR), with widening of the interspinous distance, facet diastasis and >50% vertebral body height loss or >30° kyphosis as radiographic surrogates.
  • TLICS (Thoracolumbar Injury Classification and Severity score): morphology (compression 1, burst 2, translation/rotation 3, distraction 4) + PLC integrity (intact 0, suspected 2, disrupted 3) + neurologic status (intact 0, root 2, complete cord 2, incomplete cord or cauda equina 3). Score ≤3 → non-operative; 4 → surgeon's discretion; ≥5 → operative. Note that an incomplete neurologic injury scores higher than a complete injury, because it has more to gain from decompression.
  • Brace versus no brace for a thoracolumbar burst fracture WITHOUT neurologic deficit: high-quality Canadian evidence (Bailey, Dvorak et al., Spine J 2014) showed that treatment WITHOUT a brace (early mobilisation with a 'no-brace' protocol) is EQUIVALENT to TLSO bracing in stable burst fractures without neurologic deficit, with equivalent pain, function and radiographic outcomes at 3 months and 1–2 years, and with lower cost, greater comfort and earlier mobilisation. This is a repeated and important Canadian trial.
  • The eligibility criteria matter: the trial included stable burst fractures with kyphosis <35°, no neurologic deficit and an intact PLC. Bracing remains reasonable for comfort but is not required for healing or alignment maintenance.
  • Lumbar burst fracture epidemiology: most occur at the thoracolumbar junction (T11–L2) because of the transition from the rigid, rib-stabilised thoracic spine to the mobile lumbar spine and the change in facet orientation. They result from axial compression, are more common in young men from high-energy mechanisms (falls from height, motor vehicle collisions), and the degree of canal compromise correlates POORLY with neurologic deficit — canal remodelling occurs over time and canal compromise alone is not an indication for surgery.
  • Flexion-distraction (Chance) fracture is a tension failure of the posterior and middle columns, classically from a lap-belt (seat-belt) mechanism in a motor vehicle collision — with the hallmark association of INTRA-ABDOMINAL INJURY (bowel, mesenteric, pancreatic) in up to 50% and a transverse abdominal wall ecchymosis (the 'seat-belt sign'). Always image the abdomen.
  • Bony Chance fractures (entirely through bone, with an intact disc and ligaments) can heal in hyperextension casting/bracing; ligamentous or bony-ligamentous flexion-distraction injuries (with PLC disruption on MRI, as in an L1 chance with T2 signal change in the interspinous ligaments) will NOT heal with bracing and require POSTERIOR instrumented fusion — short-segment posterior compression instrumentation is highly effective because the injury is a tension failure. This is the answer for the MRI showing PLC disruption.
  • Paediatric Chance fractures are typically lap-belt injuries in children too large for a car seat but too small for the shoulder belt to fit correctly; the same abdominal injury association applies, and remodelling potential is greater.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spine Trauma.
  • Bailey CS, Dvorak MF, Fisher CG et al. (Canadian) Orthosis versus no orthosis for the treatment of thoracolumbar burst fractures without neurologic injury: a multicenter prospective randomized equivalence trial. Spine J 2014.
  • Vaccaro AR et al. A new classification of thoracolumbar injuries: the importance of injury morphology, the integrity of the posterior ligamentous complex, and neurologic status (TLICS). Spine 2005.
  • Wood KB et al. Operative compared with nonoperative treatment of a thoracolumbar burst fracture without neurological deficit. JBJS Am 2003.
  • Bernstein MP, Mirvis SE, Shanmuganathan K. Chance-type fractures of the thoracolumbar spine. AJR 2006.
2questions

Cervical radiculopathy & degenerative spondylosis

What actually compresses the nerve root in the degenerative cervical spine.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2022

  • In degenerative cervical spondylosis, the structure most commonly responsible for nerve ROOT compression is the UNCOVERTEBRAL JOINT (joint of Luschka) osteophyte, which projects into the anterior aspect of the neuroforamen. Facet (zygapophyseal) joint hypertrophy compresses the root posteriorly, and a soft disc herniation is more common in younger patients. The uncovertebral osteophyte is the classic answer for the older patient with degenerative spondylosis.
  • Anatomy of the cervical root exit: the roots exit ABOVE the correspondingly numbered pedicle in the cervical spine (down to C7, which exits above the T1 pedicle; C8 exits below the C7 pedicle) — so a C5-6 disc/foraminal lesion compresses the C6 root, and a C6-7 lesion compresses the C7 root. This differs from the lumbar spine and is a common trap.
  • Root patterns: C5 — deltoid/shoulder abduction, lateral shoulder sensation, biceps reflex; C6 — biceps and wrist extension, thumb/index sensation, brachioradialis reflex; C7 — triceps and wrist flexion/finger extension, middle finger sensation, triceps reflex; C8 — finger flexion, ring/small finger sensation; T1 — intrinsics, medial forearm.
  • Spurling's test (extension, ipsilateral lateral bending and axial compression, reproducing radicular arm pain) has high specificity but low sensitivity — a positive test is meaningful; a negative test does not exclude radiculopathy. The shoulder abduction relief sign (placing the hand on the head relieves the pain) is also specific for cervical radiculopathy.
  • Natural history is favourable — the majority of cervical radiculopathy resolves or substantially improves within weeks to a few months with non-operative management (physiotherapy, NSAIDs, activity modification, traction, and selective nerve root/epidural steroid injection). This is the essential counselling point.
  • Surgical indications: persistent, disabling radicular pain failing 6–12 weeks of appropriate non-operative treatment with a concordant imaging finding, a progressive motor deficit, and any evidence of myelopathy. Options: ACDF (also corrects alignment and treats central pathology), cervical disc arthroplasty (for a young patient with a soft disc and preserved facets), or posterior foraminotomy (motion-preserving, ideal for a lateral soft disc or foraminal osteophyte without kyphosis or central pathology).
  • Always distinguish from shoulder pathology and from a peripheral nerve entrapment — see the 'Cervical vs shoulder pain differentiation' topic. Brachial neuritis (Parsonage-Turner) — severe pain preceding profound patchy weakness — is the classic mimic.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spinal Conditions.
  • Radhakrishnan K et al. Epidemiology of cervical radiculopathy: a population-based study from Rochester, Minnesota. Brain 1994.
  • Tong HC, Haig AJ, Yamakawa K. The Spurling test and cervical radiculopathy. Spine 2002.
  • Caridi JM, Pumberger M, Hughes AP. Cervical radiculopathy: a review. HSS J 2011.
2questions

Isthmic spondylolisthesis & pars defects

The lytic pars defect in adults.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2022

  • Isthmic spondylolisthesis results from a defect (lysis) in the pars interarticularis, almost always at L5-S1, allowing the vertebral body, pedicles and transverse processes to translate forward while the posterior arch (lamina and spinous process) remains behind. This is the key anatomic difference from degenerative spondylolisthesis: because the posterior arch is left behind, the canal is effectively decompressed and central stenosis is uncommon.
  • The consequence is FORAMINAL, not central, stenosis — the exiting root is compressed between the downward-migrating pedicle, the fibrocartilaginous pars mass and the disc. A lytic L5-S1 spondylolisthesis therefore produces an L5 radiculopathy (dorsum of the foot, great toe, weak EHL and dorsiflexion). The typical patient has back pain with bilateral posterior thigh pain, worse with extension, plus an L5 radicular pattern below the knee.
  • Wiltse classification and Meyerding grading are as described in the paediatric section. The slip angle (lumbosacral kyphosis) is a better predictor of progression and clinical outcome than the percentage slip.
  • Adult isthmic spondylolisthesis is usually a long-standing childhood defect that becomes symptomatic in adulthood as the disc degenerates. Progression of the slip in adulthood is uncommon; disc degeneration at the slip level is the usual source of new symptoms.
  • Management: non-operative first — physiotherapy, core and hamstring stretching, activity modification, and analgesia — with good results in most. Surgery for persistent, disabling symptoms: decompression (with foraminal decompression, since the pathology is foraminal) combined with fusion (posterolateral or interbody). Decompression alone in isthmic spondylolisthesis risks destabilising the segment and increasing the slip, so fusion is generally added in the adult.
  • Reduction versus in-situ fusion in high-grade slips is a genuine controversy: reduction improves sagittal alignment and lumbosacral kyphosis but carries a significant risk of L5 nerve root injury (up to 20–30%); in-situ fusion has lower neurologic risk but a higher pseudarthrosis rate and no deformity correction. Partial reduction of the slip angle with interbody support is a common compromise.
  • Direct pars repair (screw, wiring or hook-screw techniques) is reserved for the young patient with a symptomatic pars defect, minimal or no slip, a healthy disc, and a defect above L5 — it preserves the motion segment. Adding posterior instrumentation to a pars repair improves fusion rates and provides immediate stability but sacrifices motion at the segment.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spinal Conditions.
  • Wiltse LL, Newman PH, Macnab I (Canadian). Classification of spondylolisis and spondylolisthesis. CORR 1976.
  • Möller H, Hedlund R. Surgery versus conservative management in adult isthmic spondylolisthesis: a prospective randomized study. Spine 2000.
  • Kalichman L, Hunter DJ. Diagnosis and conservative management of degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis. Eur Spine J 2008.
  • Lonstein JE. Spondylolisthesis in children: cause, natural history, and management. Spine 1999.
