Marfan syndrome: Spinal manifestations

The connective tissue disorder and its spinal features.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2025

  • Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder from a fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutation on chromosome 15, with increased TGF-β signalling. Features: tall stature with arachnodactyly, arm span exceeding height, joint hypermobility, pectus excavatum/carinatum, pes planus, ectopia lentis (superior lens dislocation), and — the life-threatening feature — AORTIC ROOT DILATATION AND DISSECTION (plus mitral valve prolapse and spontaneous pneumothorax).
  • The most common spinal manifestation of Marfan syndrome is SCOLIOSIS, occurring in roughly 60%. Marfan scoliosis differs from adolescent idiopathic scoliosis: it presents earlier, progresses more rapidly and more relentlessly, is more likely to be a double or triple curve, is more rigid, is associated with thoracic LORDOSIS, and responds POORLY to bracing.
  • Other spinal manifestations: DURAL ECTASIA (present in ~60–90% and part of the Ghent diagnostic criteria — widening of the dural sac, usually lumbosacral, with vertebral scalloping and meningoceles; it causes low back pain and postural headaches and creates significant technical hazards during instrumentation and with dural tears), spondylolisthesis, atlantoaxial instability, thoracolumbar kyphosis, and basilar impression.
  • Surgical considerations in Marfan scoliosis: higher rates of blood loss, dural tear and CSF leak (dural ectasia), pseudarthrosis, infection, fixation failure/pull-out (poor bone quality and thin pedicles), and curve progression above and below the fusion — so fusion levels are usually extended. A cardiac assessment (echocardiogram) is mandatory before surgery, and perioperative beta-blockade/careful blood pressure control is important given the aortic risk.
  • Ectopia lentis in Marfan is SUPERIOR (versus inferior/nasal in homocystinuria, the key differential, which is autosomal recessive with a marfanoid habitus, developmental delay and a thrombotic risk — obtain a urine sodium nitroprusside test). Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1/2) has a similar habitus with arterial tortuosity and aneurysms and a much higher rate of cervical spine instability.
  • A patient with a marfanoid habitus, ligamentous laxity, arachnodactyly and a spinal deformity requires cardiac and ophthalmologic evaluation and genetic testing, not just orthopaedic management. Protrusio acetabuli is the classic hip manifestation, and recurrent joint dislocation and pes planus are common.
  • Least associated with Marfan: features that belong to other conditions — café-au-lait spots (NF1), blue sclerae (OI), and short stature — are the standard distractors.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine; Systemic Disease.
  • Sponseller PD et al. The thoracolumbar spine in Marfan syndrome. JBJS Am 1995.
  • Loeys BL et al. The revised Ghent nosology for the Marfan syndrome. J Med Genet 2010.
  • Jones KB, Sponseller PD et al. Symposium on the musculoskeletal aspects of Marfan syndrome. J Pediatr Orthop 2007.
2questions

Vertebral artery injury

Screening, natural history and management of blunt vertebral artery injury.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2023

  • Blunt vertebral artery injury (VAI) occurs in up to 20–30% of cervical spine fractures with specific patterns, and is far more common than historically appreciated. The majority are ASYMPTOMATIC because the contralateral vertebral artery and the circle of Willis provide collateral flow — this is the single most important fact.
  • Screening criteria (Denver/modified Denver) — the fracture patterns that mandate CT angiography: any fracture extending into the TRANSVERSE FORAMEN (the classic and strongest indication), subluxation or dislocation of the cervical spine, fractures of C1–C3, any cervical spine fracture in the presence of a neurologic deficit unexplained by the imaging, Le Fort II/III facial fractures, basilar skull fracture involving the carotid canal, severe TBI with a GCS <6, and a cervical seat-belt sign or hanging mechanism.
  • CT angiography is the screening study of choice (sensitivity and specificity now approaching conventional angiography with modern multidetector scanners); catheter angiography remains the gold standard and is used for intervention.
  • Biffl grading: I — luminal irregularity/dissection with <25% narrowing; II — dissection with an intimal flap or >25% narrowing; III — pseudoaneurysm; IV — occlusion; V — transection with extravasation.
  • Treatment of most VAI is MEDICAL — antithrombotic therapy (antiplatelet agents such as aspirin, or systemic anticoagulation) to prevent thromboembolic stroke, balanced against the bleeding risk from other injuries. Aspirin is generally as effective as heparin with a lower bleeding risk, and is the practical choice in the polytrauma patient. Endovascular intervention (stenting, coiling) is reserved for pseudoaneurysm, active extravasation or symptomatic lesions.
  • Vertebral artery injury is a recognised complication of cervical spine surgery, particularly with C1-C2 transarticular screws (where an aberrant/high-riding vertebral artery in the C2 isthmus, present in ~20%, is the key pre-operative consideration — obtain a CT/CTA), C2 pedicle screws, lateral mass screws placed too medially/anteriorly, and anterior cervical decompression extending laterally beyond the uncovertebral joints.
  • Intra-operative management of a vertebral artery injury: tamponade with haemostatic agent and direct pressure, complete the procedure without placing a screw on the contralateral side (a bilateral injury is catastrophic), and obtain a post-operative angiogram with endovascular management as required. Do not blindly attempt to ligate or explore the vessel.
  • A unilateral vertebral artery occlusion is usually well tolerated; bilateral injury or occlusion of a dominant vessel risks brainstem/posterior circulation infarction and is the feared outcome.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spine Trauma.
  • Biffl WL, Moore EE, Offner PJ, Burch JM. Blunt carotid and vertebral arterial injuries. World J Surg 2001.
  • Cothren CC, Moore EE et al. Screening for blunt cerebrovascular injuries is cost-effective. Am J Surg 2005.
  • Neo M et al. Vertebral artery injury during cervical spine surgery: a survey of more than 5600 operations. Spine 2008.
  • Bromberg WJ et al. EAST practice management guidelines: blunt cerebrovascular injury. J Trauma 2010.
1question

Complications of spine surgery: Dural tear, CSF leak & wound

Recognising and managing an incidental durotomy and its sequelae.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • Incidental durotomy occurs in ~1–5% of primary lumbar decompressions and up to 10–17% of revision procedures. It is more common with revision surgery, ossified ligamentum flavum/OPLL, ankylosing spondylitis, dural ectasia (Marfan) and in the elderly.
  • Primary repair whenever possible: a running or interrupted 6-0 non-absorbable suture (Prolene) with a taper-point needle, augmented with a dural sealant/fibrin glue and a patch (fascia, muscle, collagen matrix) where the defect cannot be closed directly. Meticulous multilayer fascial closure is the single most important step in preventing a persistent leak.
  • Testing the repair: the standard intra-operative test is a VALSALVA MANOEUVRE (or reverse Trendelenburg with sustained inspiratory pressure) by the anaesthetist while the surgeon observes the repair for leakage — this raises the CSF pressure and demonstrates any residual defect. This is the answer to 'the best way to test for a leak after dural repair'.
  • Post-operative management after a repaired durotomy: flat bed rest for 24–48 hours (though the evidence is weak and early mobilisation is increasingly favoured for a well-repaired dura), adequate hydration, and avoidance of straining. A subfascial drain should generally be AVOIDED or kept on gravity (not suction) after a durotomy, as suction can propagate the leak.
  • Recognising a post-operative CSF leak — the classic exam scenario: a patient 3 days after a lumbar decompression with severe POSITIONAL headache (worse upright, relieved lying flat), nausea, and a subfascial drain that was not draining on day 2 but is suddenly draining 150 mL every 8 hours of clear fluid. This is a CSF leak — the drain is now draining CSF. The correct management is to STOP the suction and REMOVE the drain (a drain maintains a low-pressure fistula), place the patient flat with bed rest and hydration, and monitor. If the leak persists, options are a lumbar subarachnoid drain or return to theatre for exploration and repair.
  • The critical error is to leave a suction drain in place — it perpetuates the fistula, risks a pseudomeningocele and increases the risk of meningitis. Beta-2 transferrin testing confirms the fluid is CSF if there is doubt.
  • Consequences of an unrecognised or persistent leak: pseudomeningocele, positional headache, wound dehiscence and CSF fistula, meningitis, arachnoiditis, and (rarely) intracranial hypotension with subdural haematoma.
  • Wound complications: risk factors are diabetes, obesity, smoking, malnutrition, prolonged operative time, instrumentation and revision surgery. Intrawound vancomycin powder reduces gram-positive surgical site infection in spine surgery (with a shift toward gram-negative organisms). Deep infection with retained instrumentation is generally treated with débridement, irrigation and antibiotic suppression with implant retention until fusion, rather than immediate hardware removal.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Surgical Techniques.
  • Bosacco SJ, Gardner MJ, Guille JT. Evaluation and treatment of dural tears in lumbar spine surgery. CORR 2001.
  • Guerin P et al. Incidental durotomy during spine surgery: incidence, management and complications. Injury 2012.
  • Cammisa FP, Girardi FP, Sangani PK, Parvataneni HK, Cadag S, Sandhu HS. Incidental durotomy in spine surgery. Spine 2000.
1question

Complications of spine surgery: Positioning & nerve palsy

Positioning-related nerve injuries in spine surgery.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN) palsy — meralgia paraesthetica — is a common and under-recognised complication of PRONE positioning for posterior spinal surgery. It presents with numbness, burning and dysaesthesia over the anterolateral thigh with no motor deficit (the nerve is purely sensory).
  • The mechanism is DIRECT COMPRESSION of the nerve against the anterior superior iliac spine by the pads/bolsters of the prone frame (Wilson frame, Jackson table, or chest/hip rolls) — the nerve passes just medial to the ASIS under the inguinal ligament and is very superficial there. Contributing factors: prolonged operative time, obesity, hip flexion, and excessive pressure or malpositioned hip bolsters. This is the answer to 'why is LFCN injury common after posterior spinal instrumented fusion'.
  • Prevention: position the hip pads lateral to the ASIS on the iliac crest, not over it, use adequate padding, avoid excessive hip flexion, and minimise operative time. The prognosis is good — most resolve over weeks to months with reassurance and, if needed, neuropathic agents.
  • Other positioning complications of prone spine surgery — the full list is worth knowing: post-operative visual loss (POVL) from ischaemic optic neuropathy (the most feared — associated with prolonged prone positioning, large blood loss, hypotension, anaemia and a head-down position; prevention is head-neutral or slightly elevated positioning, avoidance of direct globe pressure, and maintenance of perfusion and haemoglobin); brachial plexus and ulnar neuropathy (from arm abduction >90°, external rotation, or elbow pressure); abdominal compression raising epidural venous pressure and increasing bleeding (ensure the abdomen hangs free); pressure sores (chin, chest, iliac crest, knees); and compartment syndrome of the lower limbs in prolonged cases.
  • Lateral (transpsoas) lumbar interbody approaches carry a distinct set of neurologic risks — lumbar plexus and genitofemoral nerve injury with thigh numbness, and hip flexor (psoas) weakness — highest at L4-5, where the plexus is most anterior. Directional EMG neuromonitoring is mandatory for the transpsoas approach.
  • Anterior lumbar approaches risk retrograde ejaculation (superior hypogastric plexus, hence blunt dissection and no monopolar cautery at L5-S1 in men), vascular injury, and ureteric injury.
  • Always document a careful pre-operative neurologic examination — attributing a pre-existing deficit to positioning after the fact is a common medicolegal problem.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Surgical Techniques.
  • Mirovsky Y, Neuwirth M. Injuries to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve during spine surgery. Spine 2000.
  • Practice Advisory for the Prevention of Perioperative Peripheral Neuropathies (ASA Task Force). Anesthesiology 2018.
  • Postoperative Visual Loss Study Group. Risk factors associated with ischemic optic neuropathy after spinal fusion surgery. Anesthesiology 2012.
1question

Intraoperative neuromonitoring & spinal cord monitoring

Modalities, alert criteria and the response protocol.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • Multimodal monitoring is the standard: somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) monitor the dorsal columns (posterior cord, posterior spinal artery territory) and are more resistant to anaesthesia; transcranial motor evoked potentials (tcMEPs) monitor the corticospinal tracts (anterior cord, anterior spinal artery territory) and are the most sensitive for impending motor injury; free-running and triggered EMG monitors nerve roots and pedicle screw placement (a triggered threshold below ~6–8 mA suggests a medial breach).
  • Alert criteria: SSEPs — a >50% reduction in amplitude or a >10% increase in latency; tcMEPs — a >50–75% reduction in amplitude (many centres use an all-or-none/>75% criterion). A 70% drop in MEPs after instrumentation is a major alert requiring immediate action.
  • Response protocol (the checklist to recite): (1) Confirm the signal is real — check leads, connections, and that no anaesthetic change has occurred (halogenated agents and neuromuscular blockade abolish MEPs; a bolus of propofol or a change to inhaled agent is a common cause of a false alert). (2) Optimise physiology — RAISE THE MEAN ARTERIAL PRESSURE (to >85–90 mmHg), correct anaemia (transfuse), correct hypothermia, hypocapnia and hypovolaemia. (3) Remove the mechanical insult — release the correction/distraction, remove the rods, and check implant position (remove any suspect screws). (4) If signals do not return, perform a Stagnara wake-up test. (5) Consider steroids and imaging.
  • The commonest cause of a significant MEP drop during deformity correction is a combination of the CORRECTION MANOEUVRE (distraction/derotation causing cord stretch and vascular compromise) and RELATIVE HYPOTENSION/cord ischaemia — not usually direct screw impingement. This is why the first therapeutic action is to raise the blood pressure and release the correction.
  • Anaesthetic requirements: total intravenous anaesthesia (propofol and an opioid) with NO neuromuscular blockade and minimal or no halogenated agent is required for reliable MEPs. Failure to communicate this to anaesthesia is a common cause of unusable signals.
  • Monitoring reduces but does not eliminate neurologic injury, and it is now standard of care for deformity correction, intramedullary tumour surgery, and any procedure where the cord or roots are at risk. A loss of signals that does not recover after the full protocol should prompt abandonment of the correction and a wake-up test, and — if a deficit is confirmed — return to theatre for implant removal/decompression.
  • For peripheral nerve monitoring in a deformity case, positioning-related brachial plexus and ulnar nerve injury is a recognised cause of upper limb SSEP change; check arm position before assuming a spinal cause.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Surgical Techniques.
  • Vitale MG et al. Best practices in intraoperative neuromonitoring in spine deformity surgery: development of an intraoperative checklist to optimize response. Spine Deform 2014.
  • Nuwer MR et al. Somatosensory evoked potential spinal cord monitoring reduces neurologic deficits after scoliosis surgery. Electroencephalogr Clin Neurophysiol 1995.
  • Schwartz DM et al. Neurophysiological detection of impending spinal cord injury during scoliosis surgery. JBJS Am 2007.
1question

Lumbar total disc arthroplasty

Indications, contraindications and outcomes.

1 of 7 sittings2024F

  • Lumbar total disc replacement (TDR) is intended to treat discogenic low back pain while preserving segmental motion and, theoretically, reducing adjacent segment degeneration compared with fusion.
  • The single best predictor of a good outcome is careful patient selection: a YOUNG patient with SINGLE-LEVEL, purely DISCOGENIC pain, with PRESERVED FACET JOINTS, no instability or spondylolisthesis, no significant osteoporosis, normal alignment, minimal or no radicular symptoms, and a normal BMI, who has failed at least 6 months of good non-operative treatment.
  • Contraindications — the essential list: FACET ARTHROPATHY at the index level (the most important — motion is preserved through a degenerate, painful joint, guaranteeing persistent pain), spondylolisthesis or any segmental instability, spondylolysis/pars defect, osteoporosis or metabolic bone disease, significant scoliosis or deformity, central or lateral recess stenosis requiring posterior decompression, previous posterior decompression compromising the posterior elements, infection, morbid obesity, and allergy to implant materials.
  • Outcomes: the FDA IDE trials showed TDR to be non-inferior to fusion at 2 and 5 years for single-level degenerative disc disease, with faster early recovery and comparable satisfaction. However, the long-term promise of reduced adjacent segment disease has not been convincingly demonstrated in the lumbar spine (the evidence is stronger in the cervical spine).
  • Complications are the main practical concern: approach-related vascular injury (the anterior retroperitoneal approach places the great vessels at risk, and revision surgery through scarred tissue is extremely hazardous — an access surgeon is standard), retrograde ejaculation (superior hypogastric plexus, especially at L5-S1 in men — use blunt dissection and avoid monopolar cautery), implant subsidence, migration and wear, heterotopic ossification with spontaneous fusion, and persistent pain from an unrecognised facet source.
  • Revision of a failed lumbar TDR is a major undertaking, and the difficulty of anterior revision is a legitimate consideration in the initial decision — the durability of the implant must outlast the patient's remaining life expectancy or the revision problem becomes real.
  • In practice, the narrow indication set means TDR is appropriate for a small minority of patients with back pain, and the commonest error is offering it to a patient with multilevel disease, facet arthropathy or a predominantly psychosocial pain presentation.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spinal Conditions.
  • Blumenthal S et al. A prospective, randomized, multicenter FDA IDE study of lumbar total disc replacement with the CHARITÉ artificial disc versus lumbar fusion. Spine 2005.
  • Zigler J, Delamarter R. Five-year results of the prospective, randomized, multicenter FDA IDE study of ProDisc-L. J Neurosurg Spine 2012.
  • Van den Eerenbeemt KD et al. Total disc replacement surgery for symptomatic degenerative lumbar disc disease: a systematic review. Eur Spine J 2010.
1question

Osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture & augmentation

The commonest osteoporotic fracture and its management.

1 of 7 sittings2022

  • Vertebral compression fractures are the most common osteoporotic fracture, with the majority occurring in postmenopausal women, most commonly at the thoracolumbar junction (T12–L1). Crucially, the majority (roughly two thirds) are ASYMPTOMATIC and are discovered incidentally on imaging obtained for another reason — the classic 'which is true' answer.
  • They are stable injuries (anterior column failure only, with an intact middle and posterior column and posterior ligamentous complex) and rarely cause neurologic deficit. A vertebral compression fracture with a neurologic deficit, retropulsion, or involvement of the posterior elements is not a simple osteoporotic VCF and requires further work-up.
  • A vertebral compression fracture is a sentinel event: it confers a five-fold increased risk of a subsequent vertebral fracture and a two- to three-fold increased risk of hip fracture, and is associated with increased mortality. Every patient requires osteoporosis assessment and treatment (BMD, fracture risk assessment, calcium/vitamin D and pharmacologic therapy) — this is the most important intervention and the one most often omitted.
  • Always exclude a pathologic fracture in a patient with an atypical presentation: age <55, no significant osteoporosis, involvement above T5, a lesion involving the PEDICLE, a paraspinal soft-tissue mass, weight loss, night pain, or a known malignancy — the differential includes metastasis and MULTIPLE MYELOMA (the commonest primary malignancy causing vertebral collapse, though metastasis is more common overall). Obtain an MRI ± biopsy.
  • Initial management is non-operative: analgesia, early mobilisation, physiotherapy, and a brace for comfort if needed. Most improve substantially within 6–12 weeks.
  • Vertebral augmentation (vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty): the evidence is genuinely mixed. Two 2009 NEJM sham-controlled trials found no benefit of vertebroplasty over a sham procedure, while the VAPOUR trial (2016) found benefit in patients with severe pain of recent onset (<6 weeks). The current position is that augmentation may be considered for severe, refractory pain of relatively acute onset that has failed conservative management, and it is not indicated for chronic or asymptomatic fractures.
  • Complications of augmentation: cement extravasation (into the canal, disc or venous system — pulmonary cement embolism), and adjacent-level fracture from the stiffness mismatch. Kyphoplasty has a lower cement leakage rate than vertebroplasty because the balloon creates a cavity allowing lower-pressure injection of more viscous cement.
  • Surgery (instrumented fusion) is reserved for: neurologic deficit, progressive kyphotic deformity with pain and functional loss, instability, or a nonunion/vertebral osteonecrosis (Kümmell disease, with an intravertebral vacuum cleft). Cement augmentation of the pedicle screws is essential when instrumenting osteoporotic bone.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spine Trauma; Systemic Disease.
  • Buchbinder R et al. A randomized trial of vertebroplasty for painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures. NEJM 2009; Kallmes DF et al. A randomized trial of vertebroplasty for osteoporotic spinal fractures. NEJM 2009.
  • Clark W et al. (VAPOUR) Vertebroplasty for acute painful osteoporotic fractures. Lancet 2016.
  • Osteoporosis Canada. 2023 Clinical Practice Guideline for the management of osteoporosis. CMAJ 2023.
  • Lindsay R et al. Risk of new vertebral fracture in the year following a fracture. JAMA 2001.
1question

Scheuermann kyphosis

The rigid adolescent thoracic kyphosis.

1 of 7 sittings2024F

  • Diagnostic criteria (Sorensen): anterior wedging of ≥5° at three or more consecutive vertebrae, with thoracic kyphosis >45–50° that is RIGID (does not correct on hyperextension). Associated features: Schmorl nodes, endplate irregularity, disc space narrowing, and a compensatory hyperlordosis of the lumbar and cervical spine.
  • Two forms: thoracic (classic) Scheuermann — apex T7–T9, presenting with deformity and mid-thoracic pain; and thoracolumbar/lumbar (atypical) Scheuermann — apex T11–L2, more common in athletes and manual labourers, presenting predominantly with PAIN rather than deformity.
  • Lumbar (atypical) Scheuermann differs from the classic thoracic form: it produces less kyphotic deformity, is more strongly associated with axial back pain and with repetitive loading/athletic activity, and characteristically shows Schmorl nodes, endplate irregularity and disc narrowing WITHOUT the marked anterior vertebral wedging seen in the thoracic form. The classic ≥5° wedging of three consecutive vertebrae is a THORACIC criterion and is NOT typically found in lumbar Scheuermann — this is the recurring 'what is not commonly found in lumbar Scheuermann' answer.
  • Distinguish from postural kyphosis, which is flexible (corrects on hyperextension and prone extension) with no vertebral wedging or endplate changes — the key discriminator.
  • Natural history: most patients do well; the deformity progresses during the adolescent growth spurt and then stabilises. Back pain is common in adolescence but the long-term functional prognosis is generally good; curves >75–100° may cause restrictive pulmonary compromise.
  • Treatment: observation for curves <60°; bracing (Milwaukee or a modified TLSO) for curves 60–80° in a skeletally immature patient (Risser ≤2/3) with at least 1 year of growth remaining — the brace works by extension and requires flexibility; it has limited success in rigid curves. Physiotherapy and extension exercises for pain and postural strengthening.
  • Surgical indications: curves >75–80° with skeletal maturity, progressive deformity, intractable pain unresponsive to non-operative care, and neurologic compromise (rare — from associated disc herniation or, exceptionally, cord compression at the apex). Modern treatment is posterior instrumented fusion with multiple Ponte (Smith-Petersen) osteotomies, correcting to approximately 50% (over-correction risks proximal and distal junctional kyphosis). The distal fusion level must include the first lordotic disc and the stable sagittal vertebra to prevent distal junctional kyphosis — the commonest complication.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Spinal Conditions; Pediatrics.
  • Sorensen KH. Scheuermann's Juvenile Kyphosis. Copenhagen, 1964.
  • Lowe TG. Scheuermann's kyphosis. Neurosurg Clin N Am / JBJS Am reviews.
  • Wenger DR, Frick SL. Scheuermann kyphosis. Spine 1999.
  • Lonner BS et al. Operative management of Scheuermann's kyphosis in 78 patients. Spine 2007.
1question

Spine biomechanics & instrumentation

Rod and construct mechanics in spinal instrumentation.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • Rod stiffness is governed by the area moment of inertia, which is proportional to the RADIUS TO THE FOURTH POWER (r⁴) for a solid cylindrical rod — so a small increase in rod diameter produces a large increase in stiffness (a 6.35 mm rod is roughly 1.7× stiffer than a 5.5 mm rod of the same material). Material modulus is the other determinant: cobalt-chrome > stainless steel > titanium > PEEK, so a cobalt-chrome rod of the same diameter is substantially stiffer than titanium.
  • The stiffness–biology trade-off: a stiffer construct provides better deformity correction and resists loss of correction, but increases stress shielding at the fusion mass and increases stress at the ends of the construct (raising the risk of proximal junctional kyphosis and adjacent segment failure). A higher-stiffness construct means LESS motion of the fusion mass, not more — the classic false statement in the stress-strain/spinal construct question.
  • Increasing the stability of a spinal construct in OSTEOPOROTIC bone — the high-yield list: cement (PMMA) augmentation of the pedicle screws (the single most effective measure), increasing the number of fixation points/levels instrumented (spreading the load), using larger-diameter and longer screws to maximise the bone-screw interface, bicortical purchase, using hooks or sublaminar bands in combination with screws (hybrid constructs), undertapping the pedicle, crosslinks, and extending the construct to include the pelvis when fusing to the sacrum. Increasing rod diameter alone does NOT solve the problem — failure in osteoporotic bone occurs at the bone-screw interface, not in the rod.
  • Cement augmentation in a spine fracture (vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty): the principal risk is cement extravasation — into the canal (cord/root compression), into the disc (increasing the risk of adjacent level fracture), and into the venous system (pulmonary cement embolism). Kyphoplasty creates a cavity with a balloon, allowing a more viscous cement to be injected at lower pressure, and has a LOWER rate of cement leakage than vertebroplasty, though the clinical outcomes are broadly similar. Adjacent-level fracture after augmentation is well described and is attributed to the stiffness mismatch created by the cemented level.
  • Screw pull-out strength correlates with bone mineral density (the dominant factor), screw outer diameter, thread depth and pitch, length of purchase, and the technique of insertion (undertapping increases pull-out strength; repeated insertion/removal decreases it).
  • Crosslinks improve torsional (rotational) stability substantially but add little to flexion-extension or lateral bending stiffness.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Spine: Surgical Techniques; Principles of Orthopaedics.
  • Benzel EC. Biomechanics of Spine Stabilization, 3rd ed.
  • Serhan H et al. Biomechanics of the posterior lumbar articulating elements. Neurosurg Focus.
  • Burval DJ et al. Primary pedicle screw augmentation in osteoporotic lumbar vertebrae. Spine 2007.

ACL reconstruction: Graft choice, technique & outcomes

Graft selection, tunnel placement, LET, and the predictors of failure.

7 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022 (x2), 2023, 2024S, 2024F, 2025 (x2)

  • Graft biomechanics (load to failure): quadrupled hamstring (semitendinosus-gracilis) ~4,000 N is the strongest, followed by quadriceps tendon ~2,200 N, bone-patellar tendon-bone (10 mm) ~2,000–2,900 N, and the native ACL ~2,160 N. So the strongest graft is the quadrupled hamstring — a repeated single-best-answer item.
  • Graft trade-offs: BTB — bone-to-bone healing, historically favoured in high-demand pivoting athletes, but more anterior knee pain and kneeling pain and a small risk of patella fracture/patellar tendon rupture. Hamstring — less donor-site pain, but more residual laxity in some studies, hamstring weakness in deep flexion, and a higher failure rate in young patients. Quadriceps tendon — increasingly popular, large cross-sectional area, less donor-site morbidity than BTB. Allograft has a significantly higher failure rate in patients under 25 and in high-demand athletes, and irradiated/chemically processed allograft is worse still.
  • Risk factors for ACL graft failure/re-rupture: young age (the strongest — under 20–25 years), return to high-level pivoting sport, allograft use in the young, non-anatomic (vertical/high) tunnel placement, increased posterior tibial slope (>12°), generalised ligamentous laxity, unaddressed meniscal or extra-articular (ALL/PLC) injury, family history, and failure to complete rehabilitation/early return to sport. Female sex is a risk factor for primary ACL injury but is not consistently a risk factor for graft re-rupture — a common distractor.
  • The single most important technical factor for outcome is anatomic tunnel placement — restoring the native femoral and tibial footprints. A vertical femoral tunnel controls anterior translation but not rotation, leaving a positive pivot shift.
  • Lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET)/anterolateral ligament reconstruction: the Canadian-led STABILITY trial (Getgood et al., AJSM 2020) showed that adding an LET to a hamstring autograft ACL reconstruction in young, high-risk patients (age ≤25, high-grade pivot shift, generalised laxity, returning to pivoting sport) significantly reduced graft failure and persistent rotatory laxity at 2 years. LET is now standard in that high-risk group.
  • Timing: early reconstruction (within a few weeks) is safe provided the knee is 'quiet' with full extension and good quadriceps control; operating on a stiff, swollen knee increases arthrofibrosis. Pre-operative rehabilitation improves outcomes.
  • Tunnel mismatch with a BTB graft that is too long (the bone block protrudes from the tibial tunnel): options include recessing the femoral bone block deeper into the femoral tunnel, rotating/twisting the graft to shorten it, using a free bone block/interference screw distally on the tibia, or converting to a suspensory or two-incision technique. Deepening the femoral socket is the simplest first manoeuvre.
  • Graft contamination (the graft is dropped): it should not be discarded reflexively — the standard is serial decontamination with chlorhexidine and/or antibiotic solution followed by saline lavage (a common protocol is 4% chlorhexidine for 30 seconds followed by triple-antibiotic and saline rinses), which reliably sterilises the graft. Alternatives are to harvest a different autograft or use an allograft. Simply rinsing in saline alone is inadequate.
  • Paediatric/adolescent ACL — see the Paediatrics section; physeal-sparing techniques are chosen by skeletal age.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports.
  • Getgood AMJ, Bryant DM, Litchfield R, Heard M, McCormack RG, Rezansoff A, Peterson D, Bardana D, MacDonald PB, Spalding T (Canadian, STABILITY Study Group). Lateral extra-articular tenodesis reduces failure of hamstring tendon autograft ACL reconstruction. AJSM 2020.
  • Noyes FR, Butler DL, Grood ES et al. Biomechanical analysis of human ligament grafts used in knee-ligament repairs. JBJS Am 1984.
  • MARS Group. Effect of graft choice on the outcome of revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. AJSM 2014.
  • Kaeding CC et al. Risk factors and predictors of subsequent ACL injury (MOON cohort). AJSM 2015.
  • Plante MJ et al. Evaluation of sterilization methods following contamination of hamstring autograft during ACL reconstruction. KSSTA 2013.
8questions

Patellofemoral instability & MPFL reconstruction

MPFL anatomy, risk factors for recurrence, and the surgical algorithm.

7 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024S, 2024F (x2), 2025

  • The MPFL is the primary passive restraint to lateral patellar translation in the first 20–30° of flexion, contributing ~50–60% of the restraining force. Beyond 30° the bony trochlea provides the constraint.
  • Femoral origin of the MPFL (Schöttle's point) — the exam favourite: on a true lateral radiograph, it lies just anterior to the posterior femoral cortex extension line, distal to the posterior origin of the medial femoral condyle, and proximal to the posterior point of Blumensaat's line. Anatomically it is in the saddle between the medial epicondyle and the adductor tubercle (slightly posterior and proximal to the medial epicondyle). Its patellar insertion is on the superomedial third to half of the patella.
  • Non-anatomic femoral tunnel placement — most commonly placing the tunnel too PROXIMAL/ANTERIOR — is the commonest technical error, producing a graft that is tight in flexion, causing pain, loss of flexion, medial patellofemoral overload and eventual failure. The femoral position is far more important than the patellar position.
  • Risk factors for recurrent patellar dislocation — the highest-yield list: trochlear dysplasia (the single strongest anatomic risk factor), patella alta (Caton-Deschamps >1.2, Insall-Salvati >1.2), increased TT-TG distance (>20 mm on CT, >15–17 mm on MRI), young age at first dislocation (<18–20 years, the strongest demographic factor), skeletal immaturity, generalised ligamentous laxity, contralateral instability, and increased femoral anteversion/genu valgum. The lateral retinaculum is not a cause — a tight lateral retinaculum does not cause recurrent dislocation, and isolated lateral release does not treat instability (it may worsen it by causing medial instability).
  • Treatment algorithm: first-time dislocation without a loose body → non-operative (brace, physiotherapy, quadriceps/VMO and hip abductor strengthening). Osteochondral fragment/loose body → surgery. Recurrent instability → MPFL reconstruction as the workhorse, with the addition of a tibial tubercle osteotomy (medialisation for TT-TG >20 mm; distalisation for patella alta) and, in severe dysplasia with a supratrochlear spur, a trochleoplasty.
  • Patellofemoral mechanics: the patella increases the moment arm of the quadriceps (extensor mechanism efficiency), and patellofemoral contact area increases with flexion while contact stress is highest in mid-flexion (~30–60°) where force is high but area is still limited. The patella first engages the trochlea at ~20–30° of flexion. Contact force reaches ~3× body weight with stair climbing and up to 7× with squatting.
  • In a skeletally immature child, do not drill across the distal femoral physis — use a physeal-sparing MPFL reconstruction (soft-tissue anchor distal to the physis or an adductor magnus sling). A tibial tubercle osteotomy is contraindicated with an open tubercle apophysis (recurvatum deformity).
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports.
  • Schöttle PB et al. Radiographic landmarks for femoral tunnel placement in medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction. AJSM 2007.
  • Dejour H, Walch G, Nove-Josserand L, Guier C. Factors of patellar instability: an anatomic radiographic study. KSSTA 1994.
  • Lewallen L, McIntosh A, Dahm D. First-time patellofemoral dislocation: risk factors for recurrent instability. J Knee Surg 2015.
  • Balcarek P et al. Which patellae are likely to redislocate? KSSTA 2014.
4questions

Meniscus tears, root repair & allograft transplantation

Meniscal function, root tears and the indications for transplantation.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2022 (x3)

  • Meniscal function: load transmission (the menisci transmit ~50% of the load in extension and ~85% in flexion), shock absorption, joint congruity/stability, proprioception and lubrication. Total meniscectomy increases peak contact pressure by ~235% and reliably produces arthritis (Fairbank changes).
  • Meniscal root tear: an avulsion or radial tear within 1 cm of the root attachment. It functionally equals a total meniscectomy — the circumferential hoop stress mechanism is destroyed, so tibiofemoral contact pressure and peak contact pressure both INCREASE, and the meniscus extrudes. This is the classic single-best-answer: 'increased tibiofemoral contact area? No — increased contact pressure and peak contact pressure'. Root tears cause rapid chondral loss and are associated with subchondral insufficiency fracture of the knee (SIFK) and rapid progression to arthritis. Repair (transtibial pull-out) is indicated in patients without advanced arthritis or malalignment.
  • Repair vs meniscectomy: repair where the tissue and vascularity permit — the red-red (peripheral third) and red-white zones heal; the white-white (inner third) zone is avascular. Factors favouring healing: peripheral tear, vertical longitudinal pattern, acute injury, young patient, and concurrent ACL reconstruction (the marrow elements/haemarthrosis improve healing).
  • Degenerative meniscal tears in middle-aged patients with osteoarthritis do not benefit from arthroscopic partial meniscectomy over physiotherapy — a consistent finding across multiple high-quality RCTs (FIDELITY, METEOR, and others). This is one of the most important evidence points in modern sports medicine.
  • Meniscal allograft transplantation — the ideal candidate: a young (<50), active patient with a previous total or subtotal meniscectomy, pain localised to that compartment, essentially normal (Outerbridge ≤2) articular cartilage, a stable knee, and neutral alignment. Contraindications: advanced arthritis (the key one), uncorrected malalignment, uncorrected instability, inflammatory arthritis, obesity, and skeletal immaturity is a relative issue. Malalignment and instability must be corrected concurrently or in a staged fashion.
  • Discoid meniscus (see Paediatrics): a congenital variant (usually lateral) prone to tearing; treat symptomatic tears with saucerisation to a stable rim rather than total meniscectomy.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports.
  • Allaire R, Muriuki M, Gilbertson L, Harner CD. Biomechanical consequences of a tear of the posterior root of the medial meniscus. JBJS Am 2008.
  • Sihvonen R et al. (FIDELITY) Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy versus sham surgery for a degenerative meniscal tear. NEJM 2013.
  • Katz JN et al. (METEOR) Surgery versus physical therapy for a meniscal tear and osteoarthritis. NEJM 2013.
  • Verdonk PCM, Verdonk R et al. Meniscal allograft transplantation: indications and outcomes. KSSTA.
4questions

Multiligament knee injury & knee dislocation

Vascular assessment, the obese low-energy dislocation, and staged management.

4 of 7 sittings2023, 2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • A knee dislocation is a vascular emergency until proven otherwise. Popliteal artery injury occurs in up to ~20–30% (higher in posterior dislocations) because the artery is tethered proximally at the adductor hiatus and distally at the soleal arch. Peroneal nerve injury occurs in ~25%, particularly with posterolateral corner injury, and has a poor prognosis for recovery.
  • Vascular protocol: a serial physical examination with ankle-brachial index (ABI) is the standard. ABI ≥0.9 with normal pulses → serial observation (sensitivity for a surgically significant arterial injury approaches 100%); ABI <0.9 → CT angiography or immediate surgical exploration. Palpable pulses do NOT exclude an intimal injury, which can thrombose hours later — this is why serial examination is mandatory even when the foot is warm and pulses are present. Warm ischaemia beyond ~6–8 hours produces very high amputation rates.
  • Low-energy knee dislocations in the morbidly obese (BMI >40) are a distinct and dangerous entity: they occur with trivial trauma (tripping, a fall from standing), and are associated with a higher rate of vascular injury, peroneal nerve palsy, compartment syndrome, wound and thromboembolic complications, and a much higher rate of amputation and poor outcome than high-energy dislocations. They are frequently missed or spontaneously reduced at presentation, so a high index of suspicion with multiligament examination is essential.
  • Schenck classification by ligaments injured: KD-I (one cruciate + collateral), KD-II (both cruciates, collaterals intact), KD-III (both cruciates + one collateral: IIIM medial or IIIL lateral), KD-IV (both cruciates + both collaterals), KD-V (with periarticular fracture). Add 'C' for arterial and 'N' for nerve injury.
  • Management: reduce urgently, assess vascularity, span with an external fixator if the knee is irreducible, unstable after reduction, has a vascular repair, or in an obese patient, then reconstruct. Early (within 2–3 weeks) reconstruction/repair of the ligaments gives better stability and outcome than delayed treatment, although stiffness is more common — a balance is required.
  • The posterolateral corner should be repaired/reconstructed early (within 2–3 weeks); late PLC reconstruction is required if this window is missed. Do not reconstruct a cruciate in a knee with uncorrected varus malalignment — a proximal tibial osteotomy is required first or the graft will fail.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports; Lower Extremity Trauma.
  • Mills WJ, Barei DP, McNair P. The value of the ankle-brachial index for diagnosing arterial injury after knee dislocation. J Trauma 2004.
  • Georgiadis AG, Mohammad FH, Mizerik KT, Nypaver TJ, Shepard AD. Changing presentation of knee dislocation and vascular injury from high-energy trauma to low-energy falls in the morbidly obese. J Vasc Surg 2013.
  • Levy BA, Marx RG et al. Controversies in the treatment of knee dislocations and multiligament reconstruction. JAAOS 2009.
  • Schenck RC. The dislocated knee. Instr Course Lect 1994.
4questions

Posterolateral corner injury & lateral-sided knee instability

PLC anatomy, examination and the consequences of missing it.

3 of 7 sittings2021 (x2), 2022, 2024F

  • The three primary static stabilisers of the PLC are the fibular (lateral) collateral ligament, the popliteus tendon, and the popliteofibular ligament. Secondary/other structures: the lateral capsule, the arcuate ligament, the fabellofibular ligament, the biceps femoris, the iliotibial band and the lateral gastrocnemius. The mid-third lateral capsular ligament/anterolateral ligament and the iliotibial band are not part of the PLC proper — a classic 'all are components except' item.
  • Layers of the lateral knee (Seebacher): Layer I — iliotibial tract and the superficial biceps femoris; Layer II — patellar retinaculum and patellofemoral ligaments; Layer III — the lateral capsular layer, which splits into superficial (containing the LCL and fabellofibular ligament) and deep (containing the popliteus, popliteofibular and arcuate ligaments) laminae. This layered approach is the basis of the surgical exposure.
  • Examination: varus stress at 30° of flexion isolates the LCL/PLC (varus opening at 0° implies a cruciate injury in addition). The dial test at 30° only = isolated PLC injury; at both 30° and 90° = PLC + PCL. The external rotation recurvatum and posterolateral drawer/reverse pivot shift tests are also used.
  • The commonest and most important clinical point: an unrecognised PLC injury is the leading cause of failure of ACL and PCL reconstruction. Always assess the PLC in a multiligament or high-energy knee injury.
  • Peroneal nerve palsy accompanies PLC injury in up to 15–30% (higher with fibular head avulsion); document nerve function before and after treatment and protect the nerve during surgery.
  • Acute (within 2–3 weeks) repair/reconstruction is preferred — outcomes deteriorate substantially with delay. Chronic injuries require anatomic reconstruction (e.g. LaPrade fibular-based or Larson technique), and varus malalignment must be corrected first with a proximal tibial osteotomy or the reconstruction will stretch out.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports.
  • LaPrade RF, Terry GC. Injuries to the posterolateral aspect of the knee. AJSM 1997; LaPrade RF et al. The anatomy of the posterolateral aspect of the knee. AJSM 2003.
  • Seebacher JR, Inglis AE, Marshall JL, Warren RF. The structure of the posterolateral aspect of the knee. JBJS Am 1982.
  • Levy BA et al. Decision making in the multiligament-injured knee. Arthroscopy 2009.
2questions

Articular cartilage restoration: OATS, ACI & microfracture

Choosing a cartilage procedure by lesion size and characteristics.

2 of 7 sittings2022, 2023

  • Microfracture/marrow stimulation: best for small (<2–2.5 cm²) contained lesions in lower-demand patients. It produces fibrocartilage (type I collagen), which is biomechanically inferior and deteriorates after 2–5 years. Subchondral bone overgrowth and intralesional osteophytes compromise later procedures.
  • Osteochondral autograft transfer (OATS/mosaicplasty): the ideal candidate has a small-to-medium (1–4 cm²), focal, contained, symptomatic lesion, is young (<40–50), has a stable and well-aligned knee, and has intact opposing cartilage. It provides immediate hyaline cartilage with a bony base and allows faster return to sport. Limitations are donor-site morbidity and difficulty matching contour for large lesions.
  • Autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI/MACI): a two-stage procedure — arthroscopic cartilage harvest, cell culture, then implantation under a periosteal or collagen membrane. Indicated for large (>4 cm²) symptomatic femoral condyle or patellar lesions in young patients, especially after failed marrow stimulation. It produces hyaline-like cartilage. Drawbacks: two operations, cost, prolonged rehabilitation (return to sport 12–18 months), and graft hypertrophy/delamination. It requires an intact subchondral bone plate — a deep osseous defect requires a sandwich technique or an osteochondral allograft.
  • Osteochondral allograft: for large (>4 cm²) lesions with bone loss, revision cases, and osteochondritis dissecans with a large osseous defect. Fresh (not frozen) grafts preserve chondrocyte viability.
  • The universal rule: correct malalignment, instability and meniscal deficiency, or the cartilage procedure will fail. A concurrent or staged osteotomy, ligament reconstruction or meniscal transplant is frequently required. Patellofemoral lesions additionally require correction of maltracking (TT-TG, tubercle osteotomy).
  • Prognostic factors for a good outcome from OCD/cartilage lesions: skeletally immature patient with open physes (much better prognosis), a stable lesion, smaller size, a lesion in the classic medial femoral condyle location, and intact overlying cartilage. Unstable lesions, larger lesions, adult onset and lesions in atypical (weightbearing/lateral) locations do worse.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports.
  • Hangody L, Füles P. Autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty for the treatment of full-thickness defects of weight-bearing joints. JBJS Am 2003.
  • Brittberg M et al. Treatment of deep cartilage defects in the knee with autologous chondrocyte transplantation. NEJM 1994.
  • Bekkers JEJ, Inklaar M, Saris DBF. Treatment selection in articular cartilage lesions of the knee: a systematic review. AJSM 2009.
  • Mithoefer K et al. Clinical efficacy of the microfracture technique for articular cartilage repair in the knee. AJSM 2009.
2questions

Posterior cruciate ligament injury

PCL anatomy, natural history and the indications for reconstruction.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2023

  • The PCL is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation, providing ~95% of the restraining force, and is the strongest ligament in the knee. It has two bundles: the larger anterolateral bundle (tight in flexion) and the smaller posteromedial bundle (tight in extension) — most single-bundle reconstructions reproduce the anterolateral bundle.
  • Mechanism: a posteriorly directed force on the flexed tibia (dashboard injury) or a fall onto a flexed knee with a plantarflexed foot. Hyperextension injuries tear the PCL as part of a multiligament pattern.
  • Examination: the posterior drawer test at 90° is the most sensitive and specific. Grading is by the step-off: grade I — the tibial plateau remains anterior to the femoral condyles (0–5 mm); grade II — flush with the condyles (5–10 mm); grade III — the tibia translates posterior to the condyles (>10 mm), which implies an associated injury (usually PLC). The quadriceps active test and posterior sag sign are useful adjuncts.
  • Natural history: isolated grade I–II PCL injuries generally do well non-operatively with quadriceps-focused rehabilitation, and most athletes return to sport; however, long-term follow-up shows a significant incidence of medial compartment and patellofemoral degenerative change. The PCL has an intrinsic capacity to heal in continuity (unlike the ACL), often with residual laxity.
  • Indications for reconstruction: grade III (isolated, with >10–12 mm translation), symptomatic instability despite rehabilitation, bony avulsion of the PCL (ORIF is preferred), and any PCL injury as part of a multiligament injury or with a PLC injury — a combined PCL/PLC injury must be reconstructed.
  • Do not miss the PLC — an unrecognised posterolateral corner injury is the commonest cause of PCL reconstruction failure. Similarly, varus malalignment should be corrected before or with reconstruction.
  • Rehabilitation emphasises quadriceps strengthening and avoidance of isolated hamstring exercises early (the hamstrings pull the tibia posteriorly), and uses a dynamic PCL brace and prone-position range of motion to avoid posterior sag.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports.
  • Shelbourne KD, Davis TJ, Patel DV. The natural history of acute, isolated, nonoperatively treated posterior cruciate ligament injuries. AJSM 1999.
  • LaPrade CM et al. Posterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. JAAOS 2015.
  • Race A, Amis AA. The mechanical properties of the two bundles of the human posterior cruciate ligament. J Biomech 1994.
2questions

Proximal tibiofibular joint instability

The overlooked cause of lateral knee pain.

2 of 7 sittings2021, 2024S

  • The proximal tibiofibular joint is a synovial joint that communicates with the knee joint in ~10% of people. It has two morphologies: horizontal (more stable, larger surface area) and oblique (>20° inclination — less stable and more prone to instability and injury).
  • Function: it dissipates torsional stress from the ankle, transmits axial load (~one sixth of the static load at the ankle), and resists lateral tibial bending. The fibula bears roughly 6–17% of the axial load at the ankle.
  • Mechanism of instability: usually anterolateral dislocation (the commonest direction, ~85%) from a fall on a flexed, adducted knee with an inverted/plantarflexed foot; it occurs in parachutists, wrestlers and soccer players. Posteromedial dislocation is rare and is associated with peroneal nerve injury.
  • Presentation: lateral knee pain and a prominent fibular head, worse with ankle motion and direct pressure; often misdiagnosed as a lateral meniscal tear or an LCL injury. Chronic instability presents with a sense of the fibular head 'popping'. Radiographs should be compared with the contralateral side (a true AP with ~45° of internal rotation shows the joint best); CT confirms.
  • Treatment: acute dislocation — closed reduction (knee flexed to 90° to relax the biceps femoris and LCL, foot everted/dorsiflexed, direct pressure on the fibular head), then immobilisation for 2–3 weeks. Chronic instability — anatomic ligament reconstruction (biceps femoris tenodesis or graft reconstruction) is preferred; historical options such as arthrodesis (causes ankle pain from loss of fibular rotation) and fibular head resection are now largely avoided.
  • The proximal tibiofibular joint is not a stabiliser tested by varus stress at 20–30° of knee flexion — that test isolates the LCL/PLC, and the tibiofibular joint is a common distractor.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports.
  • Ogden JA. Subluxation and dislocation of the proximal tibiofibular joint. JBJS Am 1974.
  • Sekiya JK, Kuhn JE. Instability of the proximal tibiofibular joint. JAAOS 2003.
  • Horst PK, LaPrade RF. Anatomic reconstruction of chronic symptomatic anterolateral proximal tibiofibular joint instability. KSSTA 2010.
2questions

Stingers, burners & cervical spine in athletes

The brachial plexus stinger and return-to-play decisions.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2024S

  • A stinger/burner is a transient unilateral upper limb burning dysaesthesia and weakness following a shoulder/neck impact, most often in football and rugby. Two mechanisms: traction on the upper trunk (C5-6) with shoulder depression and contralateral neck side-bending (typical in younger athletes), and compression of the exiting nerve root in the neuroforamen with neck extension and ipsilateral rotation (typical in older athletes with degenerative foraminal narrowing).
  • Symptoms are unilateral and follow an upper trunk (C5-6) pattern — deltoid, biceps, supraspinatus and infraspinatus weakness with lateral arm/thumb paraesthesia. Bilateral symptoms or any lower limb involvement are NOT a stinger — they indicate transient quadriparesis/cervical cord neurapraxia and require immediate cervical spine imaging and work-up.
  • Most stingers resolve within minutes; an athlete may return to play in the same game only if symptoms have completely resolved, strength is full and symmetric, and the neck examination and range of motion are normal. Persistent symptoms, weakness or recurrent episodes require removal from play and further evaluation (radiographs, MRI, EMG if weakness persists >2–3 weeks).
  • Risk factors for recurrence: cervical foraminal stenosis and a reduced Torg-Pavlov ratio (<0.8), cervical disc disease, previous stingers, and poor neck strength/technique. Recurrent stingers warrant MRI and consideration of a permanent change in technique, neck strengthening and protective equipment (cervical roll/neck collar).
  • Cervical cord neurapraxia/transient quadriparesis presents with bilateral sensory and/or motor symptoms in all four limbs lasting minutes to hours. It requires MRI; congenital stenosis, cord signal change, instability or ligamentous injury are contraindications to return to contact sport, whereas an isolated single episode with a normal MRI and no stenosis may allow return after full recovery.
  • Any athlete with neck pain, midline tenderness, neurologic deficit or altered consciousness after a cervical injury is managed with full spinal immobilisation and transfer; helmet and shoulder pads are removed together in a controlled setting.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports; Spine.
  • Kuhlman GS, McKeag DB. The 'burner': a common nerve injury in contact sports. Am Fam Physician.
  • Weinstein SM. Assessment and rehabilitation of the athlete with a 'stinger'. Clin Sports Med 1998.
  • Torg JS et al. Cervical cord neurapraxia: classification, pathomechanics, morbidity, and management guidelines. J Neurosurg 1997.
1question

Biologics in sports medicine (PRP)

What platelet-rich plasma is and what the evidence shows.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • PRP is autologous plasma with a platelet concentration above baseline (typically 3–5×), delivering growth factors — PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF, IGF-1, EGF, FGF — released on activation from the alpha granules. It is not a stem cell therapy and contains very few (if any) mesenchymal stem cells — a common misconception and exam distractor.
  • Preparations differ enormously and are not standardised: leukocyte-rich (LR-PRP) versus leukocyte-poor (LP-PRP), activated versus non-activated, and varying platelet concentration. This heterogeneity is the principal reason the literature is inconsistent. Broadly, LP-PRP is favoured for intra-articular (joint) injection and LR-PRP for tendinopathy.
  • Evidence: the most consistent positive signal is for knee osteoarthritis (several RCTs and meta-analyses show benefit over hyaluronic acid and saline at 6–12 months, though the largest recent trials have been negative) and for lateral epicondylitis and patellar tendinopathy in some studies. Evidence for acute muscle injury, Achilles tendinopathy, and augmentation of rotator cuff or ACL repair is weak or negative.
  • PRP is not a proven treatment for acute Achilles rupture and does not improve healing in high-quality trials (e.g. the PATH-2 trial).
  • Practical issues: NSAIDs should be held for ~1 week before and after injection (they inhibit platelet function); PRP is not covered by most public and private plans in Canada and is an out-of-pocket cost; and it is prohibited in some competition contexts in specific formulations — check the current WADA list (intramuscular PRP is currently permitted).
  • Counsel patients honestly: the biological rationale is plausible, adverse events are rare, but the evidence base is heterogeneous and the effect sizes are modest at best.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports; Principles of Orthopaedics.
  • Bennell KL et al. Effect of intra-articular platelet-rich plasma vs placebo injection on pain and medial tibial cartilage volume in patients with knee osteoarthritis (RESTORE). JAMA 2021.
  • Keene DJ et al. (PATH-2) Platelet-rich plasma injection for acute Achilles tendon rupture. BMJ 2019.
  • Le ADK, Enweze L, DeBaun MR, Dragoo JL. Current clinical recommendations for use of platelet-rich plasma. Curr Rev Musculoskelet Med 2018.
1question

Hamstring & pelvic apophyseal avulsion injuries

Avulsion injuries around the pelvis and hip.

1 of 7 sittings2021

  • Apophyseal avulsions around the pelvis occur in adolescents because the apophysis is the weak link before fusion. Classic sites and muscles: ischial tuberosity — hamstrings (the commonest and most disabling); anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) — direct head of rectus femoris; anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) — sartorius and tensor fascia lata; iliac crest — abdominal muscles; lesser trochanter — iliopsoas; greater trochanter — abductors.
  • Mechanism-based identification is the exam skill: an avulsion occurring with the hip flexed and the knee extended stretches the hamstrings maximally → ischial tuberosity (sprinting, hurdling, cheerleading splits). With the hip extended and knee flexed, the rectus femoris is at maximal stretch → AIIS (kicking). The sartorius (ASIS) is least likely to avulse with the hip flexed and knee extended because that position shortens rather than lengthens it — the usual 'least likely' answer.
  • A lesser trochanter avulsion in an adult without significant trauma is a pathologic fracture until proven otherwise (metastasis) — an important red flag.
  • Most apophyseal avulsions are treated non-operatively: rest, protected weightbearing, and graduated rehabilitation, with excellent results. Operative fixation is considered for ischial tuberosity avulsions displaced >1.5–2 cm in an athlete, because nonunion, painful bony prominence when sitting, and sciatic nerve irritation/tethering are recognised sequelae.
  • Complete proximal hamstring tendon avulsion in an adult (a 'water-skiing' injury with sudden hip flexion and knee extension, ecchymosis and a palpable defect) — surgical repair is recommended for complete two- or three-tendon retracted avulsions in active patients, with better strength and return to sport than non-operative treatment, and much better results when repaired acutely than chronically.
  • Distinguish these from avulsion of the ischial apophysis in a growing athlete and from a hamstring musculotendinous strain, which is far more common and is treated with rehabilitation.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Pediatrics; Sports.
  • Rossi F, Dragoni S. Acute avulsion fractures of the pelvis in adolescent competitive athletes. Skeletal Radiol 2001.
  • Metzmaker JN, Pappas AM. Avulsion fractures of the pelvis. AJSM 1985.
  • Bodendorfer BM et al. Outcomes after operative and nonoperative treatment of proximal hamstring avulsions: a systematic review and meta-analysis. AJSM 2018.
1question

Medial collateral ligament & posteromedial corner

The medial side of the knee.

1 of 7 sittings2025

  • The medial structures are described in three layers (Warren & Marshall): Layer I — deep (crural/sartorial) fascia; Layer II — superficial MCL, medial patellofemoral ligament, semimembranosus; Layer III — the deep capsular layer, containing the deep MCL (meniscofemoral and meniscotibial ligaments) and the capsule. The posterior oblique ligament (POL) lies at the junction of layers II and III posteriorly.
  • The posteromedial corner comprises the posterior oblique ligament, the semimembranosus tendon and its expansions, the oblique popliteal ligament, the posteromedial capsule, and the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. The superficial MCL is the primary valgus restraint but is usually considered separately from the PMC proper, and the medial patellofemoral ligament and the pes anserinus are not components of the posteromedial corner — the standard 'all are parts except' answer.
  • Function: the superficial MCL is the primary restraint to valgus stress (tested at 30° of flexion); the POL and posteromedial capsule resist valgus in full extension and control anteromedial rotatory instability. Valgus laxity at 0° of extension implies a combined MCL + PMC ± cruciate injury.
  • Natural history: isolated MCL injuries — even grade III — heal reliably with non-operative treatment (hinged brace, early range of motion, progressive weightbearing). The MCL has an excellent blood supply and healing capacity. This is one of the most reliable non-operative outcomes in orthopaedics.
  • Indications for MCL surgery: a displaced/entrapped distal MCL avulsion (Stener-like lesion, where the ligament flips superficial to the pes anserinus), a bony avulsion, chronic symptomatic valgus instability, a combined multiligament injury, and valgus laxity in full extension with an associated PMC injury.
  • Combined ACL-MCL injury: the standard approach is to allow the MCL to heal first with bracing and rehabilitation, then reconstruct the ACL at 4–6 weeks once valgus stability and motion are restored — this reduces the risk of arthrofibrosis compared with acute combined surgery.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports.
  • Warren LF, Marshall JL. The supporting structures and layers on the medial side of the knee. JBJS Am 1979.
  • LaPrade RF, Engebretsen AH et al. The anatomy of the medial part of the knee. JBJS Am 2007.
  • Wijdicks CA, Griffith CJ, Johansen S, Engebretsen L, LaPrade RF. Injuries to the medial collateral ligament and associated medial structures of the knee. JBJS Am 2010.
1question

Patellar tendinopathy & jumper's knee

Diagnosis and the evidence for treatment.

1 of 7 sittings2022

  • Patellar tendinopathy ('jumper's knee') presents with anterior knee pain localised to the inferior pole of the patella, provoked by jumping, landing and deceleration, in volleyball, basketball and high-jump athletes. Tenderness is maximal at the deep posterior aspect of the proximal patellar tendon at the inferior pole with the knee extended, and decreases with the knee flexed (Bassett's sign).
  • Pathology is tendinosis — angiofibroblastic degeneration with neovascularisation and disorganised collagen — not inflammation. Imaging (ultrasound or MRI) shows tendon thickening and increased signal at the proximal deep fibres, but imaging findings correlate poorly with symptoms and are common in asymptomatic athletes.
  • Eccentric strengthening — specifically a decline-board single-leg squat programme — has the best evidence and is the treatment of choice. Heavy slow resistance training is at least as effective and better tolerated. Both outperform concentric exercise, rest, ultrasound and most passive modalities.
  • Corticosteroid injection is contraindicated — it gives short-term relief but weakens the tendon and risks rupture, with worse long-term outcomes (the same pattern as lateral epicondylitis).
  • Second-line: extracorporeal shockwave therapy, sclerosing injections, and PRP (inconsistent evidence). Surgery — open or arthroscopic débridement of the degenerate tissue at the inferior pole ± excision of the distal pole — is reserved for at least 6 months of failed structured eccentric rehabilitation and gives ~80% good results with a long return to sport.
  • Address contributing factors: decreased ankle dorsiflexion, quadriceps and hamstring inflexibility, poor landing mechanics, training volume and playing surface.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports.
  • Young MA, Cook JL, Purdam CR, Kiss ZS, Alfredson H. Eccentric decline squat protocol offers superior results at 12 months compared with traditional eccentric protocol for patellar tendinopathy in volleyball players. Br J Sports Med 2005.
  • Kongsgaard M et al. Corticosteroid injections, eccentric decline squat training and heavy slow resistance training in patellar tendinopathy. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2009.
  • Malliaras P, Cook J, Purdam C, Rio E. Patellar tendinopathy: clinical diagnosis, load management, and advice. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2015.
1question

Return to sport & tennis/overuse injuries

Overuse injury in racquet sports and return-to-play principles.

1 of 7 sittings2020

  • Lateral epicondylitis is the classic 'tennis' injury but the majority of patients with it do not play tennis — this is the standard 'what is false about tennis injuries' item. In tennis players specifically, it is associated with poor backhand technique (leading elbow), a grip that is too small or too large, a racquet that is too heavy or too stiff, and high string tension.
  • Other common racquet-sport injuries: rotator cuff tendinopathy and internal impingement (serving), medial epicondylitis (forehand/serve, especially with topspin), wrist ECU tendinopathy and subluxation (two-handed backhand, western grip), hook of hamate fracture, abdominal/rectus and shoulder injuries from serving, and lower limb injuries (calf/Achilles, ankle sprain, patellar tendinopathy).
  • Modifiable equipment factors that reduce load: a larger grip size, lower string tension, a more flexible/lighter racquet, and a larger head size all decrease transmitted vibration and force. Technique correction (particularly a two-handed backhand and avoiding a leading elbow) is at least as important.
  • Return-to-sport principles (applicable across sports): full pain-free range of motion, restored strength (typically ≥90% limb symmetry index), restored neuromuscular control and sport-specific functional testing (hop tests), completion of a graduated sport-specific progression, and psychological readiness (ACL-RSI). Time alone is not an adequate criterion.
  • Delaying return after ACL reconstruction to at least 9 months, and achieving strength symmetry, substantially reduces re-injury risk — each month of delay up to 9 months reduces re-injury by approximately 50% in some cohorts.
  • In the skeletally immature athlete, remember sport specialisation and excessive training volume are the strongest modifiable risk factors for overuse injury; guidelines recommend limiting to fewer hours per week than the athlete's age in years and taking 2–3 months off per year from a single sport.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Sports.
  • Grawe B, Fabricant PD et al. / Abrams GD, Renstrom PA, Safran MR. Epidemiology of musculoskeletal injury in the tennis player. Br J Sports Med 2012.
  • Grindem H, Snyder-Mackler L, Moksnes H, Engebretsen L, Risberg MA. Simple decision rules can reduce reinjury risk by 84% after ACL reconstruction (Delaware-Oslo cohort). Br J Sports Med 2016.
  • Jayanthi NA et al. Sports-specialized intensive training and the risk of injury in young athletes. AJSM 2015.

Acetabular fracture: Classification, approach & outcomes

Letournel classification, radiographic lines, approach selection and prognostic factors.

7 of 7 sittings2020 (x3), 2021 (x3), 2022 (x2), 2023, 2024S (x3), 2024F, 2025

  • The six radiographic lines on the AP pelvis define the classification: iliopectineal line (anterior column), ilioischial line (posterior column), anterior wall, posterior wall, teardrop, and the roof/sourcil. Disruption of the iliopectineal line indicates an ANTERIOR column injury; disruption of the ilioischial line indicates a POSTERIOR column injury. A disrupted iliopectineal line WITH a posterior wall fragment = an anterior column with posterior hemitransverse or an associated both-column pattern — read the lines, then name the fracture.
  • Judet views: the OBTURATOR OBLIQUE (rolled 45° toward the injured side) shows the ANTERIOR COLUMN and the POSTERIOR WALL; the ILIAC OBLIQUE (rolled 45° away) shows the POSTERIOR COLUMN and the ANTERIOR WALL. Mnemonic: obturator = anterior column + posterior wall.
  • Letournel's five ELEMENTARY patterns (posterior wall, posterior column, anterior wall, anterior column, transverse) and five ASSOCIATED patterns (posterior column + posterior wall, transverse + posterior wall, T-type, anterior column/wall + posterior hemitransverse, associated both-column).
  • The associated both-column (ABC) fracture is defined by the 'SPUR SIGN' on the obturator oblique — a spur of intact iliac wing remaining attached to the sacroiliac joint, with no part of the articular surface remaining attached to the axial skeleton (the 'floating acetabulum'). It is the only pattern that can achieve SECONDARY CONGRUENCE — the fragments rotate around the femoral head and can produce a congruent, functional hip even without anatomic reduction, which is why selected ABC fractures in the elderly can be treated non-operatively.
  • Approach selection: posterior wall and posterior column → Kocher-Langenbeck; anterior column and anterior wall → ilioinguinal or anterior intrapelvic (modified Stoppa); associated both-column → usually ilioinguinal/anterior intrapelvic (the best single approach for an ABC pattern); transverse and T-type → depends on the dominant displacement; extended iliofemoral for complex patterns (with a high HO rate). For an 86-year-old ABC fracture where the goal is to visualise, reduce and plate the QUADRILATERAL PLATE, the anterior intrapelvic (modified Stoppa) approach is the answer — it gives direct access to the quadrilateral surface and pelvic brim, which the ilioinguinal does not visualise as well.
  • The strongest predictor of a good long-term outcome is the QUALITY OF THE ARTICULAR REDUCTION — an anatomic reduction (<2 mm step) is the single most important modifiable factor (Matta). Restoring congruity of the weightbearing dome matters most.
  • Poor prognostic factors: age >55–60, femoral head damage/impaction (a marginal impaction or an osteochondral injury), posterior wall comminution and a wall fragment involving >40–50% of the wall, an initial hip dislocation (especially with delayed reduction), non-anatomic reduction (>2 mm step), acetabular dome impaction, associated femoral neck fracture, and delay to surgery >2–3 weeks. A concomitant ipsilateral femoral SHAFT fracture is NOT itself a poor prognostic factor for the acetabulum — a common distractor.
  • Posterior wall fracture indications for fixation: hip instability on examination under anaesthesia (the definitive test), a fragment involving >40–50% of the wall (>50% is always unstable; <20% is usually stable; 20–50% requires an EUA), an incongruent joint, an intra-articular fragment, and marginal impaction. Posterior wall fractures have the WORST outcomes of the elementary patterns despite appearing simple, because of associated femoral head injury, marginal impaction and sciatic nerve injury.
  • Heterotopic ossification is highest with the extended iliofemoral approach, then the Kocher-Langenbeck; consider prophylaxis (indomethacin or single-dose radiation) in high-risk patients. The sciatic nerve (peroneal division) is at risk with posterior approaches — keep the hip extended and the knee flexed.
  • An elderly patient undergoing acetabular ORIF can expect a higher rate of conversion to THA (roughly 20–30% at 2 years in some series), poorer functional outcomes, and higher perioperative morbidity than a young patient — acute or delayed THA (with or without fixation) is increasingly favoured in this population.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Pelvis and Acetabulum.
  • Judet R, Judet J, Letournel E. Fractures of the acetabulum: classification and surgical approaches for open reduction. JBJS Am 1964.
  • Matta JM. Fractures of the acetabulum: accuracy of reduction and clinical results in patients managed operatively within three weeks after the injury. JBJS Am 1996.
  • Cole JD, Bolhofner BR. Acetabular fracture fixation via a modified Stoppa limited intrapelvic approach. CORR 1994.
  • Moed BR, WillsonCarr SE, Watson JT. Results of operative treatment of fractures of the posterior wall of the acetabulum. JBJS Am 2002.
13questions

Femoral shaft fracture: Nailing, rotation & ipsilateral neck fracture

Nailing technique, malrotation, the fracture table, and the ipsilateral femoral neck fracture.

6 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021 (x2), 2022 (x4), 2024S (x2), 2024F (x2), 2025

  • Reamed, statically locked intramedullary nailing is the gold standard for adult femoral shaft fractures, with union rates >95%. Reaming improves union rates in the femur and tibia (SPRINT) without a clinically significant increase in pulmonary complications in the resuscitated patient.
  • Femoral malrotation after nailing is common (up to 20–30% have >15° of malrotation) and is functionally significant. Methods to judge rotation intra-operatively: the lesser trochanter profile compared with the contralateral side (obtained pre-operatively as a template with the patella facing forward), the cortical step sign, the diameter difference sign, the linea aspera alignment, and clinical assessment of hip rotation with the knee flexed. Comparing the fluoroscopic appearance of the knee (posterior condylar axis) with the hip on the same image is another method. Simply matching the patella position by eye is unreliable.
  • Interpreting a post-operative rotational CT: 'left retroverted 10° and right anteverted 15°' means the operated left femur has 10° of retroversion relative to a normal right of 15° of anteversion — a 25° rotational difference, which is clinically significant internal malrotation and generally warrants correction (derotation osteotomy or nail revision) if symptomatic. Note that the terminology matters: retroversion on the operated side with anteversion on the normal side means the two add.
  • Antegrade nailing on a fracture (traction) table versus a standard radiolucent table: the fracture table applies sustained traction with the limb fixed, and the classic complication is INTERNAL MALROTATION (the traction boot internally rotates the distal fragment), along with pudendal nerve palsy from the perineal post, compartment syndrome of the contralateral (well) leg from the lithotomy/hemilithotomy position, sciatic and peroneal nerve palsy, and the practical difficulty of assessing rotation and length. A fracture table does not cause fat embolism syndrome — a common distractor. Time to set up is longer and it is impractical in the polytrauma patient needing simultaneous procedures.
  • Start point errors: with a piriformis entry nail, a start point that is too anterior risks anterior cortical perforation/blowout of the femoral neck and increased hoop stress; too posterior risks the femoral neck blood supply and posterior comminution. With a trochanteric entry nail, a start point that is TOO LATERAL causes a VARUS malreduction (and medial cortical impingement), while too medial risks the femoral neck.
  • Distal femoral anterior cortical perforation with an antegrade nail is caused by the mismatch between the radius of curvature of the nail and the greater anterior bow of the patient's femur (nails are typically manufactured with a radius of curvature of 1.5–3.0 m, straighter than many femora, especially in elderly and Asian patients) — so the nail 'bottoms out' anteriorly. The other contributor is a posteriorly placed start point.
  • Ipsilateral femoral neck and shaft fracture occurs in ~1–9% of femoral shaft fractures and the neck fracture is MISSED in 20–50% of cases. It is typically a vertically oriented, minimally displaced basicervical/transcervical fracture in a young patient. Always obtain a dedicated internal rotation AP of the hip (and a CT) in any high-energy femoral shaft fracture, and inspect the hip on the post-nailing images.
  • Treatment priority is the FEMORAL NECK — it determines the outcome (AVN and nonunion are far more consequential than a shaft nonunion). Options: a reconstruction (cephalomedullary) nail, or — preferred by many — independent fixation of the neck with cannulated screws or a sliding hip screw, plus a retrograde nail for the shaft, which allows optimal, unconstrained fixation of the neck.
  • IM nailing complicated by an iatrogenic femoral neck fracture during the procedure requires immediate recognition and fixation of the neck (screws or a sliding hip screw) before completing the shaft fixation.
