  • Cannabis use and femoral shaft fracture: heavy recreational cannabis use is associated with increased anaesthetic requirements, higher post-operative pain scores and greater opioid consumption, and — in some series — a higher rate of complications; it is a relevant preoperative history.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity.
  • SPRINT Investigators (Bhandari M, Canadian). Randomized trial of reamed and unreamed intramedullary nailing of tibial shaft fractures. JBJS Am 2008.
  • Jaarsma RL, Verdonschot N, van der Venne R, van Kampen A. Avoiding rotational malalignment after fractures of the femur by using the profile of the lesser trochanter. Arch Orthop Trauma Surg 2005.
  • Riemer BL, Butterfield SL. Comparison of reamed and nonreamed solid core nailing of the tibial diaphysis / Bishop JA et al. Ipsilateral femoral neck and shaft fractures. JAAOS 2015.
  • Egol KA et al. Mismatch of current intramedullary nails with the anterior bow of the femur. J Orthop Trauma 2004.
13questions

Open fracture management: Antibiotics, débridement & timing

Gustilo classification, antibiotic choice, timing, irrigation and coverage.

6 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021 (x2), 2022 (x2), 2023 (x4), 2024F, 2025 (x2)

  • Gustilo-Anderson: I — wound <1 cm, clean, minimal soft-tissue damage; II — wound 1–10 cm, moderate soft-tissue damage, no significant contamination; IIIA — extensive soft-tissue damage but adequate soft-tissue coverage (includes any segmental fracture, farmyard injury, high-energy or gunshot injury regardless of wound size); IIIB — inadequate soft-tissue coverage requiring a flap, with periosteal stripping; IIIC — with arterial injury requiring repair. The classification is definitively made in the operating theatre after débridement.
  • ANTIBIOTICS ARE THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT INTERVENTION in reducing infection, and the key is TIMING — antibiotics within 1 hour (certainly within 3 hours) of injury. Delay beyond 3 hours is the strongest predictor of infection, more so than the time to débridement. Antibiotics, not the timing of surgery, are the mainstay.
  • Antibiotic choice: Type I/II — a first-generation cephalosporin (cefazolin). Type III — add gram-negative coverage (an aminoglycoside or, increasingly, extended gram-negative cover with piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone). Farm/soil contamination — add penicillin (or metronidazole) for clostridial cover. Fresh-water contamination — cover for Aeromonas hydrophila (a fluoroquinolone or third-generation cephalosporin); salt-water — cover for Vibrio (doxycycline plus a third-generation cephalosporin). Duration is 24 hours after wound closure (and 24–72 hours for type III) — prolonged antibiotics do not help.
  • A 25-year-old with an open forearm fracture sustained while water-skiing on a FRESHWATER lake requires, beyond I&D, coverage for Aeromonas hydrophila — a fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) or a third-generation cephalosporin added to the standard regimen, with delayed closure.
  • Timing of débridement: the historical '6-hour rule' is not supported by modern evidence. Débridement within 24 hours is acceptable for most open fractures without a significant increase in infection, provided antibiotics were given early. Urgent (immediate) débridement remains indicated for gross contamination, vascular compromise, compartment syndrome and highly contaminated farmyard/marine injuries. The FLOW and LEAP data support this.
  • FLOW trial (Canadian-led, NEJM 2015): comparing irrigation solutions and pressures in open fractures — NORMAL SALINE was superior to castile soap (soap had a higher reoperation rate), and LOW pressure (gravity flow) was equivalent to high pressure, with a trend favouring low pressure. The answer is normal saline at low (gravity) pressure. High-pressure lavage damages bone and drives contaminants deeper.
  • Timing of soft-tissue coverage: delay in definitive flap coverage beyond ~7 days markedly increases deep infection and flap failure (Godina's classic work favoured <72 hours; modern series support coverage within 7 days). The exam answer for 'delayed definitive coverage past what time is associated with increased complications' is 7 days (with <72 hours being ideal).
  • Local antibiotic delivery: antibiotic bead pouches and vancomycin powder are widely used. Intrawound vancomycin powder in tibial plateau/plafond fixation reduces gram-positive deep infection but is associated with a shift toward gram-negative organisms — the standard answer.
  • Other points: primary closure of a clean type I/II wound after adequate débridement is acceptable and may reduce infection compared with leaving the wound open; tetanus prophylaxis must be addressed; and negative pressure wound therapy is a temporising dressing, not a substitute for coverage.
  • In pregnancy with an open tibia fracture, avoid tetracyclines (fetal teeth/bone), fluoroquinolones (cartilage), and aminoglycosides (ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity — relative) — cephalosporins and penicillins are safe. The answer to 'what NOT to give a pregnant woman with an open tibia' is an aminoglycoside (gentamicin) or a tetracycline/fluoroquinolone depending on the options offered.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: General; Orthopaedic Dilemmas.
  • Gustilo RB, Anderson JT. Prevention of infection in the treatment of one thousand and twenty-five open fractures of long bones. JBJS Am 1976; Gustilo RB, Mendoza RM, Williams DN. J Trauma 1984.
  • FLOW Investigators (Bhandari M, Canadian). A trial of wound irrigation in the initial management of open fracture wounds. NEJM 2015.
  • Patzakis MJ, Wilkins J. Factors influencing infection rate in open fracture wounds. CORR 1989.
  • Godina M. Early microsurgical reconstruction of complex trauma of the extremities. Plast Reconstr Surg 1986.
  • Pollak AN et al. (LEAP) The relationship between time to surgical debridement and incidence of infection after open high-energy lower extremity trauma. JBJS Am 2010.
13questions

Polytrauma: Damage control orthopaedics & timing of fixation

Resuscitation endpoints, DCO versus early total care, and the tertiary survey.

7 of 7 sittings2020 (x4), 2021, 2022 (x2), 2023 (x2), 2024S, 2024F, 2025 (x2)

  • Damage control orthopaedics (DCO) = temporary spanning external fixation and control of haemorrhage/contamination, deferring definitive fixation until the patient is physiologically resuscitated. Early total care (ETC) = definitive fixation within the first 24 hours. The modern synthesis is 'Early Appropriate Care' (EAC) — definitive fixation of the pelvis, acetabulum, femur and spine within 36 hours provided the patient is adequately resuscitated, judged by physiologic parameters rather than by time or Injury Severity Score alone.
  • Resuscitation endpoints that indicate a patient is ready for definitive fixation (Vallier's EAC criteria) — memorise these numbers: lactate <4.0 mmol/L, pH ≥7.25, and base excess ≥ −5.5 mmol/L. Meeting these, definitive fixation within 36 hours reduces complications. Failing to meet them, DCO is appropriate.
  • Apply the numbers to the stem: a polytrauma patient 16 hours post-injury, off pressors, with lactate 3.5, base deficit 4.2 and pH 7.3 has met resuscitation criteria → proceed with definitive fixation of the pelvis, femur and spine. A patient with pH 7.2, lactate 7 and base excess −11 has NOT been resuscitated → damage control (external fixation, pelvic binder/packing, continue resuscitation).
  • Indications for DCO: persistent haemodynamic instability or coagulopathy, the lethal triad (hypothermia <35 °C, acidosis, coagulopathy), severe chest injury/pulmonary contusion with hypoxia, severe traumatic brain injury (where hypotension must be avoided), massive transfusion requirement, and a prolonged anticipated operative time in a marginal patient.
  • The 'second hit' phenomenon is the conceptual basis: the initial injury primes the systemic inflammatory response, and a prolonged, bloody definitive operation delivers a second inflammatory insult that can precipitate ARDS, MODS and death. Reamed femoral nailing in an under-resuscitated patient with a severe chest injury is the classic example.
  • Damage control resuscitation accompanies DCO: permissive hypotension (until haemorrhage control), balanced (1:1:1) transfusion of packed cells, plasma and platelets, limiting crystalloid, TXA within 3 hours (CRASH-2), and aggressive rewarming.
  • Massive transfusion of citrated blood causes HYPOCALCAEMIA (citrate chelates ionised calcium) — this is the cause of cardiac arrhythmia and hypotension during massive transfusion, and the treatment is intravenous calcium. Hyperkalaemia (from stored cells), hypothermia and acidosis are the other contributors. Citrate toxicity/hypocalcaemia is the answer to 'the cause of arrhythmia with massive transfusion of citrated red blood cells'.
  • The tertiary survey is a systematic head-to-toe re-examination with review of all imaging, performed within 24 hours and repeated when the patient is awake and communicative. Missed injuries occur in 10–40% of polytrauma patients, most commonly extremity fractures, and the tertiary survey is the single most effective tool to detect them. Missed injuries are more common at night, in patients with a reduced GCS, and in the most severely injured — and the classic false statement is that missed fracture rates are the same at night as during the day (they are higher with night-time admissions).
  • Bilateral femur fractures carry a substantially higher mortality, higher ISS, and higher rates of ARDS, fat embolism and transfusion requirement than a unilateral fracture — they are a marker of high energy and warrant a lower threshold for damage control.
  • A polytrauma patient with a pulmonary contusion, rib fractures, an APC-III pelvis, a tibial shaft and a forearm fracture, resuscitated with Hgb 100, SpO₂ 97% on 50% FiO₂, pH 7.3 and lactate 3 has broadly met resuscitation criteria — definitive pelvic fixation with fixation of the long bones is appropriate, with close monitoring.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: General.
  • Vallier HA et al. Timing of orthopaedic surgery in multiple trauma patients: development of a protocol for early appropriate care. J Orthop Trauma 2013.
  • Pape HC et al. Impact of the method of initial stabilization for femoral shaft fractures in patients with multiple injuries at risk for complications. Ann Surg 2007.
  • Scalea TM et al. External fixation as a bridge to intramedullary nailing for patients with multiple injuries and with femur fractures: damage control orthopedics. J Trauma 2000.
  • Enderson BL et al. The tertiary trauma survey: a prospective study of missed injury. J Trauma 1990.
10questions

Femoral neck fracture: Young & elderly

The young femoral neck fracture, the elderly arthroplasty debate, and the evidence.

6 of 7 sittings2020, 2021 (x3), 2022, 2023 (x3), 2024S, 2025

  • In the YOUNG patient (<50–60 years), a displaced femoral neck fracture is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY — the priorities are urgent anatomic reduction and stable internal fixation to preserve the femoral head. AVN rates are 20–30% and nonunion 10–30%, and the strongest modifiable factor is the quality of reduction; a capsulotomy to decompress the intracapsular haematoma is often added. A 19-year-old with a displaced neck fracture from a 10-foot fall requires urgent open (or closed) anatomic reduction and internal fixation — arthroplasty is not the answer in this age group.
  • Vertically oriented (Pauwels III) fractures experience high shear and are best fixed with a construct resisting shear: a fixed-angle device (sliding hip screw with an anti-rotation screw, or a cephalomedullary device) rather than three cannulated screws alone.
  • In the ELDERLY, the evidence has consolidated: displaced intracapsular fractures should be treated with ARTHROPLASTY, not internal fixation — fixation has a reoperation rate of 30–40%. The FAITH trial (Canadian-led) compared sliding hip screws with cannulated screws in fractures amenable to fixation and found no overall difference in reoperation, with sliding hip screws better in specific subgroups (displaced, basicervical, smokers).
  • HEALTH trial (Canadian-led, NEJM 2019): total hip arthroplasty versus hemiarthroplasty for a displaced femoral neck fracture in patients over 50 — no significant difference in the primary outcome (secondary hip procedures) at 24 months, but THA showed modestly better function and quality of life with a higher dislocation rate. Practical synthesis: THA for the active, cognitively intact, independent patient with pre-existing hip arthritis; hemiarthroplasty for the lower-demand, frail or cognitively impaired patient.
  • A 78-year-old with CHF who ambulates with a walker and needs assistance with IADLs is best treated with a CEMENTED hemiarthroplasty — not THA (her demand does not justify the dislocation risk) and not fixation.
  • Cemented versus uncemented hemiarthroplasty: the WHiTE 5 trial (NEJM 2022) and multiple registries show cemented stems reduce periprosthetic fracture and improve early function/quality of life with no increase in mortality. Uncemented hemiarthroplasty's commonest reason for revision is periprosthetic fracture. Modern guidance (NICE, AAOS) favours cementation in the elderly, with awareness of bone cement implantation syndrome.
  • Valgus-impacted (non-displaced) femoral neck fracture in an 80-year-old with dementia: these are frequently treated with in-situ fixation (cannulated screws) with good results, though ~10–20% displace. They are not 'stable enough to mobilise without fixation' — that is the classic false statement. Posterior tilt >20° on the lateral view predicts failure of fixation.
  • HIP ATTACK trial: accelerated surgery (within 6 hours) versus standard care for hip fracture showed no significant difference in 90-day mortality or major complications, though accelerated surgery reduced delirium, pain and length of stay. The AAOS CPG supports surgery within 24–48 hours, which reduces mortality, pain and complications.
  • Hip fracture patient on clopidogrel: current evidence supports proceeding with surgery without delay — waiting 5–7 days for platelet recovery increases mortality, pneumonia and length of stay, and the observed increase in blood loss/transfusion is modest. Do not delay surgery for clopidogrel. Regional anaesthesia may be avoided in favour of general anaesthesia.
  • Femoral neck stress fracture in a young athlete or recruit: TENSION-side (superolateral) lesions are unstable and require prophylactic screw fixation; compression-side (inferomedial) lesions can be treated with protected weightbearing, though a lesion involving >50% of the neck width or associated with an effusion warrants fixation. A 35% inferomedial (compression-side) lesion with an effusion sits in the grey zone — most would treat with strict non-weightbearing and close follow-up, with a low threshold for fixation.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity; Arthroplasty.
  • HEALTH Investigators (Bhandari M, Canadian). Total hip arthroplasty or hemiarthroplasty for hip fracture. NEJM 2019.
  • FAITH Investigators (Canadian). Fracture fixation in the operative management of hip fractures: a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet 2017.
  • Fernandez MA et al. (WHiTE 5) Cemented or uncemented hemiarthroplasty for intracapsular hip fracture. NEJM 2022.
  • AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Hip Fractures in Older Adults, 2021.
  • HIP ATTACK Investigators. Accelerated surgery versus standard care in hip fracture. Lancet 2020.
9questions

Humeral shaft fracture & radial nerve palsy

Non-operative treatment, indications for fixation, plating technique and radial nerve palsy.

5 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021 (x2), 2023 (x3), 2024S, 2025

  • Union rates with functional (Sarmiento) bracing are approximately 90–95% — the frequently quoted figure is ~94.5%, so 'union rate for non-op is over 95%' is false and 'most treated non-operatively go on to nonunion' is grossly false. Acceptable alignment: <20° apex anterior/posterior angulation, <30° varus/valgus, <3 cm shortening, and <15° malrotation.
  • Reasons for conversion from bracing to ORIF — the recognised list: inability to maintain acceptable alignment, unacceptable angulation/shortening, a fracture that distracts (particularly a transverse fracture), non-compliance or intolerance of the brace, obesity or large body habitus preventing effective bracing, delayed union/nonunion, and proximal-third or very distal fractures that the brace cannot control. A radial nerve palsy at presentation is NOT an indication to convert to ORIF — the classic 'all are reasons EXCEPT'.
  • Indications for primary operative fixation: open fracture, vascular injury, an associated forearm fracture ('floating elbow'), polytrauma requiring upper limb weightbearing, ipsilateral brachial plexus injury, bilateral humeral fractures, pathologic fracture, segmental fracture, an intra-articular extension, a secondary (post-manipulation) radial nerve palsy, and failure of non-operative treatment.
  • Plating technique: use a compression plate with at least 6–8 cortices (3–4 bicortical screws) on each side of the fracture. For a SPIRAL/oblique fracture, an INTERFRAGMENTARY LAG SCREW placed perpendicular to the fracture plane and then neutralised with a plate creates the MOST COMPRESSION — this is the answer to 'what technique creates the most compression' and 'the best method of fixation for a spiral humeral shaft fracture'.
  • Far cortical gapping with dual plating (a construct with a long plate plus a small plate, where the fracture gaps at the far cortex) results from failure to pre-bend/pre-contour the plate. A perfectly straight plate applied to a transverse fracture compresses the near cortex and gaps the far cortex — the correction is to slightly OVER-BEND (pre-bend) the plate at the fracture site so that tightening the screws compresses the far cortex first. This is a repeated question in several forms (humeral shaft, femoral shaft).
  • Radial nerve palsy accompanies 8–15% of humeral shaft fractures, most commonly with middle- and distal-third fractures (the Holstein-Lewis distal-third spiral fracture is classically associated). The great majority (>85–90%) are neurapraxias that recover spontaneously, typically beginning at 3–4 months.
  • Management of a primary radial nerve palsy is OBSERVATION with splinting to prevent contracture and EMG at ~6 weeks (fibrillations appear) and 3 months. Explore if there is no recovery by 3–4 months, or immediately for an open fracture, a vascular injury, or a palsy that develops AFTER manipulation or fixation (a secondary palsy).
  • Order of recovery: proximal to distal — brachioradialis recovers FIRST, followed by ECRL, then supinator, ECU, EDC, and EPL/EIP LAST. A patient showing signs of recovery at 2 months with a humeral shaft fracture, wrist drop and first-web-space numbness will regain EPL/extensor indicis last.
  • Humeral shaft nonunion: atrophic/hypertrophic. A hypertrophic nonunion of an oblique humeral shaft fracture indicates adequate biology but inadequate stability — treat with COMPRESSION PLATING (with a lag screw where the pattern allows), without the need for bone graft. An atrophic nonunion requires débridement, compression plating and autologous bone graft.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Upper Extremity.
  • Sarmiento A et al. Functional bracing for the treatment of fractures of the humeral diaphysis. JBJS Am 2000.
  • Shao YC, Harwood P, Grotz MRW, Limb D, Giannoudis PV. Radial nerve palsy associated with fractures of the shaft of the humerus: a systematic review. JBJS Br 2005.
  • Rämö L et al. Effect of surgery vs functional bracing on functional outcome among patients with closed displaced humeral shaft fractures (FISH randomized clinical trial). JAMA 2020.
  • Ekholm R et al. Outcome after closed functional treatment of humeral shaft fractures. J Orthop Trauma 2006.
8questions

Distal femur fracture & periarticular fixation

Lateral locked plating, nonunion, and the geriatric distal femur fracture.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2023 (x2), 2024S (x2), 2024F (x2)

  • Lateral locked plating is the workhorse, but the construct must be tuned biologically: a plate that is too stiff over a short working length produces asymmetric motion (the near cortex moves, the far cortex does not) and a NONUNION. Strategies to promote healing: use a longer plate with a longer working length, leave screw holes empty near the fracture, use fewer and more widely spaced screws, consider titanium rather than stainless steel, and use far-cortical locking or dynamic locking screws.
  • Factors contributing to nonunion of a distal femur (AO/OTA type C) fracture — the standard list: obesity, diabetes, smoking, open fracture, infection, an excessively stiff construct with a short working length, a stainless-steel plate, gapping/distraction at the fracture, and inadequate medial support in a comminuted metaphyseal fracture. An anatomic reduction with cortical contact and a well-balanced construct is NOT a cause of nonunion — the classic 'all contributed EXCEPT'.
  • Technique points: place the plate parallel to the distal femoral articular surface, and check the K-wire for the central distal screw in the lateral view — it must be parallel to the joint line and in the centre of the condyles, avoiding the intercondylar notch and the trochlea. A common error is placing the plate too anterior or in flexion, producing an extension malunion.
  • Golf-club deformity (the distal femur in varus with the shaft translated) results from plate placement too anterior/distal or failure to correct the flexion of the distal fragment by the gastrocnemius — the gastrocnemius origin pulls the distal fragment into extension (apex posterior/recurvatum) and the adductors pull the shaft medially, producing varus. Correct by anticipating these deforming forces (a bump under the knee, a femoral distractor, or a temporary joystick).
  • Malunion in VARUS with a distal femur ORIF is the classic late presentation: a patient at 1 year with hip and knee pain and varus alignment. Contributory factors: inadequate medial support, an unstable comminuted medial column, and early weightbearing.
  • Geriatric distal femur fracture — dual plating/nail-plate combination versus distal femoral replacement (DFR): DFR permits immediate unrestricted weightbearing and avoids nonunion, and is favoured for a loose or failed knee prosthesis, severe comminution with unreconstructible articular bone, and very poor bone quality. Fixation (dual plating, or a retrograde nail combined with a lateral plate) preserves bone stock and native anatomy and is favoured when reconstruction is feasible. Comparative studies show similar mortality with faster mobilisation after DFR but higher infection and extensor mechanism complication rates.
  • Periprosthetic distal femur fracture around a TKA (Rorabeck): type I/II (well-fixed component) → ORIF (lateral locking plate or retrograde nail if the femoral component has an open box); type III (loose component) → revision arthroplasty. Confirm nail compatibility with the implant before attempting a retrograde nail.
  • Nonunion of a periprosthetic distal femur ORIF at 4 months with a painful, stiff knee and a negative infection work-up in an elderly patient → revision to a distal femoral replacement is usually the answer, avoiding a further prolonged period of non-weightbearing.
  • A 64-year-old healthy woman with a closed distal femur fracture fixed with a lateral locking plate and interfragmentary screws who is still not healing at 3 months should prompt assessment for a hypertrophic nonunion from excessive construct stiffness (too many screws close to the fracture, short working length) — the correction is to revise to a biologically favourable construct, add compression or bone graft, and check for infection and metabolic factors.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity.
  • Lujan TJ, Henderson CE, Madey SM, Fitzpatrick DC, Marsh JL, Bottlang M. Locked plating of distal femur fractures leads to inconsistent and asymmetric callus formation. J Orthop Trauma 2010.
  • Rodriguez EK et al. Predictive factors of distal femoral fracture nonunion after lateral locked plating. Injury 2014.
  • Hoellwarth JS et al. Equivalent mortality and complication rates following periprosthetic distal femur fractures managed with either lateral locked plating or a distal femoral replacement. Injury 2018.
  • Ricci WM et al. Risk factors for failure of locked plate fixation of distal femur fractures. J Orthop Trauma 2014.
8questions

Intertrochanteric & subtrochanteric femur fracture

Implant selection, the tip-apex distance, and the subtrochanteric reduction problem.

4 of 7 sittings2021, 2022 (x2), 2024S (x3), 2025 (x2)

  • Implant selection: stable intertrochanteric fractures (AO/OTA 31-A1) can be treated with a sliding hip screw (SHS) or a cephalomedullary nail (CMN) with equivalent results and lower cost for the SHS. UNSTABLE patterns — reverse obliquity (31-A3), subtrochanteric extension, a fracture with a deficient lateral wall, and transverse patterns — MUST be treated with a cephalomedullary nail (a sliding hip screw in a reverse obliquity fracture will medialise the shaft and fail). Lateral wall integrity is the key determinant.
  • Tip-apex distance (TAD) = the sum of the distance from the tip of the lag screw to the apex of the femoral head on the AP and lateral views, corrected for magnification. TAD <25 mm is the target; a TAD >25 mm is the strongest independent predictor of screw cut-out. Central-central or centre-inferior positioning is optimal; a superior and anterior screw is the worst position.
  • Distal locking of a LONG cephalomedullary nail in an unstable intertrochanteric fracture: static distal locking controls length and rotation of the distal fragment, and is standard in unstable and subtrochanteric patterns. The trade-off is that static locking prevents controlled fracture-site compression/impaction, and in a stable pattern this can promote nonunion — so short nails in stable fractures are often locked dynamically or not at all. Distal locking does not increase the risk of femoral shaft fracture — an unlocked nail with a mismatch does.
  • Complications of cephalomedullary nailing — the standard list: screw cut-out (the commonest, driven by TAD and varus malreduction), varus malreduction, anterior perforation of the distal femur from radius-of-curvature mismatch, iatrogenic femoral shaft fracture at the nail tip, and lateral thigh pain. AVN of the femoral head is rare after an intertrochanteric fracture and is NOT a typical complication — the usual 'all are true EXCEPT'.
  • Subtrochanteric fractures are dominated by the deforming forces: the proximal fragment is FLEXED (iliopsoas), ABDUCTED (gluteus medius/minimus) and EXTERNALLY ROTATED (short external rotators), while the distal fragment is adducted and shortened (adductors). The consequence is a varus and procurvatum (apex anterior) malreduction if the fracture is nailed without deliberate correction.
  • Techniques to obtain and hold a subtrochanteric reduction: a LATERAL start point is wrong — start slightly medial/at the tip of the trochanter and correct the flexion of the proximal fragment; use blocking (Poller) screws, a percutaneous reduction clamp or ball-spike pusher, a unicortical plate or cerclage cable, positioning with the hip flexed (nailing on a radiolucent table in the lateral position), and temporary Schanz pin joysticks in the proximal fragment. Accept nothing worse than neutral alignment — varus malreduction is the leading cause of nonunion and implant failure.
  • A subtrochanteric fracture nailed in varus with a lateral start point, thick diaphyseal cortices and lateral cortical beaking is an ATYPICAL (bisphosphonate-related) fracture — the contributory factors beyond the start point are failure to correct the varus/flexion deformity of the proximal fragment and the pre-existing bowed, osteopetrotic-appearing femur, plus the impaired healing biology.
  • Risk factors for nonunion of a subtrochanteric fracture: varus malreduction (the dominant technical factor), gapping/distraction at the fracture, smoking, atypical/bisphosphonate-related fracture, open fracture, and inadequate fixation. A well-reduced fracture with cortical contact is not a risk factor — read the 'except' carefully.
  • A 22-year-old with a transverse subtrochanteric fracture from a trivial slip with markedly dense bone has OSTEOPETROSIS — expect extremely hard bone with obliterated medullary canals, high rates of drill/reamer breakage, delayed union and nonunion, and a high risk of iatrogenic fracture; plan for sharp new drill bits, copious irrigation to prevent thermal necrosis, and consider plate fixation.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity.
  • Baumgaertner MR, Curtin SL, Lindskog DM, Keggi JM. The value of the tip-apex distance in predicting failure of fixation of peritrochanteric fractures of the hip. JBJS Am 1995.
  • Haidukewych GJ, Israel TA, Berry DJ. Reverse obliquity fractures of the intertrochanteric region of the femur. JBJS Am 2001.
  • Kuzyk PRT, Bhandari M, McKee MD, Russell TA, Schemitsch EH (Canadian). Intramedullary versus extramedullary fixation for subtrochanteric femur fractures. J Orthop Trauma 2009.
  • Riehl JT et al. Reduction techniques for subtrochanteric femur fractures. J Orthop Trauma.
8questions

Pelvic ring injury: Classification, resuscitation & fixation

Young-Burgess, haemorrhage control, and the LC-1 stability question.

5 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021 (x2), 2022 (x2), 2023, 2025

  • Young-Burgess classification by mechanism: APC (anteroposterior compression) I — symphyseal widening <2.5 cm; II — widening >2.5 cm with anterior SI ligament disruption (posterior SI intact) — the 'open book'; III — complete hemipelvis disruption (both anterior and posterior SI). LC (lateral compression) I — sacral compression fracture on the side of impact; II — crescent fracture (iliac wing fracture with posterior SI disruption); III — 'windswept' (LC on one side, APC on the contralateral side). VS (vertical shear) — complete vertical displacement. CM — combined.
  • APC-II/III and VS patterns produce the most bleeding (the pelvic volume increases and the posterior venous plexus and internal iliac branches tear), while LC injuries have a higher rate of associated head and abdominal injuries and generally less pelvic haemorrhage.
  • Haemorrhage control sequence: pelvic binder/sheet at the level of the GREATER TROCHANTERS (not the iliac crests) → resuscitation with balanced blood products and TXA → identify the source (FAST/CT) → angioembolisation for arterial bleeding, preperitoneal pelvic packing for venous/bony bleeding, and external fixation or a C-clamp for mechanical stability. Roughly 85–90% of pelvic bleeding is venous or from the fracture surfaces, and only 10–15% is arterial — which is why binders and packing are so important.
  • LC-1 injuries — the modern controversy and a repeatedly tested topic: many LC-1 injuries are stable and treated non-operatively with early weightbearing, but a subset are occultly unstable. Examination under anaesthesia (EUA) with dynamic stress fluoroscopy is the accepted method of determining stability, and it does NOT 'displace the fracture' in a way that changes management — the statement 'you should not stress test an LC-1 because it will displace the fracture' is FALSE, and this is the classic item. Displacement on stress simply reveals the instability that was already present and identifies patients who benefit from fixation.
  • Indicators of an unstable LC-1: complete sacral fracture, displacement >10 mm on stress, an inability to mobilise/weightbear because of pain, and displacement on serial radiographs. Fixation (percutaneous iliosacral screws ± anterior fixation) allows earlier mobilisation and better pain control.
  • Pubic symphysis injuries: the symphysis widens with an APC mechanism; widening >2.5 cm implies disruption of the sacrotuberous, sacrospinous and anterior SI ligaments and warrants fixation (anterior plating), usually combined with posterior fixation for APC-III.
  • A young man with pubic diastasis whose retrograde urethrogram shows contrast outlining the bowel/extravasating into the peritoneum has a urethral (and likely bladder) injury — this indicates an intraperitoneal bladder rupture (which requires operative repair) or a urethral disruption. The appropriate next step is urology consultation with suprapubic catheterisation (NOT repeated attempts at urethral catheterisation) and operative repair of an intraperitoneal bladder rupture. Extraperitoneal bladder rupture can often be managed with catheter drainage alone. Genitourinary injury occurs in ~15% of pelvic ring injuries in men.
  • The AP pelvis radiograph should be scrutinised for: symphyseal widening, SI joint widening, sacral arcuate line disruption, an avulsion of the L5 transverse process (an indirect sign of vertical instability from the iliolumbar ligament), an avulsion of the ischial spine (sacrospinous ligament) and the sacrotuberous ligament, and asymmetry of the hemipelvis. Inlet and outlet views define anterior/posterior and superior/inferior displacement respectively.
  • Paediatric pelvic ring fractures are usually stable, heal rapidly, and — unlike adults — are rarely associated with catastrophic pelvic haemorrhage; but they mark a high-energy mechanism with a high rate of associated injuries. Triradiate cartilage injury risks acetabular growth arrest with progressive dysplasia.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Pelvis and Acetabulum.
  • Burgess AR, Eastridge BJ, Young JW et al. Pelvic ring disruptions: effective classification system and treatment protocols. J Trauma 1990.
  • Sagi HC, Coniglione FM, Stanford JH. Examination under anesthetic for occult pelvic ring instability. J Orthop Trauma 2011.
  • Bruce B, Reilly M, Sims S. OTA highlight paper predicting future displacement of nonoperatively managed lateral compression sacral fractures. J Orthop Trauma 2011.
  • Tile M (Canadian, Toronto). Acute pelvic fractures: causation and classification. JAAOS 1996.
7questions

Tibial shaft fracture & intramedullary nailing

Nail entry point, proximal-third deformity, blocking screws and the reaming debate.

4 of 7 sittings2020, 2021, 2022 (x3), 2023 (x2)

  • Reamed versus unreamed nailing (SPRINT, Canadian-led): in CLOSED tibial shaft fractures, reamed nailing showed a benefit (a reduced rate of reoperation/events) compared with unreamed; in OPEN fractures there was no significant difference. Reaming improves union rates and allows a larger-diameter nail; the historical concern about damage to the endosteal blood supply and fat embolism has not translated into worse clinical outcomes in the tibia.
  • Benefits of IM nailing versus closed treatment for a tibial shaft fracture: better maintenance of alignment, earlier weightbearing and mobilisation, faster return to function, and lower rates of malunion and shortening. It does NOT reduce the incidence of compartment syndrome (the classic 'all are benefits EXCEPT') and it introduces a risk of anterior knee pain (up to 50%).
  • Entry point is the single most important technical detail. The ideal start point on the AP is just medial to the lateral tibial spine, and on the LATERAL is at the anterior edge of the tibial plateau, in line with the anterior cortex, immediately adjacent to the articular margin. A start point too lateral causes valgus; too medial causes varus; too anterior causes apex-posterior (procurvatum); too posterior risks the posterior neurovascular structures and causes apex-anterior deformity. The safe zone avoiding intra-articular damage is between the tibial spines, and a suprapatellar (semi-extended) approach improves the trajectory for proximal fractures and reduces anterior knee pain in some studies.
  • Proximal-third tibial fractures deform into APEX ANTERIOR (procurvatum) and VALGUS because of the pull of the patellar tendon/quadriceps on the proximal fragment (extension) and the pes anserinus/anterior compartment, plus the tendency for an anteriorly placed start point. Strategies to correct this: a semi-extended (suprapatellar or parapatellar) nailing position, a more lateral and proximal-anterior start point, BLOCKING (POLLER) SCREWS placed in the concavity of the deformity (posterior in the proximal fragment for procurvatum, lateral for valgus) to functionally narrow the metaphyseal canal and direct the nail, a unicortical plate or clamp, and a femoral distractor.
  • Blocking (Poller) screws work by narrowing the effective medullary canal in the wide metaphysis, redirecting the nail and increasing construct stability — place the screw on the concave side of the deformity (i.e. in the segment that the nail must be pushed away from).
  • Distal-third tibial fracture with residual valgus after nailing — to correct: fix the fibula with a plate (restoring length and alignment on the lateral side), use a blocking screw, apply a unicortical plate, or use a clamp/femoral distractor before passing the nail. Simply exchanging for a larger nail after the deformity is established does not reliably correct it.
  • Compartment syndrome is most common with tibial shaft fractures; nailing does not prevent it and the diagnosis requires vigilance post-operatively (see the Basic Science topic).
  • A valgus malunion after tibial nailing treated by removing the nail requires correction of the deformity before or during renailing — the nail alone will follow the malaligned canal; use a blocking screw or provisional plate.
  • IM nailing versus plating for extra-articular distal tibial fractures: nailing has less wound complication and infection risk, plating has better control of alignment in very distal fractures. Both have comparable union rates; nailing does not have a higher rate of nonunion, which is a common false statement.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity.
  • SPRINT Investigators (Bhandari M, Schemitsch EH, Canadian). Randomized trial of reamed and unreamed intramedullary nailing of tibial shaft fractures. JBJS Am 2008.
  • Krettek C, Miclau T, Schandelmaier P, Stephan C, Möhlmann U, Tscherne H. The mechanical effect of blocking screws ('Poller screws') in stabilizing tibia fractures with short proximal or distal fragments after insertion of small-diameter intramedullary nails. J Orthop Trauma 1999.
  • McConnell T, Tornetta P et al. Tibial portal placement: the radiographic correlate of the anatomic safe zone. J Orthop Trauma 2001.
  • Vallier HA, Cureton BA, Patterson BM. Randomized, prospective comparison of plate versus intramedullary nail fixation for distal tibia shaft fractures. J Orthop Trauma 2011.
6questions

Hip dislocation & femoral head fracture (Pipkin)

Urgent reduction, blocks to reduction, and the Pipkin classification.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2023, 2024F, 2025 (x2)

  • A traumatic hip dislocation is a surgical emergency — reduce within 6 hours to minimise the risk of osteonecrosis, which rises markedly with delay (AVN rates of ~5% with reduction under 6 hours, rising to 20–50% or more beyond 6–12 hours). Posterior dislocation accounts for ~90%.
  • Blocks to closed reduction of a posterior hip dislocation: an incarcerated osteochondral or femoral head fragment, an inverted/interposed labrum, the piriformis or other short external rotators, a buttonholed femoral head through the capsule, and an associated femoral head or acetabular wall fracture. The most common single block is an interposed bony fragment or the buttonholed capsule.
  • Post-reduction CT is MANDATORY for every hip dislocation — to identify incarcerated fragments, marginal impaction, femoral head fractures and acetabular fractures that are invisible on plain films. Do not accept a 'concentric' plain film as adequate. Look for asymmetric joint space widening as a clue to interposed tissue.
  • Pipkin classification of femoral head fractures: type I — fracture INFERIOR to the fovea (below the weightbearing surface — better prognosis, often can be excised); type II — fracture SUPERIOR to the fovea (involves the weightbearing surface — requires anatomic fixation); type III — either type with an associated FEMORAL NECK fracture (the worst prognosis, highest AVN risk); type IV — either type with an associated ACETABULAR fracture.
  • The most likely indication to FIX (rather than excise) a femoral head fracture is a LARGE fragment involving the weightbearing (superior) portion of the head that prevents a concentric reduction or is a substantial part of the articular surface — i.e. a Pipkin type II. Small inferior (Pipkin I) fragments below the weightbearing dome are frequently excised.
  • Surgical approach for a Pipkin II fracture: the anterior (Smith-Petersen) approach gives direct access to the anterosuperior femoral head where these fragments lie, and — importantly — it does not further compromise the posterior retinacular blood supply (the medial femoral circumflex artery), which has usually already been injured by a posterior dislocation. The internervous interval is between sartorius/rectus femoris (femoral nerve) and tensor fascia lata (superior gluteal nerve). The alternative is a surgical hip dislocation (trochanteric flip, Ganz), which gives 360° access to the head with protection of the MFCA and is increasingly favoured.
  • Common Pipkin misconceptions to recognise: Pipkin type I does NOT have a worse prognosis than type II (it is better — the fragment is below the weightbearing surface); AVN risk is driven by the dislocation and the associated neck fracture (type III), not by the head fragment itself; and not all femoral head fractures require fixation.
  • Sciatic nerve injury occurs in ~10–20% of posterior hip dislocations, with the peroneal division most affected (more lateral, more tethered, less connective tissue). Most are neurapraxic with partial recovery; document the examination before and after reduction. A sciatic palsy after reduction that was not present before mandates imaging to exclude an entrapped fragment.
  • Anterior dislocations are less common, associated with femoral head impaction/indentation fractures and a higher rate of associated femoral head chondral injury; they carry a lower rate of sciatic nerve injury but a similar urgency for reduction.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity; Pelvis and Acetabulum.
  • Pipkin G. Treatment of grade IV fracture-dislocation of the hip. JBJS Am 1957.
  • Giannoudis PV et al. Operative treatment of displaced fractures of the femoral head. Injury 2009.
  • Ganz R, Gill TJ, Gautier E, Ganz K, Krügel N, Berlemann U. Surgical dislocation of the adult hip. JBJS Br 2001.
  • Sahin V et al. Traumatic dislocation and fracture-dislocation of the hip: a long-term follow-up study. J Trauma 2003.
6questions

Tibial pilon fracture

Staged management, approach selection and soft-tissue complications.

4 of 7 sittings2021, 2022 (x2), 2023, 2024S (x2)

  • The pilon fracture is a soft-tissue injury with an associated fracture — this framing dictates management. The historical experience of immediate ORIF through swollen tissue produced catastrophic wound breakdown and infection rates approaching 40%.
  • Staged protocol (Sirkin/Patterson): stage 1 — spanning external fixation (with fibular ORIF if it aids length and alignment) within 24 hours, with CT after the fixator is applied (the CT is far more useful once length is restored); stage 2 — definitive ORIF at 7–21 days, once the swelling has resolved and the SKIN WRINKLES return. This reduces wound complications dramatically.
  • Measures that reduce soft-tissue complications in high-energy pilon fractures — the standard list: staged/delayed definitive fixation, spanning external fixation, careful incision planning with adequate skin bridges, minimally invasive/percutaneous techniques, elevation, and the use of an anterolateral rather than combined anteromedial-plus-direct-lateral approach. EARLY definitive bone stabilisation (immediate ORIF) is the intervention that INCREASES complications — the classic 'all reduce soft tissue complications EXCEPT'.
  • Skin bridge: the historical rule is a minimum of 7 cm between incisions; combining an anteromedial tibial incision with a direct lateral fibular incision creates the narrowest bridge and the highest rate of skin necrosis — this specific combination is the answer to 'which combination of distal tibial approaches is associated with increased skin necrosis'.
  • Anterolateral approach: the superficial peroneal nerve limits the proximal extension (it emerges from the fascia ~10–12 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral malleolus) — this is the answer to 'what limits your proximal extension' and 'the proximal limit of the anterolateral approach'.
  • Management principles for the articular reconstruction (Rüedi & Allgöwer): (1) restore fibular length and alignment; (2) reconstruct the tibial articular surface; (3) bone graft the metaphyseal defect; (4) buttress the medial tibia. Modern practice modifies this with staged treatment and locked plating.
  • High-energy open pilon fractures: the falsehood to recognise is that these can be treated with immediate definitive internal fixation — they cannot. The options after external fixation include definitive ORIF once soft tissues permit, definitive external fixation/ring fixator (Ilizarov), and primary ankle arthrodesis in the most severe cases with unreconstructible articular damage.
  • Locking versus non-locking plates in the distal tibia — the exam presents an RCT scenario: 5/15 in the locked group and 5/20 in the non-locked group requiring hardware removal means 33% vs 25%, so the locked group had a HIGHER rate of reoperation for hardware removal (locked plates are bulkier and more prominent over the subcutaneous distal tibia). Be careful to compute the rates rather than compare the raw numbers.
  • Outcomes: even with a perfect reduction, post-traumatic ankle arthritis is common and functional outcomes are frequently poor after high-energy pilon fractures. Patients should be counselled that recovery takes 1–2 years and that a return to full pre-injury function is uncommon.
  • Radiation in pregnancy: a 14-week-pregnant patient with a pilon fracture can safely undergo the necessary imaging — a single extremity radiograph delivers a negligible fetal dose (<0.01 mGy), and no single diagnostic study approaches the 50 mGy threshold; shield the abdomen where it does not obscure the field.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity.
  • Sirkin M, Sanders R, DiPasquale T, Herscovici D. A staged protocol for soft tissue management in the treatment of complex pilon fractures. J Orthop Trauma 1999.
  • Patterson MJ, Cole JD. Two-staged delayed open reduction and internal fixation of severe pilon fractures. J Orthop Trauma 1999.
  • Rüedi TP, Allgöwer M. The operative treatment of intra-articular fractures of the lower end of the tibia. CORR 1979.
  • Herscovici D, Sanders RW, Infante A, DiPasquale T. Böhler incision: an extensile anterolateral approach to the foot and ankle. J Orthop Trauma 2005.
6questions

Tibial plateau fracture

Schatzker classification, reduction parameters, approaches and associated injuries.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2021 (x2), 2022, 2024F, 2025

  • Schatzker classification: I lateral split; II lateral split-depression; III pure lateral depression; IV medial plateau fracture (the highest-energy pattern despite the low number — associated with knee dislocation, vascular and neurologic injury); V bicondylar; VI metaphyseal-diaphyseal dissociation.
  • A medial plateau fracture-dislocation (Schatzker IV) is a knee dislocation until proven otherwise — it is associated with cruciate and collateral ligament injury, peroneal nerve injury and popliteal artery injury. A middle-aged motorcyclist with a medial plateau fracture and a warm foot with palpable pulses still requires ABI measurement and serial vascular examination — palpable pulses do not exclude an intimal injury.
  • Which structures are NOT injured: in a medial plateau fracture-dislocation with an associated lateral plateau depression, the medial joint line and the MCL are characteristically PRISTINE — the medial plateau fails in compression while the lateral side fails in tension, so it is the LCL/posterolateral corner and the cruciates that are torn. Read the imaging description carefully.
  • Parameters for an acceptable reduction of a tibial plateau fracture: restoration of the articular surface (step-off <2 mm, though the tolerance is debated and up to 4–5 mm of depression may be accepted in low-demand patients), restoration of the mechanical axis/coronal alignment (the most important determinant of long-term outcome), restoration of condylar width, and restoration of the tibial slope (sagittal alignment). Restoring the length of the fibula is NOT a parameter of tibial plateau reduction — the fibula plays no role, and this is the classic 'all are parameters EXCEPT'.
  • Coronal alignment/mechanical axis is a stronger predictor of outcome than articular step-off — a knee left in varus does poorly regardless of a perfect articular reduction.
  • Lateral plating biomechanics: for a lateral split-depression fracture, subchondral raft screws placed immediately beneath the elevated articular surface, supported by a lateral locking plate, provide the best biomechanical support against re-depression. The number and position of the subchondral screws (a 'raft' of screws just under the joint line) matters more than the plate itself. Bone void filler (calcium phosphate cement, which has higher compressive strength than calcium sulfate and reduces subsidence compared with autograft) supports the elevated fragment.
  • Posteromedial fragments are a marker of instability and cannot be controlled from a lateral plate — they require a posteromedial buttress plate through a posteromedial (Lobenhoffer) approach, often with the patient prone or in a floppy lateral position.
  • Posterior approach to the tibial plateau: gives direct access to posterior column fragments that cannot be reduced from anterior; the popliteal neurovascular bundle is protected by retracting the medial head of gastrocnemius laterally; it is technically demanding but is the correct answer for a posterior shear fragment.
  • Soft-tissue management: high-energy bicondylar fractures (Schatzker V/VI) are managed in a staged fashion — spanning external fixation first, definitive fixation at 7–14 days once the soft tissues permit — the same principle as the pilon.
  • Compartment syndrome must be actively excluded in Schatzker IV, V and VI fractures — the risk is high, and a knee dislocation equivalent with vascular injury and reperfusion is the highest-risk scenario.
  • Vancomycin powder introduced into the wound at the time of plateau fixation reduces deep gram-positive infection but shifts the organism profile toward gram-negatives — the standard answer.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity.
  • Schatzker J (Canadian, Toronto), McBroom R, Bruce D. The tibial plateau fracture: the Toronto experience 1968–1975. CORR 1979.
  • Barei DP, Nork SE, Mills WJ, Coles CP, Henley MB, Benirschke SK. Functional outcomes of severe bicondylar tibial plateau fractures treated with dual incisions and medial and lateral plates. JBJS Am 2006.
  • Russell TA, Leighton RK (Canadian). Comparison of autogenous bone graft and endothermic calcium phosphate cement for defect augmentation in tibial plateau fractures. JBJS Am 2008.
  • Lobenhoffer P et al. The posteromedial approach to the tibial plateau. Oper Orthop Traumatol.
5questions

Patella fracture

Fixation options, the modern shift away from tension band wiring, and outcomes.

5 of 7 sittings2020, 2022, 2023, 2024S, 2024F

  • The patella is a sesamoid within the extensor mechanism; its function is to increase the moment arm of the quadriceps, improving extensor efficiency by ~30%. Preserve the patella wherever possible — total patellectomy reduces extension strength by 30–50%.
  • Treatment by pattern: non-displaced (<2 mm step, <3 mm separation) with an intact extensor mechanism (the patient can perform a straight-leg raise) → non-operative treatment in a brace/cylinder cast in extension with early weightbearing. Displaced fractures or an incompetent extensor mechanism → ORIF.
  • Modified anterior tension band wiring converts the tensile force of the quadriceps into compression at the articular surface during knee flexion; it requires a simple transverse pattern with an intact opposite cortex. The dominant complication is SYMPTOMATIC HARDWARE, with reported reoperation/removal rates of 30–60% — this is the single most important practical fact about patella fracture fixation.
  • Modern practice has shifted: cannulated screws with an anterior tension band through the screws (biomechanically superior to K-wires with a wire), suture-based tension band constructs using heavy non-absorbable suture instead of metal wire (markedly reducing hardware irritation with comparable strength), and plate fixation (mesh or low-profile anterior plates) for comminuted fractures, which has better biomechanical performance and lower hardware-removal rates than tension band wiring in comminuted patterns.
  • Comminuted fractures are NOT suitable for a simple tension band — they collapse. Use a plate, or a combination of interfragmentary screws with a tension band, or (for an unreconstructible pole) a partial patellectomy with repair of the tendon to the remaining patella, which preserves function far better than total patellectomy.
  • Partial patellectomy (for an unsalvageable inferior or superior pole) requires reattachment of the tendon close to the articular surface — attaching it anteriorly tilts the remaining fragment and causes articular incongruity and anterior knee pain.
  • Outcomes: even with an anatomic reduction, patellofemoral arthritis, anterior knee pain, stiffness and quadriceps weakness are common, and a substantial proportion of patients have persistent symptoms at long-term follow-up. The articular reduction should be within 2 mm, assessed directly (through a small arthrotomy or with fluoroscopy in the skyline view).
  • Periprosthetic patella fracture after TKA: the great majority are treated non-operatively if the extensor mechanism is intact and the component is well fixed — surgical outcomes are poor with high complication rates. Surgery is reserved for extensor mechanism disruption or a loose patellar component (usually removal of the component and patelloplasty rather than revision).
  • Post-operative rehabilitation emphasises early protected range of motion, since stiffness is a major cause of disability. Weightbearing in full extension in a brace is generally permitted immediately.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity.
  • Melvin JS, Mehta S. Patellar fractures in adults. JAAOS 2011.
  • Wild M et al. Fixed-angle plate osteosynthesis of the patella: an alternative to tension wiring? Clin Biomech 2010.
  • Hoshino CM et al. Complications following tension-band fixation of patellar fractures with cannulated screws compared with Kirschner wires. JBJS Am 2013.
  • LeBrun CT, Langford JR, Sagi HC. Functional outcomes after operatively treated patella fractures. J Orthop Trauma 2012.
4questions

Fat embolism syndrome & ARDS

Pathophysiology, diagnosis, and the interventions that actually reduce embolic load.

3 of 7 sittings2021, 2022 (x2), 2024F

  • Fat embolism syndrome (FES) classically presents 24–72 hours after a long bone fracture with the triad of hypoxaemia/respiratory distress, neurologic dysfunction (confusion, agitation, coma), and a PETECHIAL RASH (in the axillae, conjunctivae, chest and neck — the most specific but least common feature, present in ~20–50%). Thrombocytopenia, anaemia, fever and tachycardia are supportive (Gurd and Wilson criteria).
  • Risk factors: long bone fractures (femur most of all), multiple fractures, bilateral femur fractures, closed fractures (higher than open, because the intramedullary pressure is contained), young patients with high-pressure marrow, and reamed intramedullary nailing. Bilateral femoral shaft fractures carry a substantially higher risk of FES, ARDS and mortality.
  • Factors that increase the risk of ARDS in a polytrauma patient with a femur fracture — the strongest is the severity of the associated CHEST INJURY (pulmonary contusion), followed by shock/hypoperfusion and massive transfusion, and prolonged/reamed intramedullary nailing performed in an under-resuscitated patient (the 'second hit'). The biggest contributing factor for ARDS in a patient with a femoral shaft fracture and multiple other injuries is the associated pulmonary/chest injury and the degree of shock, not the femur fracture in isolation.
  • Interventions shown to reduce the embolic load during nailing — the exam list: venting the medullary canal (drilling a distal vent hole to release intramedullary pressure), using a smaller-diameter reamer with sharp reamer heads and slow, gentle advancement, avoiding a tight reamer-to-nail fit and over-reaming appropriately, irrigation/lavage of the canal, using an unreamed or smaller nail in a physiologically compromised patient, and avoiding excessive intramedullary pressure. Three methods commonly cited: venting the canal, using a smaller/sharper reamer with slower advancement, and lavaging the canal.
  • Early fracture stabilisation reduces the incidence of FES and ARDS compared with prolonged traction — this is one of the foundational arguments for early fixation, provided the patient is resuscitated.
  • Treatment is SUPPORTIVE — oxygen, ventilatory support (including PEEP), haemodynamic support, and correction of hypovolaemia. Corticosteroids may have a prophylactic role in high-risk patients but are not established treatment; heparin and alcohol infusions are historical and not used. Most patients recover fully with supportive care; mortality is ~5–15%.
  • Distinguish from pulmonary embolism (usually later, with a normal neurologic examination and no rash) and from cerebral fat embolism (which may present with an unexplained decline in consciousness with a normal head CT; MRI shows a 'starfield' pattern of scattered high-signal lesions on diffusion-weighted imaging).
  • Prevention in the polytrauma patient: adequate resuscitation before definitive fixation, damage control external fixation in the physiologically compromised, and gentle reaming technique.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: General; Orthopaedic Dilemmas.
  • Gurd AR, Wilson RI. The fat embolism syndrome. JBJS Br 1974.
  • Pape HC, Giannoudis P, Krettek C. The timing of fracture treatment in polytrauma patients: relevance of damage control orthopedic surgery. Am J Surg 2002.
  • Bone LB, Johnson KD, Weigelt J, Scheinberg R. Early versus delayed stabilization of femoral fractures: a prospective randomized study. JBJS Am 1989.
  • Pitto RP et al. Prophylaxis of fat and bone marrow embolism in cemented total hip arthroplasty. CORR 1998.
4questions

Vascular injury & limb ischaemia in trauma

Hard and soft signs, the ABI, and the sequence of repair.

3 of 7 sittings2020 (x2), 2021, 2022

  • Hard signs of vascular injury (mandate immediate operative exploration or, in selected cases, on-table angiography): pulsatile bleeding, an expanding or pulsatile haematoma, a palpable thrill or audible bruit, and the signs of ischaemia (the 6 Ps — pulselessness, pallor, paraesthesia, pain, paralysis, poikilothermia). Soft signs (a history of significant bleeding, a non-expanding haematoma, a proximity wound, an unexplained neurologic deficit, a diminished but present pulse) warrant ABI measurement and further imaging.
  • Ankle-brachial index (ABI): ≥0.9 with a normal examination effectively excludes a surgically significant arterial injury and permits serial observation; <0.9 mandates CT angiography or exploration. This is the key screening tool in blunt injury, particularly in knee dislocation.
  • Palpable pulses do NOT exclude an intimal injury, which may thrombose hours later — this is why serial examination is essential in a knee dislocation and in a medial tibial plateau fracture-dislocation.
  • The sequence in a mangled or ischaemic limb: restore perfusion first. In practice: (1) reduce the fracture/dislocation (this alone frequently restores flow — always reduce before declaring a vascular injury); (2) if ischaemia persists, place a temporary intraluminal SHUNT to restore perfusion while skeletal stabilisation is performed; (3) skeletal stabilisation (usually external fixation); (4) definitive vascular repair; (5) fasciotomy (which should be liberal and is essentially routine after prolonged ischaemia and reperfusion). Warm ischaemia beyond 6 hours dramatically increases amputation rates and the risk of reperfusion injury.
  • In a haemodynamically unstable polytrauma patient with an ipsilateral acetabular fracture, femur fracture and a Gustilo IIIC pulseless, insensate tibia going for laparotomy — the priorities are damage control: control haemorrhage (laparotomy takes precedence for the life-threatening injury), place a temporary vascular shunt to the tibia, apply an external fixator, and return for definitive care once resuscitated. Definitive vascular reconstruction and complex limb salvage are deferred.
  • Compartment syndrome after revascularisation is the rule, not the exception — perform prophylactic four-compartment fasciotomy when the ischaemic time approaches or exceeds 4–6 hours.
  • Which vessels matter: the popliteal artery (tethered proximally at the adductor hiatus and distally at the soleal arch — hence its vulnerability in knee dislocation, with a ~20–30% injury rate), the brachial artery (supracondylar humerus fractures, elbow dislocation), the superficial femoral artery in the adductor canal, and the posterior tibial/anterior tibial in the leg.
  • A stab wound to the anteromedial thigh at the junction of the upper and middle thirds (the adductor canal) places the superficial femoral artery, femoral vein and saphenous nerve at risk — the SCIATIC NERVE is in the posterior compartment and is the structure LEAST at risk.
  • Duplex ultrasound and CT angiography have largely replaced conventional angiography for diagnosis; on-table angiography is used when the patient is too unstable to travel.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: General; Orthopaedic Dilemmas.
  • Mills WJ, Barei DP, McNair P. The value of the ankle-brachial index for diagnosing arterial injury after knee dislocation. J Trauma 2004.
  • Feliciano DV et al. EAST practice management guidelines for the evaluation and management of penetrating lower extremity arterial trauma. J Trauma 2012.
  • Gifford SM et al. Effect of temporary shunting on extremity vascular injury. J Vasc Surg 2009.
3questions

Gunshot wounds & ballistic injury

Ballistics, wound severity and management.

3 of 7 sittings2020, 2023, 2024S

  • Kinetic energy = ½mv² — so VELOCITY is far more important than mass in determining wounding potential. High-velocity (>2000 ft/s — military rifles, hunting rifles) versus low-velocity (<2000 ft/s — most handguns) is the fundamental distinction. A shotgun at close range behaves as a high-energy injury because the entire mass is delivered as a unit.
  • Mechanisms of tissue injury: the permanent cavity (the tissue directly crushed by the projectile) and the TEMPORARY cavity (radial stretching of tissue by the passage of the projectile, which then collapses). The size of the temporary cavity is proportional to the ENERGY TRANSFERRED to the tissue — this is the key concept and the correct answer to 'the size of the cavity is proportional to...'. Tissue with low elasticity (bone, liver, brain) is damaged most by cavitation; elastic tissue (muscle, lung, bowel) tolerates it better.
  • Factors that increase energy transfer and therefore wound severity: tumbling/yaw of the bullet, fragmentation, deformation (hollow-point/expanding bullets), a longer path through tissue, and higher velocity. A through-and-through wound (entrance AND exit) means the projectile RETAINED energy and left the body — so LESS energy was transferred to the tissue than if the bullet had come to rest inside (which deposits all its energy). Therefore the statement 'an entrance and exit wound has a higher impact than an entrance only' is FALSE — a retained bullet transferred all its energy.
  • The worst injury pattern on an exam stem is typically the high-velocity rifle wound with fragmentation and bone comminution, or a close-range shotgun blast — both transfer maximal energy.
  • Management of LOW-velocity gunshot fractures: local wound care, tetanus prophylaxis, a short course of oral or IV antibiotics (typically 24–48 hours of a first-generation cephalosporin), and treatment of the fracture on its own merits. They do NOT routinely require formal operative débridement — this is the important management point, and low-velocity gunshot fractures are generally treated as closed fractures.
  • High-velocity injuries require formal, often serial, operative débridement, are treated as Gustilo III open fractures, and frequently require staged reconstruction.
  • Specific situations requiring surgery regardless of velocity: vascular injury, compartment syndrome, an intra-articular bullet or fragment (lead can cause synovitis and systemic lead toxicity — remove intra-articular lead), gross contamination, a transabdominal trajectory (bowel contamination — these require operative treatment and broader antibiotics), significant soft-tissue loss, and neurologic compromise requiring exploration.
  • Nerve injuries with low-velocity gunshot wounds are usually neurapraxias from the temporary cavity and recover spontaneously in the majority — observation with EMG at 6 weeks is appropriate unless the nerve is known to be transected.
  • Do not attempt to determine entrance versus exit wounds or to document forensic details beyond an objective description — describe the wounds factually, preserve clothing and any retrieved projectiles, and document the chain of custody.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: General.
  • Bartlett CS. Clinical update: gunshot wound ballistics. CORR 2003.
  • Dougherty PJ et al. Gunshot wounds: epidemiology, wound ballistics, and soft-tissue treatment. Instr Course Lect 2009.
  • Hoekstra SM et al. / Dickey RL et al. Efficacy of antibiotics in low-velocity gunshot fractures. J Orthop Trauma 1989.
3questions

Trauma in pregnancy

Resuscitating two patients.

3 of 7 sittings2024S, 2024F, 2025

  • The fundamental principle: RESUSCITATE THE MOTHER — the best treatment for the fetus is optimal maternal resuscitation. Maternal hypotension and hypoxia are the greatest threats to the fetus.
  • Physiologic changes of pregnancy that mislead: plasma volume increases by 40–50% (a physiologic anaemia), heart rate rises by 10–20 bpm, blood pressure falls in the second trimester, so a pregnant woman can lose 30–35% of her blood volume before showing hypotension — and the fetus is compromised long before the mother appears unstable (uterine vasoconstriction preserves maternal pressure at fetal expense). Tachycardia and fetal distress are the early signs.
  • After ~20 weeks, tilt the patient 15–30° to the LEFT (or manually displace the uterus) to relieve aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus — supine positioning can reduce cardiac output by 30% and cause profound hypotension.
  • Imaging is NOT contraindicated. The threshold for deterministic fetal effects is 50 mGy (5 rad), and no single diagnostic study approaches this — a plain extremity radiograph delivers <0.01 mGy, a chest radiograph negligible fetal dose, and CT of the abdomen/pelvis approximately 25 mGy, which remains below the threshold and is not contraindicated when clinically necessary. Necessary imaging should never be withheld — this is the most important and most frequently tested point. Shield where it does not obscure the field, and prefer ultrasound and MRI (without gadolinium) where equally informative.
  • Teratogenic risk is greatest at 2–15 weeks (organogenesis); before implantation the effect is all-or-none; after 15 weeks the main risk is a small increase in childhood malignancy.
  • Obstetric involvement is mandatory — continuous fetal monitoring (cardiotocography for at least 4–6 hours after significant trauma, longer if there are contractions or abnormalities), assessment for placental abruption (the commonest cause of fetal death after blunt trauma, presenting with contractions, bleeding, a tender uterus and fetal distress), uterine rupture, and preterm labour. Kleihauer-Betke testing and Rh immunoglobulin for the Rh-negative mother.
  • Medications: avoid tetracyclines (fetal teeth/bone staining), fluoroquinolones (cartilage), and — relatively — aminoglycosides (fetal ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity). Cephalosporins and penicillins are safe. Avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester (premature ductus closure). LMWH is safe for VTE prophylaxis; warfarin is teratogenic.
  • Surgery: necessary orthopaedic surgery should not be delayed — the second trimester is the safest window for elective procedures, but urgent surgery proceeds at any stage with obstetric and anaesthetic input, left lateral tilt, and fetal monitoring. Perimortem caesarean section should be considered within 4 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest after 23–24 weeks.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: General; Medical Conditions.
  • American College of Surgeons. Advanced Trauma Life Support, 10th ed — Trauma in Pregnancy.
  • ACOG Committee Opinion 723: Guidelines for Diagnostic Imaging During Pregnancy and Lactation, 2017.
  • Mendez-Figueroa H et al. Trauma in pregnancy: an updated systematic review. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2013.
  • Jain V et al. (SOGC Canadian) Guidelines for the management of a pregnant trauma patient. J Obstet Gynaecol Can 2015.
2questions

Morel-Lavallée lesion & soft-tissue degloving

The closed internal degloving injury.

2 of 7 sittings2023, 2024F

  • A Morel-Lavallée lesion is a closed internal degloving injury — a shear force separates the subcutaneous fat and dermis from the underlying deep fascia, disrupting the perforating vessels and lymphatics and creating a cavity filled with haemolymph, blood, fat and necrotic debris, lined by a fibrous capsule if chronic.
  • The most common location is the GREATER TROCHANTER/proximal lateral thigh (the classic answer), followed by the flank/lumbodorsal region, the gluteal region, the knee (where it is common in American football) and the scapular region. It is strongly associated with pelvic and acetabular fractures (occurring in ~10–30% of these injuries).
  • Clinical features: fluctuance, a soft-tissue swelling with skin hypermobility, contour deformity, ecchymosis, and a characteristic area of decreased cutaneous sensation over the lesion (from injury to the cutaneous nerves). The overlying skin may be devitalised. It is frequently missed on initial assessment — a third or more are diagnosed late.
  • Imaging: MRI is the study of choice and characterises the lesion by its contents and chronicity (Mellado classification, types 1–6, based on the signal characteristics and the presence of a capsule). Ultrasound is useful for aspiration guidance.
  • The critical management point is the INFECTION RISK: a Morel-Lavallée lesion is culture-positive in up to a third of cases, and operating through or near an unrecognised lesion is associated with markedly higher rates of deep surgical site infection after pelvic and acetabular fixation. The lesion must be identified and addressed before or at the time of definitive fixation.
  • Management: small acute lesions — compression dressings and observation, with percutaneous aspiration if they persist. Larger or persistent lesions — percutaneous drainage with débridement and irrigation (often through small incisions with a brush/curette to remove the fibrous lining), followed by compression and a drain, or sclerodesis (doxycycline, talc, fibrin glue) for recurrent lesions. Chronic encapsulated lesions require open débridement with excision of the capsule.
  • Do not simply aspirate and ignore — recurrence is high, and the fibrous capsule prevents the cavity from obliterating. Cultures should be taken at the time of any drainage, and definitive fixation may need to be staged if the lesion is infected.
  • The lesion typically does not resolve spontaneously once a capsule has formed (usually beyond 3 weeks), and can persist for months to years as a fluctuant mass.
References4
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Pelvis and Acetabulum; Orthopaedic Dilemmas.
  • Hak DJ, Olson SA, Matta JM. Diagnosis and management of closed internal degloving injuries associated with pelvic and acetabular fractures: the Morel-Lavallée lesion. J Trauma 1997.
  • Tseng S, Tornetta P. Percutaneous management of Morel-Lavallée lesions. JBJS Am 2006.
  • Mellado JM, Bencardino JT. Morel-Lavallée lesion: review with emphasis on MR imaging. Magn Reson Imaging Clin N Am 2005.
2questions

Segmental bone defect: Masquelet & bone transport

The induced membrane technique and alternatives for critical-sized defects.

2 of 7 sittings2020, 2025

  • The Masquelet (induced membrane) technique is a TWO-STAGE procedure: Stage 1 — radical débridement of all necrotic and infected bone and soft tissue, insertion of a PMMA cement spacer into the defect, and stable skeletal fixation (usually external fixation, sometimes a plate or nail) with soft-tissue coverage. Stage 2 — at 6–8 weeks (the classic window, when the membrane is biologically most active), the spacer is carefully removed WITHOUT damaging the membrane, and the cavity is packed with cancellous autograft (often with allograft or graft extenders for large volumes).
  • The induced membrane is the biological engine of the technique: it is a richly vascularised, synovium-like pseudo-membrane that secretes growth factors — VEGF, TGF-β1 and BMP-2 — and osteoinductive/osteogenic factors, and it acts as a barrier preventing soft-tissue ingrowth and graft resorption while providing a vascular bed. Its bioactivity peaks at approximately 4–8 weeks and declines thereafter — hence the timing of stage 2. The membrane must be preserved at all costs.
  • Antibiotic-loaded cement is used in the spacer when infection is present or suspected, providing high local antibiotic concentrations. The spacer must fill the defect completely and overlap the bone ends.
  • Graft volume is the practical challenge: a large defect (e.g. 7–10 cm of tibia) requires a very large volume of cancellous graft. The reamer-irrigator-aspirator (RIA) from the ipsilateral or contralateral femur is the best single source, yielding 40–90 mL of graft with growth-factor content comparable to iliac crest and less donor-site pain — the answer to 'the optimal choice when 50 mL of graft is needed'. Bilateral iliac crest yields substantially less. RIA carries a risk of iatrogenic femoral fracture and blood loss.
  • The technique works for very large defects (published series up to 25 cm), does not require microsurgical expertise, and tolerates infection better than a vascularised graft. Limitations: it requires two operations, a long time to union and full weightbearing, the graft consolidates as trabecular rather than cortical bone initially, and it does not correct limb-length discrepancy — a defect of 10 cm treated by Masquelet leaves the limb short unless combined with a lengthening procedure.
  • Alternatives for critical-sized defects: distraction osteogenesis/bone transport (Ilizarov) — restores both bone and length and produces true cortical regenerate, but requires prolonged frame time and has a high rate of docking-site nonunion and pin-site infection; vascularised free fibular transfer — living cortical bone that hypertrophies, ideal for defects >6 cm in the young, but requires microsurgical expertise and carries donor-site morbidity (contracture of the FLEXOR HALLUCIS LONGUS is the classic complication of vascularised fibula harvest, producing a clawed great toe); and amputation, which remains a legitimate option.
  • Prerequisites for any reconstruction: eradication of infection, a healthy vascularised soft-tissue envelope (flap coverage as needed), stable fixation, and an optimised host (nutrition, smoking cessation, glycaemic control, vitamin D).
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas; Trauma.
  • Masquelet AC, Fitoussi F, Begue T, Muller GP. Reconstruction of the long bones by the induced membrane and spongy autograft. Ann Chir Plast Esthet 2000.
  • Pelissier P, Masquelet AC et al. Induced membranes secrete growth factors including vascular and osteoinductive factors and could stimulate bone regeneration. J Orthop Res 2004.
  • Giannoudis PV, Faour O, Goff T, Kanakaris N, Dimitriou R. Masquelet technique for the treatment of bone defects. Injury 2011.
  • Cox G et al. Reamer-irrigator-aspirator indications and clinical results: a systematic review. Int Orthop 2011.
1question

Femoral neck stress fracture

The high-risk stress fracture that must not be missed.

1 of 7 sittings2020

  • A femoral neck stress fracture in a young athlete or military recruit is a HIGH-RISK stress fracture — missed or mismanaged, it can progress to a complete displaced fracture with catastrophic AVN and nonunion in a young patient. It should be treated with a high index of suspicion for any young, active patient with insidious groin or anterior thigh pain that worsens with activity.
  • Presentation: gradual-onset groin pain worse with weightbearing and at the extremes of hip rotation, an antalgic gait, a positive log-roll and pain at the extremes of internal rotation, and — importantly — NORMAL PLAIN RADIOGRAPHS in the early stages. MRI is the investigation of choice (marrow oedema and a low-signal fracture line); bone scan is sensitive but less specific.
  • The critical distinction is TENSION-side versus COMPRESSION-side: the SUPEROLATERAL (tension) side experiences distraction forces and is UNSTABLE — these lesions have a high risk of displacement and require PROPHYLACTIC INTERNAL FIXATION (percutaneous cannulated screws) regardless of size. The INFEROMEDIAL (compression) side experiences compressive forces and is relatively stable — small lesions can be treated with strict protected/non-weightbearing and close radiographic follow-up.
  • Within the compression-side group, the size matters: a lesion involving >50% of the femoral neck width, a fracture line that progresses on serial imaging, an associated joint effusion, or failure of symptoms to settle should prompt prophylactic fixation. A 35% inferomedial (compression-side) lesion with an effusion sits in the grey zone — most surgeons would treat with strict non-weightbearing, close serial MRI/radiographs and a very low threshold for fixation, and fixation is a defensible answer.
