  • Any DISPLACED femoral neck stress fracture is a surgical emergency requiring urgent anatomic reduction and fixation, with an AVN risk of 20–40%.
  • Investigate the underlying cause: the female athlete triad / relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) — low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction and low bone mineral density — is the key association in female athletes and must be addressed with a multidisciplinary approach or the fracture will recur. Check vitamin D, calcium intake, and consider a DEXA scan and endocrine assessment; screen for eating disorders sensitively.
  • Other contributing factors: a rapid increase in training volume or intensity, a change in running surface or footwear, coxa vara, femoral neck geometry, smoking, and medications (corticosteroids, bisphosphonates in atypical cases).
  • Return to activity is gradual and guided by symptom resolution and imaging evidence of healing, typically over 3–6 months, with correction of the underlying training and metabolic contributors.
  • Other high-risk stress fractures requiring the same aggressive approach: anterior tibial cortex ('dreaded black line'), medial malleolus, tarsal navicular, fifth metatarsal base, talar neck, sesamoid, and the pars interarticularis.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity; Sports.
  • Boden BP, Osbahr DC. High-risk stress fractures: evaluation and treatment. JAAOS 2000.
  • Fullerton LR, Snowdy HA. Femoral neck stress fractures. AJSM 1988.
  • Egol KA, Koval KJ, Kummer F, Frankel VH. Stress fractures of the femoral neck. CORR 1998.
  • De Souza MJ et al. Female Athlete Triad Coalition consensus statement. Br J Sports Med 2014.
1question

Forearm shaft fracture & Galeazzi

The forearm as a joint, and the Galeazzi fracture-dislocation.

1 of 7 sittings2021

  • Treat the adult forearm as a JOINT, not as two long bones — rotation depends on the precise restoration of radial bow, length and rotational alignment. Consequently, displaced both-bone forearm fractures in adults require anatomic ORIF with compression plating (3.5 mm), which achieves union rates >95%; non-operative treatment produces unacceptable loss of rotation.
  • Restoration of the RADIAL BOW is the key technical determinant of forearm rotation — the maximum radial bow and its location should match the contralateral side; loss of the bow correlates directly with loss of supination/pronation and grip strength.
  • Galeazzi fracture-dislocation = a fracture of the distal third of the radius with an associated disruption of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ). It is called the 'fracture of necessity' because non-operative treatment reliably fails in adults — it requires ORIF of the radius, after which the DRUJ is assessed.
  • DRUJ instability is more likely with a radial fracture within ~7.5 cm of the distal articular surface; fractures more proximal than this are less likely to disrupt the DRUJ. Radiographic signs of DRUJ disruption: ulnar styloid base fracture, widening of the DRUJ on the AP, dislocation of the ulna on a true lateral, and radial shortening >5 mm.
  • Algorithm after ORIF of the radius: assess DRUJ stability. If stable, no further treatment. If reducible but unstable, immobilise in supination in a long-arm cast for ~6 weeks (or pin the ulna to the radius). If irreducible, open the joint — the usual block is an entrapped ECU tendon or the TFCC, which is then repaired to the fovea.
  • Monteggia (the mirror injury) = a proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation — anatomic reduction of the ulna reduces the radial head (see the paediatric topic).
  • Isolated ulnar shaft ('nightstick') fracture: if the fracture is in the distal two thirds, angulated <10°, and displaced <50% of the shaft width, it can be treated non-operatively in a functional brace or short-arm cast with early motion, with high union rates. More proximal, more angulated or more displaced fractures — and any suspicion of a Monteggia variant — require ORIF.
  • Complications of forearm ORIF: synostosis (higher with a single incision for both bones, high-energy injury, head injury, bone graft placed in the interosseous space, and delayed surgery — use two separate incisions), refracture after plate removal (which is why routine plate removal is discouraged; if removed, protect the arm for several months), nerve injury (PIN with the Thompson/dorsal approach), and compartment syndrome.
  • Essex-Lopresti injury — a radial head fracture with interosseous membrane disruption and DRUJ injury — is the longitudinal instability pattern; never excise a radial head without examining the wrist.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Upper Extremity.
  • Schemitsch EH, Richards RR (Canadian, Toronto). The effect of malunion on functional outcome after plate fixation of fractures of both bones of the forearm in adults. JBJS Am 1992.

  • Anderson LD, Sisk D, Tooms RE, Park WI. Compression-plate fixation in acute diaphyseal fractures of the radius and ulna. JBJS Am 1975.
  • Ring D, Rhim R, Carpenter C, Jupiter JB. Isolated radial shaft fractures are more common than Galeazzi fractures. J Hand Surg Am 2006.
1question

Geriatric fracture care & orthogeriatrics

The system of care that determines outcome in the elderly hip fracture patient.

1 of 7 sittings2023

  • Hip fracture in the elderly is a medical emergency with a surgical component. One-year mortality is approximately 20–30%, and only about half of survivors return to their pre-fracture level of function. The system of care matters as much as the operation.
  • AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline (2021) — the strong recommendations worth knowing: surgery within 24–48 hours improves outcomes (reduced mortality, pain, delirium and length of stay); regional or general anaesthesia are equivalent for mortality (REGAIN and RAGA trials); a restrictive transfusion threshold (~80 g/L, or symptoms) is as safe as a liberal threshold (FOCUS); multimodal analgesia including a regional nerve block (fascia iliaca or femoral) reduces opioid use and delirium; arthroplasty is preferred to internal fixation for displaced femoral neck fractures; and an interdisciplinary care programme improves outcomes.
  • Orthogeriatric co-management is the single most impactful system intervention — a shared-care model with a geriatrician reduces delirium, medical complications, length of stay and (in several studies) mortality, and improves the rate of osteoporosis treatment on discharge.
  • Delirium occurs in 20–50% of elderly hip fracture patients and is associated with mortality, institutionalisation and functional decline. Prevention is far more effective than treatment: early surgery, adequate analgesia (untreated pain causes delirium — opioid sparing is desirable, but under-treated pain is worse), avoidance of benzodiazepines and anticholinergics, early mobilisation, hydration, oxygenation, sensory aids (glasses, hearing aids), and reorientation.
  • Do not delay surgery to 'optimise' a patient who cannot be meaningfully optimised. Reversible issues (severe anaemia, electrolyte derangement, uncontrolled heart failure, a new arrhythmia) warrant brief correction; a chronic comorbidity does not. Clopidogrel is not a reason to delay — proceeding without delay reduces mortality and complications despite a modest increase in transfusion.
  • Weightbearing as tolerated is the standard after fixation or arthroplasty — restricted weightbearing is poorly complied with, causes deconditioning, and does not improve fixation outcomes.
  • Secondary fracture prevention is the most commonly omitted element of care: every fragility fracture patient requires calcium and vitamin D, BMD assessment, fracture risk assessment and pharmacologic osteoporosis therapy. Fracture liaison services close this gap and are cost-effective; without one, fewer than 20% of patients are treated.
  • Also address: falls assessment and prevention (medication review, vision, home hazards, gait and balance training), nutritional supplementation, and advance care planning — a hip fracture is frequently a sentinel event marking a transition in the patient's overall trajectory.
References6
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: Lower Extremity; Medical Conditions.
  • AAOS Clinical Practice Guideline: Management of Hip Fractures in Older Adults, 2021.
  • Neuman MD et al. (REGAIN) Spinal anesthesia or general anesthesia for hip surgery in older adults. NEJM 2021.
  • Carson JL et al. (FOCUS) Liberal or restrictive transfusion in high-risk patients after hip surgery. NEJM 2011.
  • Grigoryan KV, Javedan H, Rudolph JL. Orthogeriatric care models and outcomes in hip fracture patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Orthop Trauma 2014.
  • Bogoch ER, Elliot-Gibson V, Beaton DE, Jamal SA, Josse RG, Murray TM (Canadian). Effective initiation of osteoporosis diagnosis and treatment after fragility fracture. JBJS Am 2006.
1question

Mangled extremity & limb salvage

Scoring systems, the LEAP findings, and how to make the decision.

1 of 7 sittings2024S

  • The MESS (Mangled Extremity Severity Score) comprises four components: skeletal/soft-tissue injury severity, limb ischaemia (doubled if the ischaemic time exceeds 6 hours), shock, and patient age. A score ≥7 was originally reported to predict amputation.
  • The critical modern point is that MESS and all other scoring systems have POOR POSITIVE PREDICTIVE VALUE and should NOT be used in isolation to decide on amputation. The LEAP study specifically validated this: none of the available scores (MESS, PSI, LSI, NISSSA, HFS-97) reliably predicted the need for amputation or the eventual functional outcome, and their high scores did not identify limbs that should be amputated. They retain some value in that a LOW score reliably predicts successful salvage (good negative predictive value).
  • The LEAP finding that reframed the field: at 2 and 7 years, functional outcomes (SIP scores) were EQUIVALENT between reconstruction and amputation, and outcomes were predicted by psychosocial factors — self-efficacy, education, income, social support and smoking — not by the treatment chosen. Both groups had poor outcomes overall, with roughly half not returning to work.
  • Insensate plantar skin is NOT an absolute indication for amputation — this was a major LEAP finding. Of patients presenting with an insensate foot, more than half regained sensation by 2 years, and outcomes in the insensate salvage group were comparable to the insensate amputation group. The historical teaching that an insensate plantar foot mandates amputation is wrong.
  • Genuine indications favouring primary amputation: an unreconstructible vascular injury with prolonged warm ischaemia (>6–8 hours) and a non-viable limb, massive soft-tissue and bone loss that cannot be reconstructed, a physiologically unstable patient in whom limb salvage would be life-threatening (life over limb), and severe associated injuries. A near-complete traumatic amputation with only a skin bridge is a practical indication.
  • Factors favouring salvage: a young patient, an upper limb injury (salvage thresholds are much lower — always attempt salvage in the upper limb, where even a poorly functioning limb with sensation is valuable), preserved sensation, a viable vascular supply, and reconstructible bone and soft tissue.
  • Consider the whole trajectory: limb salvage typically involves multiple operations, prolonged non-weightbearing, a high rate of complications and reoperation, and a significant chance of eventual amputation anyway (late amputation after failed salvage has worse outcomes than primary amputation). This must be discussed honestly with the patient and family — the decision should be shared wherever the patient can participate.
  • The decision should be made by two experienced surgeons where possible, documented carefully, and — where the patient cannot consent and the limb is not immediately life-threatening — deferred until the patient can participate, using temporary shunting and external fixation to buy time.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas; Trauma.
  • Bosse MJ, MacKenzie EJ et al. (LEAP) An analysis of outcomes of reconstruction or amputation after leg-threatening injuries. NEJM 2002.
  • Bosse MJ et al. (LEAP) The insensate foot following severe lower extremity trauma: an indication for amputation? JBJS Am 2005.
  • Bosse MJ et al. A prospective evaluation of the clinical utility of the lower-extremity injury-severity scores. JBJS Am 2001.
  • Johansen K, Daines M, Howey T, Helfet D, Hansen ST. Objective criteria accurately predict amputation following lower extremity trauma. J Trauma 1990.

Nonunion: Diagnosis & management

Classification, the diamond concept, and the systematic work-up.

1 of 7 sittings2023

  • Definition: a fracture that has failed to unite and shows no radiographic progression toward healing over three consecutive months, generally at 6–9 months after injury (the FDA definition is 9 months with 3 months of no progression, but this is a guide — some fractures are declared earlier).
  • Classification by biology (Weber-Čech): HYPERTROPHIC ('elephant foot' or 'horse hoof') — abundant callus, good vascularity and biology, but inadequate mechanical STABILITY; treatment is improved stability (compression plating, exchange nailing) WITHOUT the need for bone graft. ATROPHIC — no callus, poor vascularity/biology; treatment requires débridement of the fibrous tissue and sclerotic bone ends, bone graft (biology), AND stable fixation. OLIGOTROPHIC — minimal callus, usually from distraction or malreduction; requires both. A SEPTIC nonunion must be excluded before any treatment.
  • The 'diamond concept' framework for assessing every nonunion: (1) osteogenic cells, (2) an osteoconductive scaffold, (3) osteoinductive growth factors, (4) MECHANICAL STABILITY, with the added considerations of vascularity and the host.
  • Systematic work-up of every nonunion — the checklist: (a) EXCLUDE INFECTION — history, examination, ESR, CRP and WBC, and intra-operative cultures and histology at the time of revision (a proportion of 'aseptic' nonunions grow organisms). (b) Assess mechanics — is the fixation stable? Is there a gap? Is there malalignment? (c) Assess biology — vascularity, soft-tissue envelope, bone loss. (d) Assess the HOST — smoking (the single most important modifiable factor), diabetes, malnutrition (albumin, prealbumin, total lymphocyte count), vitamin D deficiency (extremely common — check 25-OH vitamin D in every nonunion), NSAID use, bisphosphonates, and endocrine disorders (thyroid, parathyroid, hypogonadism — a metabolic screen identifies an abnormality in a surprisingly high proportion of nonunions).
  • Treatment principles: fix what is deficient. A hypertrophic nonunion with good alignment needs compression (plate or exchange nail). An atrophic nonunion needs débridement to bleeding bone, autologous cancellous graft (iliac crest or RIA), and stable fixation. A large segmental defect needs Masquelet, bone transport or a vascularised graft. An infected nonunion requires eradication of infection first (débridement, antibiotic-loaded cement/beads, staged reconstruction).
  • Exchange nailing is highly effective for a hypertrophic diaphyseal tibial or femoral nonunion with an intact soft-tissue envelope — reaming provides autogenous graft locally and allows a larger, stiffer nail. It is less effective in atrophic nonunions, in the presence of a gap or bone loss, and in the distal tibia.
  • Adjuncts: BMP-2/BMP-7 (osteoinductive, effective but expensive with off-label concerns), bone marrow aspirate concentrate, teriparatide (with encouraging evidence in atypical femoral fractures and some nonunions), and low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) — for which the TRUST trial (Canadian-led, BMJ 2016) found NO benefit in tibial fracture healing, substantially weakening the case for its routine use.
  • Correct malalignment at the time of revision — a nonunion in varus that is simply grafted and re-plated in varus will fail again.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Orthopaedic Dilemmas: Nonunion.
  • Weber BG, Čech O. Pseudarthrosis: Pathophysiology, Biomechanics, Therapy, Results. 1976.
  • Giannoudis PV, Einhorn TA, Marsh D. Fracture healing: the diamond concept. Injury 2007.
  • TRUST Investigators (Busse JW, Bhandari M, Canadian). Low intensity pulsed ultrasonography versus placebo for tibial fractures (TRUST): a multicentre randomised trial. BMJ 2016.
  • Brinker MR, O'Connor DP et al. Metabolic and endocrine abnormalities in patients with nonunions. J Orthop Trauma 2007.
1question

Psychosocial outcomes & recovery after injury

Why psychosocial factors dominate long-term outcome after major trauma.

1 of 7 sittings2024F

  • The LEAP (Lower Extremity Assessment Project) studies established the central finding: after severe lower extremity trauma, outcomes at 2 and 7 years were determined far more by PSYCHOSOCIAL factors than by the injury characteristics or by whether the limb was salvaged or amputated. The dominant predictors were low self-efficacy, low educational attainment, poverty/low income, lack of health insurance, smoking, poor social support, and involvement in litigation/compensation.
  • Depression and post-traumatic stress disorder are extremely common after major orthopaedic trauma — roughly 20–50% of patients screen positive for depression or PTSD in the first year, and these conditions are strongly associated with persistent pain, poorer functional outcomes, delayed return to work and lower satisfaction, independent of injury severity.
  • Fracture types associated with a high rate of post-injury psychological distress: high-energy lower extremity injuries (particularly tibial pilon, calcaneus, open tibia and severe foot injuries) and injuries requiring prolonged non-weightbearing or multiple operations. Calcaneal and pilon fractures are classically associated with prolonged disability, chronic pain, failure to return to work and depression — the injuries where the functional outcome most often disappoints relative to a technically good radiographic result.
  • Pain catastrophising and low self-efficacy are the strongest modifiable psychological predictors of persistent pain and disability, and are more predictive than the objective severity of the injury. Screening tools (PHQ-9, PCL-5, the Pain Catastrophizing Scale) can be used routinely.
  • Persistent opioid use after orthopaedic surgery: the single strongest predictor is pre-operative opioid use, followed by mental health comorbidity (depression, anxiety, PTSD), substance use disorder, and a larger initial prescription. Injury severity and pain scores are weaker predictors than psychosocial history — this reframing is important.
  • Practical implications: screen for depression, PTSD and substance use; set realistic expectations early and repeatedly; treat pain multimodally with opioid stewardship; involve social work, psychology and vocational rehabilitation; and address smoking, nutrition and social support as part of the fracture care plan. Early psychological intervention improves outcomes.
  • Counselling patients honestly about the expected 1–2 year recovery trajectory after a severe injury, and about the likelihood of some permanent limitation, improves satisfaction more than optimistic reassurance that is later contradicted.
References5
  • Hartman J. Ortho Review, 2nd ed — Trauma: General; Ethics & Principles of Practice.
  • MacKenzie EJ, Bosse MJ et al. (LEAP Study Group) Long-term persistence of disability following severe lower-limb trauma: results of a seven-year follow-up. JBJS Am 2005.
  • Bhandari M, Busse JW, Hanson BP, Leece P, Ayeni OR, Schemitsch EH (Canadian). Psychological distress and quality of life after orthopedic trauma. Can J Surg 2008.
  • Vranceanu AM, Bachoura A, Weening A, Vrahas M, Smith RM, Ring D. Psychological factors predict disability and pain intensity after skeletal trauma. JBJS Am 2014.
  • Helmerhorst GTT et al. Risk factors for continued opioid use one to two months after surgery for musculoskeletal trauma. JBJS Am 2014.

How this was built

Source

The national consensus recall workbook, sheets Fall 2025, 2024-Fall, 2024-Spring, 2023, 2022, 2021 and 2020 — seven sittings, because 2024 ran in both spring and fall.

1,328 stems were extracted; 81 were duplicates from the trailing repeat blocks several sheets carry. That left 1,247 questions, all of which were read and classified. None are reproduced here.

Classification

Each stem was assigned to exactly one topic. Matching ran on the stem only in the first pass — when the full cell was matched, answer options drove the result, and every patella fracture question landed in Elbow because “tension band” appeared among its distractors.

Regional fractures sit with their region: distal radius under Hand, radial head under Elbow, ankle and hindfoot under Foot & Ankle. Trauma keeps polytrauma, open fractures, pelvis, hip, femur and tibia.

Paediatrics and Basic Science together are roughly a third of the exam. Sports, which residents often over-prepare, is under 4%.

Figures

All 37 diagrams are original, drawn for this document rather than reproduced from any text. They are weighted toward the highest-frequency topics and together cover 335 questions worth of material.

References

Hartman's Ortho Review cited by chapter, alongside JBJS, JAAOS, CORR, JOT, AJSM, Arthroscopy, J Arthroplasty, JSES, FAI, Spine, JPO, NEJM, Lancet and JAMA. Canadian evidence is emphasised where it exists — COTS, Buckley, Willits, McKee, Bhandari, Fehlings, Schatzker, Tile, Salter, Getgood, Daniels, Fisher, Bailey and Dvorak.

One caveat worth holding onto. These are recalled questions, written from memory by candidates after the fact — not official examination material. Stems are often incomplete or paraphrased, and some recalls contradict one another. Treat the frequency counts as a reliable guide to emphasis, and the teaching points as a study framework to verify against your primary sources — not as a reproduction of the exam.
